units.la: Am unus alterque fluit annus, cum amicorum quidam, ex Belgio, Gallia & Italia redux, infamiliari colloquio, Mirari isthic bonines dicebat, quibus ex scriptis innouerim, cur in vitu pra aliis Germanis fritus sim, ut nulla vita oblectamenta queram! Ne mirentur, inquam: quia alia & plura ferre non possum. Illi vero, reddit hospes, repiciunt ad τ̀ ... Plutarchi, quod absque meinterprete intelligis. Cui ego, scire equidem velim, quot mihi sint domini! Et unde sciunt illi. quid domi mea agatur? Ne putes, respondet ille tam ignotum te esse extra Germaniam, quam intra illam es. Possum credere, ad paucos pervenire libellos meos, in quibus VERITATEM doceo: sed hoc vix credere pofsum, quemquam esse inter illos, apud quem fraudi mihi fit ad Naturæ legem vixisse. Scio ego quorsum pertineat illud τῶν ἀσώτων ,quod Latini Medicè vivere nominant: ego vero OPTIME vivo, Quia tale & tantum comedo, quantum benè fero. Nimirum, fubinfert alter, sciant hoc quoque, vivere te ad libellam, quo modo ALOYSIVS olim CORNELIVS, qui hoc vitæ genere usus, ad annum 90. accessit, quem terf minum tibi quoque optant. Nihil minus, quam ad libellam, dicebam. Videbis, si volet DEO VS, hodie. Atque utinam ad rigorem illum aspirare possim! Sed &non valdè folicitus sum, quamdiu vivam, modò DEO & proximo vivam. Mihi enim cordi est illud stoicorum sapientissimi, Non oportere fastidire senectutis extrema, & finem opperiri, non manu facere. Quando n. quod idem scribit, nostra quoque providentiâ
units.tr: A year or so ago, one of my friends, returning from Belgium, France and Italy, said to me in a familiar conversation: "I am amazed at you, for from your writings I have learned why, more than other Germans, you have made yourself so austere as to seek no pleasures in life!" "Let them not be amazed," I replied, "for I cannot bear other and greater things." He answered, returning the remark, "They refer to the passage of Plutarch, which you understand without my interpreting it." To this I said, "I would really like to know how many masters I have! And how do they know what is going on in my house?" "Do not think," he replied, "that you are as unknown outside Germany as you are within it. I can believe that my little books, in which I teach the TRUTH, reach only a few; but I can hardly believe that there is anyone among them who holds it against me that I have lived according to the law of nature. I know what the saying of the wasteful [τῶν ἀσώτων] means, which the Latins call living medically; but I live BEST, because I eat such and such an amount as I can digest well." "Surely," another added, "let them know this as well: you live by the scale, as ALOYSIUS CORNELIUS once did, who, living in this way, reached the age of ninety, which they also wish you as your limit." "Nothing less than by the scale, I said. You will see that today, God willing. And would that I could aspire to that rigour! But I am not very anxious, as long as I live, provided that I live for God and for my neighbour. For I hold dear that saying of the wisest of the Stoics, that one should not disdain the last extremities of old age, nor wait for the end with impatience, nor hasten it by hand. units.tr: to live [ζῆν] by care and diligence a longer delay can be granted to this little body, why, I said, should I give myself over to idle sloth and at the same time wear myself out with gluttony, and as it were smother that little spark which is left to me from the fire of Prometheus, so to speak? Add to this that in public life Favonius rarely breathes on me; indeed I am ordered to bear injuries without limit, and to give thanks besides, with ready effort, a task which seems to me far too hard, especially at my age. Indeed, as of old, so today too, all men hide their sins (you recognise the words of the same sage); they make use of the fruit of them and withdraw them from view themselves. For who is there who does not wish to seem kind? Who, among crimes and injuries, does not seek the reputation of goodness? Who does not put on some semblance of right over the very things he has done most arrogantly? Who does not also wish to seem to have done a kindness to those whom he has harmed? To which I may add something of my own: this has begun not today or yesterday, that it is lawful for a king to do anything with impunity. This

Apud enim Majores nostros recte factorum verus fructus erat, recte fecisse, nec tamen ideo ut facere viderentur, cum sola conscientia sufficeret : nostris moribus qui maximè fallunt, volunt etiam conscientiis suis consuluisse, adeò nullus est metus τξ ἐκἀλίκς ὁμηρ(ῶ, quod Homerus vocat. Hoc tum imprimis fit, cum duo conjurárunt in unum caput. Ut enim quod Ludovicum XII, Galliæ regem dixisse ferunt, in alio solo rapum intra biennium vertitur in napum, in alio contrà napus in
units.tr: is new and unheard of to me among the Germans: that ambition should obscure the force of honesty, and robbers should wear the garb of justice. For among our ancestors the true reward of right actions was to have acted rightly, and not in order to seem to act, since conscience alone was enough. In our customs, those who deceive most wish also to have consulted their consciences; so there is no fear of that which Homer speaks of [τξ ἐκἀλίκς ὁμηρ(ῶ]. It is indeed so, as Cicero somewhere complains: no one is so bad that he wishes to seem bad. Among us, not merely the appearance of right is thrown over what has been done most shamelessly, but men even dare to lie and to defend the contrary, not now as Plautine slaves, but even as great men. This happens especially when two have conspired against one head. Pœnorum quorundam, qui succensent mihi, quod parciuscorpore tela illorum recipiam, quod non porrecto jugulo acceptem gladios intentatos, quod non comiter assurgam infolentiæillorum, quod non : Tum vero commotiorem me videns amicus assidens, injectâ manu, Omittamus, inquit, ista inamœna, quæ- quam μικροφυχίαν quandam sapiunt, indi- gnam perfonâtuâ, quam apud exteros geris: agamus de rebus iis, ob quas huc veni. Quas vero? inquam ego. Miraberis, ubi dixero: sed ita est, princeps hæc cauía est adventus mei: Cupio à te audire, Quatenus, & quibus Medicis libros scribere liceat? Mi- ror equidem, qui istuc tibi subve- niat? ajebam. Subvenit non jam primum: sed sæpicule inter amicos ventilatum fuit, Cur scriptis inclarescere velis, & non potius, Socratis ex- emplo ἀλαζονείᾳ βιωσας, cum ea res invidiam tibi non mediocrem conciliet, & fortassis cicutam minetur! Subrisi iterum, & dixi, Quasi vero Socrates ob id, & ab invidia & à ci- cutâ immunis fuerit! Cæterum, cum Socrate neutiquam me comparo: servio D E o meo ineruendâ V ERIT A T E, securus quid Diabolus machinetur. Hujus constantis mec volantatis testem nunc advoco.
units.tr: The vices of yesterday weigh down the mind as well. In this way (which is the second point) the thought [παρεγίεαΦΘ ἐννοια] does not trouble me. Some of the Carthaginians, who are angry with me because I do not take their blows on my body, because I do not offer my throat to their drawn swords, because I do not rise courteously to their insolence, because I do not... Then a friend sitting beside me, seeing me more agitated, laid his hand on me: "Let us drop these unpleasant matters," he said, "which smack of a certain pettiness, unworthy of the character you bear among foreigners. Let us deal with the things for which I came here." "Which ones?" I asked. "You will be surprised when I tell you, but it is so: this is the main reason for my visit. I want to hear from you how far, and for which physicians, it is permitted to write books." "I am truly amazed. What gives you that idea?" I said. "It is not the first time it has occurred to me. It has often been discussed among friends: why do you want to become famous through writings, rather than live, after the example of Socrates, without boasting [ἀλαζονείᾳ βιωσας], since that matter wins you no small hatred and perhaps threatens you with hemlock?" I smiled again and said: "As if Socrates was free of hatred and hemlock on that account! But I do not compare myself with Socrates at all. I serve my God by seeking the truth, and I am unconcerned about what the Devil may plot. I now call to witness this steady will of mine."

Quo minus etiam à me exspectare debes, ut explicem feptem illa requisita, fi sic appellare possum, quæ Gal. aut quisquis fuit autor τῆς συσκότως τῆς ἰαλρικῆς deridet in illo, qui pro judice controverfiarum in disciplinis fe gerere velit. Est enim in medio hac de re oratio incomparabilis Scheerbi nostri, quam alio tempore, me
units.tr: Friend, I bid you defer to those who have never thought about this matter with you at all. So that you do not come in vain, first you should be persuaded of this: in the question proposed I am in the position Socrates was in, in Xenophon, when he was asked What is παροινία? Who truly are those who ought to write books I cannot tell you; what seems right to me I can tell you, by the example I have set. Next, I declare to you that neither time nor my strength now permits me to begin a discourse that is too long; let it be enough that it was popular. You should expect even less from me in explaining those seven requisites, if I may so call them, which Galen, or whoever was the author of the obscurity of the art, mocks in the man who wishes to act as judge of controversies in the disciplines. For in the middle of this matter stands the incomparable speech of our Scheerbius, which you may read at another time, if I furnish it to you, unless you have already read it.

As for the matter at hand, there is conveniently at hand the passage in Galen (*Anat.* 2, bk. 8) that others have passed over dry-shod, and here it is for you! I read it aloud from the open book: "Thinking it ancient, and finding nothing new, to put down in writings only that, but I did not care to write, as for myself, whatever belongs to the interpretation..." [ἀρχαῖον ἐνόμιζον ... ἐκεῖνο μόνον εἰς συγγράμματα τίθεσθαι ... ὡς ἐμοὶ γράφειν ... τοῖς προσ... ἐν ἐρμηνευ...]. You see the wholesome advice of a most serious man; would that more people observed it! I think he means by "the newer things" not only the advances of the arts, as Isocrates calls them, but chiefly the true opinions of the ancients, which others have explained less well. From my speech you understand, my good friend, that I am not one of those many whom the satirist says are possessed by an insatiable itch for writing. Indeed, I think we shall have enough trouble of our own if we read the ancients with a free judgment.

I would be more foolish than Margites if I began to recount to you the tournaments (forgive the harsh word) of certain men concerning the use of the spleen and brain, the origin of veins and nerves, the course of the blood from the right ventricle of the heart to the left, and whatever else there is. For these suddenly vanished when there appeared on stage the most powerful goddess Adrastea herself, of Galen himself, and those jugglers said to their faces: "He himself taught it, do you see?"

units.tr: In the course of time, when these slight works had received, so to speak, three judgments [Com. in de usu partium etc.], but no one wanted to come openly down into the arena, I took this as the most certain proof of victory. And I truly understood, from foreign travellers (I say nothing of private letters), that Italians, French, English and Belgians judge far more uncorruptedly. So I went on eagerly, persuaded that this labour had been divinely enjoined upon me. When I had argued subtly, another would retort: "Is it necessary that everyone wish the same? Let each abound in his own sense?" Ah, I replied, our parchment will tell you! For since Philosophy has entered into affinity with Medicine, it is right and pious that, lies being exploded, we love TRUTH alone; all the more so because this is indeed [ἐκ Θεᾶς, from God], as the poet says.

units.tr: But that other thing comes from the father, the Devil. From this you understand that, if there were no harm except in trifles and fables, some things could be borne without infection and left to their authors. But since lies so deadly are entangled, we ought not only to abhor them in mind but also to show their foulness in words. Nor is it enough to excuse them by the consent of so many centuries; rather, true things must be carefully and circumspectly distinguished from false, so that God's glory may be greater and the Devil's works more detestable. The more reason we have to withdraw from those who defend right opinions either by authority alone or by mere verbal allurement, and who not only defend them boldly but also slander those who think otherwise, as if they understand little, as if they oppose themselves in vain, as if it were better to be silent than to put forward...

Hæc adeò visest ADRASTEAS illius, cujus memini, quæ facit, ut, qui studiò velit premere Veritatem, non possit id facere perpetuò : sed vel tandem cogatur dicere, quod resest. units.tr: ...things which destroy the old concord of the schools. Oh, what concord! Consent cannot be so firm in evil that these sinister patrons differ not only from one another but from themselves. This is the Adrastea of which I spoke, which ensures that whoever wishes to suppress Truth deliberately cannot do so continually, but is at last compelled to say what is true. I invent nothing; I dare promise on my own account that all those erroneous things publicly extant under the veil of Galen can be led back to the true sense by Galen himself. Since this has already been done abundantly in the spleen, in the hermaphrodite, both masculine and feminine, in the unity of the soul, and in many other matters, enough of this for now. Meanwhile let those fume who stop their ears against the Sirens' songs, raise their brows, wrinkle their noses, and excuse, defend, affirm and deny all the most salty things. What is that to me? It is my own affair [ἀ ἔυμεὶ ἐμῆ]. But, you men of this sort, I am accustomed sometimes to say:

Dicat mihi aliquis, dum callidè potius, & ad pompam difceprat, quam simplice assensione Veritatem colit: quod sibi præmium speret hujus tam barbaræ acrimonice? tam crassæ subtilitatis? Non ego issum, qui insectatione aliorum delecter, quique præclaram operam esse ducam carpere aliena errata; & ex eâ re famam mihi quæram. Quin, ut modestiam meam comprobem omnibus, propendeo inalteram potius partem, multa commodè interpretando, speciem absurditatis avertendo, bonis, ingenuifque viam sternendo ad prosequendum Veritatis amorem. Sic enim;
units.tr: Is it a game and a joke, to raise a hand and display some sort of cleverness against those before whom you ought to be ashamed and blush? Is not divine glory trampled in this way? Is not the salvation of our neighbour put in danger? Are not good minds perverted? Are all things turned upside down? Let someone tell me, when he argues cunningly and for show rather than cultivating Truth with simple assent: what reward does he hope for from this so barbarous sharpness, this so crass subtlety? I am not one who delights in attacking others, or who thinks it a fine work to carp at others' errors and win fame from that. Rather, to prove my modesty to everyone, I incline to the other course: interpreting many things charitably, averting the appearance of absurdity, and paving the way for good and ingenuous people to pursue the love of Truth. For so...

units.la: enim cogito, Quâ facilitate, & confidentiâ acerbè alios exagitare potes tu : eâdem fieri potest, ut in te vicissim inquiratur,& culpentur prolibidine optima quæque. Equidem valdè nescio quid rigidis istis ceniforibus securitatem polliceri possit, quò minus vicissim censuram aliorum ipsi subire cogantur! Oraculum enim censendum est Homeri illud, O′ πατοῖον κ′ἐπι ... ἐᾶ Θ., τοῖον κ′ἰπαν ... Quale verbum dixeris, tale audies. Idem dico, in quibus manifesta falsitas est, five antiquitatis obstet autoribus, five novitatis offerat fe splendor, fumere animos oportet, nec Veritatem prodere metu vel infamiæ, vel alii, veldenique Diaboli ipsius. Sed neque ætatem contrâ stantis revereri oportet. Quam in rem insignis est locus apud Euripidem, ubi Orestes juvenis fenî nescio cui in os dicit.
units.tr: For I think about how easily and confidently you can savage others; the same can happen to you in turn, and every best man is blamed for his frankness. Indeed, I have no idea what security those stiff censors can promise themselves, to keep them from being forced in turn to undergo the censure of others! For that line of Homer should be taken as an oracle: "As you say a word, such you will hear." I say the same: where there is manifest falsehood, whether the antiquity of the authors stands in the way or the brilliance of novelty presents itself, one must take courage and not betray the truth out of fear of infamy, or of anyone, or finally of the Devil himself. Nor, indeed, ought one to revere an age that stands against the truth. A notable passage on this is in Euripides, where the young Orestes speaks into the face of some old man.

units.la: Idem dico de consensu isto difsono. Quod enim reprobum est, nunquam fuit probum, nunquam erit. Uerum enim verò mifcela illa, ô suavissime, nov-antiqui, quam non est cujusvis? Incrementum quotidie capere artes, certum est, & errata antiquitatis multa corrigere posteriorum sagacitatem: sed enim non propterea sperni vult antiquitas. Non raró enim accidit,ut vetera in contemtu sint, non culpâ rei ipsius, sed vel negligentiâ, vel malitiâ hominum: Tum verò reddendus fuerit potius illis splendor primus, sinceritasque, & puritas, detersa rubigine, quovis modo concilianda, quam sinenda in pædore & pulvere. Tales lapsus qui animadvertere potuerunt,non debuerunt silere ; sed indicare, ut, quos everterunt, alleventur rutsus, non aliis ruinis premantur, usque dum res ad insanabiles corruptelas delatæ, morbos fecerint plane desperatos. Sequius qui animati sunt,h.e. qui tantum abest ut fanarevelint, & tollere malum, cum possint,ut non dubitent alere quoque,& fovere,& corroborare:illos preffiùs cupio intueri fulmen illud, Maledictus,qui facit opus D o M INI fraudulenter.Servi enim nequam sunt omnes tales, nec poterunt vel mutire coràm hero, à peregrinatione reduci. units.tr: I say the same about this discordant agreement. For what is reprobate was never sound, and never will be. But what, O sweetest, is that mixture of "new-old," and who is fit for it? That the arts grow day by day is certain, and that later men's sharpness corrects many errors of antiquity; but antiquity is not therefore to be despised. It often happens that old things fall into contempt not through any fault of the thing itself, but through the negligence or malice of men. In such cases the original brightness, sincerity and purity should rather be restored, the rust scraped off and in every way recovered, than left to lie in filth and dust. Those who have been able to notice such lapses ought not to keep silent, but point them out, so that those whom they have overthrown may be raised up again and not crushed by further ruins, until matters that have been brought to incurable corruption become quite hopeless diseases. Those who are more reckless, that is, who are so far from wishing to heal, and when they could remove the evil, not hesitate instead to feed it, foster it and strengthen it: on these I would rather fix my gaze, with that thunderbolt, "Cursed is he who does the work of the LORD deceitfully." For all such are wicked servants, and they will not be able even to murmur before their master when he returns from abroad. I hear indeed from afar that it is troublesome and rash [ἀνσσι μέλειν ἐνα λέγειν τὸν αὐλίς]: but I value that as much as I would value that fly which you see wanting to settle on my nose, if I allowed it. At this he burst into laughter and said, "Ha! I praise that!"

Postquam per integrum penè quinquennium versatus sum in opere τῶν χρησμῶν θεῶν πολλογικῶν, & aliquam-multa vidi aliis invisa : ausus sum Animadverfiones has, quas vides, meditari in COMITEM MONTANUM de Morbo, eique contigua fcripram, ut publici juris faciam, fi quâ fata sinant. Ex his intelligas GALENVM quidem in hoc ipso negotio in multis maricum esse : MONTANVS autem, interpretem ipsius, in plerisque succubuisse oneri. Illum quidem facilè excusabit desultorius fcribendi modus, Plinio non diffimilis, quem necipfe deprecatur, familiarem quippe Asiaticis omnibus: hunc autem, post 25 annorum decursum, & quidem in otio rustis cano, tantum reliquatum esse, quantum hic ostendo,est quod mireris. GALENI res qui agunt, Commentatores, FvcHSIVS, VALERIOLA,IOVBERTVS, alii, quávis nive frigidiores sunt: MoNTANI securis ERASTVS, parum proficit: MONTANVS ipse in Definitione, ut vocat, feré verba dat nobis:P A CIV S,Come in Meth.med. aliquid praftat: de STVPANO & SCHERBIO, praeceptoribus opt.max. pietas me prohibet sequius quid dicere. In hisomnibus, cum varie trahatur negotium de morbis; adolescentibus vero confultum non fit omnia legere : putavi partium mearum esse in compendium redigendi vaftitiem illam, ut sub uno intuitu finttam ... quam ... Hac ratione succurrere etiam voluiinopiz, tamillorum, qui non habent omnes illos autores, quam illorum, qui habere non possunt. Atque
units.tr: Marginal note cut off; no legible text. "I praise it! Thus it is right! Thus one ought to despise that contempt!" So that you may finally understand (I went on) what I mean, I shall make it clear by an example taken from close at hand. After I had spent almost five years on the work of the most celebrated commentaries [τῶν χρησμῶν θεῶν πολλογικῶν] and had seen many things that others find hateful, I ventured to publish these Animadversions, which you see, on Montanus's Comes on Disease, and the writing that is joined to it, if the fates allow. From these you may understand that Galen, indeed, in this very business is in many things a stumbler, while Montanus, his interpreter, has in many places yielded under the burden. The rambling manner of writing, not unlike that of Pliny, which he himself deprecates, as is familiar to all Asiatics, will readily excuse the one; but that so little remains of the other, after twenty-five years, and indeed when I am grey in rural leisure, as I show here, is a thing to wonder at. The commentators on Galen, Fuchsius, Valeriola, Jobertus and others, are colder than any snow; Erastus, the axe of Montanus, accomplishes little; Montanus himself in his Definition, as he calls it, almost makes fools of us; Paccius is of some use in the Method of Medicine. Concerning Stupanus and Scherbius, my teachers of most excellent memory, piety forbids me to say anything worse. Since in all these works the matter of diseases is treated in varied ways, and since it is not advisable for young men to read everything, I thought it my duty to reduce that vast bulk to a summary, so that it might be seen at a single glance ... Thus I have also wished to help those who lack all these authors, no less than those who cannot have them. And

units.la: Atq; ut ὁχον aliquem adipisceretur opella, diffudi me in specialibus quibusdam latius, quam volent illi, qui persuasionem hanc de se habent, se jam omnia in scrinio pectoris sui habere. In convulsione precipuè,quia Erastus obstrepere voluit antiquitati, & ex motibus preternaturalibus facere naturales: placuit conculcare teterrimum commentum, ne quem porro moretur. Hoc tantò magis urgeo, quò verius est, refutasse hoc dogma magnos quosdam viros, quorum autoritate decepti adolescentes quidam commiserunt se alex valdè ancipiti. Hoc ipsum quia recta via deduxit me ad Epilepsiam& Apoplexiam, in quibus duobus affectibus tantæ hodiè sunt tenebræ, quantæ in Cimmeriâ nunquam fuere: volui hic quoque officiolus esse. In Epilepsiâ privatim ausus sum in scenam protrahere decemviros Medicorum celeber-
units.tr: And so that my little work might gain some standing, I spread myself out more broadly on certain special topics than those would wish who are persuaded that they already have everything in the casket of their own breast. Especially on convulsion, because Erastus wished to clamour against antiquity and to make natural motions out of preternatural ones, I thought it right to trample that most horrible invention, so that it should not delay anyone further. I press this all the more, because it is the truer that certain great men have refuted this doctrine, and by whose authority some young men, deceived, have committed themselves to a very precarious course. Since this very matter led me by the straight road to epilepsy and apoplexy, in which two affections there is today such darkness as never was in the land of the Cimmerians, I wished to be of some small service here too. In epilepsy, I ventured privately to bring onto the stage the ten most celebrated physicians and to show briefly to the less experienced how unsafe it is to trust oneself to this sea without a Palinurus, who indeed is here Aristoteles alone. You have, O most expectant reader, the reason for my plan, why I have written these Animadversions, new-old, which I have adapted with no violence to my other labours. I wish to adorn the Sparta I have obtained as well as I can. With this word I break off, now tired and exhausted, and I invite you to supper, not a lavish one but a Platonic one, with which you will be content, O good sir, no less than that Athenian Timotheus, so that you may see and be able to tell others how strict the life of Hofmann is. Meanwhile, Reader, take this dialogue as a preface, and farewell. Written at Altdorf, in the month of May, in the year 1639.

units.la: De Morbi definitione. CAP. I.
units.tr: On the definition of disease. CHAPTER I.

units.la: §. I. Eǽ quidem conjicit Montanus, Galenum methodum definiendi suam habuisse ab Ariftotele, quamvis illius non meminerit: malè tamen judicat, vulgatam hodiè, & ab omnibus receptam definitionem esse ϑατωδη. Quin est ἐνοχλωδης tantum,
units.tr: §. 1. Montanus conjectures that Galen had his method of defining from Aristotle, although he does not mention him. But he wrongly judges that the definition commonly accepted today by everyone is "pathodes" [παθώδης], and that it is only "enochlodes" [ἐνοχλώδης]. Indeed,

units.la: §. 2. Hoc probo ex duobus Galeni locis, altero I. de Diff. morb.2. A. altero. 1.Meth.5.B. In de Diff.venaturus definitionem morbi, his utitur verbis. Αητίεον ἀλλ' ϰαὶ ἡλίου ... ὅτι ἀρχὴν ὡς ἀπαντᾶς ἀνθρώποις, καὶ ἰα ἐφ. Quasi di-ceret, Constat inter Logicos, eum qui velit constituere definitionem essentialem, debere progressus fui initium facere à confessi omnium hominum de re propositâ notione. Ea vero est, inquam ego, definitio nominis.
units.tr: §. 2. I prove this from two passages of Galen, one in the first book On the Differences of Diseases (A), and the other in the first book of the Methodus (B). In On the Differences, when he is about to define disease, he uses these words: "Αἰτίαν δὲ ... ὡς ἅπασιν ἀνθρώποις ..." [ἀρχὴν ὡς ἅπασιν ἀνθρώποις]. It is as if he said: logicians agree that whoever wishes to set out an essential definition must begin from the notion of the matter in question that all men agree on. That, I say, is a definition of the name.

units.la: § 3. Hoc est Ciceronis illud, 1 Offic. quod in omnium ore versatur quidem, verùm à paucis rectè intelligitur. Ego vero, ab Hotomanno eruditus, principio Instit. Dialect. dico, Cicero loquitur de definitione nominis. Hinc ita infero:
units.tr: §. 3. This is what Cicero says in the first book of De Officiis, a thing that is on everyone's lips but is rightly understood by few. I, however, taught by Hotman at the beginning of the Institutio Dialectica, say: Cicero is speaking of the definition of the name. From this I infer as follows:

units.la: § 4. Quemadmodum Cicero de Officio (ita enim Scaliger vellet) scripturus, dicere debuit, quid vocet Officium, ut lecturis constet, quâ de re fit futurus sermo: ita Galenus de Morbo acturus, & consequenter de Sanitate ci contraria, debuit exponere, quid apud Græcorum vulgus fit νόσος, ἡ ὑγίεια? quid item ὑγίεια?
units.tr: §. 4. Just as Cicero, about to write On Duty (for so Scaliger would have it), ought to have said what he calls Duty, so that his readers would know what the discussion was to be about, so Galen, about to treat of Disease and consequently of its contrary, Health, ought to have set out what the common people among the Greeks mean by νόσος and ὑγίεια, and likewise what they mean by ὑγίεια.

units.la: § 5. Inquit igitur, Omnes homines dicunt fe sanos esse, cum possunt praeffe rebus suis: omnes homines dicunt fe ægrotare, cum non possunt. Ergo. (concludit.) Sanitas est tale quid, per quod agimus, quod unicuique nostrûm officii ratio mandat: Morbus est contrarium quid, per quod non licet nobis esse talibus. Hæc cum fit πρόληψις omnium hominum, sutorum, fartorum, fartorum, fabrorum, rusticorum, fubroftrariorum, ambubajarum: exfpectes ne ab his definitionem essentialem? Ad Logicas leges exactam?
units.tr: §. 5. He therefore says: All men say that they are healthy when they can manage their affairs; all men say that they are sick when they cannot. Therefore (he concludes): Health is something by which we act, which the reason of our duty requires of each of us; disease is the contrary, by which it is not permitted us to be such. Since this is the common notion of all men, cobblers, bakers, tailors, smiths, peasants, muleteers, and street-girls alike, do you expect from them an essential definition? One exact by the laws of logic?

units.la: § 6. Tu verò, quisquis es, fortassis iniquo oculo aspicis illud meü Tale quid? vellesque διάθεσιν Galenicâ? Ego verò de industriâ feci, quod feci, & jam tibi hoc lumen affero. Τὸ διάθεσις vel pressè accipitur, vel late. Presse, cum pro prima qualitatis (species apud Aristotelem in Categoriis. Late cum pro quacumque καθ' αυτο significatione volunt accipere omnes, & subito incidunt in maximam difficultatem, Non omnem tantum morbum esse qualitatem: sed & omnem caussam morbificam, omne symptoma. In hac accipi voluisse Galenum, nunc hoc tantum persuadeat, quod ponit juxta καθ' αυτο: καθ' αυτο autem fit qualitas, Illa videlicet, quæ constituit genus Logicum univocum, quod Montanus vult. Imo ne quidem genus univocum est. (quod Eraftus deducit, Anat. p. 44.) sed æquivocum. Quid igitur est? Pacius in 1, Meth. col. 242. me docuit, esse ἀιδεσι hanc Galeni ἀιδεσιν Ariftotelis. 5. Metaph. (mihi, l. 4. c. 19.) Hoc est, Dispositionis nomen non posse redigi ad unum prædicamentum: sed tanquam nomen Transcendens per plures prædicamenta vagari, uti loquitur. Hoc prior ipso scriplit Fernelius. 1. Patholog. 1. ut Montanus refert. li, 1. c. 4. extr. Iam ergo ἀιδεσις hæc extendit fe ad omnia ea, in quibus ordo partium est. Est autem in omnibus prædicamentis, ut idem Montanus habet 1. 4. c. 29. extr. Hoc fi ad Galenum referas, dicet tibi eo ipso loco, quem præ manibus habemus.
units.tr: §. 6. But you, whoever you are, perhaps look with a hostile eye at my words "something of the kind" and would prefer Galen's diathesis. I did this on purpose, and now I bring you this light. Diathesis is taken either strictly or broadly. Strictly, when it is taken for the first species of quality in Aristotle's Categories. Broadly, when everyone wishes to take it for any meaning of kath' hauto, and at once they run into the greatest difficulty: that not every disease is a quality, but also every morbid cause and every symptom. That Galen wished it to be taken in this sense, he now persuades us by this alone: he places it beside kath' hauto. But kath' hauto is quality, namely that which constitutes a univocal logical genus, as Montanus wishes. Indeed it is not even a univocal genus (which Erastus deduces, Anatomy, p. 44), but an equivocal one. What then is it? Pacius, in the first book of Methodus, col. 242, taught me that this diathesis of Galen is the diathesis of Aristotle in Metaphysics 5 (in my edition, book 4, ch. 19). That is, the name of disposition cannot be reduced to one predicament, but, as he puts it, wanders through several predicaments like a transcendent name. Fernelius wrote this before him, in the first book of Pathology, as Montanus reports (book 1, ch. 4, end). Therefore this diathesis extends itself to all those things in which there is an order of parts. And it is in all the predicaments, as the same Montanus holds (book 4, ch. 29, end). If you refer this to Galen, it will tell you the same thing in the very passage we have before us.

units.la: A 2 ἀιδεσιν διάθεσιν dici, quia per illam dicimur διaθέσεως ( ita enim lego. ) πῶς, * disponi ita vel ita. Disponimur autem aliter atque aliter, non tantum cum in qualitate mutamur, hoc est, laboramus intemperie aliquâ: sed & cum κα̈λαςκευὴ ἢ διάπλασις[?], conformatio corrumpitur, sub qua jam & quantitatem habeo, & numerum, & situm, hoc est, cum laboramus morbo aliquo organico. Hujus rei femina praebet mihi Montanus ipse, ut mox dicam. Iam enim ita concludo, Dispositio Galeni est Transcendentale, ut loquuntur quidam, non minus quam, Vnum, Verum, Bospecta quifpi witatis siv jusdan dam tum ni ab mus, hoc sin qualita bi vul triplic plex plex num, &c.
units.tr: A 2. *Diathesis* is so called because by it we are said to be disposed in such and such a way (for so I read it), *pōs*, to be disposed thus or thus. We are disposed in different ways, not only when we are changed in *quality*, that is, when we suffer from some intemperance, but also when the *kataskeuē* or *diaplasis* [κατασκευὴ ἢ διάπλασις], the *conformation*, is corrupted; under this I also have quantity, number and position, that is, when we suffer from some organic disease. Montanus himself supplies me with evidence of this, as I shall soon say. For I conclude thus: Galen's *diathesis* is *transcendental*, as some say, no less than *One*, *True*, *Good*, and so on.

units.la: §. 7. VtadGalenum faciam reditum: haæ tenus ille cum vulgo egit. In cujus ὁμολογίᾳ si subsistendum sibi ratus fuisset, non subjunxisset, ἀρχὴ δὲ καὶ ἵλᾶνδα ὁμολογυμένη. Quasi dicat: Ab hac publica confessione de Sanitate & Morbo, progredior ad aliam, non minus publicam, quæ est, sanitatem quidem consistere in συμμετρίᾳ: Morbum autem in ἀμετρίᾳ. v. g. cum febricitat quivis è vulgo, dicit, sentio calorem p. n. Cum tussit, cum dolet, quâcunque parte, communis sensus revocat illum ad statum suum priorem, in quo bene illi erat.
units.tr: §. 7. To return to Galen: up to this point he has argued along with the common view. Had he thought it enough to rest on that agreement, he would not have added: "and the beginning and the measure are agreed upon" [ἀρχὴ δὲ καὶ ἵλᾶνδα ὁμολογυμένη]. It is as if he said: from this public agreement about health and sickness I proceed to another, no less public, namely that health consists in due proportion [συμμετρία], but sickness in lack of proportion [ἀμετρία]. For example, when anyone from the common people has a fever, he says, "I feel heat." When he coughs, or aches in whatever part of the body, common sense calls him back to his former state, in which he was well.

units.la: §. 8. Quo loco moneo, sive Galenus spectata
units.tr: §. 8. Here I note that whether Galen, looking at

units.la: spectaverit,five non, hæc συμπτωσις, hæc ἀμετρία est verum & Logicum genus Sanitatis & Morbi, adeoque sunt hæc duo λόγοι πρὸς ἡ. Vt enim συμπτωσις est cuius- dam συμπτωσις : ita ἀμετρία est cujus- dam ἀμετρία. Hoc veró ad prædicamentum Relationis ducit nos tàm certâ viâ, uti absque etiam Aristotele, dicere possimus, Tam Sanitas, quàm Morbus sub uno hoc summo genere sunt, non sub alio quoque, qualitate. v.g. quod Montanus dari sibi vult. Iam igitur quia συμπτωσις pro triplici corporis nostri constitutione, triplex est : erit utique ἐν ἀμετρία tri- plex. Quare, cum Sanitatem definierimus, Est συμπτωσις temperamenti, organisationis, & unitatis : certè Morbum definiemus, est ἀμετρία temperamenti organisa- tionis, & unitatis. Vt enim Galenus, Meth. 7. Sanitas & Morbus cum sint contraria, indubitatò sunt sub eodem genere Logico.
units.tr: Whether he had this in view or not, this symptōsis, this ametria, is the true and logical genus of Health and Disease, and so these two are pros hen terms. For just as symptōsis is of a certain kind, so ametria is of a certain kind. This leads us by so sure a path to the predicament of Relation that we can say, even without Aristotle, that both Health and Disease fall under this one highest genus, and not under another, such as quality, which Montanus wants to be given to them. Now, since symptōsis is threefold according to the threefold constitution of our body, ametria will certainly be threefold as well. Therefore, since we have defined Health as the symptōsis of temperament, organization and unity, we shall certainly define Disease as the ametria of temperament, organization and unity. For as Galen says in the seventh book of the Methodus, since Health and Disease are contraries, they are without doubt under the same logical genus.

units.la: § 9. Et hæc quidem ex priori loco exsculpere potui : ex posteriori multò evidentior erit res, si hinc sumam exordium. Duplex cum sit proposita ἐρχή, unde in possessionem utriusque definitionis veniamus : alterum quidem principium longè melius & luculentiùs proponit salterum autem obscurius, involvens quip-
units.tr: §. 9. I could draw these things from the earlier passage; from the later one the matter will be much clearer, if I take my start from it here. Since there are two starting points by which we come into possession of either definition, the one sets out the principle far better and more clearly, but the other is more obscure, being wrapped up in that Asiatic verbosity.

units.la: pe fe multiloquio illi Asiatico. Quod ad illud, significantissimis verbis declarat, ut ego quidem concipio Latina. Quo igitur modo,inquit, inveniemus methodice id,quod quaerimus? Quo alio,quam inventa notione, omnibus hominibus confessa, absque qua efsentiam propositi negotii nemo invenerit? Hanc notionem dixi oportere omnibus in confesso esse, alioqui ne principium quidem futuram. Sed quae tandem est illa notio? Omnes homines dicunt fe esse sanos, cum pofsunt agere res suas : omnes homines dicunt fe esse aegros, cum non possunt. Ego sane ( concludit. ) video omnes ita usurpare & vocabulum.
units.tr: As to that, he explains it in very significant words, as I, at least, understand the Latin. "How then," he says, "shall we find methodically what we are seeking? By what other means than by finding the notion agreed upon by all men, without which no one will find the essence of the matter in hand? I said this notion ought to be agreed by all, otherwise it would not even be a principle. But what, finally, is that notion? All men say that they are healthy when they can manage their affairs; all men say that they are sick when they cannot." I, certainly, (he concludes) see that all men use the word in this way.

units.la: § 10. Ego duo subnoto. 1. Canté hic loqui Galenum, nec utivel τῆς διαθέσεως voce, fortassis, quia lites conciverant apud eos, qui, pro locutione praedicamentali habentes, vo- cant Logicum genus esse morbi.2. Duo ista opposita, ἕξις καὶ ἀσθένεια, planissimè dicere & edicere nobis, ne definitionem vulgatam pro essentiali habeamus. Ait enim expressè, Ἀλλ' hac ἕνυοια fi fit, quanquam perventuros nos ad ἀσθένειαν. Iamque adeò hæc est prima illa ἀσθένεια in de Diff. morb.
units.tr: §. 10. I note two things here. 1. Galen speaks here plainly, and he does not use the word tēs diathéseōs [τῆς διαθέσεως], perhaps because disputes had arisen among those who, holding it to be a predicamental expression, call disease a logical genus. 2. These two opposites, hexis [ἕξις] and astheneia [ἀσθένεια], tell us very plainly, and state outright, that we must not regard the common definition as essential. For he says expressly: "But if this hexis is present, although we shall arrive at astheneia..." And indeed this is that first astheneia in On the Differences of Diseases.

units.la: § 11. Huic subjiciens alteram, videtur illam adimere vulgo, per haec verba, ἐπ᾽ ἐκ τῶν προλήψεων ... ἐπὶ τῶν ἐπιστημονικῶν ἀρχῶν. Mihi videtur manca esse oratio, itaque solidanda, ἀ- ... Hoc enim popu- lant illa, quae sequuntur, ... ἐστι τίς ἀνθρώπους ἀκολουθεῖ ...
units.tr: § 11. Subjoining a second point, he seems to take away from the common view that notion, by these words: "upon the preconceptions ... upon the scientific first principles." To me the sentence seems incomplete and in need of strengthening: "... For those things which follow make the people ... there is some man who follows ..."

units.la: § 12. Propositus in exemplo oculus, fanus & æger, tacitè insinuat nobis ... cupe- ... hàc morbus. Vt dici jam debeat, Galenum ex ... bro, pervenisse ad ... ad definitionem essentialem, quae constituenda fit eo modo quo dixi. Huc ducit me infallibiliter, quod cap. feq. 7. primum quidem arguit falsas Theffali, Iuliani & Olympici fanitatis & morbi definitiones: subinde autem infert suam, Actiones partium naturales esse sanitatem: nonnaturales morbum. Dicere autem Naturale & Non-naturale, re ipsa non differt à fymmetro & ametro. Quamobrem cum tandem dicit, Neminem unquam tam fuisse stupidum, ut sub alio genere (Logico) posuerit fanitatem, sub alio morbum; idipsum vero genus fit Relatio: pro essentiali definitione habeo illam, quam dixi.
units.tr: § 12. The eye, the healthy man and the sick man, which he sets forth as an example, tacitly suggests to us ... to desire ... this disease. So that it should now be said that Galen ... has arrived at ... the essential definition, which is to be framed in the way I have said. What leads me infallibly to this view is that in the following chapter, 7, he first indeed argues against the false definitions of health and disease given by Thessalus, Julian and Olympicus, and afterwards he infers his own: the natural actions of the parts are health, the non-natural ones are disease. But to say "natural" and "non-natural" does not in fact differ from "symmetry" and "ametry". Wherefore, when at last he says that no one was ever so stupid as to place health under one (logical) genus and disease under another, and that this same genus is Relation, I hold that the definition I have mentioned is the essential one.

units.la: § 13. Et hæc quidem nunc temporis ita posita funto, tanquam probabilia: quæ fi fuerint Ariftotelis etiam dogmatis consentanea, audebo dicere, proba quoque esse. Hoc quia demonstravit Montanus ipse l. 1. c. 10, forte jam mihi quieto esse licet? Vtinam! Quia enim dicere audet, & Ariftotelem & Galenum docuisse, Morbum juxta cum Sanitate, non Relationes duntaxat esse, sed & Qualitates:
units.tr: § 13. And these things are now set forth as probable. If they also agree with the doctrine of Aristotle, I will venture to say that they are sound as well. Since Montanus himself has demonstrated this in book 1, chapter 10, may I perhaps now rest easy? Would that I might! For since he dares to say that both Aristotle and Galen taught that disease, together with health, is not merely a relation but also a quality:

units.la: — novus rerum mihi nascitur ordo:
units.tr: — a new order of things is born for me:

units.la: § 14. Vt paucis me expediam, Ex Philosophia hoc præhabendum est, distinguendas esse alterationes prævias ad formam à formā, five, quod idem est, motum ad terminum à termino ipso, scilicet à facto esse.v.g. In generatione hominis, multæ illæ & fuccessivæ alterationes sanguinis materni ad hominem, seu ad formam hominis, non sunt generatio: tum demum verò est, tunc dicitur homo generatus, in illo scilicet in quo natura imponit finem operi suo. Ita denum fit pullus, per 24. dies illos, qui bus Gallina incubat, & subinde accrescit aliquid, nondum dicitur pullus: sed tum, cum perrumpit putamen ovi. Ita in omnibus habitibus, Ergo in sanitate quoque & morbo. Sanitas igitur partis dicitur, cum &
units.tr: § 14. To deal with the matter briefly: from philosophy this must be laid down first, that the alterations preceding a form must be distinguished from the form itself, or, which is the same thing, the motion towards a term from the term itself, namely from the thing made (factum esse). For example, in the generation of a man, the many successive alterations of maternal blood into a human being, or into the form of a human, are not the generation itself. Only then is it said that a man has been generated, namely when nature sets the end of its work in that thing. Thus a chick is not yet called a chick through those twenty-four days during which the hen sits on the egg, and though something keeps growing in the meantime, but only when it breaks through the shell of the egg. So it is with all habits, and therefore with health and disease too. Thus the health of a part is said to be present when both the similar and the dissimilar parts have been altered to the point where they can act, and the dissimilar parts are so disposed that nothing is lacking for action. Conversely, disease is so called when these, or those, or both have departed from their natural state so that they cannot act. Here it must be noted that among accurate speakers the alterations which precede disease are distinguished by their own names from disease itself. For the alterations are actions [ποιήσεις], while disease is an affection [πάθημα].

units.la: & fimilaies eo usque alterate sunt, ut’ agere possint : &diffimilares ita difpofite,ut ad actionem nihil desideretur. Viciflim, Morbus appellatur, cum vel hæ,. velille, vel utræque è naturáfuá abiére ita, ut agete non possint. Vbi notandum venit, Apud áccuratè loquentes distinguì præviasad morbum alterationes àmorbo nominibus. Morbus enim véc@ ǝ véσμέα εἰ alterationes ποιῆ sunt, ἡ ποιη- ὑηματα.
units.tr: and similar parts have been altered so far that they can act; and dissimilar parts are so disposed that nothing is wanting for action. Conversely, disease is so called when either these, or those, or both have departed from their nature so that they cannot act. Here it must be noted that among accurate speakers the alterations preceding disease are distinguished by name from disease itself: for the alterations are actions, the disease is an affection.

units.la: § 15. Ergò, cum Montanus dicto: loco admittit assertionem Ariftotelis,Sanitatem & Morbum esse res factas ; sed negat inde sequi,qualitates non esse: non videt, quà in parte fit sita vis demonftrationis Ariftotelis. Si enim sunt ἀνάλγενμεῖνα , ut sunt,Esse in fieri, & Esse in fa&to : certè negato alterutro,negatur alterum. Ideò manet inconcussum hoc,fi Sanitas & Morbus sunt in facto esse, nullo: modo simul sunt in fieri. Quasi verò, inquiat quis, non dentur qualitates in facto: esse? Dantur, vocatæ ab Ariftotele in quali ἐξεῖς. Illas verò quo modo Morbis accommodabis ? Vt planius dicam, quo: modo probabis mihi,omnes morbos esse: hoc sub genere?Intemperies (forte) solæ: huc faciunt ; Organici morbi cum cohærentibus, nullâ vi huc pertrahi possunt.
units.tr: § 15. Therefore, when Montanus, in the place cited, admits Aristotle's assertion that health and disease are things made, but denies that it follows that they are not qualities, he does not see where the force of Aristotle's demonstration lies. For if they are in becoming (in fieri) and in having become (in facto esse), as they are, then certainly by denying one of these the other is denied. Hence it remains unshaken that if health and disease are in having become, they are in no way at the same time in becoming. "But," someone will say, "are there not qualities in having become?" There are: those which Aristotle called habits (ἕξεις) in the category of quality. But how will you adapt these to diseases? To put it more plainly: how will you prove to me that all diseases belong under this genus? Perhaps intemperies alone favours this; organic diseases with their cohering parts cannot be dragged into this class by any force.

units.la: Quare Logicus dicet, definitio eritangaftior definito.
units.tr: Hence the logician will say that the definition will be more uncertain than the thing defined.

units.la: § 16. Atqui Montanus refert, Ariftoteles ipse dicit, Gigni & corrumpi, alteratis quibusdam? Argumentum tale est, Morbus fit alteratis quibusdam, Alteratio est qualitas. Ergo morbus est qualitas. Heic quis non subito videt, sermonem efle de solis Intemperiebus? é quibus etiam exempla petit? Annon latet quoque confusio motus ad terminum cum termino ipso? Quidquid fit, Vera est Chriftophori à Vega positio, Morbus ita est ad aliquid, ut non fit qualitas, veluti Montanus ipse loquitur.
units.tr: § 16. Yet Montanus reports that Aristotle himself says that things are generated and corrupted by certain alterations. The argument runs: disease comes about through certain alterations; alteration is a quality; therefore disease is a quality. Here who does not at once see that the discourse concerns intemperies alone, and that it is from these that he takes his examples? Does not a confusion also lie hidden here, between motion towards a term and the term itself? Whatever the case, the position of Christophorus à Vega is true: disease is a relation in such a way that it is not a quality, as Montanus himself puts it.

units.la: § 17. Tamen Noster hic instituit c.1 1. probationem illius, Morbum tám in Relatione esse, quàm in qualitate. Hanc in rem sumit sibi ab initio ... riftotelem & Galenum idem sentire. Sentiunt idem, fi recte explicentur: non sentiunt idem, fi Montanum audias. Arifotelem eo adigi, ut omnem morbum dicat esse qualitatem, indignum cogitatu. Est. Quid Montanus probarit, audivimus in hoc vestigio. Galenum velle idem, non credam, etiam ubi dixero me credere. Vt enim non semel dixi, Duipofitio ipsius non pertinet ad solas qualitates, nec potest nec gare ipsus Montanus ut videbimus. Sed de consensu & dissensu fatis: Montanus, utiapparet, iterum peccat in eo, quod particulare vult esse universale. Sed & (hei mihi!) quàm frigidè stat in particulari illo ! Cum enim in Intemperiebus deberet ostendere & Relationem, & Relationis fundamentum:quidfacit? Temperies carnis ( hanc enim pro exemplo sumit. ) inquit, quatenus calida & humida est, Qualitas est:quatenus συμπεπλεως talis est, Ad aliquid est. Temperies eo usque vitiata,ut actio lædatur, Qualitas est:quatenus ἀμέλεῳ fit, Ad aliquid. Quid multis? Qualitas illa tua. (in rei veritate.) fundamentum est Relationis, & tàm non pertinet ad prædicamentum qualitatis, quàm cœlum non attingit terram. Quanta enim Logices ποιότης est, unam, eandemque rem, eodem modo consideratam, esse in diversis Categoriis! Ab hac ποιότητα absolvo Galenum,quod Dispositionem suam nunquam intruferit in censum prædicamentorum, indagans quippe definitionem nominalem tantùm.
units.tr: § 17. Nevertheless, our author here undertakes in chapter 11 to prove that disease lies as much in relation as in quality. For this purpose he takes it upon himself from the start ... that Aristotle and Galen think the same. They think the same, if they are properly explained; they do not think the same, if you listen to Montanus. That Aristotle was driven to say that every disease is a quality is unworthy of consideration. What Montanus has proved we have heard in this place. That Galen wished the same I will not believe, even when I say that I believe it. For, as I have said more than once, his disposition does not pertain to qualities alone, nor can Montanus himself, as we shall see, manage it. But enough about agreement and disagreement. Montanus, as is clear, errs again in this, that he wants what is particular to be universal. But, alas, how feebly he stands in that particular case! For when in intemperies he ought to show both a relation and the foundation of the relation, what does he do? "The temperament of the flesh (for he takes this as his example)," he says, "insofar as it is hot and moist, is a quality; insofar as it is in proportion (συμπεπλεγμένη), it is a relation. A temperament so far vitiated that action is harmed is a quality; insofar as it is out of proportion (ἀμέλει?), it is a relation." What more need be said? That quality of yours, in the truth of the matter, is the foundation of a relation, and it no more belongs to the category of quality than heaven touches earth. How great a quality of logic this is, that one and the same thing, considered in the same way, should be in different categories! I absolve Galen from this quality, because he never brought his disposition into the list of categories, since he was investigating only the nominal definition.

units.la: § 18. Vt constans jam esse possit sententia Ariftotelis & Galeni, Sanitatem quidem esse solam συμπεπλεγμένην : morbum autem solam ἀμέλειαν, adeoque utramque affectionem esse inter Relata. Quod solum facit umbram Montano, est, quod Galenus praeter duo illa, asciscit διαθεσιν.
units.tr: § 18. So that Aristotle's and Galen's opinion may be consistent: health is indeed only a proportion (συμπεπλεγμένη), while disease is only a lack of proportion (ἀμέλεια), and therefore both affections are among relatives. What alone gives Montanus a shadow is that Galen, besides those two, admits a disposition (διάθεσις).

units.la: Is verò ampliorem facit sibi umbram,. cum explicat illam de qualitate solá.Non propterea ( dixi ego ) Galenus exagitandus est; multò minùs credendum est, ex διαθέσει & συμμετρίᾳ fieri unam fanitatem ; ex διαθέσεω & ἀμετρίᾳ fieri unum morbum. Quin ipsa rerum Natura abhorret ab hac μισγαγγεία.
units.tr: Montanus, however, casts a broader shadow for himself when he explains that disposition as a quality alone. I say that Galen is not on that account to be censured; much less should we believe that from disposition and symmetry one health arises, and from disposition and ametry one disease arises. Indeed the very nature of things shrinks from this mixing (μισγαγγεία).

units.la: § 19. Quamobrem denuò clarà voce & distincte dico. I. Definitio illa πολυρυκῶν non est definitio essentialis, inquam. I I. Διαθέσεως Galeni non magis pertinet ad hoc, illudve praedicamentum, quàm Vnum, Verum, Bonum, &c. I I I.Si omninò Galenus, additis aliis quibufdam, conficit definitionem, quae usui Medico sufficit : non ob id illa legibus Logicisfubjicienda est. τεόπ@ enim ἐπισήμης: hæc & alia permittit. Restat ergò sola συμμετρίαι € ἀμετρίαι, quae dant nobis verum genus Logicum Sanitatis & Morbi.
units.tr: § 19. Wherefore I say again, clearly and distinctly: first, that the definition of the many-rhythmed (πολυρρύθμων?) is not an essential definition, I maintain. Second, Galen's disposition belongs no more to this or that category than One, True, Good, and so on. Third, if Galen, by adding certain other things, constructs a definition sufficient for medical use, that definition is not on that account to be subjected to the laws of logic. For it is in the manner of a science (τρόπῳ ἐπιστήμης): this and other things it allows. There remains, therefore, only symmetry and ametry, which give us the true logical genus of health and disease.

units.la: § 20. Nec hilum valet assertio Mortani infrà l. 2. c.12. Bonam , malamque temperiem esse, non solas qualitates ; sed & relationes, ideoquè symmetriam & ametriam. Quo modo enim probatur? Multò viliot est illa in Ant-Eraft. f. 78. a. Galenus non consideravit ametriam nudam, quae fit inter ipsas qualitates : sed actiones omnes, que à qualitatibus istis emanant, Et paulò antè, Morbi sunt qualitates, ut difpositiones sunt : sunt eorum, que ad aliquid, ut sunt immoderatae, que immoderatio pertinet ad subiectum qualitatum. Heic primum omnium abominabilis plane mihi est mifcela illa praedicamentorum. Deinde scirevolam, quae fit Nuda illa ametria? Quantum intelligo, que non includit actiones: que non connotat subiectum, cuius est actio. Ergone ametria vestita includit & actionem & subiectum? Mirabilis sermo! Si ametria est inter Relata; ista autem omnia considerantur cum suo subiecto, fundamentove: quomodo ulli fano fuccurrere potest ulla ametria nuda? vel ideo, quia Galenus tam expresse alligat difpofitionem suam partibus? Tertio, nec illud forte praetereundum est, Nunquam, inquit, Galenus conftitutit temperiem cordis proportionem quandam inter calidum eq frigidum, cum proportio illa non babeat vim agendi. Imo, tu ipse l.1.c.3. sanitatem quidem collocas in symmetria quatuor primarum qualitatum: morbum autem in dissolutione earundem, quae actionibus noxam inferat. Sed quid ego hac?
units.tr: § 20. Nor does Montanus's assertion below, book 2, chapter 12, have any force: that good and bad temperament are not only qualities but also relations, and therefore symmetry and ametry. For how is this proved? Much less compelling is that passage in Anti-Erasmus, folio 78a: "Galen did not consider bare ametry, which exists between the qualities themselves, but all the actions which emanate from those qualities." And a little earlier: "Diseases are qualities, insofar as they are dispositions; they are of things which are said in relation, insofar as they are immoderate, and this immoderation pertains to the subject of the qualities." Here, first of all, that mixing of categories seems to me plainly abominable. Next, I would like to know what this bare ametry is. As far as I understand, it is that which does not include actions, which does not connote the subject whose action it is. Does ametry, then, clothed in a subject, include both action and subject? A remarkable statement! If ametry is among relatives, and all these things are considered together with their subject or foundation, how can any sane person conceive of any bare ametry? Is it not so, if only because Galen so expressly binds his disposition to the parts? Third, it perhaps must not be passed over that Galen never established the temperament of the heart as some proportion between the hot and the cold, since that proportion has no power of acting. Indeed, you yourself in book 1, chapter 3, place health in the symmetry of the four primary qualities, but disease in the dissolution of these, which inflicts harm on the actions. But why do I dwell on these things?

units.la: Dic mihi denique, o vir magne, quae tibi spes fugae ex istis angustiis? Certe Mirmillo invenit heic retiarium! An pet hac,
units.tr: Tell me finally, great man, what hope of escape you have from those narrows. Surely the Mirmillo has found a retiarius here! Or by this?

units.la: hæc., quæ magnus tui admirator, SCHERBIVS, adnotárat? Sanitas cum morbus sunt qualitates, ut dispositiones sunt: ad aliquid referuntur, ut moderate, vel immoderate sunt. Eatenus enim referuntur ad subjectum dispositionum ipsarum. An per hæc? In definitione morbi Galeni expressè ponitur cum relatio, cum relationis fundamentum. Illa est in duobus istis vocabulis, πρὸς τι Φύσιν: hoc in διαθέσει ipsa. Unde fit, ut morbus sit dispositio immoderata. Parcant mihi manes venerandi doctoris! Non video heic quidquam solidi. Primo omnium recidunt hæc in idem, nec differentia est ulla, præterquam in verbis.
units.tr: These things, which your great admirer Scherbius had noted: health and disease are qualities, just as dispositions are. They are referred to something, as moderate or immoderate, for they are referred to the subject of the dispositions themselves. Or by these? In Galen's definition of disease the relation is expressly stated, and also the foundation of the relation: the former in the two words "πρὸς τι φύσιν" [pros ti physin, "in relation to nature"], the latter in "διαθέσει" [diathesei, "disposition"] itself. Hence it follows that disease is an immoderate disposition. May the shades of that venerable teacher forgive me! I see nothing solid here. First of all, these points come down to the same thing, and there is no difference except in words.

units.la: Deinde quis subito credat, cum τὸ διάθεσις tot habeat significata, complectatur (inquam) non Morbum tantum, sed Caufam quoque cum Symptomate triplici: hæc capi de morbo solo? Videantur super hac de re litigia mutua Erasti, in Anat. f. 55, & feq. & Montani in Ant-Erast. f.29.b. & feq. Tertio cum eadem διάθεσις jam fit profl gata extra limitesCategoriarum, quis ultro iecipiat? Quarto, nisi egregie fallor, impedit hæc manifestam ai urditarem cnim tota ergo e diffe-runt, ut ad hoc fit ei: quia pro-fit Cua-litas: nemo fanus ... ut Hujus sensus est ... ad eit, Morbum esse Relatio-nem.
units.tr: Next, who would suddenly believe that, since the word τὸ διάθεσις [to diathesis] has so many meanings, it embraces (I say) not only disease but also the cause together with the threefold symptom: that these things are to be taken of disease alone? Let the mutual disputes of Erastus on this matter be consulted, in the Anatomy, f. 55 and following, and those of Montanus in the Anti-Erastus, f. 29b and following. Thirdly, since this same διάθεσις has now been pushed beyond the limits of the Categories, who would readily accept it? Fourthly, unless I am greatly mistaken, this hinders a manifest absurdity: for the whole argument differs, so that to this end, because quality is produced, no sane person... The sense of this is ... that disease is a relation.

units.la: {a} Cf. Galenum, De differentiis morborum. nem, falsum est : morbum includere Relationem, verum est. Heic enim est Relatio, ἀπελθία : heic est fundamentum, corpus ἀπελθον, Video nimirum,ad talia diverticula cogi eos, qui Diffofitionem progenere Logico habent, quod Galeno me quidem sub mentem fuit, Hac in re confirmat me,quod negant Montano, Morbum esse tantum qualitatem: imo dicunt, esse in diversis praedicamentis, quatenus accedit illis ametria. His vero annon juvatur Pacii sententia de natura Transfcendentali,ut quidam loquuntur? Plumá levius est, quod amplius dicitur, Galenus per Diffofitionem intellexit partem ita difpositam. Vbi enim tum qualitas stabit? Pauci s Calor, ( ita de reliquis quoque ) qua calor, abstractive, non facit morbum : sed Calor ἀπελθ cum suo fundamento. Haec duo juncta morbum faciunt, & habet alterum rationem Relationis, alterum fundamenti.
units.tr: {a} See Galen, On the Differences of Diseases. That disease is a quality is false; that disease includes a relation is true. For here is the relation, [ἀπελθία], here is the foundation, the body [ἀπελθον]. I see, of course, that those who hold disposition to belong to the logical genus are driven into such detours; this, as I think, was in Galen's mind. In this matter I am confirmed by the fact that they deny to Montanus that disease is merely a quality; indeed they say it belongs to different categories, insofar as dyscrasia [ametria] attaches to them. Surely the view of Pacius on the transcendental nature, as some put it, does not help them here? What is said further is lighter than a feather: that Galen by "disposition" understood a part so disposed. For where, then, will the quality stand? Heat (and likewise with the rest), taken as heat in the abstract, does not make disease; but heat [...] together with its foundation does. These two joined together make disease, and the one has the character of relation, the other of foundation.

units.la: § 22. Concludo igitur denuo negotium totum, GALENVS non valt habeat definitionem suam pro essentiali, & frustra sunt omnes machinae : ipsa rei Natura repugnat, & dicit, Orbis est in solo praedicamento Relationis, & definiendus, ut scripsi § 8.
units.tr: § 22. I conclude, therefore, the whole business once more: Galen does not want his definition to be taken as essential, and all the machinery is in vain. The very nature of the thing opposes it, and says that disease lies in the category of relation alone, and must be defined as I wrote in § 8.

units.la: De eadem definitione Cap. II.
units.tr: On the same definition, Chapter II.

units.la: § 1. Vidimus, quàm felix in ftabiliendis suis fuerit Comes Inoster: videamus, quàm firmus fit in refellendis aliis. Tibi vero, qui quis es, permifsum esto saltu superare. Mihi enim animadversiones meditanti, necessitas hanc legem imponit vel levi brachio tangendi.
units.tr: § 1. We have seen how successful our Comes was in establishing his own views; let us see how firm he is in refuting others. You, whoever you are, are allowed to leap over this. For me, while I weigh his remarks, necessity imposes the rule of touching him only with a light arm.

units.la: § 2. Cap. 5, nimis praeceps est in affirmativâ sententiæ illius, Ἀριστοτέλης Galeni esse eandem cum διαθέσει Ariftotelis. Neuter enim eodem semper modo accipit. Non Ἀριστοteles, qui in Categoriis quidem ftrictius accipit quàm Galenus, pro eâ scilicet tantum, ob quam aliquid dicitur Quale: in Methaphyficis autem tribus modis, fecundum locum, potentiam, & speciem. Vbi propono confiderandum Pacio, Annon morbus κατὰ δύναμιν fit is, qui infrà dicetur Futurus seu Fiens ἐν ᾧ, status athleticus solvendus est, licet morbus nondum fit. Non Galenus, qui, ut dictum est nuper, aliquando latiffimè accipit, pro eo omni, quod p. n. est: aliquando pressè, pro morbo tantum. Hoc stabilire oportet quibusdam locis. 2. Meth. 3. diserte ait, ἐπεὶ τὸ ἑτερὸν ἕξιν, ὃ ἐν ... quomodocunque fe habeat, omnino dicitur effe indiabicus aliquâ fen ftatu altquo,ut Cicero loqueretur. Ne dubites, in veftigio ait, τὸ δ' ἐν δυσλύλ διαθέσει, καθ' ἕξιν ἤδη διαλεκτικῶς quod vero διαθέσεων habes firmam, jam καθ' ἕξιν ἐστὶ effe difpofitum. Vt tamque fignificationem exprimit s. in 6 Epid.4. ubi ait, Vocare fe difpofitiones morbificas, non eas tantum, quæ jam funt: fed eas quoque, quæ fieri incipiunt. Quibus verbis innuit morbum in potentia jam dictum. Quò minus facilè credat Montanus, Galenum femper in ftrictâ illâ fignificatione habere, quam exponit de Diff. fym.1, ibi, Καθόλης δὲ ὃ διαπθεσις, &c. Quin imò, paulò antè meminit etiam latè fignificationis, ibi ἐ ξαν τῶν ἐντων, &c. Quin, quod jam deprehendo, Infrà c.29. ut & in Ant. Eraft. f. 20. b. de induftria ftabilit idipfum.
units.tr: § 2. In chapter 5 he is too hasty in asserting that Galen's [ἀριστοτέλης] is the same as Aristotle's [διάθεσις]. Neither of them always takes the term in the same way. Aristotle, in the Categories, takes it more strictly than Galen does, meaning only that by which something is called "quale". In the Metaphysics, however, he uses it in three ways: according to place, power and species. Here I propose that Pacius consider whether morbus [κατὰ δύναμιν] is not what is called below the future or becoming disease [ἐν ᾧ], the athletic condition that must be dissolved, even though the disease does not yet exist. Galen, as was said recently, sometimes takes the term very broadly, for everything that is in any way, and sometimes narrowly, for disease alone. This must be established by some passages. In 2 Meth. 3 he says plainly that whatever state a thing is in, it is called, to use Cicero's phrase, in some state or other. Do not doubt it: in the same place he says that what is [διάθεσις] firm is already [κατ' ἕξιν] disposed in that way. He expresses the same meaning in 6 Epid. 4, where he says that he calls morbific dispositions not only those that now exist but also those that are beginning to arise. By these words he hints at disease already present in potency. Montanus would be less ready to believe that Galen always keeps to that strict sense, which he sets out in De diff. symp. 1, where he says, [καθόλης δὲ ὃ διάθεσις], and so on. Indeed, a little earlier he also mentions the broad sense, where he says [ἐξ ὧν τῶν ἐντων], and so on. What is more, as I now find, he deliberately establishes the same thing below in chapter 29, and in Ant. Erast. f. 20b.

units.la: § 3. Tollatur ergò totum hoc, tamquam frivolum & inane, & anquiratur in id potiùs,Quo modo Galenus acceperit διαθέσεως in negotio, quod præ manifestus eft? Accepit, ut ego, tanquam Trans- fcendens. Hoc fi fenfiffe quoque Montanum probâro, jure merito— Phyllida seius habebo. Hem tibi autem! Initio cap.
units.tr: § 3. Let all this, then, be set aside as frivolous and empty, and let us inquire instead how Galen understood διαθέσεως [diatheseōs] in a matter that is clear enough. He understood it, as I do, as Transcendent. If I prove that Montanus also thought so, I shall rightly say, "Phyllida shall be mine alone." Well, there you are! But at the beginning of chapter

units.la: 6. hæc funt ipfius verba, & quidem ex Simplicio,Com. in Categ. Qualitatem, licet
units.tr: 6. these are his own words, taken from Simplicius's Commentary on the Categories: "Quality, although it is a genus in itself

units.la: zet fit genus per fe,ex ab aliis novem separatumilate tamenfe fundere,ex reliqua omnia occupare. Hoc dum per exempla explicat, quid facit aliud, quam is, qui pro Transfcendente declarat hoc demto, quod qualitatem vocare audet? Hoc dum munit autoritate D. Thomae, 1. 2. quaest. 49. art. 2. quid aliud facit, quam quod ego defidero? Hem tibi iterum! Cum cap. prae. 5. ait, Hac vox in nullo praedicamentorum esse potest, quia in quocunque fit, excludit morbos aliorum: dicit, quod ego volo. Hoc cum fulcit autoritate Turrifani, tanto mihi affinior fit, quo clariora sunt verba Monachi, Compositio (ita barbari olim vertebant διαθεσιν) est unio. Pnum non est in genere, sed genera transscendit, sicut Ens, Quare de omnibus generibus dici potest. Hem aliud quoque! Cum lib.4. c.29. extr. Ordinem quidem concedit esse in praedicamento ad aliquid; posse tamen in omnibus praedicamentis reperiri: annon tacite hucc tendit? puta, quatenus διαθεσεις est ἐξις apud Ariftotelem in Metaph. qua de re heic fine cap.7. Iam ergo ab ipsomet Montano hoc beneficii habeo, ut confidentius dicere ausim, Αυξησις Galeni innullo praecise praedicamento est, sed in omnibus, quatenus Transscendens est. Et tolerat significationem vulgi tam Græca, quàm Latina lingua : verùm à prædicamentis aspellit illum rerum natura, & recto tramite ducit nos ad ametriam, ut dixi.
units.tr: and separated from the other nine, yet spreads itself and occupies all the rest." While he explains this by examples, what else does he do than someone who declares, for the Transcendent, this removed, which he dares to call quality? While he supports this with the authority of St Thomas, 1.2, q. 49, art. 2, what else does he do than what I desire? Well, there you are again! In the preceding chapter 5 he says, "This word can be in none of the categories, because in whatever it is found, it excludes the diseases of others." He says what I want. When he supports this with the authority of Turrisanus, it is all the more to my liking, since the words of the Monk are the clearer: "Composition (as the barbarians once translated διάθεσιν [diathesin]) is a union. It is not in a genus, but transcends genera, as Being does; hence it can be predicated of all genera." Well, here is another! When in book 4, chapter 29, at the end, he concedes indeed that order is in the predicament of relation, yet can be found in all predicaments, does he not tacitly tend to this point? That is, insofar as διαθέσεις [diatheseis] is ἕξις [hexis] according to Aristotle in the Metaphysics, on which see here, without chapter 7. Now, therefore, I have this benefit from Montanus himself, that I may more confidently dare to say that the augmentation [αὔξησις] of Galen is not in any one precise predicament, but in all, insofar as it is Transcendent. He tolerates the common meaning in both the Greek and the Latin language; but the nature of things draws him away from the predicaments and leads us by a straight path to ametria [ἀμετρία], as I said.

units.la: § 4. Nisi penitissimè fallor, eodem tendit Parolinus,Prof. Ferrarienfis, (hoc à Scherbio habeo.) quem Montanus refutare vult in Ant-Eraft, f. 75. De Parolino hoc imprimis miror, Concedere quidem esse morbum ad aliquid : sed divellere telàtionem à fundamento suo. Formaliter quidem, inquit,morbus est ἀμετεία : atmaterialiter, ratione termini, sed fundamenti, quod Medicus principaliter respicit, connotat. Quid connotat, ò Paroline? Exspectabam equidem Qualitatem Montani : sed dissimulas, usus interim iifdem poenè verbis, Eodem ducunt illa, Dispositionis nomen ad qualitatem referri : non ita tamen, ut non possimus dicere, aliaquid esse morbum, quod non aliquam ejus speciei qualitatem in fe contineat. Sufficit enim quod fit modò substantia, &c. Quæ verba, cum Montani verbis collata, eamdem & longitudinem & latitudinem habent. Sed neque aliò vergunt illa in Digref. f. 77. b. ext. Hinc patet, cum dicimus; Sanitatem esse συμμετρίαν &c. Cupiam autem ab utroque audire, quâ fronte divellere ausint ἀμετρίαν ἢ ἀμε- τεῖα.
units.tr: § 4. Unless I am very much mistaken, Parolinus, professor at Ferrara (I have this from Scherbius), tends to the same place, and it is him that Montanus wants to refute in the Ant-Erast, f. 75. About Parolinus I am especially surprised: he concedes that disease is a relation, but tears the relation away from its foundation. "Formally," he says, "disease is ἀμετρία [ametria]; but materially, by reason of the term, it connotes the foundation, which the physician principally regards." What does it connote, O Parolinus? I was indeed expecting Montanus's quality, but you dissemble, meanwhile using almost the same words: "These things lead to the conclusion that the name disposition is referred to quality; not so, however, that we cannot say that something else is a disease which does not contain in itself some quality of its kind. For it is enough that it is now a substance," and so on. These words, when compared with Montanus's words, have the same length and the same breadth. Nor do those words in the Digression, f. 77 b, extend elsewhere. Hence it is clear when we say, "Health is symmetry" [συμμετρίαν], and so on. But I would like to hear from both of them with what face they dare to tear apart ἀμετρίαν ἢ ἀμετρία [ametrian ē ametria].

units.la: τεῖα.
units.tr: (the end of the Greek word just cited)

units.la: ɣεοῦ,ut pridem innui? Alterum enim ponit alterum,ut vara vibiam, quod in proverbio est. Summa λόγω μακρὰς diceret Galenus, qualis (addam ego.) inter Efernios & Pacidianos ( quo adagio ex Cicerone libenter utitur Comes ) esse solet.
units.tr: As I hinted before? For one thing is put for another, like "vara vibiam", which is the proverb. In sum, Galen would say, [λόγῳ μακρὰς], what kind of thing (I would add) is usually found between the Eternians and the Pacidians, an adage which Comes gladly borrows from Cicero.

units.la: § 5. Quidquid fiat de Parolino:Montanus ipse, dum Fuchfiumrefutat, tantùm non obviam mihi it. Hoc interest, quod nimis longis utitur ambagibus; cum breviori via,quam SCHERBIVS olim, ὁ ἀεὶ μόνι ... nobis sternebat,pervenire posset.Cum hoc ergo dicam. Calculus, v.g. nec morbus est , nec in calculo morbus est : sed calculus in parte, cui infidet,facit eam dispositionem,fi cum vulgo loqui tibi placet,eam ἀμετεῖν,si cum Philosophis, quæ morbus est, Obstructio. scilicet,ex conformationis vitiis illis,quæ sunt in viis angustis. Ita in Obstructionibus reliquis , humor impactus , nec morbus est,nec in eo morbus: sed pars morbi illa, quæ Relationis fundamentum est. Quod cum ita fit,quis ferat illum,qui velit dicere : Morbus est substantia,quia calculus est substantia ? quia humor est substantia ? Non minor est ἀ τοῦτο illa,quærere in talibus qualitatem , quod Montanus facit.
units.tr: § 5. Whatever becomes of Parolinus, Montanus himself, while refuting Fuchsius, barely comes to meet me. The difference is that he uses overly long circumlocutions, whereas by a shorter road, the one Scherb once paved for us, one could arrive at the goal. So I will say this: a calculus, for example, is neither a disease, nor is there a disease in the calculus. Rather, the calculus in the part where it lodges makes that disposition, which, if you wish to speak with the common people, you may call [ἀμετρία], but if with the philosophers, which is a disease, namely obstruction, arising from those faults of conformation which lie in the narrow passages. So in other obstructions, an impacted humour is neither a disease nor is there a disease in it; rather that part of the disease is the foundation of the relation. Since this is so, who could endure a man who says that disease is a substance because a calculus is a substance, or because a humour is a substance? It is no less absurd to seek quality in such things, as Montanus does.

units.la: § 6. Et quia ad Fuchfium pervenimus,de cap. quidem 6. nihil amplius di. cam : de 7, autem non nisi pauca.Abfurdiffimum est, causas quoque esse fubftantias, quod Galenus illas vocet dispositiones. Cadente enim illo, cadit simul hoc. Interim Montanus labitur in retia noftra, Causas esse dispositiones, quatenus sunt qualitates transscendentes. Quæ quia improprie sunt dispositiones,quippe ἀλλοιώσεις,Constitutiones, quoque, quæ nullâ ratione dici possunt qualitates, proprie, inquam; stat argumentum Fuchfii & Valleriolæ,nec quidquam agit Montanus,cum simpliciter ἀνδρεῖα. Et quàm ridiculus fit, cum ait, Quemadmodum sanitas fine controversiâ est qualitas, ita morbus quoque! Sunt qualitates, sed quales tu cap. anteced. dixti, improprie dicte, non autem quales ab Ariftotele dicuntur in Categ. Hoc prorsus vult Philofophema ex Simplicio, quod annectit Comes, & comprobat Eraftus, Anat. p.31,
units.tr: § 6. And since we have come to Fuchsius: I will say nothing more about chapter 6, and only a little about chapter 7. It is most absurd that causes too are substances, which Galen calls dispositions. For if that falls, this falls with it. Meanwhile Montanus slips into our nets, saying that causes are dispositions insofar as they are transcendent qualities. Since they are dispositions only improperly, being alterations, and constitutions too, which can in no way properly be called qualities (I say properly), the argument of Fuchsius and Valleriola stands, and Montanus achieves nothing when he simply [ἀνδρεῖα]. How ridiculous it is when he says: just as health is without controversy a quality, so disease is too! They are qualities, but such as you yourself said in the preceding chapter, improperly so called, not the qualities which Aristotle names in the Categories. This is exactly what the philosophy from Simplicius wants, which Comes adds and Erastus confirms, Anat. p. 31.

units.la: § 7. Dum profunde contemnit cap.8, primum,(ut ipse quidem collocat.) Chr, à Vega argumentum, ostendit fe parum prudentem & pudentem. Hoc ita formo, Genus complectli debet omnes species morbi,qualitas non complectitur,Ergo. Minor probatur, Morbos in Magnitudine
units.tr: § 7. While he deeply scorns chapter 8, the first argument (as he himself arranges it) of Christopher à Vega, he shows himself little prudent and little modest. I put it thus: a genus ought to embrace all the species of disease; quality does not embrace them; therefore quality is not the genus. The minor is proved: quality does not embrace diseases in magnitude, and so on. What does he say to that? It does not comprehend them in the way that species are in a genus, but as in a subject. A dangerous answer, Erastus used to say. The question concerns species, not subject. Hence it follows that, while he admits diseases are not contained in magnitude under...

units.la: non complectitur, Quid ille? Non comprehendit eo modo, quo species in genere sunt : sed quo tanquam in subjecto. Periculofa refponfio, dicebat Eraftus. De specie quaeritur, non de subjecto. Inde fit, ut dum fatetur, morbus in magnitudine non contineri sub genere dato (quantitas enim non est qualitas, & viciflim.) concedit argumentum. Tandem cum addit, Morbus non est quantitas ipsa, sed vitium, & mala dispositio : manibus & pedibus repit in castra nostra.
units.tr: does not comprise. What does he mean? He does not comprehend it in the way species are in a genus, but as in a subject. Erastus said this is a dangerous answer.
