The question concerns species, not subject. So when he admits that disease is not contained under the given genus in magnitude (for quantity is not quality, and vice versa), he concedes the argument. Finally, when he adds, "Disease is not quantity itself but a defect and bad disposition," he creeps into our camp hand and foot.

units.la: § 8. Postquam cap. 9. introduxit Vegam dicentem, Absurdum dictu esse, Calor est ametria, quod haec locutio causae potius morbificae conveniat, quam morbo : regerit, Non est absurdum, fi de calore p. n. accipias. Pax!
units.tr: § 8. After chapter 9 he brought in Vega saying it is absurd to call heat an ametria, since this expression fits a morbific cause rather than the disease. He retorts, "It is not absurd if you take it of preternatural heat." Peace!

units.la: § 9. De cap, 10, & 11. jam dixi, quod fatis esse possit.
units.tr: § 9. What I have already said about chapters 10 and 11 may be enough.

units.la: § 10. Adea, quae cap. 12 de Erafto scribit, quia respondit ipsius, Anat. p. 12: non ego ero frustra tedium sus. Consistit enim resinfacto. Alter ait, alter negat. Eadem ratio quia valet de duplici Digreffione in Ant-Eraft. f. 7 & 9, verbum non commutabo. Et quia merae λογικα sunt, quae in iisdem sunt, à f. 11. ufque ad. 29. An excessus primarum qualitatum morbi potius sint, quam causae pariter abjicio. Causam dico, quam SCHERBIVS sæpe; Omnes linguæ utuntur Relativis, loco absoluti, seu fundamenti. Et hæc est septima regula inter illas, quas Relatis transscribit P H. ME. LANCHTHON. Hanc ita accommodare oportet, ut pateat dolus. Cum dico Temperamentum, intelligo qualitates ita temperatas, non in abstracto, sed in concreto.
units.tr: § 10. As for what he writes in chapter 12 about Erastus, since he answers his own words (Anat. p. 12: "I shall not be a burden to you in vain"), it stands on the deed. The one affirms, the other denies. The same reasoning holds against the double digression in Ant-Erast. ff. 7 and 9; I will not change a word. And since these are merely logical matters, which occur in the same passages from f. 11 to f. 29, I equally set aside the question whether excesses of the primary qualities are rather the disease than the cause. I call it a cause, as Scherbius often does. All languages use relatives in place of the absolute, or foundation. This is the seventh rule among those which Ph. Melanchthon transcribes concerning relatives. It must be applied so that the trick is evident. When I say temperament, I understand qualities so tempered, not in the abstract but in the concrete.

units.la: § 11. Cap. 13. incipit agere contra Argenterium, cujus argumenta ibinumerat.Horum I. est cap.14. Dispositionem esse vocem ambiguam. Nihil mali, dico ego.Mens enim Galeni nunquam fuit ea, quæ affingitur illi, quærendi (inquam) genus Logicum, constituendive definitionem essentialem. Quæ contra Fuchfium in Inftit. obiter denotat, profecto sapiunt insolentiam aliquam. Vtut enim definitio non fit: rectè tamen ait, fi rectè intelligas, Ἀσάθεσιν capi aliquando pro omni eo, eâ quo corpus nostrum afficitur.Et hoc favet rebus quoque meis.
units.tr: § 11. Chapter 13 begins to argue against Argenterius, and there he lists his arguments. The first of these, in chapter 14, is that "disposition" is an ambiguous word. I say there is no harm in that. For Galen never intended what is attributed to him, a logical kind of inquiry (I mean) or the constructing of an essential definition. What he remarks in passing against Fuchsius in the Institutions certainly savours of some insolence. Although it is not a definition, he rightly says, if you understand it rightly, that διάθεσιν is sometimes taken for any condition by which our body is affected. And this favours my own case too.

units.la: § 12. II. III. IV. Argumentum
units.tr: § 12. II. III. IV. Argument

units.la: copulat cap.15. & rursus lacessit Fuchfium, Ego de Argenterio quidem dicam, quod SCHERBIVS oræ codicis fui adscripserat. Multa ille peperit, sed fine obftetrice, hoc est, fine organo Logico, ut vocat
units.tr: He takes up chapter 15 and again attacks Fuchsius. As for Argenterius, I will say what Scherbius had added in the margin of my copy. He produced many things, but without a midwife, that is, without the logical instrument, as he calls it.

units.la: car Plato: de Fuchfio autem, quod idem, solet bonas causas male agendo perdere. Res breviter ita fe habet. Duae sunt voces apud Graecos, διὸ νῦν ἢ μόνιμοι, quas Galenus jungere solet τῇ διαιρέσει. Hinc quaestio instituitur, fitne de effentiâ morbi, ut & sensilis fit, & stabilis? Distinguo, ut infrà, Aliter fe habet in ὑγιεινῇ : aliter in θεραπευτικῇ. In illa fatis est, fi fit laefurus actionem : in hac necesse est, ut laesio fit sensibilis, five illa duret per medium horas, five per totum diem. Coeterum, cogere velle Galenum, ut vel semper cum Ariftotele fit, vel semper cum illo loquatur, insania est.
units.tr: as Plato says. But of Fuchsius, the same charge applies: he is accustomed to waste good causes by arguing badly. The matter stands briefly thus. There are two words among the Greeks, [διηνεκής ἢ μόνιμος], which Galen is accustomed to join to division. Hence the question arises whether it belongs to the essence of disease to be both sensible and lasting. I distinguish, as below. It is otherwise in hygiene, and otherwise in therapeutics. In the former it is enough that it harm the action; in the latter it is necessary that the harm be sensible, whether it lasts half an hour or the whole day. Moreover, to want to force Galen either always to agree with Aristotle or always to speak with him is madness.

units.la: § 13. Hinc aestimet aliquis. V. quod est cap.16. Morbus infenfilis (in Therapeuticis) oppositum habet in adjecto, ne dicam ἀεὶ προσδιαν introducere. Oportet igitur sensilis fit juxtà, & laedat actionem. Quod fi Galenus alicubi negat, respicit ad axioma suum, Lafo instrumento leditur actio ipsius. To μόνιμον igitur pertinet, non ad durationem temporis : sed ad factum quid, quo distinguitur ἀπὸ τῆς πάθου. Quidquid fit, recte Montanus ait, Est quaestio Logica.
units.tr: § 13. Let someone judge from this. V., which is chapter 16: disease that is insensible (in therapeutics) has its opposite in the adjunct, to say nothing of introducing [ἀεὶ προσδιάν]. It is necessary, therefore, that it be sensible and harm the action. If Galen somewhere denies this, he looks to his own axiom: the action is harmed by an injured instrument. The [μόνιμον] therefore pertains not to the duration of time, but to some fact by which it is distinguished from [πάθος]. Whatever the case, Montanus rightly says it is a logical question.

units.la: § 14. V I. Causam esse dispositionem (cap.17.) nihil absurdi est, ut & laedere actionem, Morbus enim primò laedit: causa secundario, ut Mont. ipse cap.seq. Vanum verò est, causam esse aliam à Relatione, hoc est, considerari posse in se, tanquam qualitatem: non autem ratione causati. Iam igitur hoc non tollit πρώτως.
units.tr: § 14. V I. That disposition is the cause (chapter 17) is no more absurd than that it impairs the action. For disease first impairs, and the cause does so secondarily, as Montanus himself says in the following chapter. But it is empty to say that the cause is something other than the relation, that is, that it can be considered in itself, as a quality, and not in respect of what it causes. Therefore this does not remove primarily [πρώτως].

units.la: § 15. VII. Facultatem ledi an- tequam ledatur actio (cap.18.) multò minus absurdi est.
units.tr: § 15. VII. That the faculty can be impaired before the action is impaired (chapter 18) is much less absurd.

units.la: Verum enim verò assertio hæc opus habet παςχμυδίαις quibusdam. I. Temperamentum vocat ille aliquando Facultatem, etiam Animam, Medicâ consideratione. Et sunt hæc duo apud ipsum revera unum, nec dici potest alterutrum esse prius aut posterius. Hinc Montanus in Ant-Eralt. f. 64. b. ait, Morbum non lædere facultatem : sed esse ipsammet læsam facultatē. Quo loco admonendus fuerit Eraftus, Anat. f. 23. Galenum 1. quod animi, conficere, quod vult, Temperamentum esse animam. Non enim Philosophum agit sed Medicum, ut mox amplius dicam. II. Non raro à Temperamento recedit, Facultatemque vocat Spiritus, ex partibus principibus influentes, abs quibus temperamenti actio nulla est. Hoc alii ita efferunt, Actiones fluunt non à solo temperamento proprio, sed & à communi, quod à corde est.
units.tr: But this assertion does need certain qualifications [παςχμυδίαις]. I. He sometimes calls the temperament the faculty, and even the soul, from a medical point of view. In him these two are really one, and it cannot be said that one is prior or posterior to the other. Hence Montanus, in Ant-Eralt. f. 64 b., says that disease does not impair the faculty, but that the faculty itself is what is impaired. On this point Erastus should be admonished, Anat. f. 23, where Galen, to establish what he wants, makes the temperament the soul. For he is not acting as a philosopher but as a physician, as I shall say more fully below. II. He not rarely departs from the temperament and calls the faculty the spirit, flowing from the principal parts, on which the action of the temperament has no bearing. Others express this as follows: the actions flow not from the proper temperament alone, but also from the common one, which comes from the heart.

units.la: III. Cum triplex sit corporis nostri constitutio,ut mox dicetur in diff. morb. actio dependet,non à solâ partium Temperie : sed & ab Organisatione, & tandem Vnione earundem. IV. Eædem non fiunt,non tantùm affectâ parte, quæ laborat,sed & alterâ, hoc est, affectus alii fiunt per ἰδιοπαθείαν, alii per συμπαθείαν, Vide Montanum infrà cap.26. Hæc tot,& forte plura cum requirantur; Galenus verò modò hoc tantùm dicat, modò plura,pauciorave:quis propter inconstantiam ( ut interpretantur σχεσιν) quidam ) velit illum objurgare potius, quàm excusare,ille possit. Mihi vel vultu aspernari liceat,tàm illa, quæ Mont. colligit heic : quàm ista ,quæ cap.19. & 20. contrà I. Alexandrinum & Fuchsium. Eâdem licentiâ utar in concul candis Valleriolæ, cap.21. 22. & 23. absurditatibus. Multò enim absurdior sim ipse , si refutare tentem, quæ liberali consideratione indigna sunt.
units.tr: III. Since the constitution of our body is threefold, as will be said presently in the differences of diseases, action depends not only on the temperature of the parts but also on their organisation, and finally on their union. IV. The same parts are affected not only in the part which suffers, but also in the other part: some affections happen through [ἰδιοπάθεια], others through [συμπάθεια]. See Montanus below, chapter 26. These many, and perhaps more, are required; but Galen sometimes says only this, sometimes more or fewer. Because of this inconstancy (as they interpret [σχέσιν]), someone may prefer to rebuke him rather than excuse him, and he may be able to. For my part I may be permitted to scorn with a look both those things Montanus gathers here and those in chapters 19 and 20 against Alexandrinus and Fuchsius. I shall use the same licence in shaking off the absurdities of Valleriola in chapters 21, 22 and 23. For I should be far more absurd myself if I tried to refute things unworthy of liberal consideration.

units.la: § 16. Cæterùm, quia occasione huius argumenti, natum est Capivaccio. (hunc enim Scherbius nominatim producebat.) dictatum illud, quod Mont. refutat in Ant-Eraft. f. 61. & seq. fas est de illo dicam tria verba. Insultat ille Montano, quod dixerit, Temperiem esse facultatem. Cui ego confidenter in os:
units.tr: § 16. Moreover, since this argument gave rise to Capivaccio (for Scherbius named him expressly), and to the saying which Montanus refutes in Ant-Erast. f. 61 and following, it is right to say three words about him. He insults Montanus because he said that temperament is a faculty. To which I reply confidently to his face:

units.la: Fecit autoritate Galeni.At quo habitu ille? Non enim utar diverticulo, quo Montanus. Si Philosophico, procul dubio vehementissimè erravit & dux, & comes. Sim Medico, excusari debent & possunt. Prosecto, quod Aristoteles non semel nos docuit, distinguere oportet ἐπιστήμην [?] ἢ πρὸς τρόπον ἐπιστήμης [?]. Neque enim eadem est ratio scientiarum & artium. In scientiis oportet ubique locorum sectari, quod subjectum vult: in artibus propter finem licet (ita loquor) digredi ab illâ regulâ, sicubi fini, vel non obstet, vel propius ad illum ducat. Ita in proposito negotio. Temperies, nec Facultas est nec [?] tamen Medicus dicit utrumque. Cur? In reddendis actionum causis, adeoque in curatione ipsâ, præcipuè respicit temperiem, quia, servatâ temperie, fervat animam. Hoc facit ad profligandum Epicurifmum, qui & olim objectus fuit Galeno, & superiori sæculo à magno Cratone in epistolâ quâdam ad Donzellinum, Montano nostro. Quin mihi quoque objectus fuit quondam atheismus à magno quodam ICto in disput. de Naturæ officio, Profectò accidit talibus, quod apud Terentium hostibus Comici, Ne faciunt intelligendo, ut nihil intelligant.
units.tr: "He did it on Galen's authority." But in what capacity? I shall not use the sidestep Montanus used. If as a philosopher, without doubt both leader and companion erred most gravely. If as a physician, they ought to be and can be excused. Surely, as Aristotle has taught us more than once, one must distinguish knowledge [ἐπιστήμην] from the manner of knowing. The reasoning of the sciences and of the arts is not the same. In the sciences one must everywhere follow what the subject demands; in the arts, for the sake of the end, it is permitted (so I speak) to depart from that rule wherever it does not hinder the end or leads more directly to it. So in the present matter: temperament is neither faculty nor [?]; yet the physician says both. Why? In giving the causes of actions, and so in the cure itself, he chiefly regards temperament, because, with the temperament preserved, he preserves the soul. This serves to overthrow Epicureanism, which was objected to Galen of old, and in the last century by the great Crato in a letter to Donzellini, our Montanus. Indeed, atheism was once objected to me too by a certain great jurist, in the disputation on the Nature of Duty. Surely what Terence's comic poet says of enemies happens to such people: "They do not understand, by pretending to understand, so that they understand nothing."

units.la: § 17. VIII. Ad hoc (cap. 24.) simplex est refponfio, Est ab errore externo, Vide, si placet, Ant-Erast. f.23.a. ext. & iterum f. 73. b.
units.tr: § 17. VIII. To this (chap. 24) the reply is simple: it comes from external error. See, if you please, Ant-Erast. f.23.a ext., and again f.73.b.

units.la: § 18. IX. Symptomata (cap.25.) primò lædere actiones, est inter ea quæ διαφθαρτικὰ negari debent. Sed & si obtineatur quid, Logicum est.
units.tr: § 18. IX. That symptoms (chap. 25) first impair actions is one of those claims that must be denied as destructive. But even if something were granted, it is a point of logic.

units.la: § 19. X. Hoc sequi debebat VII. quatenus Galenus aliquando non meminit morborum per συνεχὲς ὄνομα. Ideo Montanus recte inscribit, Actiones non lædi fine læsione partis, vel illius, quæ acit, vel alterius, tu puta, τῆς συμπτωσεως. Vbi fortassis addere licet παραμυθίας superioribus, In ordine partium, ad unum aliquem effectum insignem coeuntium, fingulis καὶ ἐντελεχείαν agentibus, vel non fieri aliquid, vel male, si una illarum non fit in officio. v.g. Effectus valde operosus est sanguinis alendi confectio: quare si vel despectissima pars cespitet, sanguis laudabilis non fit.
units.tr: § 19. X. This ought to follow from VII, inasmuch as Galen sometimes does not name diseases by the common term (συνεχὲς ὄνομα [synekes onoma]). So Montanus rightly entitles it: actions are not impaired without injury to the part, either to the part that acts or to another, namely the sympathy (τῆς συμπτωσεως [tes symptōseōs]). Here it may perhaps be permissible to add a qualification to the above: where several parts converge on one notable effect, each exercising its activity (καὶ ἐντελεχείαν [kai entelecheian]), either nothing is produced or it is produced badly if one of them is not doing its duty. For example, the making of nourishing blood is a very laborious effect; so if even the most despised part stumbles, healthy blood is not produced.

units.la: § 20. In XI. (cap.27.) jure dubitat Montanus de sequelâ. Recte etiam respondet, Non distingui morbos ratione læsarum partium, sed naturæ propriæ. v.g. hæc est inflammatio, hic est Organicus morbus. Hac de re videsis, Erastum, Anat. f.218. & Ant-Erastum. f.14. & a.
units.tr: § 20. In XI (chap. 27) Montanus rightly doubts the sequel. He also responds rightly that diseases are not distinguished by the parts injured but by their own nature. For example, this is inflammation, this is an organic disease. On this matter see Erastus, Anat. f.218, and Ant-Erastus f.14 and a.

units.la: § 21. Cur Galenus (cap.28.) in definitione posuerit unicum hoc symptoma, Actionem lefam, falsam uti autumo, caufam attulit Montanus, Quia actio laesa cum morbo simpliciter συμπεφυκεναι cum reliquis duobus symptomatis non item.
units.tr: § 21. Why Galen (chap. 28) put this single symptom, the impaired action, into the definition, I suppose is a false question; Montanus gave the reason: because the impaired action has simply grown together with the disease, but the other two symptoms have not.

units.la: Veram dedit Pacius, Com. in Meth. col. 274. quaeque SCHERBIO etiam placebat, Actione primum et maxime ipsa digemus, utpote in quā sanitas consistit, et iam vulgi judicio, è quo Galenus desumit.
units.tr: Pacius gave the true reason, in Com. in Meth. col. 274, and this also pleased Scherbius: we should treat action first and foremost, since health consists in it, and by the judgment of the common people, from whom Galen takes it.

units.la: § 22. Examen definitionis Argentee- rii & Fernelii, cap.30. & 31. non magnae rei est: quin definitabilis est innovatio illa ingenio ad majora properanti. Scribunt licet.
units.tr: § 22. The examination of the definitions of Argenterius and Fernelius, chapters 30 and 31, is of no great importance; indeed, that innovation is one a mind hurrying towards greater things might well define. Still, they write...

units.la: Turpe est difficiles habere nugas, et sultus labor est ineptiarum.
units.tr: It is disgraceful to have troublesome trifles, and the sweat of labour is spent on nonsense.

units.la: CAPUT III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: § 1. Recte Montanus cap. 2. & 3. venatur triplex morborum genus ex triplici corporis nostri constitutione. Vt enim Sanitas constat, si tria bene habeant: ita Morbus adest, si unum, plurave ex illis è natura suā abierit. Tria illa in Sanitate sunt. I. Si partes omnes justum (quod ipsum naturale est) habeant temperamentum, per quod agere
units.tr: § 1. Montanus rightly, in chapters 2 and 3, traces a threefold kind of disease from the threefold constitution of our body. For as health consists in three things being well, so disease is present if one or more of them has departed from its nature. These three things in health are: I. If all the parts have a just temperament (which is itself natural), by which

units.la: nata est unaquæque illarum, quod suum est. II. Si eædem partes rectè sint organifatæ, ut sic dicam, hoc est, fi singulæ fimilares,ad constitutionem diffimilaris alicujus,seu organi concurrentes, & rectè conformatæ sint, & nulla ex iis, vel defit,vel superfit,& nulla fit major, minorve,& nulla situm ad vicinam partem alium habeat,quam habere fecundùm naturam debet. III. Si eædem continuatæ & unitæ sint eo modo, quo f. n.debent.
units.tr: each of them is born to perform what is its own. II. If the same parts are rightly organised, as I may put it, that is, if the similar parts that combine to form some dissimilar part or organ are rightly shaped, and none of them is either lacking or superfluous, none is larger or smaller, and none has a position relative to a neighbouring part other than it ought to have by nature. III. If the same parts are joined and united in the manner they ought to be.

units.la: § 2. Tria hæc ʏ:tiata faciunt I. Intemperiem, morbum similarem dictum, cum partes non bené & fecundum naturam temperatæ sunt, sed vel calidiores, vel frigidiores, &c. Hoc accidit duobus modis, aut fine, aut cum materia. Sine materia dicitur Intemperies nuda: cum materiâ, Intemperies cum materiâ seu affluxu substantiæ.
units.tr: § 2. These three, when they are vitiated, produce: I. Intemperies, called a similar disease, when the parts are not well and naturally tempered but are either hotter or colder, and so on. This happens in two ways, either without matter or with matter. Without matter it is called bare intemperies; with matter, intemperies with matter, or with an influx of substance.

units.la: § 3. Tot numero Intemperies sunt, quot sunt qualitates primæ, eaque vel simplices vel compositæ. Illæ carent nomine:hæc sunt tumores p.n. dicti. Simplices sunt Calida, humida, frigida, sicca: compositæ, calida & humida, frigida & humida, calida & sicca, frigida & sicca. Tumores p.n. totidem sunt,sed nominibus distincti. Sunt autem & hi vel simplices, vel compositi. Simplices sunt, legi-
units.tr: § 3. There are as many intemperies as there are first qualities, and these are either simple or compound. The simple ones have no name; the compound are the tumours praeter naturam. The simple ones are hot, moist, cold and dry; the compound are hot and moist, cold and moist, hot and dry, cold and dry. The tumours praeter naturam are equally many but distinguished by names. These too are either simple or compound. The simple ones, also called legitimate, are:

units.la: timi etiam dicti, Inflammatio ex sanguine ne:Erysipelas ex bile:Oedema ex pituitā: Scirrhus ex melancholiā. Compositi seu spurii, Inflammatio erysipelatodes, ex sanguine quidem prævadente, bile autem ammistā: Erysipelas inflammatorium, ex bile superabundante, ammisto sanguine.
units.tr: inflammation from blood; erysipelas from bile; oedema from phlegm; scirrhus from black bile. The compound or spurious ones are: erysipelatous inflammation, arising from blood that predominates but with bile mixed in; and inflammatory erysipelas, arising from excess bile with blood mixed in.

units.la: Et sic de cæteris.
units.tr: And so on for the rest.

units.la: § 4. Post Intemperies faciunt Morbum organicum, qui secundum sermonem jam habitum, quadruplex est. Aut enim in Conformatione est: aut in magnitudine: aut in numero: aut in situ. Rursus quia Conformatio consistit in tribus, siunt tres inde morbi, In figurā: in cavitatibus strictioribus vel arctioribus: in superficie, vel asperatā, vel lævigatā. Quamobrem morbus organicus jam sextuplex est.
units.tr: § 4. After the intemperies comes organic disease, which, according to the account just given, is fourfold. For it lies either in conformation, or in magnitude, or in number, or in position. Again, since conformation consists of three things, three diseases arise from it: in figure; in cavities that are too narrow or too wide; and in the surface, whether roughened or smoothed. Therefore organic disease is now sixfold.

units.la: § 5. Post hos omnes est morbus communis dictus, quem Galenus Continui vel Vnitatis solutionem vocat, & comprehendit Dolores, Vlcera, & Vulnera.
units.tr: § 5. After all these, there is the so-called common disease, which Galen calls the dissolution of the continuum or unity, and which includes pains, ulcers and wounds.

units.la: § 6. De tribus his tria sunt præcipua dubia. In Intemperiebus, An, quemadmodum Temperies facultas dicitur, cum secundùm naturam se habet, possit Organisatio & Vnio pariter ita dici? Mont. ait, ego cum Erafto nego. Si vis tempus perdere, abi ad Anat. s.85. & Ant-Erast-
units.tr: § 6. Three main doubts arise about these three. First, concerning intemperies: since temperament is called a faculty when it is in its natural state, can organisation and union likewise be so called? Montanus says yes; I, with Erastus, say no. If you want to waste time, go to Anat. s.85. and Ant-Erast-

units.la: f. 58.b. In morbis organicis. ( non minus quàm in Intemperiebus.) nodus in scirpo quæritur, Annon potiùs Causæ sint, quàm Morbi? Disceptabitur illud 1.4. €.28. hocl.2.c.ro.In Continui solutione quæritur, quà ratione Communis morbus dicatur ? Dico paucis, Cum dolor aliquis fupervenit, five cum,five fine materiâ,est Intemperies: cum vulnus infligitur parti alicui, aut ulcus est, est morbus Organicus : cum vulneri aut ulceri succedit inflammatio, adest uterque morbus.
units.tr: f. 58.b. In organic diseases (no less than in intemperies) a knot is sought in a bulrush: are they not rather causes than diseases? That will be discussed in 1.4. c.28. and here in 2.c.10. On the dissolution of the continuum, the question is in what sense it is called a common disease. I answer briefly: when some pain arises, whether with or without matter, there is an intemperies; when a wound is inflicted on some part, or there is an ulcer, there is an organic disease; when inflammation follows a wound or ulcer, both diseases are present.

units.la: AD LIBRUM II. De Intemperiebus, CAP. IV.
units.tr: TO BOOK II. On Intemperies, CHAPTER IV.

units.la: § 1. VT docere posset Montanus natu-ram Intemperierum, seu morbum fimiliarium, fatis quidem altè orditur rem: veruntamen non ad euftum meum. Ego hoc solum vellem docuiffe illum, quod ego alibi. Apud Græcos, à quibus fere pendemus, duo sunt vocabula, ἀτίς καὶ κρᾶσις, quorum illud Corporum est, de quibus ägunt Physici, de miftione inferibentes: hoc Qualitatum, de quibus Medici, in lib. de Temperamentis. Hæc cum Montanus confundit, non fatis explicare fe potest ex multis. Hujus criminis.
units.tr: § 1. Although Montanus starts his account of the nature of intemperies, or the disease of the similar parts, rather far back, it does not serve my purpose. I would have liked him to teach only what I have taught elsewhere. Among the Greeks, from whom we largely depend, there are two words, ἀτίς [κρᾶσις] and κρᾶσις, of which the first belongs to bodies, the subject of the natural philosophers who write about mixture, and the second to qualities, the subject of the physicians in their book on temperaments. Montanus confuses these, and cannot, for many reasons, explain himself well. Erastus is also guilty of this fault.

units.la: Ad Lib. de Temperamentis. criminis reus est Eraftus quoque Anat. pag.18. & 21.
units.tr: Erastus is also guilty of this fault, as in the book on temperaments, in the Anatomy, pages 18 and 21.

units.la: § 2. Quæ cap.2. disputat,reverà supra Medicum sunt,vel ideò, quia in confusione persistit. Hinc adeò sit ut cap.3. quasi eximprovifo arripiat temperiem, dicatque qualitatem esse. At si præmonuisset lectorem, de Corporum mistione se non agere, attulisset rebus suis lucem. Ita autem ratiocinari debebat. Quoniam miscentur inter se corpora non nisi illa, quæ contrariis qualitatibus prædita sunt,ipsa quidem corpora, in tenuissimos vapores soluta, tota per tota coëunt : qualitates autem illorum invicem se refringunt, & accipit mistum nomen ab eâ qualitate, quæ superat. Illa est,ut pulcrè loquitur Erastus,Anat. pag.28, cui se omnes alię,tanquam communi actui subjecerunt, quæque simul omnes in amiciti â, mutuaque consensione detinet, Hinc pag.31, rectè dicitur, Temperies est qualitas, distinêta ab omnibus primis quatuor, licet in his, tanquam in subjecto, insideat.
units.tr: § 2. What he discusses in chapter 2 really lies beyond the physician, partly because he remains in confusion. Hence in chapter 3 he seizes on temperament as if unexpectedly and says it is a quality. Yet had he forewarned the reader that he was not dealing with the mixture of bodies, he would have shed light on his own subject. He ought to have reasoned thus: since bodies mix with one another only when they are endowed with contrary qualities, the bodies themselves, dissolved into the finest vapours, unite wholly through the whole; but their qualities mutually check each other, and the mixture takes its name from the quality that prevails. That quality, as Erastus nicely puts it (Anat. p. 28), is the one to which all the others submit as to a common act, and which holds them all together in friendship and mutual agreement. Hence at p. 31 it is rightly said: temperament is a quality distinct from all four primary qualities, although it inheres in them as in a subject.

units.la: § 3. Res declaratur exemplo. In pipere quia præponderant elementa calida, dicimus piper esse calidum. Hinc adeò rectè Avicenna & Alexander definierunt temperiem per qualitatem.Sed quæ est illa?Quemadmodum in rerum Naturâ ma-
units.tr: § 3. The matter is explained by an example. In pepper, because the hot elements predominate, we say that pepper is hot. Hence Avicenna and Alexander rightly defined temperament through a quality. But what is that quality? As in the nature of things ma-

units.la: *Pulchrè hæc explicat Erast p.19.& seq. B
units.tr: *Erastus explains this well at p. 19 and following. B

units.la: gna ejus varietas est,pro corporis cujufque varietate : ita in corpore humano partes variant temperamento, prout hæc vel illa destinata est huic vel illi actioni. Quo habito, dico , quemadmodum fanitas partis uniuscujusque consistit in temperie illius nativá,hoc est, in eá qualitate, aut potius, in eo qualitatis gradu , qui parti illi f.n. est : ita morbus in intemperie fit, cum qualitas illa , ille qualitatis gradus vitiatur, hoc. est, intensior, vel remiffior fit.
units.tr: § 4. Here Fernelius, another Davus of Terence, creates confusion. Montanus, in chapter 4, indeed answers Fernelius's objections to quality, but in chapter 5 he destroys the harmony and consent of the qualities. "If," says Fernelius, "temperament is a certain fifth quality, the other four must necessarily have vanished. But we see that they survive, indeed that they are present in the highest degree." To this Montanus replies: with what face do you attribute to Avicenna a certain fifth quality, different from the rest? By no means is it different; it is one of those four, relaxed indeed and checked, yet so that it has dominion over the others, as I may put it. And on what Parnassus, O Fernelius (he means to say), have you been dreaming, if one quality prevails and the others are for that reason dissipated into air? Indeed not. They survive, but are conquered and repressed by that one, by which the thing under discussion is said to be of such and such a kind.

units.la: § 4. Heic cum Fernelius,alter Davus Terentianus, turbet : Montanus, cap.4. quidem diluit objectiones ipsius contra qualitatem ;cap.5. autem destruit Harmonian & concentum ejusdem. Si,inquit,ille, Temperamentum est quinta quædam qualitas, necesse est , reliquas quatuor evanuiffe. Atqui videmus illas superstites esse : quin in summo gradu esse. Huic Montanus,quâ fronte affingis tu Avicennæ quintam quandam qualitatem , à reliquis diversam ? Neutiquam diversa est: sed una ex quatuor illis , remissa quidem illa , & refracta, ita tamen , ut supra reliquas dominium habeat, ut sic loquar. Et in quo Parnaffo , ò Ferneli ( vult dicere) fomniafti, fi una superat, reliquas propterea in auram dissipatas esse ?Imò.fuperfti-
units.tr: "If," the innovator adds, "the other qualities no longer exist, there will be no conflict in the body. If," as schoolboys say, "a donkey flies." For there remain two causes of conflict, Montanus adds: one natural, the other preternatural. At this point our author's double error must be rebuked. The first is that he makes innate heat the cause of our death, although Galen in the book on the cause of death excuses it so carefully. The second is that he joins the two causes proposed in the first book on health into one, which he nevertheless afterwards divides into two again. "If," he adds further, "the elements vanish, they will not, once the mixture is dissolved, be able to return to their own kinds." There is no consequence in this, says Montanus. As for me, I laugh again at so absurd a hypothesis! So much on chapter 4.

units.la: tes sunt, sed victæ & repressæ ab unâ illâ, à qua res, de qua agitur, dicitur qualis. Si (addit novator) reliquæ non amplius adsunt, non erit ulla in corpore repugnantia. Si ( ajunt pueri in schola ) asinus volat. Restant enim duæ causæ repugnantiarum, subjicit Montanus, Naturalis altera, altera Praeternaturalis. Quo loco castigandus venit duplex Nostri error. Primus, quod Calidum nativum facit causam interitus nostri, cum Gal. l. de Marsimo tam diligenter excuset. Secundus, quod duas causas, 1. San. tu. 2. propositas, compingit in unam, quam tamen posteà iterum dispescit in duas. Si (addit amplius Iste) evanscunt elementa, in dissolutione misti non poterunt redire ad sua congenera. Nulla consequentia, dicit Montanus. Ego vero rideo iterum hipothesin tam ineptam! Et hæc de cap. 4.
units.tr: tes are present, but overcome and held down by that one quality from which the thing in question is called such-and-such. "If," the innovator adds, "the rest are no longer present, there will be no conflict in the body." "If," say the boys at school, "an ass flies." For two causes of conflict remain, Montanus adds: one natural, the other preternatural. At this point our double error must be corrected. The first is that he makes the innate heat the cause of our death, although Galen in his book On Marasmus excuses it so carefully. The second is that he joins into one the two causes proposed in 1. San. tu. 2., and then again divides them into two. "If," he adds further, "the elements vanish, then in the dissolution of the mixed body they will not be able to return to their own kindred." "No consequence," says Montanus. But I laugh again at so inept a hypothesis! And this is on chapter 4.

units.la: § 5. Cap. 5. Proposita denuo sententiâ gladiatoris nostri, ait Montanus, Repugnare harmoniam & sensui & rationi, à nemine percipi, ne ab autore quidem suo. Quod num verè dictum sit cum dispicio, adeò resilit animus à commemoratione refponsionum, ut pudor hominis occupet faciem meam. Quò minus imperare mihi possum, ut referam; quin video consulendum mihi esse oculis & auribus
units.tr: § 5. Chapter 5. Having again stated the opinion of our gladiator, Montanus says that harmony is repugnant both to sense and to reason, and is perceived by no one, not even by its own author. When I examine whether this has truly been said, my mind so recoils from recalling the replies that a man's shame overcomes my face. All the less can I bring myself to report it; indeed I see that I must consult the eyes and ears of good men, lest they feel this Camarina.

units.la: bonorum,ne Camarinam hanc sentiante, § 6. Loco igitur affaniarum illarum, proponam genuině Philosophantibus dapes has Peripateticas,quas in fronte codicis fui (ita Veteres appellabant marginem)scripserat SCHERBIVS, ὁ πεῖν. I. Diruit Fernelii sententiam natura miftionis, quæ est alteratorum. At alterari elementa non possunt,nisi remiffione qualitatum. IT. Elementa in miftione aut agunt in fe, aút non agunt. Si non agunt, non fit miftio. Conditiones enim mifcibilium proponens Ariftoteles, ait, Mifcibilia necessario esse inter fe agentia. Et patientia, et próprie non misceri, que non egunt invicem et patiuntur, 2.Gen. & Corr.t.48. III. Sidicat Orator, Ariftoteles est intelligendus de viribus,negabo. Loquitur enim de remissione qualitatum, & hoc vult, Neutrum simpliciter, neque calidum, neque frigidum : sed est calidum frigidum,hoc est,calidum refrigeratum. Ita Zabarella in Phyf. In misto non sunt calor & frigus, tanquam duæ diftinctæ qualitates : sed est una qualitas media, quæ aliquibus gradibus calorem refert,aliquibus frigus. Quo dato sequitur, Vires esse posterius quid, post remissionem, inquam, qualitatum. IV. Et quì non falsum fit illud, Primas qualitates in summo manere : & tamen habere vires agendi remissas ? Hæc pugnant inter fe,fi habent.vires remiflas , oportet etiam fecundum gradus sint remissæ. Vide Arift. 4.Gen.3. ibi, Causa utfolvatur, debiliteturque actio, &c. V. Non nego, adesse illas proportiones : fedcum vim agendi non habeant, non spectant etiam ad Medicum, qui confiderat causas actionum. Hæc Doctor ibi : quem postea reperi fusè omnia explicaffe in Phyfiolog, qua de Temp. Verum ego ifon putavi operæ pretium me facturum , fi huc transferrem. Si quis ita velit, adeat nostrum l. r. c.8. & iterum l.2. €. 12. & 15. necnon in Ant-Eraft. f.77.& 78. Inveniet etiam Eraftum volvisse hoc saxum, Anat. f.24. cui respondere voluit antagonista , AntEraft. f.11, & 13.
units.tr: § 6. Instead of those troubles, I will set before genuine philosophers these Peripatetic dishes, which Scherbius wrote on the front of his codex (the ancients called the margin by that name), ὁ πεῖν: (1) The nature of mixture overthrows Fernelius' opinion, that mixture is a matter of things being altered. But elements cannot be altered except by a remission of qualities. (2) Elements in a mixture either act upon one another or they do not. If they do not act, there is no mixture. For Aristotle, setting out the conditions of things that can be mixed, says that mixable things must necessarily act upon one another; and those that neither act nor are acted upon are not properly mixed (On Generation and Corruption 2, t. 48). (3) If the orator says that Aristotle is to be understood of powers, I deny it. For he speaks of the remission of qualities, and means this: neither simply, neither hot nor cold, but it is hot-cold, that is, hot made cool. So Zabarella on the Physics: in a mixed body there are not heat and cold as two distinct qualities, but one intermediate quality, which in some degrees presents heat and in others cold. Granted this, it follows that powers are something posterior to the remission, I say, of qualities. (4) And how is it not false that the primary qualities remain at their height, and yet have powers of acting that are remitted? These contradict one another: if they have remitted powers, they must also be remitted according to degrees. See Aristotle, On Generation 4.3, where he says: the cause why action is loosened and weakened, etc. (5) I do not deny that those proportions are present; but since they do not have the power of acting, they do not concern the physician either, who considers the causes of actions. So the Doctor says there; and I later found that he had explained all these matters fully in his Physiology, on Temperaments. Yet I did not think it worth my labour to transfer it here. If anyone wishes to see it, let him consult our book 1, chapter 8, and again book 2, chapters 12 and 15, and also Anti-Erastus pp. 77 and 78. He will also find that Erastus rolled this stone (Anat. p. 24), to which the antagonist wished to reply (Anti-Erastus pp. 11 and 13).

units.la: § 7. Post hæc ( cap. 6.) rectè quidem. Montanus explicat , tam latitudinem temperamenti partium , interfe collatarum, quam sanitatis : ego verò duo defidero. Horum alterum est, quod non distinguit Intemperies naturales, (eu salubres, 2. Temp.4. ext. & 3.Meth.9. quas curat ὁ ὑγιεινὸς : à non naturalibus,seu morbofis,quas ὁ Θεραπευτής. Alterum,quodnon docet, quæ fit Intemperies illa nuda? An prorsus fit , quod dicitur,ut vulgo crediB 7. tur? an potius aliquando fit cum materia tantilla?non eo usque,inquam,progressa, ut Tumor p.n. dici possit,ut ego deduco in Pathologicis? Vide illa c. 51. & 52. De latitudine sanitatis quae complectitur Batum Neutrum Herophili, legeris quaedam ibid. c.10.
units.tr: § 7. After this (chapter 6), Montanus rightly explains both the latitude of the temperament of the parts compared with one another, and that of health. But I miss two things. The first is that he does not distinguish natural or healthful intemperies (2 Temp. 4 ext. and 3 Meth. 9), which the hygienist [ὑγιεινὸς] cures, from non-natural or morbid ones, which the therapeut [Θεραπευτής] treats. The second is that he does not teach what a bare intemperies is. Is it entirely what is commonly said and believed? Or is it sometimes accompanied by a little matter, not having progressed so far that it can be called a tumour, as I deduce in my Pathologica? See those chapters 51 and 52. Concerning the latitude of health, which includes the neuter of Herophilus, you may read some things in the same chapter 10.

units.la: § 8. His explicatis, debuit Montanus agere de singulis intemperiebus,tam simplicibus,quam compositis:& facit cap. 7. & 8. concludens ,in universum 16. esse, excepto aequali.. Quo loco cum inferret fc Argenterii improbitas, volentis, Intemperies non esse morbos , sed causas morborum : insumit Montanus in eam rem tria cap.10. 11. & 12. Ego contentus unica SCHERBII refponfione, Vt, dicebat, formam & materiam concipimus tanquam res diversas, cum neutra feorfim fine altera fit : ita intemperiem calidam , & calorem febrilem pro diversis habemus, cum sint res eadem. Hoc dixeris de omnibus intemperiebus, tam simplicibus quam compositis. Vno verbo, Intemperies sunt ipsi morbi.
units.tr: § 8. Having explained these points, Montanus ought to deal with each of the intemperies, simple and compound alike. He does so in chapters 7 and 8, concluding that there are sixteen in all, apart from the equal one. At this point, when he argues against the rashness of Argenterius, who held that intemperies are not diseases but causes of diseases, Montanus devotes three chapters, 10, 11 and 12, to the question. I am content with the single reply of Scherbius, who said that we conceive form and matter as different things, since neither exists apart from the other; so we regard hot intemperies and febrile heat as different, though they are the same thing. You may say this of all intemperies, simple and compound alike. In a word, intemperies are themselves diseases.

units.la: § 9. Porro in cap.12. est sedes litis, An l. Gal. de Opt. secta , ad Thrafyb. fit genuinus ? Neganti Montano opponit fe Eraftus,Anat. p.73. cui respondet illefufc in Ant-Eraft. f,38. Vbi obiter notas illud, Indicationem curandi non fumi a causa, verum esse in Therapeuticis : fumi omnino in Hygienis, seu in τεγφυλακῆ, quod exemplo habitus athletici docui alibi. Vide fis Eraftum, Anat. p.74.
units.tr: § 9. Further, in chapter 12 lies the heart of the dispute: is the passage of Galen in On the Best Sect, addressed to Thrasybulus, genuine? Erastus, in his Anatomy, p. 73, opposes Montanus, who denies it, and Montanus replies in his Anti-Erastus, p. 38. There he remarks in passing that the principle that the indication for treatment is not taken from the cause holds true in the Therapeutics, but that it is wholly otherwise in the Hygienics, or in the tērophylakē, as I showed elsewhere by the example of the athlete's condition. See Erastus, Anatomy, p. 74.

units.la: § 10. Numero Intemperierum fedenario,& olim fe opponebant quidam, & inter Recc. Averroës. 3. Coll. I. Illos quia refutavit Galenus. 1. Temp. 2. nolo ego actum agere. Hujus epicheremata, dicebat SCHERBIVS, quia volutant, & lucent subtilitate suâ, ut vitrum, non minus interim fragilia quam vitrum : nolim quenquam de illis folicitum esse, vel ideo, quia Logica sunt.
units.tr: § 10. Some have opposed the sedentary number of intemperies, both in the past and among the more recent writers, Averroes among them (3 Coll. 1). I do not wish to take up the case of those whom Galen refuted (1 On Temperaments, 2). Their arguments, as Scherbius said, are like glass: they roll and gleam with their own subtlety, yet are no less fragile than glass. I would not have anyone worried about them, if only because they are mere logic.

units.la: § 11. Contra utilis & jucunda est quæstio,tractata cap.16. An, & quatenus temperies calida & humida fit laudabilis?Ipse concludit,Tamdiu esse, adeoque eandem cum temperie æquali,quæ cæterarum canon est, quamdiu utraque qualitas moderata est:fieri morbosam,quamprimum mediocritatem amittunt. Hic duo defidero I. Quod est signum moderationis hujus? Quamdiu nonfætent, At verò cum hircorum more fætere incipiunt, putredo adest. II. Quando illa fe ostendit? Cum calor fit humore inferior,nec dominari illi potest.
units.tr: § 11. A useful and pleasant question, treated in chapter 16, is whether and to what extent a warm and moist temperament is praiseworthy. He himself concludes that it is healthy, and the same as the equal temperament that is the standard for the others, for as long as both qualities remain moderate. It becomes morbid as soon as they lose the mean. Here I have two wants. I. What is the sign of this moderation? While the humours do not stink. But when they begin to stink like goats, putrefaction is present. II. When does that show itself? When the heat becomes weaker than the humour and can no longer dominate it.

units.la: § 12. Huic opponas inutilem & con-
units.tr: § 12. Against this you may set the useless and tangled dispute:

units.la: fragosam disputationem, An detur intemperies calida & frigida? an item sicca & humida? Breviter, an per rerum naturam fieri possit, ut corpus, fecundum partes easdem, contrariis qualitatibus laborare possit? Insumit quidem Montanus, in ventilanda illa, septem integra cap. 17, 18.19. 20. 21. 22, 23. & recte judicat, Per rerum naturam fieri non posse. Quod autem quidam dicunt, aegros in febribus lipyriis & epialis tale quid percepisse, luforium est. Neque enim uno modo decipiuntur aegri, quod pluribus exemplis demonstrari poterat. Sed & tactus est sensus confusus, ut facilis fit deceptio.
units.tr: whether there is a hot and cold intemperament, or a dry and moist one? Briefly, can it happen by the nature of things that a body, in the same parts, suffers from contrary qualities? Montanus indeed spends seven whole chapters, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22 and 23, in sifting this, and rightly judges that it cannot happen by the nature of things. As for what some say, that the sick in shivering fevers (lipyriae) and hot fevers (epiales) have perceived something of the kind, it is trifling. The sick are not deceived in only one way, as many examples could show. Touch, moreover, is a confused sense, so deception is easy.

units.la: § 13. In his cum consensum suum silentio fassus effet Eraftus: inventus tamen est Capivaccius(de indicio SHERBII) qui fe opposuit. Hujus rationes affert, solideque refutat Montanus in Ant-Eraft, f. 122, & feq.
units.tr: § 13. When Erastus had tacitly given his assent to these matters, Capivaccius was found (on the indication of Scherbius) to have set himself against them. Montanus brings forward his arguments and solidly refutes them in the Anti-Erastus, f. 122 and following.

units.la: § 14. Nec quidquam prodest adverfariorum rebus, quod ex Gal. dicunt, viscera quidem uri: extrema autem frigere. Hoc enim in controversia non est, & fieri omnino potest, natura tantopere oppressa, ut calorem ad superficiem pel. lere non possit. Quod autem Simonius contra Eraftum de Putred. f. 62. ait, Qualitates repressas aeque inter fe pugnare, ac summas, veritati consonum noh est. Confunditur enim res fiens cum facta. Dum res eftin fieri, in motu ad terminum, dum ταὐτόν est, non negavero tale quid accidere posse. Cum res facta est, cum est in termino, nego & pernego. Si enim pugná superesset, res non effet, quod esse dicitur. Et quomodo duo contraria ita possunt imprimi uni subjecto, ut utrumque fit actívum? Vnum, qua unum, non agit in fe. In tota rerum natura distinctum est agens à patiente actu. Et quid? Ne in speciebus quidem verum est, v.g. oculus non recipit album & nigrum, fecundum easdem partes pupillæ. Hoc demonstrat Valdanius I, de Mift, f.64. Sed quo dilabor?
units.tr: § 14. Nor does it help the opponents' case that they quote Galen to say that the viscera indeed burn while the extremities grow cold. For that is not in dispute, and it can certainly happen that nature is so overpowered that it cannot drive heat to the surface. But when Simonius, against Erastus, On Putrefaction, p. 62, says that repressed qualities fight with one another just as extreme ones do, that is not consistent with the truth. For he confuses a thing in the process of becoming with a thing already made. While a thing is becoming, in motion toward its end, while it is still the same thing, I will not deny that something of the kind can happen. When the thing is made, when it has reached its end, I deny it absolutely. For if the fight still went on, the thing would not be what it is said to be. And how can two contraries be impressed on one subject so that each is active? One thing, as one, does not act upon itself. In the whole of nature the agent is distinct from the patient in act. And what of this? Even in the senses it is not true: for example, the eye does not receive white and black at once in the same parts of the pupil. Valdanius demonstrates this in On Mixtures, I, p. 64. But where am I slipping to?

units.la: § 15. Non minus laboriosum, spinifque horridum est iter, quod Mont. ingreditur cap.24. & continuat usque ad 32. de Intemperie inæqualis, de qua habemus singularem Gal. librum. Hunc qui Aureum vocant, Plumbeum esse intelligent denique, ubi legerint cum judicio. Quin fatebuntur mecum, indignissimum. Galeno foetum esse. Quiad Commentatores fe convertere volent, Calanum, Fuchfium, Brachelium, Vallefium, Bufennium, Villanovanum, Agricolam, (hui tot! de re NIHILI!) verum fuisse
units.tr: § 15. No less laborious, and thorny with briars, is the road that Montanus enters on in chapter 24 and follows to 32, concerning the unequal intemperament, on which we have a singular book by Galen. Those who call it the Golden book will at last understand it to be leaden, once they have read it with judgement. Indeed they will confess with me that it is a most unworthy offspring of Galen. As for the commentators to whom they wish to turn, Calanus, Fuchsius, Brachelius, Vallesius, Busennius, Villanovanus, Agricola (oh, so many, about a matter of NOTHING!), they have said something true.

units.la: Nostrum dicent, cum ait, Ne titulum quidem libri eos intellexisse, quid fi audeam hanc audaciam, Nec Montanum habere ubi tuto pedem figat; Sed finit haec protenus alba: ubi, quaeso vos, o patroni nugarum, ubi haec intemperies docum habet, vel in cognitione morborum, vel in curatione, vel in praedictione? Vide, fi ad manus Pathologica nostra, cap. 50.
units.tr: § 7. I add this to it: a bare intemperament cannot be defined better than by negation. It is not inflammation; it is not erysipelas; it is not oedema; it is not scirrhus; it is not any of the compound tumours. Therefore it is a bare intemperament. From this it will be understood in which class the fevers lie. All say they lie in the latter. I say they lie in the former. Otherwise the distinction between primary fevers, which are without inflammation, and symptomatic fevers, which are with it, would be pointless.

units.la: § 16. Quae sequuntur, usque ad finem h. l. non minus spinosa sunt anterioribus, ut bene calceatum esse oporteat, qui velit fe committere viae. Sed hem ducem tibi! Primo omnium, quam Montanus dicam impingit Galeno de Tumoribus p.n.ex Avicenna originem habet ex ignorantia veteris instituti, quid illi vocarint intemperiem undam? illam, inquam, quae e regione opponitur Intemperiei cum materia, cum affluxu substantiae? Ego hic
units.tr: § 7. I have worked this out in my Pathological Work, chapter 25, from which I now take only this. Wine is called wine, not vinegar, even when it has gone flat, but it can return to its natural state. Plethora is called plethora, not cacochymia, even when there is some corruption of the blood, but with the addition of "bilious" and so on. So a bare intemperament remains so as long as it consists in this: that it cannot be called inflammation, or anything of these kinds. On this matter you may see certain passages of Galen cited by Montanus in chapter 32.

units.la: § 7. dixi aliquid: cui hoc addo, Intemperies nuda melius definiri non potest quam negando. Non est Inflammatio: non est Eryfipelas: non est Oedema: non est Scirrhus: non est compositorum tumorum aliquis: Ergo est Intemperies nuda. Hinc intelligetur, in utro ordine sint febres? In posteriori, dicunt omnes: Ego vero, In priori sunt. Alioqui frustra erit distinctio inter febres primarias, quae
units.tr: § 7. I have said something. To this I add that a bare intemperament cannot be better defined than by negation. It is not inflammation; it is not erysipelas; it is not oedema; it is not scirrhus; it is none of the compound tumours. Therefore it is a bare intemperament. From this it will be understood in which order fevers belong. All say they belong to the latter; I say they belong to the former. Otherwise the distinction between primary fevers, which are without inflammation, and symptomatic fevers, which accompany it, will be pointless.

units.la: fine inflammatione sunt, & symptomaticas,quæcum illa. Hanc rem deduxi in d. Pathologicis, cap.25. è quo nunc hoc tantum. Vinum dicitur,non acetum, etiam cum vappuit,sed potest redire ad naturamfuam. Plethora dicitur, non cacochymia , etiam cum aliqua sanguinis corruptela est,sed cum additione, biliosa &c. Ita intemperies nuda est , quamdiu confiftitres in eo , ut nec Inflammatio, nec quidquam horum dici possit. In hanc rem videris loca. Gal. quædam. apud Mont. c.32.
units.tr: I have worked this matter out in my Pathological work, chapter 25, from which I now take only this. Wine is called wine, not vinegar, even when it has turned sour, because it can return to its nature. Plethora is called plethora, not cacochymia, even when there is some corruption of the blood, but only with the addition of "bilious" and so on. So a bare intemperament remains such for as long as it consists in this, that it can be called neither inflammation nor any of these. On this point see the passages of Galen cited in Montanus, chapter 32.

units.la: § 17. Huic vicina est alia quæstio, quatenus differant, aut non differant Intemperies cum affluxu substantiæ à Tumoribus p. n ? Paucis. Cum affluxus est modicus,est Intemperies ; cum tantus est, ut magnitudine lædat , jam est Tumor, morbus,inquam , organicus in magnitudine.Ergòne magis & minus variant speciem ? Ita in artibus omnibus , In Medicina,quia mutat Indicationes.
units.tr: § 17. Close to this is another question: how far do intemperaments with a flow of substance differ, or not differ, from tumours against nature? Briefly: when the flow is moderate, it is an intemperament; when it is so great that it harms by its bulk, it is already a tumour, a disease, I mean an organic one in respect of size. Do they therefore vary in species more or less? So it is in all the arts, and in medicine, because it changes the indications.

units.la: § 18. In utroque quantopere declinat.Noster ! Quod ad prius, cum dicitur, In intemperie nuda esse materiam aliquam:responsat ille, Humor tum non est morbus , sed causa, v.g.cum bilis influit ventriculo,& facit intemperiem calidam. Κενσ Φυχῶν toti antiquitati incognitum! Sed
units.tr: § 18. In each case, see how far he departs from our author! As to the former, when it is said that in a bare intemperament there is some matter, he replies that the humour is then not the disease but its cause: for example, when bile flows into the stomach and produces a hot intemperament. [Κενσ Φυχῶν] A thing unknown to all antiquity!

units.la: d & confusio hic non est toleranda. influxus bilis ex hepate est morbus Conformationis in viis laxioribus: hic influxus causatur alium morbum, Intemperiem. Vtamur igitur commodiori exemplo, Ventriculus refrigeratus, vel ab aëre, vel à potu frigido,tam actu, quam potestate, vel alio quocunque modo, gignit pituitam. Hæc pituita potestne dici causa Intemperiei frigidæ? Non puto,quia præfuit intemperies. Licet igitur pituita auget intemperiem: causa tamen illius non fuit. Quid ergo dicemus heic de pituitâ? Nihil hæreo. Quemadmodum in Intemperie cum materiâ, materia illa est pars morbi, fundamentum quippe Relationis: ita in Intemperie nuda quoque. Ergo erit oppositum in adjecto? dicis. Nuditatem enim pessundat materia. Ita veteres constituerunt: hoc utile est in arte. Tu fi quid melius,quid utilius habes,profer, ut miremur sapientiam tuam!
units.tr: And confusion is not to be tolerated here. The influx of bile from the liver is a disease of conformation in the looser passages; here the influx is caused by another disease, an intemperament. Let us use then a more convenient example: a stomach cooled by air, or by cold drink, whether actually or potentially, or by any other means, generates phlegm. Can this phlegm be called the cause of a cold intemperament? I think not, because the intemperament came first. So although phlegm increases the intemperament, it was not its cause. What then shall we say here about phlegm? I hesitate about nothing. As in an intemperament with matter that matter is part of the disease, being the foundation of the relation, so it is also in a bare intemperament. "So there will be a contradiction in the adjunct?" you say, "for matter destroys the nakedness." So the ancients established it, and this is useful in the art. If you have anything better or more useful, bring it forward, that we may marvel at your wisdom!

units.la: § 19. Quod ad posterius: Tumor, inquit Comes,qui non lædit magnitudine, non est morbus,sed symptoma. Eja vero, mi Domine, quale fymptorna est? In qualitatibus mutatis,ait, ex mente Turrifani, cap. 34. Quia addit, Gal. Diff. morb. 5., scribit corpus fieri aliquando durius, aliquando mollius, & sic de cæteris. Hoc figmentum cum displicere cæpiflet dicit, Mutatam esse qualitatem vifilem & tačilem. Hui tantumne? Ego enim dico. Cum adsit & relatio & fundamentum, cur Morbus non fit?Et est, fi proprie loqui velis, Intemperies cum materia, quæ transibit in Tumorem p. n. cum magnitudine lædet.Sed fit hoc parùm:Symptoma,qua symptoma, nihil indicat. At hic est indicatio curativa.
units.tr: § 19. As for the latter point: "A swelling," says Comes, "which does not harm by its size, is not a disease but a symptom." Well then, my dear sir, what kind of symptom is it? "A change in qualities," he says, "according to Turrisanus, chapter 34." Because he adds, from Galen, On the Differences of Diseases, book 5, that he writes that the body sometimes becomes harder, sometimes softer, and so on for the rest. When this fiction began to displease him, he says that the quality changed is visible and tangible. Is that all? For I say: since both a relation and a foundation are present, why is it not a disease? And it is, if you wish to speak properly, an intemperie together with matter, which, when it passes into a swelling, will harm by its size. But this happens rarely. A symptom, as a symptom, indicates nothing. Yet here there is an indication for treatment.

units.la: § 20. Agedum, inspiciamus exempla quæ dam intemperierū.De febribus interrogatus respondet cum distinctione, Heċtice, inquit, sunt nudæ: putridæ cum afiluxu substantiæ. Dixi jam,Omnem febrim ( primariam) esse intemperiem nudam:quia opponitur fymptomaticæ,quæ est cum inflammatione aliqua.
units.tr: § 20. Come, let us look at some examples of intemperies. Asked about fevers, he answers with a distinction: hectic fevers, he says, are bare; putrid ones are with an afflux of substance. I have already said that every primary fever is a bare intemperie, because it is opposed to the symptomatic fever, which comes with some inflammation.

units.la: § 21. Paralysin esse Intemperiem cum materia recte negat Avicenna : est enim intemperies nuda, propter rationem datam, Interim recte etiam Obstructio dicitur , ob ferum meatibus nervorum fe insinuans, Hoc ferum, quod pituitam aqueam vocare possis , non est causa, sed pars morbi, cum distinctè loquimur.
units.tr: § 21. Avicenna rightly denies that paralysis is an intemperie with matter. For it is a bare intemperie, for the reason given. Meanwhile obstruction is also rightly named, because a serous humour insinuates itself into the passages of the nerves. This serous humour, which you could call watery phlegm, is not the cause but a part of the disease, when we speak precisely.

units.la: § 22. Locus Gal. in calce. 9. Meth. claré ostendit, Intemperiem nudam quandam,esse cum fluore quodam materiæ, quæ materia est de effentiâ morbi, nullo autem modo causa,nisi nihil interest, quo modo loquamur,
units.tr: § 22. The passage of Galen at the end of book 9 of the Method clearly shows that a certain bare intemperie is with a certain flux of matter, which matter belongs to the essence of the disease, but in no way is the cause, unless it makes no difference how we speak.

units.la: § 23. In ostentandá Gal. (ut vocat. ) repugnantia, princ. cap.32. valdè súdat, cum facilè, & ad meam mentem sedetur illis verbis, Zinc colligostumores interdum, &c. quæ vide & conlidera.
units.tr: § 23. In his display of what he calls contradiction, at the beginning of chapter 32, he sweats greatly, although it is easily settled, and to my mind, by those words, "For they sometimes gather swellings," and so on. Look at these and consider them.

units.la: § 24. In difficultatibus duabus,quas restare ait, partim benè se gerit, partim male.Benè:cum in priori delet ⊙ Magnus, quod est Diff. morb.s. Malè:cum ita colligit, si tumor est symptoma inflammationis, inflammatio ipsa erat symptomæ. Hoc enim planissime sequitur admissa distinctione, quam vult. Sed vocarit Gal. ipsam etiam inflammatiouem tumorem: quid inde? Non oportet ubique rigidam censuram adhibere.
units.tr: § 24. In the two difficulties which he says remain, he does partly well and partly badly. Well, when in the first he deletes "Magnus," which is in On the Differences of Diseases, book 5. Badly, when he concludes thus: if a swelling is a symptom of inflammation, then inflammation itself was a symptom. For this follows quite plainly from the distinction he admits. But perhaps Galen called inflammation itself a swelling as well: what follows from that? One should not apply a rigid censure everywhere.

units.la: § 25. Explicatio loci.2.x. ⊙π.τ, grata quidem mihi est: sed non video, quo modo sensus ille possit elici.
units.tr: § 25. The explanation of the passage "2.x. ⊙π.τ" is indeed pleasing to me, but I do not see how that sense can be drawn out.

units.la: § 26. In quatuor capp. sin. longa & intricata agitatur quæstio, Materia affluens in his intemperiebus, estnè morbi pars (ita enim loquar potius) an causa? Et, si est causa, estnè efficiens, an materialis? estnè antecedens? conjuncta? connectinens? Nam omnia hæc invenerunt patronos. Respondeo direcè. Ff morbi pars,est fundamentum relationis illud,quod cum eum parte affeƈtâ facit ἀιτɛɛ̄ιαν illam, quæ morbus est. Hinc tria fiunt clara I. Efficientem nullo modo esse. Oportet enim separare influxum materiæ, quia alius est morbus, ab intemperie, quam facit materia influens. I Quatenus fit mate-rialis Montani? Non ex quà, sed in quà, utipfus fe explicat. III. Continentem esse, & non esse. Hoc, fi distinguere velis illam à morbo: illud fi non distinguas. Revera enim causa illa continens, quatenus in morbo jam facto queritur, nihil aliud est quam pars morbi, fundamentum morbi.
units.tr: § 26. In the four chapters at the end a long and intricate question is debated: is the matter flowing into these intemperies a part of the disease (to speak thus rather than otherwise), or a cause? And if it is a cause, is it efficient or material? Is it antecedent, conjoined, or connecting? For all of these have found defenders. I answer directly. It is a part of the disease, the foundation of the relation, which, together with the affected part, makes that cause [αἰτίαν] which is the disease. From this three things become clear. First, it is in no way efficient, for one must separate the influx of matter, since it is a different disease, from the intemperie which the flowing matter produces. Second, as to how Montanus makes it material: it is not that from which, but that in which, as he himself explains. Third, it is and is not a container: this holds if you want to distinguish it from the disease, but not if you do not distinguish it. For in truth that containing cause, insofar as it is sought in a disease already made, is nothing other than a part of the disease, the foundation of the disease.

units.la: § 27. Has tricas qui bene meditatus secum fuerit, non mirabitur, fi Montanum c.25. timidum fuisse repererit. Excusari autem debere & illum, & me, fi ειχο̃ tantum attulimus. Logica enim sunt.
units.tr: § 27. Whoever has thought these trifles through well will not be surprised if he finds Montanus, chapter 25, to have been timid. Yet both he and I should be excused, if we have brought only probable arguments [εἰκότα]. For these are matters of logic.

units.la: AD LIBRVM. III.
units.tr: To the Third Book

units.la: De morbis materia Fernelii, C A P. V.
units.tr: On the Matter of Diseases, by Fernelius, Chapter 5

units.la: § 1. Vod vulgò dicitur, ὠβὶ non sunt lites, docti ferunt lites, non esse universaliter verum, vel hinc evincam. Præsumo autem, dici debere doctos, non omnes eos, qui pro doctis fe gerunt : sed eos tantum,qui recte instituti sunt, quos vel simpliciter ϰεπωιδευμένες, vel cum adjectione, νομίμως, Gal. vocat. His qui opponuntur, ὁ ὑμεδεὶς dicebantur olim, ἀσεβοὶ εἰσαγόμενοί, quod alibi demonstravi. Inter vere Philosophos dum collocat Fuchfius Fernelium, prosecto facit illi injuriam. Quod quia ante me,in hoc ipso negotio, ostenderunt summi viri, Montanus, Planerus, Eraftus, Scherbius, Sonerus, alii : non est nunc opus aliis, quam ut compendio dicam, quæ instituti mei ratio postulat. Feci autem prolixius in Rejectaneis meis, Stoicorum imitatione ita dictis.
units.tr: § 1. The common saying that there are no disputes among the learned is not universally true, and I will show this from the following. I assume that by "the learned" we should mean not everyone who presents himself as learned, but only those who have been properly trained, whom Galen calls simply "educated [πεπαιδευμένους]" or, with an addition, "lawfully [νομίμως]". Those who are opposed to them were once called "the unlearned [ὁ ἀμαθής]" and "impious [ἀσεβοὶ]", as I have shown elsewhere. In placing Fernelius among the true philosophers, Fuchsius certainly does him an injustice. Since distinguished men, Montanus, Planerus, Erastus, Scherbius, Sonerus and others, have already shown this in this very matter, there is no need now for anything beyond a brief statement of what the plan of my work requires. I have treated it at greater length in my Rejectanea, in the manner of the Stoics, as they are called.

units.la: § 2 Ringeris, òadolefcens, quod amafium tuum tam audacter contrectem? Non fit ex ullo affectu: sed quia VERITAS, cuifacramentum dedi, ita vult. Atqui CRATO, tantus vir, longè aliter judicabat? Non nego ego Craton. meritiffimo suo inter viros maximos censeri debere : sed hac in re phalerifmo aulico usum fuisse ajo, dum praeconem fe praebet typographis, merces venales extrudere volentibus. Atqui ftilus etiam egregius est, quique non dedecet discentem.Stylus Plantii est, quodé Gallis fehabere SCHERBI V S affirmabat. Sed fit cujuscunque : Non debet lingua Latina disci ex Fernelio. Quia volumus studiosos tales, qui jam fatis versati sunt in utraque linguâ. Accedit incommodum illud, quod Fernelius, deferta Philosophiâ Peripateticâ, applicuit fe Stoicæ, quod intolerabile est. Sed hæc obiter:
units.tr: § 2. Ringer, my young friend, why do I handle your darling so boldly? It is not from any ill feeling, but because the TRUTH, to which I have sworn my allegiance, requires it. But did Crato, so great a man, judge quite differently? I do not deny that Crato deserves to be counted among the greatest men, but I say that in this matter he used court rhetoric, playing the herald for printers who wish to push their wares. Yet his style is also excellent and does not disgrace a learner. It is the style of Plantius, which Scherbius used to claim the French possessed. But whatever its origin, the Latin tongue should not be learned from Fernelius, since we want students who have already been well practised in both languages. There is also the further drawback that Fernelius, having abandoned Peripatetic philosophy, attached himself to the Stoics, which is intolerable. But this in passing.

units.la: § 3. In refutatione argumentorum
units.tr: § 3. In refuting the arguments

units.la: utar filo Ariadnes, à Montano nostro tenfo. I. ait in enumeratione qualitatum peccatum fuisse in eo, quod allatis primis tantum, fecundæ & tertiæ insuper habitæ sint. Hæ sunt mollities & durities, raritas & densitas &c.que cum pendeant à conditionibus materiæ, vocat defectus illarum Morbos materiæ. Huic Mont. cap. 3. ex Arift. 2. Gener. & corrupt. 13. & Gal.5.Simpl.4. ostendit,quot modis fiat unumquodque seipso mollius aut durius? Et infert. Non fieri ab uno solo morbo, sed pluribus. Deinde ait, Mollitiem & duritiem esse qualitates secundas, quae pendent ab intemperie primarum. Has Gal.3. Cauf.sym.ult. expresse vocat symptomata mutatarum qualitatum tactilium, quae pendent ab intemperie modo hac, modo illa.
units.tr: I shall follow the thread of Ariadne, as laid down by our Montanus. First, he says that the fault in the enumeration of qualities was that only the primary ones were given, while the secondary and tertiary were disregarded. These are softness and hardness, rarity and density, and so on. Since these depend on the conditions of matter, Fernelius calls their defects Morbos materiae, "diseases of matter." Against this, Montanus, in chapter 3, drawing on Aristotle, On Generation and Corruption 2, and Galen, On the Simple Medicines 4, shows in how many ways each thing becomes softer or harder in itself. He then concludes that these are caused not by a single disease but by several. Next, he says that softness and hardness are secondary qualities, which depend on the intemperature of the primary ones. Galen, in On the Causes of Symptoms, book 3, at the end, expressly calls these symptoms of altered tactile qualities, which depend now on this intemperature, now on that.

units.la: § 4. Hujus generis vult esse Laxitatem & Adstrictionem, cap.4. Respondet Montanus, sunt morbi Conformationis, & C pertipertinent ad vias ftrictiores, laxioresve. Ego vero non sum creduhus illi. Sunt morbi in modo substantiæ, ut Vallef. vocat, & hac ratione commodius reducuntur ad Temperies primarum qualita- tum.
units.tr: § 4. Fernelius wishes Laxitas and Adstrictio, looseness and tightness (chap. 4), to be of this kind. Montanus replies that they are diseases of Conformatio, shape or structure, and pertain to passages that are narrower or wider. I, however, do not trust him. They are diseases in the mode of substance, as Vallesius calls it, and on this account they are more conveniently traced back to the temperament of the primary qualities.

units.la: § 5. Idem volo dictum de Raro & Denso, licet Mont. etiam ad Conformationis vitia referat. Idem proprius de Tenui & Crasso, licet ille ad morbos Magnitudinis relatum velit.
units.tr: § 5. I would say the same of rare and dense, although Montanus also refers them to defects of conformation. The same holds more closely for thin and thick, although he wants these referred to diseases of magnitude.

units.la: § 6. De sensu acri, cap. 5 .quærit Mont. à Fern. & Argent. quei fieri id possit, cum sensus acrimonia fit res quædam naturalis? Ita hebetudo sensus est talis difpofitio, quæ facit, quo minus quis facile percellatur,
units.tr: § 6. In chapter 5, Montanus asks Fernelius and Argenterius how this can happen, since sharpness of sense is a natural thing. Thus dullness of sense is a disposition which makes it so that a person is not easily struck.

units.la: 5. Ego vero ulterius quid defidero, quid eftillud, quod facit, ut facile quis fingultiat? facile cardialgia laboret? facile vomat? Contrà, ut contrà? Mihi persuasum est, effeab eodem substantiæ modo Vallefii. Interim sæpè fit ratione ingestorum, ut fi quis piperis pulverem copiosius sumat, singultit. Ad auditus sensorium quod perrinet, non credo ego, sibilos ullos fieri ob acrimoniam organi, quamvis Gal. dicat: quin sibili omnes sunt à frigiditate, quatenus fc. ex materia frigida flatus exsistunt. Ad yifum fi quis diverti
units.tr: 5. But what more do I want? What is it that makes someone prone to hiccups, to heartburn, to vomiting? And conversely, what is the contrary? I am persuaded that it arises from the same kind of substance, as Vallesius says. Meanwhile it often happens from what is taken in: if someone swallows a larger amount of powdered pepper, he hiccups. As for the organ of hearing, I do not believe that any whistling sounds arise from the sharpness of the organ, although Galen says that all whistlings come from cold, inasmuch as winds arise from cold matter. If anyone wishes to turn to sight, I will say that it is impossible for someone to see too sharply. As for the symptoms similar to suffusion, they occur when the stomach is affected while the eyes remain unharmed.

units.la: volet, dicam, Impossibile cffe,aliquem nimis acuté videre. Quod ad symptomata fuffufioni similia, incidunt illa affecto ventriculo, oculis illæsis.
units.tr: Let me say no more about that.

units.la: § 7. Intricatum hoc quidem est problema : sed multo intricatius, quod cap. 6. & 7, ventilatur,quei fiat,quod in Iđtericis quibusdam,reddito toti corpori colore naturali, non possit reddi ille Cornea?Fitid autem modo in tota Cornea, & videntur omnia esse flava:modo in postica parte tántum, qua Sclerotica dicitur barbaris,& nihil obest visioni, inter quos ego sum, Montanus quidem firmat fe in Obstru&ione meatus fellei ad Duodenum,symptomata dicens fe ipsa excipere, Sed revera, morbus est nimis longe diffitus, Dic mihi quid facit Corneam flavefcere? I. Alexandrinus heic quoque ad Obstru&ionem confugit, sed alio modo, cum dicit, Vasa cornea obstrui,& impediri seu potius depravari nutritionem. Verum Argenterius rectè illi objicit,Fore hac ratione, ut pars similaris laboret morbo organico.Propterea ito ego in veligio, Est morbus similaris, quatenus temperamentum cornea est cum hoc modo substantia. Cornea fit tam crafla, ob admistam sanguini bilem, utfpeciebus visibilibus transitus negetur. Hac ratione C tione respondero etiam ad ὑπόθεσιν, in quo obstructionem locum habere ne ipsi quidem dicent, puto. Cornea recipit in fe sanguinem inalteratum, à quo vitiatur modus substantiæ ipsius.
units.tr: § 7. This is indeed a tangled problem, but a far more tangled one is treated in chapters 6 and 7: why, in some jaundiced people, when the whole body has regained its natural colour, the cornea cannot be restored to its colour. Sometimes the whole cornea becomes yellow and everything appears yellow; sometimes only the back part, which barbarians call the sclerotica, is affected, and this does not harm vision. Among those who hold this view I count myself. Montanus indeed asserts that it is an obstruction of the bile duct to the duodenum, saying that the symptoms confirm it. But in truth the disease is too far removed from that. Tell me, what makes the cornea turn yellow? Alexandrinus also has recourse here to obstruction, but in another way, when he says that the vessels of the cornea are obstructed and that nutrition is impeded or rather corrupted. But Argenterius rightly objects to him that, on this account, a similar part would suffer from an organic disease. Therefore I follow his track: it is a similar disease, insofar as the temperament of the cornea is of this kind of substance. The cornea becomes so thick, because bile is mixed into the blood, that passage to the visible species is denied. In this way I will also answer the hypothesis [ὑπόθεσιν], in which I think even they themselves would not say that obstruction takes place. The cornea receives unaltered blood into itself, and by this the mode of its own substance is corrupted.

units.la: § 6. Post hæc (cap.8.) instituit Montanus novam argumentorum Fernelii aciem, & orditur ab eo, quod palmarium putant isti,Constat pars quælibet, inquit, præterquam Temperamento, & Materia & Forma ideò, præter morbos temperamenti, erunt quoque morbi materiæ & formæ. Hoc Fuchfius pro nectare Philofophico habet; cum fit φιλόσοφος. Formabo syllogismum, ut pueri quoque rideant sophisticam. Ex quo rebus constat quælibet pars agens, tot lefionibus ex morbis erit obnoxia. At verò constat ex tribus, temperamento, materia & forma, Ergo. Hæc major est salsissima, quod duplicitèr ostendo. I. Vulneretur aliquis in manu, v.g. Ibi est cutis, caro, vasa, ligamenta, musculi,offa,cartilagines, octo in universum partes, Ergo octo erunt morbi, & octo læsiones. Quod qui dicet, meritò subsannabitur, quod nesciat ægro ... simul in arte nostra. II. Eamus vero ad Inftit. Physicas,quæ docent,Actiones esse compositorum, non componentium. Totum enim, ex tot partibus factum, agit,non (omittam enim partes similares) temperamentum, non materia, non forma.Tu quidem cogitatione separas at in rei natura non est ita, Quo modo enim materia informis (separas enim) actionem habere potest? Quo modo,sua natura ἐνοπ, in materiam immersa, agit fine sua materia? Sed & absque hoc, Forma,quæ non habet contrarium, quei dici potest agere? Materia, separatim accepta,non est ens in actu;forma,separatim accepta,non est ens in actu; ideo neutra sola agit quidquam. Totum hoc (ut repetam) ex materia & forma constitutum, agit. Ergo toti huic, non partibus ejus singulis debetur læsio actionis, adeoque est unus tantum morbus. Et hoc primum est acumen generosi Fernelii.
units.tr: § 6. After this (chapter 8) Montanus sets up a new line of Fernelius's arguments, and begins with what these men think their chief point: any part whatever, he says, consists of temperament, matter and form; therefore, besides the diseases of temperament, there will also be diseases of matter and of form. Fuchsius holds this as philosophical nectar. I will frame the syllogism so that even boys may laugh at the sophism. From this: any acting part whatever is liable to as many injuries from diseases as it has constituents. But it is established that it consists of three things, temperament, matter and form. Therefore... This major premise is utterly foolish, and I show this in two ways. First, suppose someone is wounded in the hand. There are skin, flesh, vessels, ligaments, muscles, bones and cartilages: eight parts in all. Therefore there will be eight diseases and eight injuries. Whoever says this will rightly be laughed at, since he does not know that the patient... at the same time in our art. Second, let us go to the Physics of the Institutes, which teach that actions belong to compounds, not to their components. For the whole, made up of so many parts, acts, not the temperament, not the matter, not the form (I will leave out the similar parts). You separate these in thought, but in the nature of things it is not so. For how can formless matter (for you separate it) have any action? How can form, immersed in matter by its nature [ἔνυλον], act without its matter? But even apart from this, how can form, which has no contrary, be said to act? Matter, taken separately, is not a being in act; form, taken separately, is not a being in act; therefore neither alone acts at all. The whole thing (to repeat) constituted of matter and form acts. Therefore the injury to its action is owed to this whole, not to its single parts, and so there is only one disease. And this is the first keen point of the noble Fernelius.

units.la: § 9. Accipe hoc alterum quoque: Temperamentum inquit, constat ex qualitatibus elementorum, & est in genere accidentium.
