Materia vero ei substerni- tur, & ab hac materia habet pars, ut fit laxa &c. Miror & demiror, fi unquam intellexit seipsum! Falsum est, materiam substerni temperamento! Non enim est ens in actu, ideoque nihil ei accidit, nec potest recipere temperamentum, quia qualitas est. Propterea manifesta est repugnantia. Si enim temperamento subjiciut materia, quomodo temperamentum est accidens ? Quod enim informat, non est accidens, sed forma substantialis, Ergone temperamentum est forma substantialis? Hui Philosophum !
units.tr: § 9. Take this second point as well: temperament, he says, consists of the qualities of the elements, and is in the genus of accidents. But matter is placed under it, and from this matter the part has its laxity, and so on. I marvel and wonder whether he has ever understood himself! It is false that matter is placed under temperament! For it is not a being in act, and therefore nothing accrues to it, nor can it receive temperament, since temperament is a quality. Therefore the contradiction is plain. For if temperament is subjected as matter, how is temperament an accident? For what gives form is not an accident but a substantial form. Is temperament then a substantial form? Oh, what a philosopher!

units.la: § 10. Accipe vero tertium quoque, In generatione similarium, non tantum contemperantur qualitates Elementorum,quæ est temperamenti origo : sed & corpora illorum miscentur,quorum corporum quidni sint peculiares morbi? Incerta deductio, ut lenissime dicam. Respicit quidem discrimen inter μιξιν ᾳ̈ ἐργ᾽ ἀν, supra propositum : sed non efficit, quod vult. In generatione enim corpus aliquod fit tale, non tantum ratione materiæ subjectæ, sed & ratione qualitatum agentium. Quare, prout superat hæc vel illa qualitas,corpus fit tale,vel tale.
units.tr: § 10. Take the third point too. In the generation of similar parts, the qualities of the elements are not only tempered together, which is the origin of temperament, but their bodies are also mixed. Why should those bodies not have their own peculiar diseases? The inference is uncertain, to put it most gently. It does notice the difference between mixture and compound, mentioned above, but it does not achieve what it wants. In generation a body becomes such not only by reason of the underlying matter but also by reason of the qualities acting upon it. So, according as this or that quality prevails, the body becomes such or such.

units.la: § 11. Eadem responsio debetur objectioni illi,quæ cap.9. est.Differre,inquit, materiam à temperamento, oftenditillud, quod partes quædam conveniant temperamento,differant materia; & contra.Dico; Non pendet res à sola materia, sed & à qualitatibus.
units.tr: § 11. The same answer is owed to that objection which is in chapter 9. He says that matter differs from temperament, since certain parts agree with temperament yet differ in matter, and conversely. I say: a thing depends not on matter alone but also on qualities.

units.la: § 12. Atqui experientia probat hos morbos ? cap.10. Corpora enim probè temperata,propter raritatem,mollitiem-que que facilè patent externis injuriis: contra, corpora densa & dura. Negatur, corpus temperatum esse rarum & molle: quin caret omni excessu. Si quod igitur corpus, vel rarum est, vel molle, vel densum & durum: hoc jam intemperatum est. Sed esto, ne pugnemus. Concedatur, inquam, corpus aliquod non ferre injurias externas, propter raritatem & mollitiem, & laboret jam morbo: quis erit ille? Certè non alius ab illo, quem vel calor, vel frigus induxit. Et quid? Densitas & raritas cutis suntnè morbi? Imò verò, dispositio illa, quæ vel à calore, vel à frigore introducta est, illa est morbus. Præterea, cum sint qualitates fecundæ, quarum nulla est vis agendi, quei possunt facere morbos? Præterea, proclivitas illa in morbos & vicissim resistentia illa, sæpe sunt à genere vitæ, ab aliis. Rusticus plus ferre potest quam umbratilis aliquis. Iuvenis plus quam senex, Mas quam fœmina, Tu puta, cæteris paribus. Sed age, quid facit corpus rarum & molle? Nunquid, quod spongiam? Quid densum & durum? Nunquid quod lignum? Vnde statim aparet, quam latè inutilia sint talia? Vis corpus densum rarefacere: calefac. Vis rarum densare: refrigera. Hæc parant indicationes, & deducunt
units.tr: § 12. But does experience prove these diseases? See chapter 10. Bodies that are well tempered, on account of their rarity and softness, lie open easily to external injuries; on the contrary, dense and hard bodies do not. I deny that a temperate body is rare and soft; indeed it lacks every excess. So if any body is either rare, or soft, or dense and hard, it is already intemperate. But let us not quarrel: grant, I say, that some body does not bear external injuries on account of rarity and softness, and is already suffering from disease. Who will that be? Certainly no other than the one whom heat or cold has brought about. And what then? Are the density and rarity of the skin diseases? Rather, that disposition which has been introduced by heat or by cold is the disease. Besides, since these are secondary qualities, none of which has any power of acting, how can they produce diseases? Moreover, that proneness to diseases, and conversely that resistance to them, often arise from one's way of life and other such things. A countryman can bear more than a man who lives in the shade. A young man can bear more than an old man, a man more than a woman, other things being equal, you may suppose. But come, what does a rare and soft body do? Does it do what a sponge does? What about a dense and hard body? Does it do what wood does? From this it immediately appears how widely useless such notions are. Do you want to rarefy a dense body? Heat it. Do you want to densify a rare one? Cool it. These prepare indications and lead us to the method of healing.

units.la: cuṅt nōs ad methodum medendi : illā? §. 13. Interim Gal, ipse accipit ab his indicationes? cap. 1 r. Iñ affectiis enim viceribus utitur adstringentibus ; remotis laxantibus. Quaero ego cum Montano, quae sunt illa adstringentia? Certè frigida & sicca. Contrà ; quae fiunt illa laxantia, quaeremovet? Certè ; calida & humida. Quod porrò deabsumtione spirituum, de aliis allinitur ex, 12. Meth. 5: tam est soluẽs, ut pudeat me dicere verbum.
units.tr: ...to the method of healing. § 13. Meanwhile Galen himself takes his indications from these: in chapter 11 he uses astringents in affections of the viscera and removes laxatives. I ask, with Montanus, what those astringents are? Surely cold and dry. On the contrary, what are those laxatives which he removes? Surely hot and moist. As for what is further said about the consumption of spirits, it is pieced together from other things, from 12, Method 5; it is so loose that I am ashamed to say a word about it.

units.la: § 14. Supersunt duo alia argumenta exMeth. cap. 12. Haustus olei tepentis laxat ventriculum, Ref. Oleum huméctat: humectationem sequitur laxitas. Et ita à fecundis qualitatibus venitur ad primas, quae solæ vim habent agendi & mutandi. Eadem refponsio debetur alteri. Si quid fit rarum, oportet densare. v. g. si quis sudoribus. diffluat, præ raritate cutis. Breviter, præstant hæc frigida & sicca. §. Simp. 1. & prox. 10.
units.tr: § 14. Two other arguments remain, from Method chapter 12. A draught of warm oil relaxes the stomach; oil moistens; moistening is followed by looseness. And so one passes from the secondary qualities to the primary ones, which alone have power to act and change. The same answer is owed to the other: if something becomes rare, it must be densified, for example if someone flows with sweat on account of the rarity of the skin. In short, cold and dry things are the better remedies. See Simple Medicines 1 and the following chapter 10.

units.la: De morbis Forma Cap. VI.
units.tr: On the Form of Diseases, Chapter VI.

units.la: § 1. Hic ab iritio miror, dari his morbis totnomina! Vocat enim hos Fernelius Infimi spiritum, Divinā ejus calorem, Facultates, Substantiam, Totam substantiam, Formam, cujus Cœruleam finit.
units.tr: § 1. Here, first of all, I wonder that these diseases are given whole names! For Fernelius calls them the "spirit of the lowest", his "divine heat", "faculties", "substance", "whole substance", "form", and he finishes off the "cerulean" of it.

units.la: Voluit,credo, homo prepofterus Peripateticum fe ostendere, & prioribus vocibus duabus exponere <bl>ᾧ</bl> κακλγμενον Ϙεχεδν Arift.2. Gen.3.quod Philosophus ait esse in femine, & proportione respondere Elemento stellarum, Verum fallitur aperte 1. quod spiritum à Gaza subministratum temeré acceptat, adeoque esse ἱσοδυνα- μεῖν ᾧ Ϙεχεδν, ᾗ τὸ πνεῦμα:sed huic loco affingere fas non est. II. quod Insitum appellat, sed nōn.explicat fe, de utro loquatur,ἑκάτερα, qui formalis est? ονμϙὐἡ,qui materialis? III. Sed & ubi fe explicarit,scio foreillum transfugam in cāftra Stoicorum. Divinum enim illum cālorem(coelestem,inquam,non elementarem) quem quærit, in ἑκσιροπλο non inveniet. Ne dubites, ἀναλογον τῶν ἰδίων ἀπερέων soιχείω appellat. Atqui quod analogum est alicui rei, non est res ipsa. Quo nomine irridet alicubi Stoicos Vallefius, Mittamus, inquit,ἀλλὰ: quæ omnia apud ipsos divina sunt! Hoc vero dicit ideò, quia Stoici omnibus fublunaribus ammiscebant aliquid divinæ substantiæ, ut alibi deduxi. IV. Dum confundit substantiam cum Facultatibus apparet ingenii folertia! Vna enim Anima habet diversas Facultates. V, Sed cur substantiam, Essentiam, Speciem absolute vocat?
units.tr: He wished, I believe, to show himself a Peripatetic, and by his first two words to explain the phrase which Aristotle, in Generation of Animals 2.3, says is in the semen and corresponds by proportion to the element of the stars. But he is plainly mistaken. First, he rashly accepts the spirit supplied by Gaza, so that it is [isodynamein] equivalent to the semen; but it is not right to attach this to that passage. Second, he calls it innate but does not explain himself: which is it, formal or material? Third, when he does explain himself, I know that this deserter will go over to the camp of the Stoics. For the divine (heavenly, I mean, not elementary) heat which he seeks he will not find in the semen. Do not doubt it: he calls it [analogon] analogous to the elements of its own kind. But what is analogous to a thing is not the thing itself. For this reason Vallesius mocks the Stoics somewhere: "Let us pass over," he says, "that all these things are divine among them!" But he says this because the Stoics mixed something of divine substance into all sublunary things, as I have shown elsewhere. Fourth, while he confuses substance with faculties, the cleverness of his wit appears! For one soul has various faculties. Fifth, why does he call it substance, essence, species, absolutely?

units.la: C
units.tr: C

units.la: An quia forma est Substantia? Egregie? VI Cur deinde Totam substantiam? Si Formam suam voluit esse id, quod Gal. vult, toto coelo errat. Et quei Forma dicatur Tota substantia? Si enim hoc vellet, possim illi aures tribuere, quemadmodum etiam, fi per Formam intelligeret Temperamentum, ut alibi scripsi. Quidquid fit de his omnibus: haec rerum & nominum, in ipso vestibulo, miserrima consufio, cui non suspectum reddat totum negotium?
units.tr: Is it because form is substance? Splendid! Sixth, why then "whole substance"? If he wished his form to be what Galen means, he is wholly in error. And how is form called whole substance? For if he meant this, I could grant him ears, just as I could if by form he understood temperament, as I have written elsewhere. Whatever be the case with all these things, is not this most wretched confusion of things and names, right at the threshold, enough to make the whole business suspect?

units.la: § 2. Sed eamus cominus, & videamus, quomodo proponatur fabula, c. 1 3, Si morbi est actiones ledere, Actiones autem a forma pendent, quidni lafa forma laedantur actiones? Struthiocamelus v. g. qua vi coquit ferrum? Non vi materiae, non infito temperamento; non elementorum calore: sed forma. Ne longe abeam, Partes corporis nostri, dicunt, quomodo alimentum trahunt, retinent, coquunt, excrementa pellunt? Non certe temperamento, non calore elementari: sed forma, specie, effentia. In hanc sententiam inducere volunt Galen. 2. ad Glauc. 2. V. Quin audent dicere, ut nuper admodum innui, Totam substantiam Gal. esse eandem cum forma hac Ferneliana, Nec fatis est hoc: accusant Gal. quod in Meth. omiserit curationem eorum morborum, qui sunt à 7ota fulfiantia. Hac in re jungit fe Fernelio Argenterius.
units.tr: § 2. But let us come to close quarters and see how the tale is put forward, in chapter 13: if disease is to harm actions, and actions depend on form, why should actions not be harmed when form is harmed? The ostrich, for instance, by what power does it digest iron? Not by the power of matter, not by an innate temperament, not by the heat of the elements, but by its form. To pass over distant examples, our bodily parts, they say, how do they draw in nourishment, retain it, digest it, and expel excrements? Certainly not by temperament, not by elementary heat, but by form, species, essence. They want to lead us into this opinion by citing Galen, On the Method 2, to Glaucon 2. Nay, they even dare to say, as was just now hinted, that Galen's "whole substance" is the same as this Fernelian form. Nor is that enough: they accuse Galen of having omitted from the Method the cure of those diseases which arise from the whole substance. In this matter Argenterius joins himself to Fernelius.

units.la: § 3. Quid heic Montanus? Fuchfium quidem ille cap. 14. apprehendit:sed non est res magnæ rei. Mihi libet statim in arcem causæ invadere,& genuinis Gal. amicis ostendere,quà fit eundum.Qui ajunt, Galenum in suis Physicis non agnovisse formam aliam, quam temperamentum: partim bene loquuntur,partim malè. Vt ordiar à posteriori, quis unquam adstrinxit Gal. ad Physicam? Non profitetur ille scientiam, (sed artem,in quà τῶν ἐπιςήμης multa permittit, quæ in Physicis falsa sunt, v.g. temperamentum esse formam,esse animam, ut supra deduxi. Hoc temperamentum cum duplex esse ajunt, rectè ajunt,si rectè se explicent, Ita enim seres habet, Temperamentum est duplex, proprium & commune. Proprium est, quod singulæ partes nactæ sunt: commune quod à corde illis affluit. Vt trumque nisi bene habeat, actio nulla sit. Rursus, proprium iterum duplex est, & consistit alterum in manifestis qualitatibus, sub quo sunt sedecim illa temperamenta intemperata, de quibus in sup. alterum in Totà substantiâ, ut loqui Gal. C
units.tr: § 3. What about Montanus here? He indeed takes hold of Fuchsius in chapter 14, but that is no great matter. I am pleased to attack straight at the citadel of the cause and show the genuine friends of Galen where one must go. Those who say that Galen in his Physics recognised no form other than temperament speak partly well and partly badly. To begin with the latter: who ever bound Galen to Physics? He does not profess science but art, in which he permits many things for the sake of the art that are false in Physics, for example that temperament is form, that it is soul, as I have deduced above. When they say that temperament is double, they speak rightly, if they explain themselves rightly. For thus the matter stands: temperament is double, proper and common. Proper is what the individual parts have obtained; common is what flows to them from the heart. Unless both are sound, there is no action. Again, the proper temperament is itself double, and consists one in the manifest qualities, under which lie those sixteen intemperate temperaments of which I spoke above, and the other in the whole substance, as Galen is accustomed to speak

units.la: solet,ầ qua,hon à caliditate,non à frigidi- fate,non ab ulla harum,editur actio Iam igitur,ut certissimum est,Galénum superstruxisse methodum suam solis qualitatibus manifestis : ita mancus dici neutiquam debet, fi omisit Totam fubftantiam. Cur ? Quia methodus ejus nulla est , inquit differtè 13,Meth.6. pene extr. Qua igitur fronte scribere jubes illum methodum earum rerum , quarum Methodus non est ? Et cur non est ? Quia non cognoscuntur refnedia ratione, non devenimus ad ea per indicationem : sed experientia. Quamobrem fi concedis morbos substantiæ esse eos,quos Gal.describit, non sunt cortimentum: sed revera sunt morbi tales,qui, & ortum futm habent à causis , tota substantia agentibus; & curantur alexiteriis , per experientiam cognitis.
units.tr: ...by which action is produced, not from hotness, not from coldness, not from any of these. Now then, as is most certain, Galen built his method solely on manifest qualities, so he ought by no means be called defective if he omitted the whole substance. Why? Because there is no method for it, he says expressly in Method 13 (Book 6), near the end. With what face, then, do you order him to write a method for those things for which there is no method? And why is there none? Because they are not known by reason; we do not arrive at them through indication but through experience. Wherefore, if you concede that the diseases of the substance are those which Galen describes, they are no trifle. In truth they are such diseases as both have their origin from causes acting on the whole substance, and are cured by alexiteric remedies known through experience.

units.la: § 4. Hactenus ergo male, & indiftincte locuti sunt illi: bene loquuntur, cum in Temperamento subsistunt , nec ulterius ascendunt,ad formam,inquam,Physicam,quae Anima est.Interim pessundant totum id,quod declarant,eum diversos à temperamento morbos quaerunt, in quibus corrumpatur forma, ut loquuntur,
units.tr: § 4. Thus far these men have spoken badly and indistinctly. They speak well when they keep to the temperament and do not rise further to the Physical form, which is the soul. Meanwhile they ruin everything they set out to explain, when they look for diseases different from the temperament, in which the form, as they put it, is corrupted.

units.la: § 5. Quain re quanta fit absurditas juxta & sallitas, audite quæso , quicunque μισοπονηρος ... non estis: Corrumpi formam, ajunt. Si corrumpitur, habet contrarium & proprie dictum contrarium. Atqui substantiæ nihil contrarium est, apud omnes sanos Philofophos. Hoc Montanus ita inducit, cap. 15. Corruptela formæ, quam isti somniant, aut fit, aut jam facta est: fi ita vis, aut est in motu ad terminum, aut jam est in termino. Si posterius hoc fit, jam res est exsuta sua forma, jam cadaver est, quod morbo amplius non laborat. Si prius illud, ne locum quidem habet objectio.
units.tr: § 5. Consider, I beg you, how great an absurdity and falsity this is. Whoever you are, you are not a hater of wickedness [μισοπονηρος]: they say the form is corrupted. If it is corrupted, it has a contrary, and a proper contrary at that. But according to all sound philosophers, a substance has no contrary. Montanus introduces this in chapter 15: "The corruption of the form that these men dream of either is happening or has already happened. If you like, it is either in motion towards its end or already at its end. If the latter, the thing has already been stripped of its form; it is already a corpse, which no longer suffers from disease. If the former, the objection does not even arise."

units.la: Hoc explico amplius,
units.tr: I explain this further.

units.la: § 6. Vt in generatione substantiali distinguere oportet alterationes prævias formæ ab ipsa forma: ita in corruptione, v.g. dum pullus in ovo fit, totis illis 24. diebus semper fit aliquid, hodie adest hæc pars, cras alia, postridie alia, usque dum rete illud fit integrum, ut Orpheus comparabat generationem, neque unquam tamen pullus dicitur, nisi ἐν τῷ νῦν illo, in quo testam rostro pertundit. Sic in homine corruptelæ dicinon possunt morbosæ illæ dispositiones, quæ formam (temperamentum) labefactant: sed alterationes ad corruptelam tendentes. At vero fi eò deventum, ut pars laboret fphacelo, jam indicatio oritur, Vre. seca.
units.tr: § 6. Just as in substantial generation we must distinguish the alterations that precede the form from the form itself, so in corruption, for example while a chick is being formed in the egg, something is always happening throughout those twenty-four days: today this part is present, tomorrow another, the day after another, until that net is complete. Orpheus compared generation to this. Yet the chick is never called a chick until the moment [ἐν τῷ νῦν] when it pierces the shell with its beak. Likewise in a man, those morbid dispositions which weaken the form (the temperament) cannot be called corruptions; they are alterations tending towards corruption. But if it has come to the point where a part is affected by gangrene, then the indication for treatment arises: burn, cut.

units.la: Eadem est ratio totius. Postquam enim cadaver heic iacet, quod est, cum forma periit: inutilis est omnis cura. Et hoc est illudin vulgus ἀπεψυχθεν, quod prositeor, Quamdiu vita fuperefi, tam diu fanis tatis aliquid est. Secus enim fi fit, nemo ex morbo convalesceret.
units.tr: The same reasoning holds for the whole body. For once a corpse lies here, which is what it is when the form has perished, all care is useless. This is the common saying that I acknowledge: "As long as life remains, there is still some health." Otherwise, if it were not so, no one would ever recover from disease.

units.la: § 7. Atqui inquit Fern. fi concedis, quaedam in corpore agere tota fubftantia,quei negare audes, inducere morbum totius substantiae? Effectus enim redolet causam. Primum delictum hic est, quod, ceu dixi, formam suam putant esse eandem cum tota substantia Gal. Alterum est, quod, neglecta experientia, Andabarum more feriunt. Dantur agentia a tota substantia: sed causæ sunt,non morbi. Deinde, morbi ipsi non subito alii sunt, & a cognitis diversi: sed sunt ii ipsi, quos novimus. v. g. Contagium phthisi. cum agit quidem tota substantia: sed facit ulcus, morbum notum. Contagium pestilens, quid facit? Febrim bubonariam, dysenteriam, &c. Ita Cantharides quid faciunt? Exulcerant renes. Et sic de exteris. Atqui est transubstantiatio, ut cum barbaris loquar? Nego. Cum yentriculus Socratis fenis non coquit, quae coquebat Socratis juvenis, estne transfubftantiatio? estne corruptio forma? Minime
units.tr: § 7. But, says Fernelius, if you grant that some things act on the body by the whole substance, how dare you deny that the whole substance can induce a disease? For the effect smells of its cause. The first error here, as I said, is that they think the form is the same as the whole substance of Galen. The second is that, neglecting experience, they strike like Andabatae. There are agents that act by the whole substance, but they are causes, not diseases. Furthermore, diseases themselves do not suddenly become different and alien from those we know; they are the very ones we already know. For example, the contagion of phthisis acts indeed by the whole substance, but it produces an ulcer, a known disease. What does the plague contagion produce? Bubonic fever, dysentery, and so on. What do Spanish flies do? They ulcerate the kidneys. And so with other things. Is there then a transubstantiation, to speak with the barbarians? I deny it. When the stomach of an old Socrates does not digest what the stomach of a young Socrates digested, is this a transubstantiation? Is it a corruption of form? Certainly not.

units.la: Minimè gentium, Calor, proximum instrumentum,est debilior. Ita,cum oculus meus, qui septuagenarius sum , non videt , quæ videbat cum vicenarius essem, estne transsubstantiatio? Summa, Nugæ nugarum! Interim quia semel hoc consisti occæpi, scquor ἑxœῦ, ἀξιοῦλιγε Ϙυμα.
units.tr: Certainly not. Heat, the nearest instrument, is weaker. So when my eye, which I am now seventy years old, does not see what it saw when I was twenty, is this a transubstantiation? In short, trifles of trifles! Meanwhile, since I have begun to stand on this ground, I follow on, as the saying goes: "Hold fast, spirit, and speak with clear voice" [ἕξω, ἀξιοῦ λίγε θυμέ].

units.la: § 8. Ergo Mont. cap.16. triplicem conficit rationem, & distinĉte respondet. I. Vt unum quodque tria requirit actionem, materiam suam, formam suam, temperamentum : ita uno horum læso fit morbus. Ideo triplex fit ordo morborum similarium. Hei mihi, hoccine philosophari est? subruere fundamenta omnium scientiarum & artium? Ita Paracelsiste, cum Hermeta suum in scenam protraxerunt, & sciunt parare duo paria oleorum, quatuor sahum, quinque magisteriorum, &c. jam sunt Philosophi reales. Sed ad rem. Cùm materia cum sua forma constituat unum ὁδὸς ἡ sic temperatum, quod demum agit: quid tu mihi seorsim collocas singula? Et, supra dixi quod Materia sola quæ potest agere, cum actu non sit? Forma sola quæ, cum contrarium non habeat? Vere contrarium, dico iterum. Nam privatio aliò tendit. Et hoc quidè principium
units.tr: § 8. Montanus, in chapter 16, makes a threefold argument and answers it point by point. I. Just as each thing requires three things for its action, namely its matter, its form and its temperament, so when one of these is harmed a disease arises. Hence there is a threefold order of similar diseases. Alas, is this what philosophy is? To undermine the foundations of all sciences and arts? That is how the Paracelsians behave when they bring their Hermes onto the stage, and they know how to prepare two kinds of oils, four kinds of salts, five kinds of magisteries, and so on. Now they are real philosophers! But to the point. Since matter together with its form makes one whole [ὅλον] thing, tempered in this way, which in the end acts, why do you set out the parts separately for me? And did I not say above that matter alone cannot act, since it is not in act? And that form alone, since it has no contrary? Truly it has no contrary, I say again; for privation tends elsewhere. And this indeed is the

units.la: Physicum est, quod isti sübruunt : turfus; § 9. Cum tropus ἐπισύμεης in arte noftrà jubeat, ut temperamento tribuamus, quod formæ est: curtu alio is? Nimirum, à temperamento sumimus indicationes tam curativas, quàm præfervativas. Hoc enim stante ut sànitas est: ita hócalterato, morbus. Hoc est fundamentum methodi medendi, quo concusso, quid erit nobis reliquum. Hinc adeò Gal.in Arte, (siquidem illam quoque in partem vocare debeo) in Meth. med. in omnibus scriptis suis vocat nos ad solum temperamentum, reliɛtà formà. Nec frustra fuére hactenus, qui secuti sunt inoffenso pede. Habuerunt enim secum adamantinum Hipp. argumentum, ἀναλύει ἐ ἢ ἱνσι. Salvum igitur nobis fit temperamentum, quæ nobis forma est, quæ anima.
units.tr: physical principle, which they undermine. Next, § 9. Since our art rightly bids us attribute to the temperament what belongs to the form, why do you say otherwise? Clearly, it is from the temperament that we draw both the curative and the preservative indications. For while this stands, there is health; when this is altered, there is disease. This is the foundation of the method of healing, and once it is shaken, what will be left to us? Hence Galen, in the Art (for I must also bring that work into this discussion), and in the Method of Healing, in all his writings, calls us to the temperament alone, leaving the form aside. Nor have those who have followed him until now done so in vain; they have walked safely, for they had with them the adamantine argument of Hippocrates: nature resolves [ἀναλύει ἡ φύσις]. Let the temperament therefore remain safe for us, which is for us the form, which is the soul.

units.la: § 10. II. Actiones omnes, dicunt, sunt à certà forma, quæ agit heic tantum, heic etiam tantum agit hoc. v.g. Struthiocamelus coquit ferrum, capra salices amaras, bos fænum, gallina muscas & araneas, pavo & ciconia serpentes, & sic de cæteris omnibus. Respondeo, Struthiocamelus, non minus quam magnes, est
units.tr: § 10. II. They say that all actions come from a definite form, which acts here alone, or here alone acts this. For example, the ostrich digests iron, the goat bitter willows, the ox hay, the hen flies and spiders, the peacock and the stork serpents, and so with all the rest. I reply that the ostrich, no less than the magnet, is

units.la: * Gefn.3. Hift. anim. e. proprio, Aldrovandus t: Ornitho'. 9. 6.2, Iordanus contra Iouh.7, Decade ā negānīt.
units.tr: * Gesner, Hist. anim. 3, de proprio; Aldrovandus, Ornitholog. 9, 6.2; Jordanus against Jovius, 7, Decade ... (they deny it).

units.la: est crux Philosophorum. Sed fit ita: O. mnia fiunt à certo temperamento, quod in hac animalis specie tantum est, non in ullá alia, & propterea nec scribi, nec dici potest. Hujus rei alia tibi subministro exempla. Faciat fufor orichalceus viginti campanulas ex eadem materia, eodem tempore, ad eundem ignem, in eodem typo: nulla tamen habebit eum prorsus sonitum, quem altera illarum. Nec discedam longius, sint simul in eadem mensa 20 homines, ejusdem sexus, aetatis, condi- tionis, roboris, etfiquae alia dari pofsunt: inspice singulorum palata, confidera conformationem, non reperies ovum ovo similius, quam isti inter fe: tamen singuli habent diversam vocem. Hinc ita infero, fi in similibus tanta est dissimilitudo effectus: quanto magis in dissimilibus erit? Videmus id fieri, quamvis dicere non possimus unde fit. Atque hic pervenire potest animus humanus: at qui in sublime subvolant, & formas fpecificas crepant, necesse est falli. Cur? Nufpiam exponunt fe, & sunt perpetuo innumero eorum, qui nihil docent. Quo sapientius fecerimus nos, fi intra positos à Gal. limites steterimus! Fit hoc à temperamento, quod ulterius verbis ornare non possum. Et haec est idoovyxgiaw illa, &c.
units.tr: the cross of the philosophers. But it happens thus: all things come about from a definite temperament, which is found in this species of animal only and in no other, and therefore it cannot be written or spoken of. I supply you with other examples of this. Let a brass founder cast twenty little bells from the same material, at the same time, at the same fire, in the same mould: yet none of them will have exactly the same sound as another. Nor shall I go further. Let twenty men of the same sex, age, condition and strength, and whatever else can be given, sit together at one table; examine the palates of each, consider their conformation: you will not find one egg more like another than these are among themselves; yet each has a different voice. From this I infer: if among similar things there is so great a dissimilarity of effect, how much greater will it be among dissimilar things? We see that this happens, though we cannot say how it happens. And the human mind can reach this point; but those who fly aloft and prattle of specific forms must necessarily be mistaken. Why? They never make themselves plain, and they are always an innumerable crowd of those who teach nothing. How much wiser we shall be if we stay within the limits set by Galen! This happens from the temperament, which I cannot adorn with further words. And this is that idiosyncrasy [ἰδιοσυγκρασία], etc.

units.la: {y} de qua idem Gal, ait, fi possem in fingulis individuis assequi illam,talem fore me existimarem, qualem Æsculapium mente concipio.
units.tr: {y} Of this same thing Galen says: "If I could grasp it in each individual, I would think myself to be such as Aesculapius is conceived to be in the mind."

units.la: § 11. III. Denique recurrunt ad afylum curationis. In hac, inquiunt, utimur aliquando iis, quæ agunt manifestis qualitatibus, aliquando alexipharmacis. Et certum est ex fup. Galenum hæc diftinxisse. Ne longius excurram cum Mont. Egregia hæc est agendi ratio, Gal, distinxit, ergo ad formam, à temperamento diversam, ivit. Actionem temperamenti fecit duplicem, ceu ostensum est.
units.tr: § 11. III. Finally, they retreat to the refuge of cure. In this, they say, we sometimes use those things which act by manifest qualities, and sometimes alexipharmics. And it is certain from what has been said above that Galen distinguished these. Not to digress too far with Montanus: this is an excellent way of proceeding. Galen distinguished them, therefore he went to a form different from the temperament. He made the action of the temperament twofold, as has been shown.

units.la: § 3. non propterea tecum in cœlum ascendit, & ibi perquisivit occultas proprietates; quin distinxit manifestas qualitates à modo substantiæ. Scilicet, hoc agit piper, hoc agit arsenicum, licet eodem fere gradu calidum fit utrumque. Hic modus comprehendit sub fe qualitates omnes, tam primas, quam secundas & tertias, facitque, ut aliquid cito actuetur, aliquid tarde, aliquid in momento, aliquid in vesica demū, & ficporro. Summa summarum, Gal. in Meth. adstrinxit (quod ad morbos similares) nos ad solum temperamentum, à quo indicationes petit. Quare, qui ad occulta & cœlestia properant, evertunt Methodum.
units.tr: § 3. He did not therefore ascend to heaven with you and there search out hidden properties; rather he distinguished manifest qualities from the mode of the substance. Clearly, pepper acts in this way and arsenic in that, although each is hot to nearly the same degree. This mode comprehends under itself all qualities, first, second and third alike, and it brings it about that one thing acts quickly, another slowly, another in a moment, another only in the bladder, and so on. In sum, Galen, in the Method, has bound us (as far as similar diseases go) to the temperament alone, from which he draws his indications. Therefore those who hasten after hidden and heavenly things overturn the Method.

units.la: Exempla morborum formalium. CAPVT VII.
units.tr: Examples of formal diseases. CHAPTER VII.

units.la: § 1. Orat Fernelius, absque exemplis nihil rite adstrui posse, Propterea accingit fe operi quidem: verum tam frigide stat, ut praestiterit filuiffe. Et quia sequor Montanum, quid cap, 17.initio frigidius dici possit,quam morbos occultos fubdiuidi in manifestos & occultos? Nec locus est tergiuerfationi, fi quis vel verba ipsius authoris intueatur,vel paraphrafin Montani, Non minus frigidum est, Morbos istos novos esse ex causis direćto sibi oppositis, cum & fine putredine,eaq; vel simplici,vel profunda.
units.tr: § 1. Fernelius prays that nothing can be properly established without examples. He girds himself to the work, but he stands so coldly that it would have been better for him to keep silent. And since I follow Montanus: what could be said more coldly at the beginning of chapter 17 than that hidden diseases are subdivided into manifest and hidden? Nor is there room for evasion, if anyone looks either at the author's own words or at Montanus' paraphrase: "It is no less cold to say that those diseases are new, arising from causes directly opposed to them, both without putrefaction and with putrefaction, whether simple or profound."

units.la: § 2. Post ulcera, cap.18. sunt morbi formales ex Putredine. Vbi fi queras, Cum putrescere possint partes tres Hippocrati dićte, dequibus loquatur? De omnibus, dicet tibi Mont. adducto loco ex l. de Abd. Cui aflertioni quia objici poterat, Intemperies indigent simplici alteratione, ad putredines mistam ... ex alteratione & vacuatione, Dicam primo loco, Putredines istas non esse morbos: sed causas, Secundo, Reducitur pfeudophilofophema illud, in quo confunduntur motus praevii ad terminum cum termino ipso.De quo termino fi loqui voletille, diceturilli,ut supra, Iam non amplius est morbus: quia cadaver est. Inflammetur v.g. digitus, & eò res deveniat, ut metus fit gangrænæ. Hanc quamdiu avertere potes, simplex eftalteratio : cum invaluit,absciñde. Quid hic novi morbi est? Imo est,inquit;alterationes enim illæ tandem corrumpunt formam.Miror admodum non tacuisse Hac ratione omnes morbi lethales erunt morbi formales, neque opus erit catalogo peculiari. Nos loquimur de putredine,quæ est in fieri,quæ est cum additione hac:non autem de putredine simpliciter, quæ aliena est à nostro instituto. Objicias, Fernelium voluisse, non putredines esse morbos formæ,sed morbos à putredine ortos. Hoc modo funditus ille perierit, ut præmonui. Causam enim esse concedet. Nec quidquam valet, Putredo est distincta ab Intemperie, ergò diftinctum facit morbum. Hoc apud Fuchfium est Philosophari; apud Montanum & me est ineptire. Tamen Mont. refutat, cui laudem inde quæsitam non invideo.
units.tr: § 2. After ulcers, in chapter 18, there are formal diseases arising from putrefaction. If you ask here which of the three parts that Hippocrates mentions can putrefy, and which of them he means, Montanus will say all of them, citing the passage from the book On Joints. Since it could be objected to this assertion that "intemperies need only simple alteration, but putrefactions are mixed ... from alteration and evacuation," I will say first that these putrefactions are not diseases but causes. Second, that pseudo-philosophical notion is refuted, in which the movements that lead up to an end are confused with the end itself. If he wants to speak of that end, I will say to him, as above: it is no longer a disease, because it is a corpse. Let a finger, for example, become inflamed, and let the matter come to the point where there is fear of gangrene. As long as you can avert this, it is a simple alteration; once it has taken hold, cut it off. What is new about this disease? "Indeed," he says, "those alterations finally corrupt the form." I am quite astonished he did not keep quiet. By this reasoning all lethal diseases will be formal diseases, and there will be no need for a separate catalogue. We are speaking of putrefaction which is in the process of becoming, which carries this addition, not of putrefaction simply, which is foreign to our undertaking. You may object that Fernel meant that putrefactions are not diseases of form but diseases arising from putrefaction. In this way he would perish utterly, as I forewarned, for he will concede that it is a cause. Nor does it help to argue that "putrefaction is distinct from intemperies, therefore it makes a distinct disease." Among Fuchsius this is philosophizing; among Montanus and me it is silly nonsense. Yet Montanus refutes him, and I do not begrudge him the praise he thereby seeks.

units.la: § 4. Post putredinem,cap. 19. Phthisis est, ni tu mavis, Pththoë. Heic eruditè Montanus, Phthisis non est morbus, sed conflues morborum. Est enim «leg Qua
units.tr: § 4. After putrefaction, in chapter 19, comes phthisis, or, if you prefer, phthoe. Here Montanus learnedly says that phthisis is not a disease but a conflux of diseases. For it is

units.la: quæ est morbus magnitudinis. Est febris hectica, quæ ad intemperies pertinet. Est ulcus pulmonis, quod est continui solutio. Reliquum ergo est, ut putredo pulmonis fit formale illud. Atqui jam demonstratum est, putredinem non esse morbum. Tu accipe eo modo, quo dixi.
units.tr: a disease of size. There is hectic fever, which belongs to intemperies. There is an ulcer of the lung, which is a dissolution of continuity. It remains, therefore, that putrefaction of the lung is that formal disease. But it has already been demonstrated that putrefaction is not a disease. Take it in the sense I have said.

units.la: § 5. Post phthifin, cap.20. sunt putredines,non viscerum tantum inferioris ventris, sed & extimarum partium. Vt res exemploinclarefcat. Affluat ad hepar putrida (v.g.) bilis, quæ ita tabefaciat parenchyma ipsius, ut diffluat : hunc morbum ait ille esse incognitum, ideoque formæ. Credin’ tu? Mihi cognitiffimus est. Tibi fi ridere placet (mihi enim hoc rerum statu non libet) videper otium, quomodo Montanus conficiat hominem propriis sagittis! Nimirum, hoc est Adrafteas imperium, de quo sæpe dico.
units.tr: § 5. After phthisis, in chapter 20, there are putrefactions not only of the viscera of the lower belly but also of the outer parts. To make the matter clear by an example: let putrid bile (say) flow to the liver and so melt its parenchyma that it dissolves. This disease, he says, is unknown and therefore formal. Do you believe it? To me it is very well known. If you like to laugh at it (for in the present state of affairs I am not inclined to), see at your leisure how Montanus makes the man with his own arrows! Surely this is the rule of Adrasteia, about which I often speak.

units.la: § 6. Heic dum cap.21.intueor Innati spiritus dissolutionem, incipio meditari mecum.Quo modo dissolutio hæc cohæreat cum morbis jam numeratis? Qui enim vult novum genus constituere, & in digitos ponere species, ille debet ante omnia docere, quod fit commune illud, quod in species omnes fe extendit? Id vero nullibi est, adeoque funis est ex arena contextus. Sed non yocetur hoc in considerationem:
units.tr: § 6. Here, as I look at chapter 21, the dissolution of the innate spirit, I begin to reflect to myself. How does this dissolution cohere with the diseases already listed? For whoever wants to set up a new kind and lay out its species on his fingers must first teach what that common thing is which extends to all the species. But nowhere is there such a thing, and so it is a rope woven of sand. Yet let this not be taken into consideration.

units.la: § 7. Quærit Montanus , O Ferneli, quem spiritum intelligis ? Influentem an Insitum? Illum non potes : habes enim inter Contenta , in quæ sola causa cadit, non Morbus. Ergo illum debes intelligere. Is vero cum cœlestis tibi fit, nihilque aliud quam Causa continens Stoicorum, quam neque Gal.agnoscit, neque ipsa rerum natura ; quid dices? Imo vero,regerit , Gal. acceptat 12. Meth, 5. & alibi. Heic fatendum est , Montanum in multis esse ambagiosum. Modo enim à morbo ad causam deerrat , modo ad symptoma in excretis , modo alio. Ego simpliciter dico, Pertinet res ad Influentem, & conftituit morbum in numero. Ita dico l. Gal.enim procul dubio respexit ad divifionem partium Hippocraticam , in qua quia spiritus sunt, fiillifatifcant, non poteft alius esse morbus quam in defectu partis.Et quis credat,defectum illum esse ab intemperie , quia lipothymia subitò curatur. An hæc ratio non valet in spiritibus?Si enim crassiores sint, quam ut libere ire poilint,odorata attenuando curant intemperiem. Tum vero crassities est morbus notus , &qui nullatenus huc facit. Eadem ratio obstructionis est à crassis
units.tr: § 7. Montanus asks: O Fernel, which spirit do you mean? The influent or the innate? You cannot mean the influent, for you have it among the contents, in which only the cause falls, not the disease. Therefore you must mean the innate. But since that spirit is heavenly for you, and is nothing other than the containing cause of the Stoics, which neither Galen acknowledges nor nature itself, what will you say? "Indeed," he retorts, "Galen accepts it, in Method 12.5 and elsewhere." Here it must be admitted that Montanus is very roundabout in many things. Now he strays from disease to cause, now to symptom in the excretions, now elsewhere. I simply say that the matter pertains to the influent spirit and constitutes a disease in its own right. So I say, for Galen doubtless had regard to the Hippocratic division of the parts, in which, because the spirits are there, if they fail no other disease can exist than a defect of the part. And who would believe that this defect comes from intemperies, because lipothymia is cured quickly? Does this reasoning not hold for spirits? For if they are too thick to move freely, odours cure the intemperies by attenuating them. Then indeed thickness is a known disease, and it has nothing to do with this. The same reasoning applies to obstruction from thick

units.la: éraffis vaporibus, a quibus lipothymiam frequentissime esse puto,
units.tr: thick vapours, from which I think lipothymia most frequently arises.

units.la: § 8. Quia Fern. post Spiritum innatum ponit Calidum innatum, cupiam aut dire ab ipfofciveritne affinitatem horum duorum inter fe? Tam arcta est illa apud Arift. & Gal. ut Spiritus fit Calidum, & Calidum Spiritus. Differunt autem ut Causa & Causatum. Calidum, in corde stabulans, constituunt reliquiæ feminis masculi, per solidam cordis substantiam ita dispersæ, ut coagulum per caseos, fermentum per panes, ut Arift, negotium explicat. Hoc Calidum, in sanguinem agens, facit ζωοποιοῦντες, quæ ipsæ sunt Spiritus illi influentes, fine quibus actio fit nulla. Calidi fi hæc est origo, facilis est refponfio, An restituatur ab alimento? Non refituitur, Non tam facilis est, An seipsum interimat? Est quidem pro affirmativa Hipp, sententia apud Gal. de Marafmo.3. Verum, refutat diligenter Gal. ibidem, referendo fe ad 1, San. tuen. 2.
units.tr: § 8. Since Fernel, after the innate spirit, posits the innate heat, I would like to ask whether he himself knows the affinity between these two. It is so close in Aristotle and Galen that spirit is heat and heat is spirit, though they differ as cause and effect. The heat dwelling in the heart is constituted by the remnants of male seed, dispersed through the solid substance of the heart in the way that rennet works through cheese and leaven through bread, as Aristotle explains the matter. This heat, acting on the blood, produces the vital spirits, which are themselves those influent spirits, without which no action occurs. If this is the origin of the heat, the answer is easy to the question whether it is restored by nourishment: it is not restored. The question whether it destroys itself is less easy. Indeed, the Hippocratic opinion in Galen's De marasmo favours the affirmative. But Galen diligently refutes it in the same place, referring the reader to De sanitate tuenda, book 1, chapter 2.

units.la: § 9. Ex his intelligi possunt, quæ Mont. cap. 22. disputat contra Fernelium. Ariftotelis cum ille non meminerit, integrabo ego sermonem, & ita exponam rem, Exstinguitur Calidum hoc apud Philosophum duobus
units.tr: § 9. From these things can be understood what Montanus disputes in chapter 22 against Fernelius. Since Fernel makes no mention of Aristotle, I will complete the discussion and set the matter out thus: this heat is extinguished, according to the Philosopher, in two

units.la: modis, vel per εὔεον, vel per μεέφνον? dic, Ferneli, uter modus est tibi formalis? Apud Gal. cum fiat etiam duobus, sed ita, ut posterior fubdividi possit: dic, ό gratiose, quam ex his eligere velis? An cum alimento (ὑσιάκωνμεα vocat Hipp.) destituitur? An cum privatur motu fursum? Ancum motu deorsum? Ponis tu quidem, & strangulatum & frigus: sed non fatis te explicas. Quamobrem Montanus quaerit, Loquerisne de exstinctione facta? Non puto. Ita enim morbus ame plius non est, ut in fup. comprehensum fuit. Loquerisne de fiente? Hæc fi fiat à frigore, an non erit intempleries? fi àlaqueo, fi à sanguine affatim irruente in syncope Cardiaca dicta; fi à vaporibus in febribus malignis, in suffocationibus uterinis, fià carbonum fumo aut calcis recens exstinctæ, &c. annon erit morbus conformationis in viis? Hæc cum nullam instantiam habeant, jure cum Montano dixerim, Fernelius nescit,quid scribat.
units.tr: ways, either by one means or by another. Tell me, Fernel, which mode is formal for you? According to Galen, since it too happens in two ways, but so that the latter can be subdivided, which of these would you choose? Do you mean the lack of nourishment (which Hippocrates calls [ἀτροφίη])? Or the privation of upward motion? Or downward motion? You indeed posit both strangling and cold, but you do not explain yourself enough. Wherefore Montanus asks: are you speaking of an extinction already accomplished? I think not, for then it is no longer a disease, as was comprehended above. Are you speaking of what is happening? If this comes from cold, will it not be an intemperies? If it comes from a noose, or from blood rushing in abundantly in what is called cardiac syncope, or from vapours in malignant fevers, in uterine suffocations, or from the smoke of charcoal or freshly slaked lime, and so on, will it not be a disease of conformation in the passages? Since these cases have no instance to support them, I may rightly say with Montanus that Fernel does not know what he is writing.

units.la: § 10. Post hæc cap.25. Montanus fylvam horridam ingreditur; à qua mihi pene timeo, ob ingressum tam tenebricofum. Cui enim,ut dudum etiam quæftus sum, morbi illi apud Fern. manifesti sunt, qui simul occulti sunt? Sed audetmus, prævio imprimis Comite tam ani- mo(o! mofo! Is primum laudat Alex. Maffariæ lib. de Peste verè aureum. Deinde monet adolescentes, Caveant sibi à Fernelii lectione! Id ipsum publicè, privatimque faciebat PH. SCHERBIVS, vir & ætatis constantis, & judicii dexterrimi. Tum vero rem aggrediens, impugnat cum dicto Maff.divisionem Fernelianam morborum pestilentium & malignorum, quam non repeto. Mox fuse docet, quid differat pestilens à maligno? Subinde, quatenus vel multi, vel pauci sint morbi, quibus debeantur hæc nomina? Tandem, aggressus causas, vellet quidem obtinere, Pestem esse à solo aëre: sed defcendit denique illò, Frequentius id esse. Ego ex G. Agricola (quem cap. feq. laudat) didici, jussus eò ire ab SCHERBIO, tres esse causas. I. Aërem, in fubftantia corruptum, five fit à μιάσματσιν aliunde importatis, five in certo loco genitis. II. Aërem eundem, sed in qualitatibus tantum mutatum, tum vid. cum ὥρα ἐχ ὥρας ἀποδίδωσι, cum tempora non sunt tempora, ut Hipp. loquitur. 3 Aph.8.III. Victum malum, praesertim famis tempore. Prius illud non nisi rarissime fit, & moritur tum tertia pars hominum, aves è tectis decidunt: duo reliqua frequentius accidunt. Hæc tria constituunt futuunt tres causas communes, quæ efficiunt morbum unum communem, Pestem. Neutiquam enim pestis est morbus aliquis peculiaris: sed in quocunque concurrunt hæc duo, Vt fit à causa communi, Vt occidat multos. Hoc vero per rerum naturam non potest convenire multis. Ex his pendet quæstio, An febris pestilens & pestis sint unus morbus? Minimè. Pestis enim latius patet, & plures sub fe morbos habet, in quorum censu febris pestilens est. Quin imò, datur febris pestilens fine peste, tum vid. cum à causa quidem communi est: sed non-dum occidit multos. Pendet quoquo modo hæc altera etiam quæstio, Quæ fit differentia inter has tres febres, Putridam, Malignam, Peftilentem? Vulgaris & quantum judico, vera est sententia, à Comite nostro heic tacta, sed tractata prolixè à Cæfalpino, 1. quæst. Med, 12. differre majore minore putredine. Tu puta. In putrida (benigna) esse putredinem primi gradus, qui paululum fit supra qualitates manifestas: in maligna esse jam ulteriorem, & qui tendit ad corruptionem: in pestilenti in excellenti gradu, quæ dici possit sordida, profunda, larga, tenax, contumax, omnino talis, quæ (ob crassitiem forté, ut in arsenico, cum pipere collato) vinci à calore nostro non possit, ut scripsi jam olim in D. de Febribus malignis. Nunc ut nihil nuto [?] : ita, explicationis doctrinæ gratiâ, hoc superaddo. Putridarum benignarum statum in eo esse, ut Combustio potius sit (quæ intra limites manifestarum qualitatum stat) quam Putredo: Pestilentium contra,ut vera sit Putredo, & quæ jam Totâ substantiâ sit mortalis: Malignarum, ut medio modo se habeant. Majoris aut minoris malitiæ indicium fere est Contagium. Quo minus enim contagiosæ sunt istæ febres, eò longius à peste absunt : quo magis, eò propius accedunt : cum maximè, jam sunt ipsa pestis. Hoc loco videtur anquirendum esse in id quoque, licet Nostro intactum, An putredo illa extrema, quam vocasse Veteres, docui alibi, dici pos- sit Venenum? Non ego quidem à domate SCHERBII, Disp. de Pestil. 28, discedo, Si proprie & Medicè loquimur, non posse dici : sin improprie & cum vulgo, posse. Hoc autem adjungo, Quamdiu in corpore quod obsedit, hospitatur, non est, nec dicitur Venenum : at, cum ex hoc corpore in aliud corpus transfertur ille Hippoc. fomes illepatridus, qui de subjecto in fubjectum transit,non posse commodiore alio nomine dici, quam venenum, vel ideo, quia agit Tota substantia. Quidquid fit: Ferneli, ubi heic est forma tua?
units.tr: § 10. After this, in chapter 25, Montanus enters a dreadful forest, and I am almost afraid of it because the entrance is so gloomy. For as I have already complained, how can those diseases in Fernelius be clear when they are at the same time obscure? But let us venture on, with such a bold companion (oh, so bold!). First he praises Alexander Massaria's book on the plague as truly golden. Then he warns young men to beware of reading Fernelius! PH. SCHERBIUS, a man of steady age and most skilled judgment, did the same thing both in public and in private. Then, taking up the matter, he attacks Massaria's division of pestilential and malignant diseases, which I shall not repeat. Soon he explains at length how the pestilential differs from the malignant. Next he asks how many diseases, few or many, these names should apply to. Finally, when he takes up the causes, he would indeed like to establish that the plague comes from the air alone, but at last he descends to this: that it is more often so. I learned from G. Agricola (whom he praises in the following chapter), at Scherbius's bidding that I should go there, that there are three causes. (1) Air corrupted in its substance, whether by miasmata [μιάσματσιν] brought in from elsewhere or generated in a particular place. (2) The same air, but changed only in its qualities, as when the seasons give back season from season [ὥρα ἐχ ὥρας ἀποδίδωσι], when the times are not times, as Hippocrates puts it (Aph. 3.8). (3) Bad food, especially in time of famine. The first happens only very rarely, and then a third of the people die, and birds fall from the roofs; the other two occur more often. These three causes, which are common, bring about one common disease, the plague. For the plague is by no means some peculiar disease, but wherever these two concur, as a result of a common cause, it kills many. But this by the nature of things cannot happen to many. On this depends the question whether pestilential fever and the plague are one disease. By no means. For the plague has a wider range and has several diseases under it, among which pestilential fever is counted. Indeed, there is a pestilential fever without the plague, when it does come from a common cause but has not yet killed many. In some way this other question also depends on the first: what is the difference among these three fevers, putrid, malignant and pestilential? The common and, as far as I judge, true opinion, touched on here by our author but treated at length by Caesalpinus (Quaest. Med. 1.12), is that they differ by a greater or lesser putrefaction. Consider it thus: in the putrid (benign) fever there is putrefaction of the first degree, which is a little above the manifest qualities; in the malignant it is further along, tending towards corruption; in the pestilential it is in the highest degree, which may be called foul, deep, broad, tenacious, stubborn, altogether such that (perhaps because of its thickness, as with arsenic mixed with pepper) it cannot be overcome by our heat, as I wrote long ago in my De febribus malignis. Now, without changing anything, for the sake of explaining the doctrine I add this. The state of benign putrid fevers is that it is more combustion (which stays within the limits of manifest qualities) than putrefaction; of the pestilential, on the contrary, that it is truly putrefaction, and already mortal in its whole substance; of the malignant, that it is in an intermediate condition. An indication of greater or lesser malice is almost always contagion. For the less contagious these fevers are, the further they are from the plague; the more contagious, the closer they come; when most contagious, they are already the plague itself. At this point it seems we must also inquire, though untouched by our author, whether that extreme putrefaction, which I showed elsewhere the ancients called by a name, can be called poison. I do not, indeed, depart from the opinion of Scherbius, in his disputation on the plague, thesis 28: if we speak properly and medically, it cannot be called so; but if improperly and with the common people, it can. I add this, however: as long as it lodges in the body it has possessed, it is not, nor is it called, poison; but when that Hippocratic fomes, that putrid thing, passes from one body into another, it cannot be called by a more suitable name than poison, if only because it acts with its whole substance. Whatever the case: Fernelius, where is your form now?

units.la: §. 11. Credam oboluisse illi,tale quid quaesitum iri ab illo, Ideo 2. Abdit.12. valde satagit, ut extundat illam. Hujus loci examen dum instituit Montanus cap.24. ostendit quidem studium suum perpetuum conculcandi mendacium: sed non video, cur tantopere laudet illum, quem mox tot injuriosis vocibus laceffit? Legi, nescio ubi, Leonis laudibus qui murem ornet, non ornet, sed obterat. De Phocione olim Demosthenes, Securis venisti meorum sermonum: de Montano non idem dicat Fernelius? An ostentare voluit triumphum de hoste glorioso? Glorioso vero, cujus peccata, errores, falsitates, oscitationes, ineptias, inadvertentias, inscitias, quin portenta dogmatum tam liberè enumerat? Quem causas apertas ad obscuras ait redegisse, cum contra deberet? qui ita agat, ut existimationem Medici amittat? ut Hipp. familia indignus fit? cujus assertiones, necà Philofophis,nec à Medicis admittantur? qui adeò coecus fit, ut confirmet ex Gal. quae contra ipsum ex Gal. afferri possunt? qui
units.tr: § 11. I suppose he was hard pressed that such a question would be put to him, so in Book 2 of De abditis 12 he struggles hard to beat it out. While Montanus, in chapter 24, examines this passage, he indeed shows his constant zeal for trampling on falsehood; but I do not see why he praises so highly the man whom he soon assails with so many insulting words? I read somewhere, I know not where, of the praise of a lion which does not adorn a mouse but crushes it. Demosthenes once said of Phocion, "You have come as the axe of my speeches." Does Fernelius not say the same of Montanus? Or did he wish to display a triumph over a glorious enemy? Glorious indeed, whose sins, errors, falsehoods, carelessness, silliness, inadvertences, ignorance, and even the monstrous doctrines he so freely lists! Whom does he say reduced obvious causes to obscure ones, when he ought to have done the opposite? One who acts in such a way as to lose the esteem of a physician? who is unworthy of the family of Hippocrates? whose assertions are admitted neither by philosophers nor by physicians? who is so blind that he confirms from Galen what can be brought from Galen against himself? who

units.la: aliorum errores notet, ut ipse in errore perfifteret? cum hoc,inquam,cur ineptit, veluti concludit ipsemet? Et quae tanta ipsius authoritas est? Apud adolescentes, qui cito volunt figri Doctores? apud viros,quos pudet dediscere? apud senes bis pueros? Hiccine peritiflimus est utriusque linguae, qui Graeca quidem extremo digito non attigit : Latina tam perverse didicit, ut opus habeat reformatore styli? Hiccine in optimis disciplinis verfatiffimus est, cui superiora omnia objici pofsunt? & quidem ex hoc solo cap.
units.tr: notes the errors of others, while he himself persists in error? Why, I ask, does he, with this man, trifle, as he himself concludes? And what is his authority so great? Among young men, who want to be called teachers quickly? Among men, who are ashamed to unlearn? Among old men who are twice children? Is this man most skilled in both languages, who has not touched Greek even with the tip of his finger, and has learned Latin so perversely that he needs a reformer of his style? Is this man most versed in the best disciplines, to whom all the above can be objected? And indeed from this chapter alone.

units.la: Quo minus à me expectet quifquam,ut sim referendarius Montani, adeò lateinutilia sunt omnia! Vnum tamen, imitatione SCHERBII, levi brachio excutiam, in quo fere summa rei consistit, μίαςμα, seu inquinamentum illud pestilens, quod è coelo derivat ille. In hoc architeCtando cum tantos labores imposuerit stellis, scire quis, non fine causa fortassis, aveat,cujusid vel authoritate fecerit, vel qua experientia didicerit? Ex doctrina Stoica hausisse facile credo, imitando araneas,quae, ex quibus floribus apes conficiunt mella sua, ex iis illae venenum.Huc inducar,quod Medici illi Siculi, quorum Montanus facit mentionem, pestem suam non ausi fuerint
units.tr: Let no one expect from me that I will act as a champion of Montanus, since all these things are so utterly trifling! Yet I will shake off one point with a light arm, in imitation of Scherbius, since the sum of the matter rests almost entirely on it: the pollution [μίασμα], or that pestilential contamination which he derives from heaven. In constructing this, he has laid such great labours on the stars. One may well ask, not without reason perhaps, on whose authority he has done so, or from what experience he has learned it. I readily believe he drew it from Stoic doctrine, imitating the spiders, which make poison out of the same flowers from which bees make their honey.

units.la: appellare pestem,sed filiam pestis.Ridiculè profectò!Forte an idem senserunt,quamvis aliter locuti sunt, tres illi HIERONYMI, summi viri, CAPIVACCIVS, MERCVRIALIS, FABRICIVS ab Aquapendente. Hi enim sunt Patavini illi, quos Montanus producit in scenam, quique anno 1575 Venetias vocati,confultique,An,qui tum ibi grassabatur morbus, pestis effet? refponderunt,Non esse. Verum,cum postea res sequius caderet, tres illi pene infamia notati sunt,eoque necessitatis adducti,ut scripto edito persuadere vellent, Successisse demum aëris corruptionem, Quasi vero necesse fit semper eo devenire rem, nec possit fomes mali aliunde inferri! Compertum enim tum quoque fuit denique,ex agro Tridentino cum letis infectis pervenifle hospitem hunc terrificum.
units.tr: I will adduce this: those Sicilian physicians whom Montanus mentions did not dare to call their plague a plague, but "the daughter of the plague." How ridiculous! Perhaps those three famous men, Hieronymus [Capivaccius], Mercurialis and Fabricius ab Aquapendente, thought the same, although they spoke otherwise. They are those Paduans whom Montanus brings onto the stage, who in 1575 were summoned to Venice and consulted whether the disease then raging there was the plague. They answered that it was not. But when matters afterwards turned out worse, those three were almost branded with infamy, and were driven by necessity to wish to persuade people, by a published writing, that the corruption of the air had come on afterwards. As if it must always be so, and the source of the evil could not be brought in from elsewhere! For it was in fact afterwards discovered that this terrible guest had come from the Trentino region with infected goods.

units.la: § 13. Adrem, quam agimus. Hoc μίασμα quid est in Medicina? Non Medicum, sed Metaphysicum! dicebat SCHERBI V S cum suavi risu.Oportet omnino ex animo delere omnem caeli morbum, ut Virg. vocat: & firmiter credere, Quidquid heic est,elementare esse. Tum vero hoc alterum persuadere sibi,Impune quidem venenum nominari
units.tr: § 13. To the matter we are treating. What is this pollution [μίασμα] in medicine? "Not a medical matter, but a metaphysical one!" Scherbius used to say, with a pleasant laugh. We must wholly erase from our minds every "disease of the sky," as Virgil calls it, and firmly believe that whatever is here is elemental. Then one should persuade oneself of this further: that a poison may indeed be named with impunity, but a disease not without impunity, since (to put it in one word) it is a cause. For it is in attacking this that the whole diligence of all physicians labours. So in the venereal pox, is that poison which passes from the infected to others anything other than a cause? So too in the rabies of dogs, and so in all other poisons.

units.la: posse : sed morbum haud impunè, cum (uno verbo ) causa sit. In hac enim expugnanda omnis omnium Medicorum desudat industria. Ita in lue Veneria, virus illud , quod ab infectis transfertur in alios , quid aliud sit, quam Causa ? Itain rabie caninā. Ita in omnibus venenis aliis. Hæc,ut dixi suprà, morbos quidem faciunt Gal. notos : sed curatio est Empirica,ut Gal. ipse tradit in Meth. Hinc intelligitur vanitas illorum , quide morbis occultis integra dant nobis volumina! Qui si dicant nobis, Atqui hi morbi propriis alexipharmacis curantur: respondebitur iterum,Illa causam respicere , non morbum.
units.tr: These things, as I said above, do indeed make diseases known to Galen, but the treatment is empirical, as Galen himself teaches in the Methodus. Hence the vanity of those men is evident, who give us whole volumes on hidden diseases! If they should say to us, "But these diseases are cured by their own specific antidotes," the answer will again be: those remedies aim at the cause, not at the disease.

units.la: § 14. Hæcipsa dicta mihi sunto de febre,carbunculo & bubone pestilentibus c.25.Reenim verà profunda illa putredo non præbet alias indicationes ab iis, quæ in putridis benignis sunt. Vt enim in benignis alteramus,quod putrescit ; vacuamus,quod putruit:ita in malignis,hac solum differentiâ,quod in illis utimur simpliciter alterantibus , in his totâ substantiâ,experientiâ cognitis.Qua in re placet mihi Montani studium,qui observat,Fernelium ipsum aliquando Causam vocare, & tamen adscribere illi , quod Morbi est, Viden' tu, ut Adrastéa caput exserit ?
units.tr: § 14. Let these same things be said by me concerning the fever, carbuncle and plague-bubo, c. 25. For that deep putrefaction does not offer indications different from those in benign putrid conditions. For just as in benign cases we alter what putrefies and evacuate what has rotted, so in malignant cases the only difference is that in the former we use simply alterative remedies, in the latter remedies that act on the whole substance, known from experience. In this matter I like Montanus's zeal, who observes that Fernelius himself at times calls it a cause, yet ascribes to it what belongs to the disease. "Do you see how Adrasteia thrusts out her head?"

units.la: § 15. Quid istuc vero est? Animadverto eandem divam sese ostentare quoque in Exanthematis cap. 2 5. ut ille vocat Variolas & Morbillos nostros. Quo minus foliciti esse debemus in posterum. Interim monere oportet, Recte à Montano refutari Fernelium, qui vult, d. Morbos fuisse Græcis olim cognitos, & quidem sub nomine Ex anthematum, Recterefellitur idem, cum Avicennæ fe opponit, ajentes, Reliquias esse sanguinis materni. Hanc causam accepto, quamvis (quod objiciunt quidam) non in omnibus appareant. Si enim inter mille millenos uni eafelicitas contingat, ut immunis fit, non obid falsa causa est. Stat igitur Arabis sententia vel ideo, quia substituta à Gallo causa nihil valoris habet. Stat illud quoque, Causam, non morbum ipsum esse, quod in sanguine superest, & ebullitionem facit certis temporum intervallis. Tandem & illud, quamvis hi duo assectus etiam pestilentes sint cum febre:non propterea semper ita est, ut Fern. vult cum Agricola. Caeterum, paraplegiam Hipp. 1. Epid. 2. t, 59. & 60. accenfendam fuisse pestilentibus, clare negat Gal. in Com. ut Mont. observat.
units.tr: § 15. But what is this? I notice that the same goddess also shows herself in the Exanthemata, chapter 25, where he calls our smallpox and measles by that name. So we should be less anxious about them from now on. Meanwhile it is right to point out that Montanus rightly refutes Fernelius, who holds that these diseases were known to the Greeks of old under the name of exanthemata. Fernelius is also rightly refuted when he opposes Avicenna, saying they are remnants of maternal blood. We accept this cause, although (as some object) it does not appear in every case. For if one in a thousand thousand is lucky enough to be immune, that does not make the cause false. The Arabian's opinion therefore stands, if only because the cause put forward by the Frenchman has no value. That also stands: the cause, not the disease itself, is what remains in the blood and produces the eruption at set intervals. Finally, although these two affections are also pestilential when accompanied by fever, it is not always so, as Fernelius maintains with Agricola. Moreover, Galen clearly denies in his commentary that paraplegia (Hippocrates, Epidemics 1, sect. 2, texts 59 and 60) should be counted among pestilential diseases, as Montanus observes.

units.la: § 16. Quia dux noster cap. 27. testatur eandem divam prebere fe confpicien-
units.tr: § 16. Since our leader testifies in chapter 27 that the same goddess shows herself to be seen

units.la: dam in venenofis & contagiosis morbis,, temere huc accersitis: quid opus est cura nostra? Sed agamus cominus, I. Affert Torpedinem marinàm. Quemadmodum non negatur, actionem esse à tota substantia : ita negari non potest, inducere morbum cognitum, intemperiem nervorum frigidam, & quidem quatenus causa est. Quin credere lubet, non esse morbum, sed symptoma primi generis. I I. Opium adducit. De hoc sciendum est, esse inter medicamenta, quae nobis simplicia venturcum reapse compositum fit. Licet enim in confesso fit, frigidum esse in 4. gr. adeoque frigiditate interficere habet tamen calidas partes multas, quae vehiculum praebent frigidis, ut eo citius enecet. Interim sum ejus sententiae, ἐφ' ᾧ potius Dvvapeu agere, quam manifesta. Quidquid fit, iterum occentandum est hoc Fernelio, causam esse, non morbum. Damus enim Malvaticum illis, qui plus juvo ejus hauserunt. Et haec est antidotus ipsius. III. Rabies est canina, unde Hydrophobia. De hoc quam certum est agere totâ substantiâ: tam certum est caufam intemperiem calidam & siccam, cujus antidotus ex Aetio effet aqua frigida copiose hausta, fi modo admitterent. Antendit eo pulvis cancrorum marinorum. Dis Æschrionis? Habent enim νόσους? Taterim & heic causa tantum est. I V. Vno manipulo scorpionum, omniumque ioβόλων, quemadmodum & telorum veneno infectorum, ictus. Refponsio est eadem: Sunt causæ morborum notorum, & quæ cura per antidotos affertur, opponitur eidem causæ, Et hæc de venenatis.
units.tr: in venomous and contagious diseases, rashly brought in here: what need is there of our concern? But let us come to close quarters. I. He cites the marine torpedo fish. Just as it is not denied that its action comes from its whole substance, so it cannot be denied that it induces a known disease, a cold intemperament of the nerves, insofar as it is the cause. Indeed, I am inclined to believe it is not a disease but a symptom of the first kind. II. He cites opium. About this it must be understood that among medicines, those which come to us as simples are in fact compound. For although it is agreed that opium is cold in the fourth degree, and so kills by its coldness, it nevertheless has many warm parts which provide a vehicle for the cold, so that it kills more quickly. Meanwhile I hold the opinion that it acts in virtue of a certain property [ἐφ' ᾧ] rather than by manifest qualities. Whatever the case, this must again be set against Fernelius: it is the cause, not the disease. For we give malmsey to those who have drunk too much of it, and this is its antidote. III. There is the bite of a rabid dog, whence hydrophobia. About this, it is as certain that it acts by its whole substance as it is certain that the cause is a hot and dry intemperament, whose antidote, according to Aëtius, would be cold water drunk copiously, if only they would allow it. Against it is applied powder of sea crabs. Why Aeschrion's? Do they have diseases [νόσους]? Therefore here too the cause alone is at issue. IV. The sting of a single handful of scorpions, and of all venomous creatures [ἰοβόλων], as also of weapons infected with poison. The answer is the same: these are causes of known diseases, and the cure by antidotes is opposed to the same cause. And so much for poisonous things.

units.la: § 17. Inter contagiosos in primâ acie collocat Iuem Venerism. De hac in specie declarat Fernelium Montanus pro reo,ab Adrastéa accusato juxta, & legitimè damnato, Saniem illam, quam alastor aliquis in συνεχία,osculove, ut & in consudatis lectis accipit, esse Causam efficientem intemperiei, non frigidæ & humidæ(qua in re pueriliter lapsus est Rondeletius)sed calidæ & siccæ. Hoc docuisse ait Cassanum, Fracanzanum & Frifimelicam,persuadetque hoc Massaria,alii. At curamus Guajaci decocto, quod calidum & siccum est. Solemus etiam ulcera, gummata, aliaque symptomata infignire peculiari hoc nomine, videlicet quod Gallica sint. Primum, do instantiam. Curamus etiam Chinæ decocto, quo Ægyptii pinguefaciunt uxores suas, authore Pr. Alpino, de Med, AEg. Sed scio, quid responderi possit: dico igitur sum Montano, Curatio illa sumiturà causa,
units.tr: § 17. Among contagious diseases, in the first rank he places the venereal pox. On this in particular Montanus declares Fernelius guilty, accused and rightly condemned by Adrasteia, that the pus which some evil spirit [ἀλάστωρ] receives through continual contact [συνεχία], or by a kiss, and likewise in infected beds, is the efficient cause of an intemperature, not cold and moist (in which matter Rondelet slipped childishly) but hot and dry. He says this was taught by Cassanus, Fracanzanus and Fracastorius [Frisimelica?], and Massaria and others persuade of it. Yet we treat it with a decoction of guaiacum, which is hot and dry. We are also accustomed to mark ulcers, gummata and other symptoms with this special name, namely that they are "Gallic." This is the first instance I give. We also treat it with a decoction of China, by which the Egyptians make their wives plump, on the authority of Prosper Alpinus, in his work on Egyptian medicine. But I know what can be answered: I say therefore to Montanus that the cure is taken from the cause,

units.la: eaufa,quam disjicere & perdere volumus sudoribus,&c. Fortassis igitur Causa continens est?Non est:sæpe enim remota hac causa manet Intemperies,nimis jam fortiter impressa. Propterea , quo maturius curatio instituitur , eo felicior solet esse.
units.tr: which we wish to dispel and destroy by sweats, and so on. Perhaps then the cause is containing? It is not: for often, with this cause removed, the intemperature remains, already too strongly impressed. For that reason, the sooner the treatment is begun, the more successful it usually is.

units.la: § 18. Post d. luem Elephantiafis est,in qua Montanus hominem valde duriter tractat , quod temere obstrepat Gal. omnibufque doctis , qui nunquam quidquam heic veneni invenerint. Mihi fatis fit hoc indicaffe.
units.tr: § 18. After the said pox comes elephantiasis, in which Montanus treats the man very harshly, because he rashly clamours against Galen and all the learned, who never found any poison here. For me it is enough to have indicated this.

units.la: § 19. Post Elephantiafin Fpilepfia est, quam saltu supero,ut feorfim de illa agere, possim , cum solā hac attestatione, Morbum formæ non esse.
units.tr: § 19. After elephantiasis comes epilepsy, which I shall leap over, so that I may deal with it separately, with this single testimony only: that it is not a formal disease.

units.la: § 20. Atque ut libenter fateor, magnam esse cognationem Epilepsiæ cum tribus illis morbis,de quibus cap,3 2.agit Montanus,suffocatione uterina, syncope & palpitatione , quatenus à vapore sunt : ita pernego,esse à veneno intus genito,a quo morbi sunt formales. Sed vocet vel blityri, vel fcindapfum. In suffocatione uterinā,vapor ille ex putri vel femine, vel fanguine, vel utroque ortus , nihil aliud est quam Causa. illa est in intemperie uteri, vasorumque feminalium , non frigida, ut Montanus vult : sed calida , quæ, non minus ac ventriculo , indicibiles.
units.tr: § 20. I gladly admit that epilepsy is closely related to those three diseases that Montanus treats in chapter 32: uterine suffocation, syncope and palpitation, insofar as they arise from a vapour. But I flatly deny that it arises from a poison generated within the body, from which the formal diseases come. Let him call it either "blityri" or "scindapsum." In uterine suffocation that vapour, arising from putrid seed or blood or both, is nothing other than the cause. The cause lies in an intemperature of the uterus and the seminal vessels, and it is not cold, as Montanus holds, but hot, and it produces, no less than in the stomach, indescribable corruptions.

units.la: corruptiones causatur. At flatus fiunt à frigiditate, dicat aliquis pro Montano? An opus est heic distinctione, siquidem accurati esse volumus? Flatus enim vulgo dicti, qui borborygonos faciunt, doresque colicos,fiunt à manifestis qualitatibus, caliditate, inquam, non proportionata ad materiam : at vapor, de quo loquimur, tota substantia agit, similis corruptioni nidorulentæ in ventriculo, de quo dixi, & dicam mox iterum.
units.tr: But do the flatulences, which Montanus says come from cold, arise from cold? Is a distinction needed here, if we want to be precise? For the flatulences commonly so called, which cause rumbling in the bowels and colicky pains, arise from manifest qualities, namely from a heat not proportionate to the matter. The vapour we are speaking of, however, acts by its whole substance, like the foul corruption in the stomach of which I spoke and of which I will speak again shortly.

units.la: § 21. Syncope, ex corrupto sanguine, non est à frigida cordis intemperie : sed à vapore illo,qui tota substantia est alienus à natura cordis,adeoque non refrigerante,sed comprimente, & compressione sua obstruente orificia vasorum cordis, quo minus fiat caloris distributio. Est igitur in extremis frigus privativum.
units.tr: § 21. Syncope arising from corrupt blood does not come from a cold intemperature of the heart, but from that vapour which, in its whole substance, is foreign to the nature of the heart, and so acts not by cooling but by compressing, and by its compression blocks the openings of the heart's vessels, so that the distribution of heat does not take place. In the extremities, therefore, there is a privative cold.

units.la: § 22. Palpitatio cordis est à calore, faciente intumefcentiam sanguinis in corde. In his tribus affectibus quid est formale?
units.tr: § 22. Palpitation of the heart comes from a heat that causes the blood to swell in the heart. In these three affections, what is formal?

units.la: § 23. Venena externa, aconitum, taxus, ephemerum, cantharides, quæ cap. 33. intruduntur tanquam furcillis, quid aliud sunt, quam causæ, morbos tamen notos causantes, ut sæpe est dictum?
units.tr: § 23. External poisons, aconite, yew, ephemerum, cantharides, which in chapter 33 are introduced as if on forks, what else are they than causes, causing diseases that are nonetheless known, as has often been said?

units.la: § 24. Cap.34. & ult:miror cur repetat Montanus cramben, supra tam claré refurefutatam,& toties!Causa à tota fubftantia facit morbum à tota substantia. Vt pauca dicam, Inprimis hoc mihi moleftum est,quod credi volunt,Morbos formæ Fernelii esse eosdem cum Morbis totius substantiæ Gal. Nihil minus. Tota enim substantia est elementare quid : at Forma illa est cælestis, astralis,uno verbo, Causa continens Stoicorum. Deinde dohanc instantiam. Cum cibi in ventriculo calidiore corrumpuntur, quam mira est varietas symptomatum? Alii videntur sibi percipere odorem ovorum frixorum, quamvis non comederint ova. Alii putres pisces,alii indicibile quid. Hæc tamen omnia ab uno calore, ratione individuorum variante,inducta sunt. Vide I. Alexandrinum l.de Theriaca.Propterea persto in eo.in quo Montanus quoque : Tota substantia parit morbos notos : tamen curatio illorum non perinde succedit per indicationes rationales, sed opus est experientia.
