Hinc adeo fit, ut aliquando frustra sint omnia remedia. Cur? Nescimus modum corruptionis humorum. Hujus rei exemplum præbuit nobis ante hos aliquot menses D D. ZACHARIAS BRENDEL, Iunior, ut de indicio amicorum Ienenfium habeo. Ex his jam patet, (concludit Montanus) D quam præclara sint inventa Fernelii,quibus artem ampliasse se gloriatur in præf. Ampliavit, dicam ego, si nomen hoc debetur sementi putidarum litium, quod Sophistarum esse, Galenus alicubi scribit.
units.tr: § 24. In chapter 34 and the last one, I wonder why Montanus repeats the cabbage, already so clearly and so often refuted! A cause acting by its whole substance produces a disease by its whole substance. To say a few things briefly: first, I am troubled by this, that they want the formal diseases of Fernelius to be the same as the diseases of the whole substance of Galen. Nothing could be less so. For the whole substance is something elemental, but that form is celestial, astral; in a word, it is the "containing cause" of the Stoics. Next, consider this example. When food is corrupted in a hotter stomach, how wonderful is the variety of symptoms! Some seem to perceive the smell of fried eggs, although they have eaten no eggs; others, rotten fish; others something indescribable. Yet all of these are induced by one heat, varying according to the individual. See Alexandrinus, in his book on theriac. Therefore I stand by what Montanus also holds: the whole substance produces known diseases, yet their cure does not succeed in the same way by rational indications, but experience is needed. Hence it comes about that sometimes all remedies are in vain. Why? We do not know the manner of corruption of the humours. An example of this was recently given to us some months ago by Dr. Zacharias Brendel, the younger, as I have from the report of Jena friends. From these things it is now clear (Montanus concludes) how excellent are the discoveries of Fernelius, by which he boasts that he has enlarged the art, in his preface. He has enlarged it, I would say, if that name is due to the sowing of rotten quarrels, which Galen somewhere writes is the mark of the Sophists.

units.la: De Convulsione contra Erastum, CAPVT. VIII.
units.tr: On Convulsion, against Erastus, Chapter VIII.

units.la: § 1. Vandoquidem in maleferiata ista forma restat nobis Epilepsia ; illius vero natura inclarescere non potest, nisi certi quid de Convulsionibus dicatur : age dum sumamus in manus Erasti * disputationem, celebrem magis, quam doctam, quam ille Heidelbergæ anno 1575. habitam,appendit Anatomæ suæ. Est etiam inter eas, quæ Tiguri sunt excusæ 1595.
units.tr: § 1. Since epilepsy remains for us in this ill-wrought form, its nature cannot be made clear unless something definite is said about convulsions. Come, let us take in hand the disputation of Erastus, more famous than learned, which he delivered at Heidelberg in 1575 and appended to his Anatomy. It is also among those printed at Zurich in 1595.

units.la: § 2. In D. r. statim admiratione dignum est, quod vir tantus confundit σπασμὸν ἡγὴ σπάσμα ! Σπασμὸς est asse- ctus ille, de quo agimus : σπάσμα est solutio continui quædam. Hac de re ego sæpè Notis in Gal.. Ibidem, cum meminerit motus arbitrarii, eundemque D.3, ex sententia Medicorum distinguat à naturali : officii ipsius erat, ex fundamentis ista explicare, hoc forte modo. Apud Arift. quidem distinctionis hujus vesti- * Quid ipse judicet, vide in Epist.n.33. gium.
units.tr: § 2. In the Dr. [D. r.] passage it is at once remarkable that so great a man confuses spasmos [σπασμὸς] with spasma [σπάσμα]. Spasmos is the affection we are discussing; spasma is a certain solution of continuity. I have often treated this matter in my Notes on Galen. There, although he mentions voluntary motion and in D.3 distinguishes it from natural motion according to the opinion of the physicians, it was his duty to explain these things from their foundations, perhaps in this way. Among Aristotle there is indeed no trace of this distinction.

units.la: * Quid ipse judicet, vide in Epist. n. 33. gium nullum est: Galenus autem usu sic deposcente, à Stoicis sumtum discrimen inter Naturam & Animam, hunc quidem Naturalem vocavit,illum autem Animam- lem, Arbitrarium, Voluntarium, laté accepto vocabulo, ut brutis etiam competit.
units.tr: * For what he himself judges, see Epist. n. 33. [the trace is missing]. But Galen, as usage demanded, took from the Stoics the distinction between Nature and Soul. He called the one natural and the other animal, arbitrary, voluntary, using the word in a broad sense, as it applies also to the brute beasts.

units.la: illæsus, vel non agat sua, vel prave, fi vid. vel non habeat spiritus, vel male difpofitos. Et hic est sensus Gal. 1, Loc. affect, ult, nec vel somnium pugnæ ibi est.
units.tr: either does not act its own action, or acts badly, if it lacks spirits or has badly disposed ones. And this is the sense of Galen in Loc. affect., last book; nor is there any dream of a fight there.

units.la: § 4. In D.2. & 5. nescio an fatis Medicè loquatur, Convulsionem duo significare, Imo vero ex 2 Meth. 2. dicere debuerat, Morbum hunc nomen habere à symptomate. Quamobrem etiam D. 6 laborat. Cum enim symptoma incurrat in sensus, non indiget ullà curà: indiget autem causa, ut tollatur. In D. 7. quid est, Musculos non prorsus naturaliter esse affectos? Si enim sunt τρὸς ἄχον, utrinque simpliciter laborant. Verum, cum hoc adversetur commento ipsius, usus est hac verborum circuitione.
units.tr: § 4. In D. 2 and 5 I do not know whether he speaks medically enough, in saying that convulsion signifies two things. Indeed, from 2 Meth. 2 he ought to have said that this disease has its name from a symptom. Wherefore D. 6 also labours. For since a symptom falls under the senses, it needs no cure; but the cause needs to be removed. In D. 7, what is the meaning of "the muscles are not altogether naturally affected"? For if they are [πρὸς ἄχον] [pros achon], they suffer simply in both respects. But since this runs against his own invention, he used this circumlocution of words.

units.la: § 5. In D. 9. quam veré docet, Motum esse actionem organicam, impedimentum motus à mo: bo organico: tam involutè id proponit. Vbi enim sunt partes, motum constituentes? Caeterum, non debet heic morari quenquam, quod mufculos aliquin habeo inter partes simila res. Sunt similares fecundum dici, non fecundum esse, ut me explico Tract. de Part. fimil. Concurrunt enim ad actiones perfectorum organorum, oculi, brachii, pedis.
units.tr: § 5. In D. 9 he teaches truly that motion is an organic action, and that an impediment to motion comes from an organic obstacle, but he proposes this so obscurely. For where are the parts that constitute motion? Moreover, no one should linger here over the fact that I otherwise count muscles among the similar parts. They are similar according to name, not according to being, as I explain in my treatise On Similar Parts. For they concur in the actions of the perfect organs: the eyes, the arm, the foot.

units.la: § 6. Hinc expediet fe illæcuiex D. 10.
units.tr: § 6. Hence it will be useful to disentangle that matter from D. 10.

units.la: hoc dubium oriatur » Quomodo pars fimilaris possit esse musculus , qui constet extribus partibus,Carne, tendine & nervo? Non est pars similaris fecundum esse. Imo vero, nisi addideris, Fibras, partem potiffimam,quippe in qua roburipforum consistit,errabis. Hæc unde fit,cognosces ex iis Gal. locis, quibus generationem musculorum docet. An dicet Eraftus, fe sub tendinibus comprehendisse?Non poteft. Nam D. 11. fatetur , non omnes musculos tendines habere, 1.Met. muf. 3. Quia ipsa D. quia incipit dispicere, quæ fit pars princeps musculi ? jure veneritalicui in animum,Rectene,an secus id fiat? Iam alibi διαίρεσις dixi, duce Ill. D. ab Aquapendente. Vbicunque opus aliquod perfectum editur à pluribus partibus, καὶ ἐντελεχείαν agentibus , non esse quærendam partem principem in hac, vel illa : quin unam aliquam totam esse illam. In oculo jure quæriturilla, quia visio fit ab oculo solo. In motu non poteft : quia fit à tot partibus , quot dictæ sunt. Quæigitur eftilla ? dicis fortasse. Musculus totus. Ita in brachio, musculi hunc locum principem habent, 1. Vf. part. Vt res fiat manifestior ,accipe hoc quoque. Valde fe effundit Gal.6. Sent. Hipp.8.de omnibus visceribus sanguineis
units.tr: Here a doubt arises: how can a similar part be a muscle, which consists of three parts, flesh, tendon and nerve? It is not a similar part according to being. Indeed, unless you add fibres, the chief part, since the strength of the muscle consists in them, you will go wrong. You will learn whence this comes from those passages of Galen in which he teaches the generation of muscles. Will Erastus say that he has comprehended them under the tendons? He cannot, for in D. 11 he admits that not all muscles have tendons (Met. mus. 3). Since he himself begins to examine which is the principal part of a muscle, it has rightly come into my mind to ask whether this is done correctly or otherwise. I have already spoken elsewhere of division (διαίρεσις [diairesis]), following the illustrious Fabricius ab Aquapendente. Wherever a perfect work is produced by several parts acting together and in actuality (ἐντελέχεια [entelecheia]), one should not seek a principal part in this or that one; rather, the whole of it is that one. In the eye that question is rightly asked, because vision comes from the eye alone. In motion it cannot be asked, because motion comes from as many parts as have been named. What then is it? you may perhaps say. The whole muscle. So in the arm the muscles hold this principal place (1. Us. part.). To make the matter plainer, take this too. Galen writes very copiously, in his commentary on the sixth book of Hippocrates' Sentences, on all the blood-containing viscera

units.la: loquens, & 4. Vf, part.12. de hepate in specie,in laudes carnis hujus,hanc fc.esse in singulis propriam uniuscujusque vi- fceris substantiam, partem principem, ut alibi loquitur. At vero fi intimius infpicias,caro illa nihil aliud est,quam tomentum (ϡlix ny sǫiβns ait ) vasis circumjecta, ne in motu violentiore periclitentur. Ita in musculis quoque fe habet. Vt dicere possim, per te , ò Erafte,ut tendo non est pars princeps,propter causam dictam;ut nervus non est, propter tria argumenta, D.12.narratacita caro non est,(ed praebet tantum fibris tomenti usum.
units.tr: speaking, and in book 4 of the Ars, chapter 12, on the liver in particular, in praise of this flesh, that it is in each organ the proper substance of that organ, its principal part, as he says elsewhere. But if you look more closely, that flesh is nothing other than a padding (as he says) placed around the vessel, so that it is not endangered in more violent motion. So it is also with the muscles. I can say, through you, O Erastus, that as the tendon is not the principal part, for the reason given, and as the nerve is not, for the three arguments set out at D. 12, so the flesh is not, but merely supplies the padding's use to the fibres.

units.la: § 7. Quid nervi ad motum conserant,duplex erat veterum opinio,Altera, trahere musculos instar habenarum : altera , esse tubos seu canales facultatis, Priorem nimis operose refutat à D. 12. usque ad 26. Posteriorem nudis verbis asserit D. 27.
units.tr: § 7. As to what nerves contribute to motion, there were two opinions among the ancients. One was that they draw the muscles like reins; the other was that they are tubes or channels of the faculty. He refutes the former at too great length, from D. 12 to 26, and asserts the latter in bare words at D. 27.

units.la: § 8. Inhoc discursu tria mihi difplicent. 1. quod. D. 17. tractionem ideo negat, quod nervi inferantur etiam in alias partes mobiles , os ventriculi , veficam, renes &c. quae tamen non moveantur. Diversitatis ratio hac est,quod nulla praeter musculos pars eam habeat constitutionem , ut impleri possit, & brevior fe ipsa fieri. Musculus autem solus
units.tr: § 8. Three things in this discourse displease me. (1) At D. 17 he denies traction on the ground that nerves are inserted also into other moving parts, the mouth of the stomach, the bladder, the kidneys and so on, which nevertheless do not move. The reason for the difference is this: no part except the muscle has that structure by which it can be filled and become shorter of its own accord. The muscle alone

units.la: ventrem habeat, inania inter fibras fpacia, quibus, instar follis, occupatis ab spiritu animali, fit rigidus. II. quod D. 18. tantum tribuit huic suo argumento, ut amplius urgeat. Non enim sufficit exortus, substantia & temperies: oportet adsit quoque (& quidem principaliter) conformatio. III. quod D. 20, improbat simile Gal. 1, Sent.Hipp.9. à vecti defumtum. Gal. enim non dicit, nervum immobilem movere musculum: sed musculum, per nervum accepto spiritu animali, factum rigidum instar vectis, movere loco offa.
units.tr: has within its belly empty spaces between the fibres, which, being filled by the animal spirit, become rigid, like a bellows. (2) At D. 18 he gives so much weight to this argument of his that he presses it further. For origin, substance and temperament are not enough; conformation must also be present, and principally so. (3) At D. 20 he disapproves the comparison, taken from a lever, which Galen makes in Sent. Hipp. 9. For Galen does not say that an immobile nerve moves the muscle; he says that the muscle, having received the animal spirit through the nerve and been made rigid, moves the bone from its place like a lever.

units.la: § 9. Quo minus morari quenquam potest metus, quem D. 21, sumit à mollitie nervorum. Non enim nervus movet, sed musculus, eo modo habilitatus, ut sic dicam. Multò minus id, quod D.22. crepat, Nervos non disseminari per totos musculos. Sufficit enim spiritui quoquo modo præberi aditum. Et quei tufcire potes, quam altè fe immergat nervus? Cum enim fibrulæ sint minutiffimæ, finiles ... ἀπεσπασμένοις, statim abrumpuntur, fi trahas. Præterea, cum substantiam ferant tenuissimam, non opus habent eâ capacitate, qua venæ & arteriæ. Quam etiam ob rem, non est opus
units.tr: § 9. The fear he draws at D. 21 from the softness of the nerves can detain no one, still less does what he rattles off at D. 22, that nerves are not spread through all the muscles. For it is enough that the spirit be given access in some way. And how deeply can you tell that the nerve sinks in? Since the little fibres are very minute, similar to those torn away, they break off at once if you pull. Moreover, since they carry a very thin substance, they do not need the capacity that veins and arteries have. For this reason there is no need

units.la: oculis advocatis, ex. 1. Loc. aff.6, Humanis , inquam , cum nec aquilini eò fe penetrent. Hoc ipsum absolvit nos à parvitate, quam urget D, 23. Hoc idem à modo infertionis, D 24. Sufficit,ut dixi, spiritui patere viam , cum musculus moveat, non nervus. Quin fatetur ipse D. 27. 35. 68. & alibi, Nervi hoc tantum esse officiu,ut deferat vim agendi.
units.tr: to call in eyes, as in Loc. aff. 6, human ones, I mean, since not even eagles' eyes penetrate there. This very point frees us from the smallness which he presses at D. 23. The same holds for the mode of insertion, D. 24. It is enough, as I said, that a path be open to the spirit, since the muscle moves, not the nerve. Indeed he himself concedes at D. 27, 35, 68 and elsewhere that the nerve has only this office, to convey the power of acting.

units.la: § 10. Quam recte igitur concludit D.25. Certo certius esse, musculos non ideo contrahi &c. negando primum usum, §. 7; qua bene declarat alterum D. 27. tam finiftre repetit D. 29. axioma suum de carnis principatu. Vtenim dixi, usum praebet tantum fibris, ne in validiffimis istis motibus periclitentur. Fit autem motus,ut pariter dixi, non trahendo,sed implendo, instar utris seu sacci. Quo magis perfifto in sententia , veteres ob hanc solam causam tribuisse musculis ventrem,quamvis λέγω potius Σωθηνῶν, quam ἀεὶ ἡδύν, ut Græce dicam.
units.tr: § 10. How rightly, then, does he conclude at D. 25 that, with more than certain certainty, the muscles are not contracted on that account, and so on, thereby denying the first use (§ 7). He declares the second well at D. 27. How wrongly he repeats at D. 29 his axiom about the primacy of the flesh! For, as I said, the flesh provides use only to the fibres, so that they are not endangered in these very violent motions. Motion happens, as I likewise said, not by drawing but by filling, like a bladder or a leather sack. The more I persist in this view, the more I think the ancients attributed the belly to the muscles for this reason alone, though to put it in Greek I would rather say [Σωθηνῶν] than [ἀεὶ ἡδύν].

units.la: § 11. Quæigitur ,inquis , pars princeps est in musculo? In ipso musculo nulla est: sed musculus, in illa congerie partium,ad motum necessarium supra § 3. est pars princeps. Hinc adeo fit, ut recte scribat D. 30. Depravatam musculi contractionem, esse primam & proximam
units.tr: § 11. What, then, you ask, is the principal part in a muscle? In the muscle itself there is none; but the muscle, within that aggregate of parts needed for motion (see § 3 above), is the principal part. Hence he rightly writes at D. 30 that the depraved contraction of the muscle is the first and nearest

units.la: Convulsionis causam. Quas vero subnectit D. 31. Causas secundarias, non unam habent ἐνσεσιν. Prima & levicula est,fi modo est, quod Convulsionem facere videtur morbum in figura. Figura enim illa est paroxysmi, seu τῶ πνῖζος non morbi. Evidentior est altera, quod nimis inconditam farraginem illarum struit. Evidentiffima tertia, quod non distinguat Vapores ab Humoribus. Illi enim huc pertinent,non hi, nisi quà materiam præbent vaporibus.
units.tr: cause of convulsion. But the secondary causes he adds at D. 31 do not agree with one another. The first, and a rather slight one, is that convulsion seems to make a disease of form, if indeed it does; for that form belongs to the paroxysm, or to the suffocation [τῷ πνίγος], not to the disease. The second is more evident: he piles up a very disordered hodgepodge of these causes. The third is most evident of all: he does not distinguish vapours from humours. For the former belong here, not the latter, except insofar as humours supply matter to the vapours.

units.la: §. 12. Hæc posterior culpa fit confpectior, quod D.32. de propinquis caufis acturus, iterum temere projicit humores & vaporcs. Nec fatis exputate possum, quo modo Repletio & Inanitio possint esse causæ propinquæ: imo vero nec pro remotis agnosco. Tanto magis, quod ἐx πνεύμα ponat humorem,vaporemveacrem, quem pro tertia causa acceptat. Nec potest effugere crimen negligentiæ, cum non distinguit Epilepsiam (ad hanc enim delabitur) per consensum ab ea,quæ per essentiam,siquidem bonus Galenifta esse vult. Imo sum ejus fententiæ,Convulsionem non proportionatam ad materiam esse Cramfum nostrum. Qui ut est à vapore (solo) apud adversarios quoque: ita omnis Epilepsia,omnis convulfio est ab illo,ut probabitur infra.
units.tr: § 12. This latter fault is more conspicuous, because at D. 32, about to treat of the proximate causes, he again rashly throws in humours and vapours. Nor can I sufficiently work out how repletion and emptying could be proximate causes; indeed I do not even admit them as remote. All the more so because he posits as a humour the vapour or windy air which he takes as the third cause. Nor can he escape the charge of carelessness, since he does not distinguish epilepsy by sympathy (for into this it slips) from epilepsy by essence, if he wishes to be a good Galenist. Indeed I hold the opinion that a convulsion not proportionate to its matter is our cramp, which, as it arises from vapour (alone), is so also among our adversaries. So every epilepsy, every convulsion, comes from that, as will be proved below.

units.la: § 13. D. 33. excusare fas est, quod loquatur ex aliena sententia, Refutat enim inanias illorum, qui interrogati, Quomodo Repletio & Inanitio causent convulsionem? responsant, Quatenus utraque nervos contrahit, brevioresque facit. Hoc enim, ut-fere loquitur D. 37, homo nullus credet, qui Anatomiæ gnarus fit, & rem ipsam examinarit. Revera dexterrimum de hoc λέγειν λόγῳ Averrois est judicium 3: Coll. 33. esse verba Musicorum, hoc est Cerletanorum, & Montembancorum, quos Itali vocant. Hoc tanto acceptius est mihi, quod video Eraftum quoque damnaffe falsam hypothefin, ut vocat D. 34, & pulcre explicuiffe D.37. Imo addo, Quam irrationabile est in cerebro per essentiam affecto, exhypothefi:tam absurdum eftin affectu ter consensum. V trobique enim fymptomata sunt gemina, quæ omnia ducunt nos ad Vaporem, de quo dicetur.
units.tr: § 13. At D. 33 one may rightly excuse him for speaking from another's opinion. For he refutes the silliness of those who, when asked how repletion and emptying cause convulsion, answer: insofar as each contracts the nerves and makes them shorter. For, as he says roughly at D. 37, no one who knows anatomy and has examined the matter itself will believe this. Indeed the most skilful judgment on this, to use Averroes' phrase, is at 3 Coll. 33, that these are the words of musicians, that is, of the Cerretani and the Montimbanchi, as the Italians call them. This is the more welcome to me because I see that Erastus too condemned the false hypothesis, as he calls it, at D. 34, and explained it beautifully at D. 37. I add further: just as it is irrational in a brain affected in its essence, on the hypothesis, so it is absurd in an affection by sympathy. For both have twin symptoms, all of which lead us to vapour, of which more will be said.

units.la: § 14. Quæ cum ita fe habeant, ne opus quidem est triplici Gal. testimonio, D.35. & 36. ex 1.Mot. mufc. de Conftit.4. de Palp. & trem.3. Quibus cum nihil clarius, certius, efficacius excogitari possit, multo minus opus erat longa illa contra Repletionem & Inanitionem ἐξηγήσεις, à D. 38. usque ad D.68. Sed ita est : voluit pervicacię & stupori recalcitrantium obviam ire, Legant igitur ii potius, qui falsis delectantur præveris: at bonæ mentis juvenes ad utiliora properent.
units.tr: § 14. Since these things stand so, there is not even need for the threefold testimony of Galen at D. 35 and 36, from De motu musculorum, De constitutione 4, and De palpitatione et tremore 3. Nothing clearer, surer or more effective can be devised than these, and there was much less need for that long explanation against repletion and emptying, from D. 38 to D. 68. But so it is: he wished to meet the obstinacy and dullness of the recalcitrants. Let those rather read who delight in false prejudices, but let young men of sound mind hasten to more useful things.

units.la: § 15. Ego obiter duo moneo, propter Avicennam & Averroëm. Illum D. 58. accusat, quod scripserit, nervos per convulsiones impleri crasso humore, cum tenui dicere debuerit, fi omnino ita fieret. Ego in mea ed. Venetiâ anni 1507. in 4, reperio ista verba Autor propter ventum grossum, retentum in transitibus spiritus, fecundum quod visum est Philosopho magno Arifl. Et vidit, addit, ipsam esse unam causarum Epilepsiæ. Quo ex loquendi modo fatis patet, Principem nihil definire, sed acervare tantum Veterum sententias. Hunc D.61 ait probabilia fcripfiffe, cum à flatu distendi censuerit: verum imaginarium hoc esse. Ego in mea pariter Venetiâ ed. anni 1514. inf. reperio, Meminisse quidem humoris aërei, qui diftendat, sed nihil determinaffe. Hoc etiam offendo, Ferre Arabem judicium, non de suâ sententiâ, sed de Hippocraticâ. An dicere mihi licet, Eraftum sententiam suam, de qua mox, hausisse ex iis, que immediatè substant? Sed quando fit hæc contractio, nascitur bellum inter duos motus, etc. Manifesté discedit ille quoque à Gal. in genere symptomatis, de quo mox. Quidquid fit:
units.tr: § 15. I make two brief remarks, on account of Avicenna and Averroes. He accuses Avicenna at D. 58 because he wrote that the nerves are filled during convulsions with thick humour, whereas he should have said thin, if it happened at all. In my edition, Venice 1507, in quarto, I find these words: the author, on account of a thick wind held back in the passages of the spirit, as it seemed to the great philosopher Aristotle. And he saw, he adds, that this itself is one of the causes of epilepsy. From this way of speaking it is quite clear that the prince defines nothing, but merely heaps together the opinions of the ancients. He says of this one at D. 61 that he wrote probable things when he judged it distended by flatus; but this is imaginary. In my likewise Venetian edition of 1514, further down, I find that he indeed recalls an airy humour which distends, but determined nothing. I also find this objectionable: the Arab sets forth the judgment not of his own opinion but of the Hippocratic one. May I say that Erastus drew his own opinion, of which presently, from those things which lie immediately beneath? But when this contraction occurs, war arises between two motions, etc. He also clearly departs from Galen in the genus of the symptom, of which presently. Whatever the case:

units.la: § 16. Elevat D.61. flatum, seu vaporem nostrum exemplo spasmi vulgaris, quem Cramfum vocamus. Hic vult dicere, quia fanis omnibus supervenit, et facile solvitur, fi convulsiones quoque inde effent, nec tam periculose effent, nec tam curatu difficiles. Eja vero, vir magne, fi nobis omnibus familiaris spasmus, unius quippe & alterius musculi motus fuperficiarius, tam contemtibilis est, fueritne etiam univerfalis? Non, credo, diceres, fi, quemadmodum ego, videres & curaffes illum. Sed & universalis ille multis parafangis abest à diritate Tetani & affinium, quippe qui aliquando subito occidunt. Referam tamen & de spasmo nostro ridiculum quid. Senex quidam, qui spasmum noftrum senserat nunquam, nisi uno, alterove mense aute mortem, cum fupervenifset tum, conclamavit familiam magna voce, O helft/helft/ Der Tod faft mich am Fuß an! Puras hunc avaiofu, fuisse? Dico igitur, Cramfus est ima convulsionis species, & consistit quidem in vapore, qui tota substantia peccat: sed qui & quantitate & qualitate exiguus est, Reliquæ convulsiones à vapore sunt & copiofo , & infigniter malitioso , genito ex corruptione indicibili , differentiam habentem ex individuis,&c.Quo loco forté illud moneri debet , D. 78. iterum contemni Cramfum, quod convulsio fit improprie dicta. Hoc quanti fit ponderis, videt quilibet.
units.tr: § 16. He also raises the flatus, or our vapour, using the example of the common spasm, which we call the cramp. He wants to say that, since it comes upon all healthy people and is easily relieved, convulsions too would not be so dangerous or so hard to cure if they arose from it. Well then, great man, if the spasm is familiar to all of us, a superficial movement of one muscle or another, why is it so contemptible, even if it is universal? I do not think you would say so if you had seen and treated it as I have. But that universal spasm is also many parasangs away from the rigidity of tetanus and its kin, which sometimes kill suddenly. Still, I will relate something ridiculous about our spasm. An old man, who had never felt our spasm except once or twice in the month before his death, when it came upon him then, cried out to the household in a loud voice: "O help, help! Death is seizing me by the foot!" Do you think he was joking? I say, then, that the cramp is the lowest form of convulsion, and it consists indeed in a vapour which affects the whole substance, but a vapour that is small both in quantity and in quality. The other convulsions arise from a vapour that is both copious and remarkably malignant, generated from an indescribable corruption, and differing according to the individuals, and so on. At this point it should perhaps be noted that at D. 78 he again despises the cramp, because a convulsion is improperly so called. Anyone can see how much weight this carries.

units.la: § 17. In D.62. observo ἀναxόλυθον in verbis illis, Quibus addi potest, &c. Quomodo enim cohærent cum antecedentibus? Imò,ubi dixit Averroës,Paralyfin præcedere convulsionem, adeoque combibi prius humorem à nervis,qui vel posteà in flatus , vaporesve vertatur, unde convulsio ? vel cui humori succedant aliunde flatus, qui sint convulsionis autores? Quid somniis vicinius , quam ista talia? Hic enim est ordo, Vapores,vel intra cranium geniti, vel ex inferioribus sursum lati,& nervis intrufi , descendunt propter continuationem in musculos , & rigidos faciunt.
units.tr: § 17. At D. 62 I notice an anacoluthon [ἀνακόλουθον] in the words "To which may be added," and so on. For how do they cohere with what precedes? Indeed, where Averroes said that paralysis precedes convulsion, so that the humour is first soaked up from the nerves and afterwards turned into flatus or vapours, whence the convulsion arises; or else flatus comes from elsewhere to follow upon some humour, and these are the authors of the convulsion? What is closer to dreams than such things? For the order is this: vapours, either generated within the skull or carried upwards from the lower parts and forced into the nerves, descend, because of their continuity, into the muscles, and make them rigid.

units.la: § 18. Quam facilè verò dicuntur illa D.63 ? Fieri non posse,ut plures negvi eodem modo impleantur, &c quæ feq. Voluntaria omnia folijs leviora caducis omnia. Si enim humorem mutes in vaporem, cavitatibus nervorum quodammodo analogum, habebis, quod quærebas.
units.tr: § 18. But how easily are those things said in D. 63? That it cannot happen that several nerves are affected in the same way, and so on, all those things lighter than leaves and all as fickle. For if you change the humour into a vapour, which is somewhat analogous to the cavities of the nerves, you will have what you were seeking.

units.la: § 19. Hujus generis sunt illa quoque E D.64.
units.tr: § 19. Of this kind also are those things in E, D. 64.

units.la: D.64. Nec fatis est accufaffe alios dementiæ,cujus ipse fis reus, Viderunt alii quoque nervos tam cerebri, quam spinalis medullæ, antequam durá matre induantur , nec pro impossibili habuerunt id, quod,Arift.duce, doceo. Quo minus neceffarium fuerit examen D.65,& 66. Abfurda enim illa duo facilè male ruunt fuà. Non magnizetiam momenti est explicatio Hipp. D.67, quamvis sciam Saxoniæ quoque meo amicam fuisse. Rondeletii mentio D.68 ἀπεγοσθόνυς est. Conclusio tandem D.69. & 70. tantum non odiosa est illi,qui expectat,quid tandem futurum fit defubjecto convulsionis adæquato.
units.tr: D. 64. It is not enough to accuse others of the madness of which you yourself are guilty. Others too have seen the nerves both of the brain and of the spinal marrow before they are clothed by the dura mater, and they did not regard as impossible what I teach on Aristotle's authority. So much the less necessary, then, will be an examination of D. 65 and 66, for those two absurd points will easily collapse under their own weight. The explanation of Hippocrates at D. 67 is not of great importance either, although I know it was also pleasing to my friend in Saxony. The mention of Rondelet at D. 68 is an "apegosthonus" [ἀπεγοσθόνυς]. The conclusion finally at D. 69 and 70 is almost hateful to anyone who waits to see what will at last become of the subject adequate to convulsion.

units.la: § 20. De quo subjecto antequam dicere occipiam , necessitas me compellit circumspiciendi , ex quo symptomatum genere fit convulsio? Notum est omnibus,tria esse. Aut enim fiunt à natura folà:aut à morbo solo:aut à natura & morbo simul. Dic , Erafte, sub quá classe velis colloeatam tuam sponsam ? Si Galenum sequi maluisses,quam nescio quas cogitationes tuas, constanti calamo scripsisses ex 2. Cauf. fym.1. & 2. infecundo genere esse , àmorbofolo , itaque excussisses humeris tuis, ingens onus. Nunc quia trepidas , nec dicere audes , quod res est, ἀναξεφεύνῶν περιγραφα διάνοις, ut Græ- ci loquuntur, Ego quidem cum attentis oculis, & vigili animo, tanquam Methragyrtes quidam, folicitè perquiror D.tuas, nec vola, nec vestigium occurrit simplicis assertionis. Quid igitur? Ex confequenti tantum elicitur, velle te ex tertio genere esse, in quo suæ quoque partes sint Naturæ. Quà in re quantis opus habeat machinis, iisque omnibus fallacibus, videbimus in feq.
units.tr: § 20. Before I begin to speak about that subject, necessity compels me to look around: to which kind of symptoms does convulsion belong? It is known to all that there are three. For they arise either from nature alone, or from disease alone, or from nature and disease together. Tell me, Erastus, under which class you wish to place your bride? If you had preferred to follow Galen rather than I know not what thoughts of your own, you would have written with a steady pen, from the Causes of Symptoms, books 1 and 2, that it belongs to the second kind, from disease alone, and so you would have shaken off your shoulders a huge burden. But now, because you tremble and dare not say what the matter is, you are, as the Greeks say, "sketching the outline of the thought" [ἀναξεφεύνῶν περιγραφα διάνοις]. I, indeed, with attentive eyes and a watchful mind, like some charlatan, search diligently through your D.'s, and neither a trace nor a footprint of a plain assertion turns up. What then? It is only by inference that one draws out that you wish to belong to the third kind, in which nature too has its parts. What great machinery you need for this, and all of it deceptive, we shall see in what follows.

units.la: § 21. Harum prima, eaque futilis adeò, utad primum contactum diffiliat, est de ταῦτα Δεῖ. D.71. Heic D. 72. statim offendit, cum ad motum requirit tres tantum partes, Cerebrum, nervum & musculum. Vbi enim cor est? quo fine tam præstans actio fiat? Sed poffit excusari: Nervum ille subitò dimittit, me non invito, & concludit, Ergo inerit ea (causa immediata & prima) vel in musculi corpore, vel in cerebro. Mirabilis ratio argumentandi! Cur enim non musculos quoque ablegat, ut nervos, & firmat fe in solo cerebro? Prose&to, hoc non est explicare, sed implicare.
units.tr: § 21. The first of these, and so trivial that it falls apart at the first touch, is the matter of "these things must be" [ταῦτα Δεῖ], D. 71. Here at D. 72 he immediately stumbles, when for motion he requires only three parts, the brain, the nerve, and the muscle. For where is the heart? By what means is so excellent an action performed? But it might be excused: he suddenly dismisses the nerve, not against my will, and concludes: therefore that cause (the immediate and first one) will be present either in the body of the muscle or in the brain. What a marvellous way of arguing! For why does he not also send away the muscles, as he did the nerves, and fix himself in the brain alone? Truly, this is not explaining but entangling.

units.la: § 22. Sed benè fecerit: Musculum quò modo aspellit? Proponit D.73. quinque modos, quibus musculi fiant breviores, E 2 & & refutat omnes.Ego vero brachio arteptum pertraham ad D. 78. & dicam illi in os, Eftinfufficiens enumeratio. Te ipso enim fatente, à flatu quoque fit convulfio. Hac de re jam dixi quædam, & dicam mox plura.
units.tr: § 22. But let him do well: how does he approach the muscle? At D. 73 he proposes five ways in which muscles become shorter, and he refutes them all. But I will seize him by the arm, lead him on as far as D. 78, and say to his face: "The enumeration is insufficient." For by your own admission convulsion also arises from flatus. I have already said some things about this matter, and I shall soon say more.

units.la: § 23. Refutat omnes, dixi, siquidem refutare est ex solido Taciti fundamento loqui,ut quidam jocari solent. Cur enim duos priores modos saltu superat? Nec dici potest, actuarii culpam esse. Quei enim Repletionem accersere potest, qui illam in superioribus tam fuse refellit? Dicat aliquis ex D.52. Non rem,sed modum negavit. Det igitur alium modum. & contentus ero. Ille vero tacet.Congelationem (cio Rondeletium, aliosque admifisse,non heic tantum,sed & in Catalepsi: sed quis credat fieri posse in corpore vivo? An quia pudebat, dissimulavit quidem heic : substituit autem D. 77. frigus vehementius? Dicit ille quidem Insolens esse : ego confidenter, Impossibile esse. Quid illud vero est,quod,post quinque illos modos, addit hunc sextum? Imo, quid illud est, quod, post sex modos, superdat D. 78. septimum? Flatus? ADRAS TEAS hoc factum est. Ejus rei argumentum esto, quod litem de re transfert ad litem de nomine, ut jam
units.tr: § 23. He refutes them all, I said, if indeed to refute is to speak from the solid foundation of Tacitus, as some are wont to joke. For why does he pass over the first two ways with a leap? Nor can it be said that the fault lies with the copyist. For who can call up Repletion, when he refutes it so at length above? Let someone say from D. 52: "He denied not the thing but the manner." Let him then give another manner, and I shall be content. But he is silent. I know that Rondelet and others admitted congelation, not only here but also in catalepsy; but who would believe it can happen in a living body? Did he hide it here out of shame, and substitute at D. 77 a more violent cold? He says indeed that it is "unusual"; I confidently say that it is impossible. And what is that which, after those five ways, he adds this sixth? Or rather, what is that which, after six ways, he adds at D. 78 a seventh? Flatus? "ADRAS TEAS" [ἀδρᾶς τέας] this has been done. Let the proof of this be that he shifts the quarrel about the thing into a quarrel about the name, as I have already forewarned.

units.la: præmonui.Et quid illud est,quod statum controversiæ ita format, Quæri causam motus, qui fiat illæso musculo ? Quei enim hoc per rerum naturam fieri potest? Potestnè credi, Epilepticos tantopere dolere,tantoperè rigidos habere musculos,ut nec à fortissimo viro dirigi possint membra, illæsismusculis? Hoc experiuntur illi, qui pollices contractos eripere illis volunt.
units.tr: And what is that which so frames the state of the controversy: that the cause of motion is sought which arises while the muscle is unharmed? For how can this happen by the nature of things? Can it be believed that epileptics suffer so greatly, and have their muscles so rigid, that their limbs cannot be straightened even by the strongest man while the muscles are unharmed? This is what those experience who want to pull contracted thumbs out of them.

units.la: § 24. Rebus sic stantibus, quæram ab Erasti patrono, unde fit illud Ergò, D.79? item Necessarium illud? Musculum enim affectum minimè esse, tam non probavit,quam ego probare non possum, Nivem esse atram. Et deserit Necessitatem suam istis verbis, Nisi cum à flatu distenditur. Profectò, hæc altera ADR ASTEAS vox est,quam qui non exaudit, surdus est.
units.tr: § 24. With matters standing thus, I will ask the patron of Erastus where that "Therefore" at D. 79 comes from, and likewise that "Necessary" one? For he has no more proved that the muscle is not affected at all than I can prove that snow is black. And he abandons his necessity with these words: "Unless when it is distended by flatus." Truly, this is another "ADRAS TEAS" word, and whoever does not hear it is deaf.

units.la: § 25. Vtigitur libentissimè concedo, fine etiam Gal. autoritate, s.Aph.s . Disp. eâdem, fine etiam ratiónibus, D.80. illatis : ita musculos esse affectos ψαυσεως mihi dicta claré ostendunt. Vt etiam libenter doilli, D.81. maximam esse latitudinem symptomatum Epilepticorum: ita cupio mihi quoque dari,Ex uno flatu, vaporéve pendere omnia. Et quærsum alias confusum illud chaos causarum remotarum cum propinquis? Imprimis Humoris cum Vapore, quos tam diligenter distinguit Gal? Et rursus, inimicæ cerebro aurææ cum qualitate? habetne quadrilitas vim agendi? Atqui Gal. etiam jungit? Loquitur ex ore Pelopis, Valet enim heic Lucretii illud,
units.tr: § 25. Therefore I most willingly grant, even without the authority of Galen (Aphorisms 5, Disputation of the same kind), even without the arguments brought in at D. 80, that the muscles are affected in this way: the words of mine, "touched" [ψαυσεως], clearly show it. And as I also gladly grant, at D. 81, that the range of epileptic symptoms is very wide, so I wish to be given also this: that everything depends on one flatus or vapour. And why otherwise that confused chaos of remote causes mixed with proximate ones? Above all humour with vapour, which Galen distinguishes so carefully? And again, the air hostile to the brain with its quality? Does a quadrilateral have the power of acting? But does Galen not also join them? He speaks from the mouth of Pelops, for that saying of Lucretius applies here:

units.la: Tangere, vel tangi, nisi corpus, nulla potest res,
units.tr: Nothing can touch or be touched except a body.

units.la: § 26. In numerandis convulsionis speciebus. D.84. videtur alter esse Herac litus. Quæ enim est illa, quæ in solis musculis est, non affecto cerebro? An Cramfus noster? Res incertissima! Quæ est illa, quæ per consensum fit, à solâ qualitate reali? Quid est qualitas reali? diftinction à substantiâ halituosâ, mordaci, putrida? Reverâ, ut calor solis non calefacit, sed aër, à Sole calefactus: ita qualitas nulla facit morbum per consensum, nisi alteratis partibus continuis, velut Gal. loquitur, 3. Loc. aff. 7. Quodsi non femper addit, subintelligendum est. Quâ in re ne te fallere videar, hem tibi Eraftum confitentem, D.86.87. & 88.
units.tr: § 26. In enumerating the species of convulsion. D.84. Heraclitus seems to be the other one. For what is that convulsion which exists only in the muscles, without the brain being affected? Is it our Cramfus? A most uncertain matter! And what is that which occurs through sympathy from a quality alone, a real quality? What is a real quality? Is it a distinct thing from a vaporous, biting, or putrid substance? Truly, as the heat of the sun does not warm, but the air warmed by the sun does, so no quality produces disease by sympathy, unless the continuous parts are altered, as Galen says in Loc. aff. 3.7. But if he does not always add this, it must be understood. In this matter, lest I seem to deceive you, behold Erastus confessing it, D.86, 87 and 88.

units.la: § 27. Iamque tandem, post tot, tanquam ambages, D. 90. comparet Ef-fiens convulsionis, contra quam Montanus lib. 3. cap. 31. non minus quam
units.tr: § 27. And at last, after so many circumlocutions, D.90, the efficient cause of convulsion appears, against which Montanus, lib. 3, cap. 31, thunders no less than Salmoneus, as we shall see.

units.la: Salmonéus fulminat,ut videbimus. Nec est cur mireris, me tam animose loqui. Cum homine enim ἐχ ρεπ̃ς ἀτόπῳ non oportet timidè agere. Sed videamus. Ait Eraftus fe ostendisse, Nervos per convulfiones obstructos non esse: sed virtutem movendi liberè deportare. Ostenderis, ò vir magne: non est quæstio de obstructione nervorum, ad musculos euntium, sed de musculis ipsis. Tum verò, fi virtus movendi liberè it, cur non fit motus liberquo modo motus f. n. tamfubito fit p.n? quomodo contrarii effectus possunt habere idem nomen? ut motus voluntarius fit motus convulforius, & motus convulforius fit motus voluntarius? ut idem sint habitus & privatio?lux & tenebræ?
units.tr: Nor is there reason for you to wonder that I speak so boldly. For one must not act timidly with a man [ἐχ ρεπ̃ς ἀτόπῳ] so absurd. But let us see. Erastus says he has shown that the nerves are not obstructed by convulsions, but that the power of moving passes freely. Show it, great man: the question is not about the obstruction of the nerves going to the muscles, but about the muscles themselves. Moreover, if the power of moving passes freely, why is voluntary motion not made freely, as it is when the natural motion is made? How can contrary effects have the same name, so that voluntary motion becomes convulsive motion, and convulsive motion becomes voluntary motion? So that the same things are a habit and a privation, light and darkness?

units.la: § 28. O,inquit D.9 r. dicat tibi Gal.2. Cauf. fym.2. Sive motus f.n. fiat trabentibus nervis musculos ad sua principia: five impletis musculis spiritu animali: eodem modo co convulsiones fiunt. Inlignis audaciane dicam,an malitia? Aut ipse fuit cæcus, aut alios putavit cæcos esse. An tantum sibi autoritatis acquisivisse putavit,ut neminem futurum crederet, qui vel locum inspiceret, velnudè in considerationem vocaret? I. Nulla heic est assertio. II. Sit, & præyaleat modus E posterior: sensus hic erit, Siquidem motus naturalis fit,impletis musculis spiritu animali ita, ut rigeant, vectis adinftar, 1.Sent.Hipp. 10. motus p.n. fiet,vapore quodam crasso,spiritum animalem mentiente. III. Hanc in rem assertio Gal. pura est,non ibi tantum, mox pòst allata verba, sed & c.1. Convulsionem esse de genere depravatorum motuum illorum, qui fiunt afolo morbo, nihil conferente, vel facultate,vel spiritu naturali, accepto vocabulo Natura eo modo,quo Gal, dicit. I V. Huc tam manifeste tendit D. 92.fi absque praejudicio legatur, ut veris meis non fit opus. Tu vero viden' ADRASTEAN?
units.tr: § 28. "O," he says, D.91, "let Galen tell you, Causes of Symptoms 2. Whether natural motion is made by the nerves drawing the muscles to their origins, or by the muscles being filled with animal spirit, convulsions are made in the same way." What a remarkable audacity, shall I call it, or malice? Either he himself was blind, or he thought others were blind. Did he think he had gained so much authority that no one would believe there was anyone who would look at the matter or call it openly into question? I. There is no assertion here. II. Let it be granted, and let the latter clause prevail: the sense will be this: if natural motion is made by the muscles being filled with animal spirit, so that they grow stiff like a lever (Sent. Hipp. 10), then natural motion will be made by a certain thick vapour pretending to be animal spirit. III. Galen's assertion on this point is clear, not only in the words quoted soon afterwards, but also in c. 1, that convulsion belongs to the class of those depraved motions which arise from disease alone, with neither faculty nor natural spirit contributing, taking the word Nature in the sense in which Galen uses it. IV. D.92 tends so manifestly to this, if it is read without prejudice, that my true words are not needed. But do you see the ADRASTEIA?

units.la: § 29. Propter hanc libet mihi paululum immorari, ut falsitas, fi pote, in oculis fit. Vulgaris sermo est, Contracto cerebro, tam validum esse motum, ut simul contrahantur musculi. Hoc per rerum naturam fieri non posse cum Eraftus (ciret (non enim cerebrum tam longe exporrigi potest,quam procul abest musculus,quasi manu attrahendus, ut leviter immutem verba ipsius D.86) quid fecit? Quia, inquit, & nervus & musculus liber est ab obstructione, nec prohibetur effluvium spiritus e cerebro: spiritus ille ciet motus convulforios. Quis
units.tr: § 29. For this reason I wish to linger a little, so that the falsehood may, if possible, be made plain. It is a common saying that when the brain is contracted, the motion is so strong that the muscles are contracted at the same time. That this cannot happen by the nature of things, Erastus (I think) did not see, for the brain cannot stretch out so far as the muscle lies distant from it, as if it were to be drawn by a hand (I lightly alter his words from D.86). What did he do? "Because," he says, "both the nerve and the muscle are free from obstruction, and the outflow of spirit from the brain is not hindered; that spirit stirs up convulsive motions." Who

units.la: Gorgo
units.tr: Gorgon

units.la: Quis heic non obftrupefcat, quasi viso Gorgonis capite? Maximum postulatum est, tam nervum, quam musculum haberefe f. n. Multò maximum;motum p. n. ab omnibus dictum;ab ipso etiam Erafto, nescio quà metamorphosi Ovidianà, transire subitò in motum f. n; adeoque motum depravatum fieri naturalem. Venerit & hoc alicui in mentem, Si, ut loqui solemus, detentæ sùnt in Epilepsiâ facultates tam principes,quam ministræ, ob defectum (credo) spirituum: unde est spiritus ille motorius? Imo verò, cum idem nervus vehat & sensum & motum: cur motus adest,sensus abest? cur, discusso paroxysmo, simul redit & sensus & motus? Venerit & hoc, Cum aura maligna à pede v.g. ascendit ad cerebrum, & subito pereunt omnes sensus: quei manere poffit solus motus, sensui tam conjunctus? Ex his, & forte aliis concluserit aliquis, & detentionis sensuum, & motus hujus depravati reddendam esse causam unicam, quà positâ tollatur utrumque fymptoma. Quæ illa verò alia fit quam Vapor? § 30. Argumentum insolubile D. 93, & 94. non fine risu intueor,quantumvis me reprimam. Tam enim manifeste est oppositum in adjecto, ut infans videat. Vt enim inane est, Est virgo corrupta, E 5 ergo
units.tr: Who here would not be struck dumb, as if he had looked upon the head of the Gorgon? It is a very great demand that a nerve be held to be a muscle as well, or rather (much greater still) that motion, called p. n. by everyone, and even by Erastus himself through some Ovidian metamorphosis, passes suddenly into motion f. n., and so a depraved motion becomes a natural one. Someone may also think this: if, as we commonly say, the principal faculties and the subordinate ones are held in epilepsy, owing (I suppose) to a lack of spirits, then where is that motor spirit? Indeed, since the same nerve carries both sensation and motion, why is motion present while sensation is absent? Why, when the paroxysm is over, do sensation and motion return together? Someone may also object: when a malignant air rises from the foot, say, to the brain, and all the senses suddenly perish, how can motion alone remain, when it is so closely joined to sensation? From these and perhaps other considerations someone will conclude that the one cause of both the suspension of the senses and this depraved motion is to be assigned, and that once it is posited, both symptoms are removed. But what else is that cause than vapour? § 30. I cannot look at the insoluble argument of D. 93 and 94 without laughing, however much I restrain myself. For the contradiction in the added term is so plain that even a child can see it. Just as it is empty to say, "A virgin is corrupt, therefore she is a virgin," so it is empty to say, "An action of an animal is depraved by disease, therefore it is an action of an animal."

units.la: ergò est virgo:ita inane est, Est actio animalis malis depravata,Ergo est actio animalis. Quare dico,Convulsio non est actio animalis,& fit fine efficientiâ animæ,ab solo morbo. Et quidni fatear, convulsionem non esse operationem nostram?Nec edi à solo instrumento,sed cooperante morbo? O, inquit D.94. Res non agunt propter dispositionem hanc, illamve: sed agunt melius & deterius. Quid hoc est? Annon sanitas est dispositio f.n. & morbus p. n? Propter illam bona fit actio, propter hunc mala.
units.tr: Wherefore I say that convulsion is not an action of an animal, and it comes about without the efficiency of the soul, from the disease alone. And why should I not confess that convulsion is not our operation, and that it is produced not by the instrument alone but by the disease cooperating? "Oh," says D. 94, "things do not act because of this or that disposition, but act better or worse." What is this? Is not health a disposition f. n., and disease p. n.? Because of the former the action is good, because of the latter it is bad.

units.la: § 31. Non dissimilis est ἀνεγολογία D.95.c.um distinguit actionem & actionis vitium. Differunt omninò, quia actio est sanitas, vitium actionis est morbus. Si negas, dic mihi, Quod est vitium illud,à morbo diversum?quæ est modificatio illa, D.ead.Rursus,quæ est actio illaimproprie efficiens, differens à morbo? D.eadem.
units.tr: § 31. The anegologia [ἀνεγολογία] of D.95 is not unlike this, where he distinguishes an action from a defect of action. They differ entirely, because action is health, and a defect of action is disease. If you deny this, tell me: what is that defect, if it is different from the disease? What is that modification, D. ead.? Again, what is that action, improperly efficient, that differs from the disease? D. eadem.

units.la: § 32. InD.96. manifestè laterem laeat. Recte dicitur, Omnis causa lædit actionem,non fine morbo: sed non rectè infertur, Ergo causa quoque. Hæc causa facit morbum instrumentalem. Flatus enim seu vapor, spiritum animalem mentiens, deducit musculos ad eum statum, ad quam anima folebat.
units.tr: § 32. In D.96 he manifestly hides a brick. It is rightly said that every cause harms the action, not without disease; but it is not rightly inferred, "Therefore the cause too." This cause makes the disease instrumental. For the breath or vapour, pretending to be animal spirit, draws the muscles to that state to which the soul used to draw them.

units.la: § 33. InD.97. nisi abundat 9 Non,
units.tr: § 33. In D.97., unless it abounds. 9 No,

units.la: sensus nullus est, Tum verò recte dico, Motum convulfivum esse contrarium motui,qui per sanitatem fit.Ita enim leg. est pro Societatem. Et qui sunt Medici illi, qui motus convulfivos fieri volunt ab animâ non recte agente ? Quia nulli sunt, qui unquam id ausi sunt , recte dico ego, Omnes Medicos causam transferre , non in animam ,sed in dispositionem instrumenti,ut est in fine D.
units.tr: there is no sensation. Then indeed I rightly say that convulsive motion is contrary to the motion which occurs through health. For so the text is to be read, instead of "Societatem." And who are those physicians who wish convulsive motions to arise from a soul not acting rightly? Since there are none who have ever dared this, I rightly say that all physicians transfer the cause not to the soul, but to the disposition of the instrument, as at the end of D.

units.la: § 34. Sunt quidem hæ προσθαοτίας: sed quæ sequuntur multò graviores. Agam igitur strictim. D,quidem 98. prorfusnon intelligo : quam verò orditur telam D.99. usque ad 105. de duplici appetitu, rationali, & irrationali , aquo (irrationali ) motus convulfivi fiant:non sperem me intellecturum , nisi ab ipso Erafto redivivo. Stuporis mei causa est, ni fallor, quod rem non illustravit accommodatis exemplis,Ita loquor.Quæ enim, urgente Montano,in Anatome, f.193.& feq. exempla numerat, accommodata non sunt. Cupio enim audire ab ipso, quam similitudinem cum motibus convulforiis habeant motus naturales illi, qui fiunt nobis non advertentibus, v.g. dum per somnum ambulamus,per deliria hæc vel illa loquimur, aut agimus ? Fiunt enim omnia talia fine molestiâ ullâ,mufE
units.tr: § 34. These are indeed preliminaries, but what follows is much more serious. I shall therefore proceed briefly. Indeed, D.98 I do not understand at all; but the web he weaves from D.99 to 105, concerning the twofold appetite, rational and irrational, by which (the irrational) convulsive motions are made, I do not hope to understand, unless from Erastus himself, come back to life. The cause of my astonishment is, unless I am mistaken, that he has not illustrated the matter with suitable examples. I say this because the examples he lists, following Montanus, in the Anatome, p. 193 and following, are not suitable. For I wish to hear from himself what likeness those natural motions have to convulsive motions, which occur without our noticing them, for instance when we walk in our sleep, or speak or act in this or that way in delirium? For all such things occur without any discomfort, with the muscles in good condition; but what is it here? This is too well known, and I have said it myself above.

units.la: culis benè fe habentibus:at heic quid fit? Nimis hoc notum est, & dixi ego supra.
units.tr: Hence I have said enough on this point.

units.la: § 35. Hucusque provectus,cum quaero cohaerentiam orationis, & nullam invenio :nescio quò me vertam. Si divinationi locus est,ita putem, Eraftum, de bonitate causae defperabundum, obdormivifle, & fomniaffe certitudines & demonstrationes plurimas: Solemus enim plerique contraria somniare. Expergefactum per ἀναχεῖ collegifle primum καὶ ἐπὶ τὰ ... sua: deinde conatum fuifle respondere dubitationibus. Quas dum inspicio, tantum abesse video illum à triumpho, quantum Alexandri ara ab Herculis columnis. Quod ut clarius fiat, redigam illas in ordinem.
units.tr: § 35. Having come this far, when I look for the connection of the argument and find none, I do not know where to turn. If divination has any place here, I would guess that Erastus, despairing of the goodness of his cause, fell asleep and dreamed up many certainties and demonstrations; for most people are accustomed to dream the opposite. Awake, he gathered together first, by a kind of [ἀναχεῖ] ... and [καὶ ἐπὶ τὰ] ... his own points; then he tried to answer the objections. As I examine these, I see him as far from triumph as the altar of Alexander is from the Pillars of Hercules. So that this may become clearer, I shall arrange them in order.

units.la: § 36. Harum agmen ADRESTEA ducat,
units.tr: § 36. Let Adrestea lead the column of these,

units.la: Et tuba terrifico praecedat vanca fragore, Subinde intercalante dea ex D. 105.
units.tr: and let the trumpet go before with a terrifying crash, the goddess interposing from time to time, from D. 105.

units.la: illa, Hac unà excepta, quae à flatibus confertim ex subito irrumpentibus, cietur. Item illa, ex D. 124. Si de eo fbafmo interpreteris, qui à flatu fit. Item illa ex D.39. Talem fere fbafmi esse descriptionem etc. Hanc in rem memineris eorum, quae dicta sunt ad D.78.
units.tr: Except this one, which rushes in all at once from sudden gusts, and is set in motion. Likewise that one, from D. 124, if you interpret it of the convulsion that comes from wind. Likewise that one from D. 39: "Such is roughly the description of a convulsion," etc. For this purpose you should remember what was said at D. 78.

units.la: § 37. I. Dubitatio incipit D.106. & pertingitad D.127. tantis implicita importunitatibus, quantis dici non poteft ab eo, qui rerum veltigia fumma fequatur. Confiftit autem in eo, ut falvet thefin fuam, Motus convulfivos effe ab appetitu fenfitivo,et fieri à fpiritu animali,tanquam inftrumento, perinde ac motus f.n. A quâ affertione cum fubito refulturum fciret animum non plane ftupidum : quid non moliatur? Precipuus obex heic eft,Annon motus dicti fiant à facultate cerebri expultrice? Ab hacita fe expedit,ut D.111. concedat, Epilepfiam per confenfum, v. g. ex pede,fieri ab hac facultate, non à phantafiàveruntamen non effe veram & proprie dictam Epilepfiam, D. 114. & 115. Miferum effugium, quod in folo nomine fpem ponit ! Propterea non femel dixi, Quia fymptomata utriufque Epilepfiæ tam gemina funt, ut fæpe à Medico difcerni non poffint: fi concedatur unam effe ab expultrice, neceffario concedendum effe, omnem inde effe. Nec quidquam valet, quod fine D.115. afpergitur ex Gal. ex 3. Loc. aff.7. Epilepfias per confenfum effe leviores. Multò minus valet xabvyaoua illud D.116. Convelli hoc modo artis principia. Quæ vero? inquam ego, Indubitate veritatis axioma eft, fcribit D.117. &c. quibus fimpliciter
units.tr: § 37. I. The first objection begins at D. 106 and runs on to D. 127, entangled in such great difficulties that they cannot be told by one who follows the tracks of things from the top. Its aim is to save his thesis: that convulsive movements arise from the sensitive appetite and are produced by the animal spirit as an instrument, just as voluntary movements are. He knows that from this assertion the mind, which is not wholly stupid, will at once rebound; so what does he not attempt? The chief obstacle here is this: do not the movements called convulsions arise from the expulsive faculty of the brain? He extricates himself from this by conceding, at D. 111, that epilepsy through sympathy, for example from the foot, arises from this faculty and not from the imagination; but that it is not a true and properly so-called epilepsy (D. 114 and 115). A wretched escape, which places its hope in a mere name! For this reason I have said more than once: since the symptoms of the two kinds of epilepsy are so alike that they often cannot be distinguished by a physician, if it is granted that one arises from the expulsive faculty, it must necessarily be granted that all do. Nor does it help that what is sprinkled in at D. 115 from Galen, On the Affected Parts book 3, chapter 7, that epilepsies through sympathy are milder. Much less does that [xabvyaoua] saying at D. 116 help: "the principles of art are convulsed in this way." But what are they? I ask. He writes at D. 117 that it is an axiom of indubitable truth, etc., to which I simply oppose that other statement, "The difference lies in this" [...]. All the more do I wonder at that [...] at D. 119. I wonder most of all at the free confession at D. 121, which agrees with that empty evasion at D. 114, and which he repeats at D. 124 to the great disgust of the reader. Thus far, then, Erastus helps me, in so far as he concedes that something of the peccant matter is in the brain, which is discharged from there into the muscles.

units.tr: E

Maximè miror liberam confessionem, D. 121. conformem illi tergiverfationi inani , D.114. quam maximo cum legentis fastidio repetit D.124. Haetenus ergò juvat me Eraftus, quatenus concedit, aliquid p.n. esse in cerebro, quod inde expellatur in musculos.
units.tr: I oppose to those things what he says in the same place, the difference lies in this, etc. All the more do I wonder at that passage of D.119. I most wonder at his frank confession at D.121, which agrees with that empty evasion at D.114 and which he repeats at D.124 to the great disgust of the reader. So far Erastus helps me, in that he concedes that something is in the brain which is expelled from there into the muscles.

units.la: § 38. II. Dubitatio incipit D.127. & pertinet usque ad D. 140. nec minus intricata est quam prior. Cum convulsio fit symptoma in motu depravato, à quo morbo est? Et Eraftus quidem subito sibi cavet, praetenía negotii difficultate, inde usque à Gal. deducta, & felicioribus ingeniis commissa: in ipsa autem re nudior est leberide. Cum enim insistit phantasiae suae D. 128. risum debet dupondiis nostris. Cum D.129. accentat nobis actiones vel puré similares, vel puré instrumentales, vel mistas: novitatis merito arguitur. Cum D. 130. morbum instrumentalem agnoscit, sed ita ut ab intempere etiam induci possit: confusionis reus est. Quò magis probo illud, fine D. 131. nolle fe progredi ulterius eò vehementius detestor ἀγρίωχουχ D. feq. 6. Abjicio etiam obscuram determinationem D.138. Cenvulfionem esse morbidam spiritum
units.tr: § 38. II. The doubt begins at D.127 and runs to D.140, and is no less tangled than the first. Since convulsion is a symptom of depraved motion, what disease is it from? Erastus, to be sure, quickly takes precautions for himself, pleading the difficulty of the matter, which he derives from Galen onward and entrusts to more gifted minds; but in the matter itself he is barer than any charm. For when he clings to his fancy (D.128) he deserves our laughter, worth a dupondius. When he sets before us actions that are either purely similar, purely instrumental, or mixed, he is rightly charged with novelty. When he acknowledges an instrumental disease, but in such a way that it can also be induced by an intemperies, he is guilty of confusion. Hence, to prove that he refuses to go any further (D.131), I detest it all the more vehemently [ἀγρίωχουχ] D. seq. 6. I also reject his obscure determination at D.138, that convulsion is a morbid spirit

units.la: {f}piritus um c cerebri dispositionem , a quae vitietur imaginatio cum appetitu. Dic mihi morbi nomen , & sciam, quid facto opus fit. Quam amicus mihi est spasmus, D. 139 : tam inimica est mihi vertigo , D. 140. V iden’ tu nuditatem hominis? Ego paucis me expedio , Non est unus morbus,sed triplex. I. est Intemperies,vaporis istius mater,in quacunque parte fit. 11.est Obstructio in vasis cerebri , vel omnibus, vel plerisque,prefertim iis,quae circa nervorum principium sunt, III, est Obstructio in musculis a vapore huc translato.
units.tr: of the disposition of the brain, by which the imagination is vitiated together with appetite. Tell me the name of the disease, and I shall know what must be done. As friendly to me as spasm is (D.139), so hostile to me is vertigo (D.140). Do you see the man's nakedness? I free myself in a few words: it is not one disease but three. First, an intemperies, the mother of that vapour, wherever it occurs. Second, an obstruction in the vessels of the brain, either all of them or most of them, especially those which lie around the origin of the nerves. Third, an obstruction in the muscles from the vapour carried thither.

units.la: § 39. Tertium locum occupent problemata, a D. 141. usque ad finem , de quibus unicuique suum fit arbitrium. Ad Medicum enim vix pertinent, Logica quippe. Ego vero me hinc abripio , cum hoc monito, Magne felicitatis esse, a prima statim juventute incidere in tales magistros, qui fine ambagibus Veritatem doceant.Contra, maximae infelicitatis esse, incidere in eos , qui etiam admoniti abominentur Veritatem. Hanc in rem cum aliquammulta scripserim Praef. in libb. de Vsu part, libet mihi nunc obsignare hac hiftoriola. Lis eratinter duos ICtos Altorsinos, quorum nominibus parco, & erat major a minore in publica disputatione eo redactus , ut non haberet amplius,
units.tr: § 39. Let the problems from D.141 to the end take the third place; each reader may judge them as he pleases, for they hardly belong to the physician, being matters of logic. I, however, withdraw from here with this warning: it is a great happiness to fall, from the earliest youth, among such teachers as teach the truth without circumlocution, and the greatest unhappiness to fall among those who, even when admonished, abhor the truth. Since I have written a good deal on this in the preface to the books De usu partium, I now wish to seal the matter with this little story. There was a dispute between two Altorf jurists, whose names I spare, and in a public disputation the elder was reduced to having nothing more to say

units.la: quod diceret. Tamen in lectionibus postea multus fuit in tuendà opinione suà. Quæ cum detulisset auditorum quidam ad alterum, postquam legit, renidens dixit. Domine, percepistine mentem meam? Intelligisne quid hic velit ? Tuam, inquit ille, videor mihi bellè intelligere : hanc non possum. Bene, respondit doctor : Nam neque ego intelligo. Hoc igitur, addit, habeas tibi hodiè à me, sæpenumero fieri, ut quò major quis est, eò major videri velit, adeoque Pythagoras quidam! Hoc ego accommodo nunc rebus noftris. Eraftus veré fuit vir magnus : sed in hoc negotio habericum vellet pro aquila, habetur suo merito pro talpa. Qua in reutar,cum bonorum venià, hac ἀπρόσσιε, O juvenes, nisi temporis jacturam facere vultis, inspectà harum ϑ'σαν inscriptione, deponite. πείθω χρὴ μὴ αἰσχρόνις. Hinc adeò fit, ut, qui defendere volunt phantasticum hoc somnium, in multò tetriores labantur errores. Tu verò, fi curæ tibi Veritas, ægrorumque salus est, accipe à me hæc pauca, per quæ reditum mihi paro ad Montanum.
units.tr: in reply. Yet afterwards, in his lectures, he was long-winded in defending his opinion. When one of his listeners reported this to the other, after reading it, the other smiled and said: "Sir, did you grasp my meaning? Do you understand what he wants here?" "Your meaning, he replied, I seem to myself to understand well enough; his I cannot." "Good," answered the teacher, "for neither do I understand it." "Take this from me today as a lesson," he adds: it often happens that the greater someone is, the greater he wishes to appear, so that he becomes a sort of Pythagoras! I apply this to our present affairs. Erastus was truly a great man, but in this business, though he would like to be taken for an eagle, he is rightly taken for a mole. Hence, with the good men's leave, I say to you, O young men, unless you wish to waste your time: [ἀπρόσιτε], look at the inscription on these matters and put them down. [πείθω χρὴ μὴ αἰσχρά.] Hence it comes about that those who want to defend this fantastic dream slip into far fouler errors. But you, if the truth and the health of the sick are your concern, take from me these few words, by which I prepare my way back to Montanus.

units.la: De Convulsionibus, precipuè Epilepsia, sententia propria, CAP. IX.
units.tr: On Convulsions, Especially Epilepsy: My Own Opinion, Chapter IX.

units.la: § 1. Ifi penitiffime fallor, & mecum boni alii, quæ dicam & veterum autoritate fulta sunt, & naturæ rerum consentanea, ideoque praxi etiam viciniora. At quæ hic subjungam ἐλεγχος ἀ{x}catenus grata spero futura, quatenus benè dictis amplior fides conciliatur. Quemadmodum enim in communi vitâ, non opus tantum est alimento, quo corpus sustentatur, sed & helleboro aliquando, cammonio, lathyride, & his talibus, quæ sentinam corporis exhauriant: ita heic utrumque suum habet locum.
units.tr: § 1. If I am not greatly mistaken, and other good men agree with me, what I shall say is supported by the authority of the ancients and accords with the nature of things, and is therefore closer to practice too. I hope that what I add here, which is a refutation [ἔλεγχος], will be welcome insofar as a fuller trust is won for well-stated views. For just as in ordinary life the body needs not only the food that sustains it but sometimes also hellebore, cammonium, spurge and such things that drain the sink of the body, so here each has its own place.

units.la: § 2. Principiò, spero haud difficulter datum iri mihi à fanis, quibus partibus benè fe habentibus, bene fit motus voluntarius: iis malè fe habentibus, aut non fieri, aut malè fieri motum hunc. Hujus enim posterioris generis sunt præscripta symptomata.
units.tr: § 2. First, I hope it will not be hard for me to get from sane people the agreement that when the parts are in good condition, voluntary motion is produced well; and when they are in bad condition, this motion either does not occur or occurs badly. For the symptoms described belong to this second kind.

units.la: § 3. Deinde & hoc, Quo modo fit motus voluntarius: ei non valde diffimili fieri convulfivum. Hoc tamen observato discrimine. Vt motus f. n. fiat, necesse est partes omnes recte fe habere: ut motus p. n. fatis est, fi unaillarum, pluresve vitientur. Vt motus fiat, necessarium est I. Cor mittat sursum ad cerebrum fpiritus Vitales dictos, & in quantitate, & in qualitate laudabiles. I I. Cerebrum oportet spiritus hos refrigeret, non simpliciter sed fubftantificè, ut jam Animales dici possint,rursus & in quantitate, & in qualitate laudabiles. I I I. Spiritus hi ex cerebro per Nervos proprie dictos ire debent in Musculos deferentes secum facultatem motricem. I V. Spiritus iidem, in Musculorum ventres delati, debent illos duros & turgidos facere, instar sacci frumento distenti, aut potius vectis inftar, ut Gal. comparat. I.Sent. Hipp.10. Vt motus male fiat ( de hoc enim solo agimus) fatis est fi spiritui misceatur Vipor quidam, undecunque ad principium nervorum delatus,qui per Nervos ad Mufculos descendens, faciat turgescere mufculos, & eo modo elevet, quo Spiritus elevabat.
units.tr: § 3. Next, consider how voluntary motion comes about: convulsive motion comes about in a manner not very different from it, though with this difference noted. For voluntary motion to occur, all the parts must be in good order; for convulsive motion it is enough that one or more of them be damaged. For motion to occur, it is necessary (1) that the heart send up to the brain the so-called vital spirits, both in quantity and in quality sound; (2) that the brain cool these spirits, not merely but substantially, so that they can now be called animal spirits, again sound in quantity and quality; (3) that these spirits, passing from the brain through the so-called nerves, carry the motor faculty with them into the muscles; (4) that the same spirits, once delivered into the bellies of the muscles, make them hard and swollen, like a sack stuffed with grain, or rather like a lever, as Galen compares in his commentary on the first book of Hippocrates' Sentences [Comparat. I. Sent. Hipp. 10]. For motion to occur badly (for this alone is our concern) it is enough that some vapour, carried from wherever to the origin of the nerves, be mixed with the spirit, and that it, descending through the nerves to the muscles, make the muscles swell, and lift them in the same way the spirit used to lift them.

units.la: § 4. v. g, In Epilepsia ( quæ jam sola restat inter morbos formales Fernelii) in quâ omnia sunt evidentiora, propter paroxyfmos crebrò repetentes, quid facit xλόγον illum, quem Græci vocant? Neque Cor, neque Cerebrum affecta esse extra paroxysmum, ostendit id,quod non tantum bene valent Epileptici: sed &c, quod
units.tr: § 4. For example, in epilepsy (which alone now remains among Fernelius' formal diseases), in which everything is more evident because of the paroxysms that recur often, what makes that irrational [ἄλογον] thing which the Greeks call so? That neither the heart nor the brain is affected outside the paroxysm is shown by the fact that not only do epileptics enjoy good health, but

units.la: plerique eorum ζζῥιυοοι sunt, ut Hercules, Cæsar, Mahomet, Carolus V. Imp. alii innumeri. Vt propius accedam, etiam agili sint corpore. Novi Pataviį saltatorem, Zachariam nomine, qui in isto exercitio præferebatur aliis. Sed & nemo in his solidis partibus quærit Epileptiæ caufam, ut neque in Nervis & Musculis, Cur? Quia reddi ratio non potest, curtam fæpe repetat infortunium. Restat ergò, ut vel in Humoribus fit, vel in Spiritibus, Humores quia plane absolvit Gal, 2. Caus. sym.2.M. quà de palpitatione relinquuntur Spiritus, vapore quodam inquinati, ceu dixi.
units.tr: most of them are very sharp-witted, like Hercules, Caesar, Mahomet, Charles V the Emperor, and countless others. To come closer to home, they are even nimble of body. I knew at Padua a dancer named Zacharias, who excelled others in that exercise. But nobody seeks the cause of epilepsy in these solid parts, neither in the nerves nor in the muscles. Why? Because no reason can be given why it so often attacks a man who is otherwise sound. It remains, therefore, that the cause lies either in the humours or in the spirits. Galen plainly disposes of the humours, since he says that after the palpitation the spirits are left behind, polluted by a certain vapour, as I said.

units.la: § 5. In hujus rei demonstratione fas est nos admirari folertiam antiquorum, ex Θαυμασίοις procedentium ad ἐναργή vocata, ex sensu ad intellectum, Quo vero modo Cum in Macrocosmo, dicebant sterremotus fiant ἀπὸ τῶν ἀνευμάτων ἀ spiritu, flatu, vapore, potius à spiritu flatuoso, vaporoso: verisimile est, convulsiones in Microcosmo fieri eodem modo. Hæc sententia est Arift. 2, Meteor. 8. & Gal. duobus locis, 2. Caus. sym. 2. D. de Palp. & trem. ult. A. Quà in re cum fatendum sit, Galenum fuisse interpretem Arist. ageamus præssus. Instituit Gal. duas comparationes, valde mihi favorabiles.
units.tr: § 5. In demonstrating this point we may admire the acuteness of the ancients, who proceeded from wonders [θαυμασίων] to what is evident [ἐναργῆ], from sense to intellect. As to how earthquakes arise in the macrocosm, they said they come from winds [ἀπὸ τῶν ἀνέμων], that is, from breath, from vapour, or rather from a windy, vaporous spirit. It is likely that convulsions in the microcosm come about in the same way. This is the opinion of Aristotle, Meteorologica 2, chapter 8, and of Galen in two places: On the Causes of Symptoms 2, and On Palpitation and Tremor, the last chapter. In this matter, since it must be admitted that Galen was the interpreter of Aristotle, let us proceed. Galen draws two comparisons, very favourable to my view.

units.la: Primo
units.tr: First.

units.la: Primò enim confert motum naturalem cum motu præternaturali. Deinde (piritum naturalem cum p.n. & hoc vult dicere. Quà ratione in motu naturali, mus fculus, (piritu naturali plenus, rapit partem, cui inseritur, versus principium suum : eà ratione in p.n, idem mufculus, (piritu quodam flatuofo turgidus, trahit partem suam eodem. Illud egregiè explicat simile à vecti defumtum, quo uti illum dixi.1. Sent. Hipp.1o, C.Nisi fallor, eodem nos perducit, ποιλία, venter mufculi, ut pariter dixi. Hoc persuadet analogia. Quemadmodum igitur in doctrinâ Gal. confeffiffimum est, (piritum naturalem,motus naturalis antorem, esse ex cerebro, adeoque cerebro non dispensante illum,non fieri motum ullum : ita dubium apud bonos, sapientesque non est ullum, exeodem cerebro, licet aliunde receptum, esse (piritum illum flatuofum, convulsionis autorem. Quin dicit Gal. ipse 5. Aph.5, ne alia loca cumulem.
units.tr: For first he compares natural motion with unnatural motion. Then he compares the natural spirit with the unnatural one, and this is what he means. In natural motion a muscle, full of natural spirit, draws the part into which it is inserted towards its origin; in the same way, in unnatural motion the same muscle, swollen with a certain windy spirit, draws its part in the same direction. The simile taken from the lever, which I mentioned in the first book of Hippocrates' Sentences 10, explains this well. If I am not mistaken, the same comparison leads us to the belly [ποιλία], the belly of the muscle, as I also said. Analogy persuades us of this. Therefore, just as in Galen's teaching it is most certain that the natural spirit, the author of natural motion, comes from the brain, and that without the brain's supplying it no motion at all occurs, so among good and wise men there is no doubt that the windy spirit, the author of convulsion, comes from the same brain, though it is received from elsewhere. Indeed Galen himself says so in Aphorisms 5, section 5, not to pile up other passages.

units.la: § 6. Hanc rem validiffima demonftratione conficit Cafalp.2, Quaft.Med. 16.Convulsio,vult dicere;fit à corpore quodam. Corpus hoc non potest esse aliud, quam quod ... cum impetu : quodidem fit ... ... vim habet agendi velocissimam, simulque vehementisimam. Tale in rerum naturâ nullum est praeterquam Spiritus seu Vapor , seu Aér , quippe qui et arbores et domos subruit , adeoque terram ipsam concutit. Hoc ratiocinio sæpe utebatur SCHERBIVS, & ita applicabat. Symptoma hoc non potest fieri nisi à morbo ( non à facultate ) qui est factum quid, cum convulsio fit in fieri. Hujus morbi causa debet esse talis, ut subito adfit & absit. Neutrum hoc fieri potest, nisi à flatu. Hoc plane evincit Gal. * exemplo palpitationis,quam ob id ab humore esse negat. Persuadet & ratio. Mortui enim rigerent : at veró subito relaxantur,evanescente scil.corporeillo,quod tendebat.
units.tr: § 6. Casalpinus, in *Quaestiones Medicae* 2, question 16, makes this point with a very strong demonstration. He wants to say that convulsion is caused by some body. This body cannot be anything other than what ... with impetus; which is the same as ... has a most rapid power of acting, and at the same time most violent. Nothing of this kind exists in nature except spirit, or vapour, or air, which indeed overturns trees and houses, and so shakes the very earth. Scherbius often used this argument, and applied it thus: this symptom cannot arise except from a disease (not from a faculty), which is a thing made, since the convulsion is in the process of becoming. The cause of this disease must be such that it comes on suddenly and goes away suddenly. Neither of these can happen except from a blast.
