Galen plainly proves this by the example of palpitation, which for that reason he denies arises from humour. Reason also persuades us. For dead bodies grow stiff, but suddenly relax when that bodily thing which was stretching them has vanished.

units.la: § 7. Hanc demonstrationem si Gal.
units.tr: § 7. If Galen knew this demonstration, as he does know it, you would wonder why he does not stand firm on it.

units.la: nôrat, ut nôrat : mireris , cur non stet in vestigio? Qui allati sunt duo loci,manifestâ in luce offerunt Veritatem , ab Arift. proditam. Iis verò locis,quibus defensare vult Repletionem & Inanitionem Hipp. inclinat se ad ruinosum parietem , Vicifsim iis ,quibus Epilepsiam , desertâ Inanitione,à solâ Repletione ventriculorum cerebri deducit, corruit cum pariete suo. Hic casus ipsius tantò minus latere potest, quod , desertâ Epilepsiâ per consensum, eam , quæ per essentiam fit, solam ab Repletione ventriculorum dictorum petit.
units.tr: The two passages he cites set forth the truth, taught by Aristotle, in plain light. But in those passages where he wishes to defend the repletion and inanition of Hippocrates, he leans on a crumbling wall, and conversely, in those where he derives epilepsy solely from repletion of the ventricles of the brain, setting aside inanition, he falls together with his wall. This lapse of his can be all the less concealed because, setting epilepsy aside through consent, he seeks from those ventricles' repletion only the epilepsy that arises through essence.

units.la: * 2 Caus. Sym. 2.
units.tr: * 2 Caus. Sym. 2.

units.la: Hæ verò fluctuationes quid non portendunt? Accedit, quod nesciam, an cuiquam diligentiori persuasurus fit, Epilepsiam, quæ symptomata affert tã sibi vicina, esse à causis tam longè à fe invicem distantibus? Accedit & hoc, quod Epilepsiam jungit cum Apoplexiâ. Cuienim vel leviter attento non fit suspecta res, duos morbos, diverfiffimis comitatos fymptomatis, esse ab eádem causa? Obstructione, inquam, ventriculorum cerebri?
units.tr: What do these fluctuations not portend? Add that I do not know whether he will persuade any careful person that epilepsy, which brings symptoms so close to one another, arises from causes so far distant from each other. Add also that he joins epilepsy with apoplexy. For who, even slightly attentive, would not suspect the thing: that two diseases, accompanied by very diverse symptoms, come from the same cause? Obstruction, I mean, of the ventricles of the brain?

units.la: § 8. Quid igitur pro Gal. dicemus? Id, quod alias quoque, Morem ipsius esse, aliis quidem locis Veritatem profiteri: aliis autem Communes sententias, Quia igitur duobus locis, de Cauf. fym. & de Palp. ex Arift. dixit, quod res est: quidni acceptemus? Quia aliis locis defensionem Hipp. suscepit, & studiosè comsit: causæ non est, cur non deferamus, Et hoc omninò boneftius est, quam vel indignari, vel falsa defendere, cum detrimento ægrorum. Hoc exaudire volo illos, qui sub nomine Gal. superbire solent: non enim deterior est conditio mea, quam istorum, fi omnino autoritatibus pugnamus,
units.tr: § 8. What then shall we say on behalf of Galen? That which we say elsewhere too: it is his custom to profess the truth in some places, but common opinions in others. Since, therefore, in two places he spoke, from Aristotle, about the cause of symptoms and about palpitation, and spoke as the matter really is, why should we not accept it? Since in other places he took up the defence of Hippocrates and labored over it diligently, there is no reason why we should not follow him there; and this is altogether more honourable than either to be indignant or to defend falsehoods to the detriment of the sick. This I want to say to those who are wont to pride themselves on Galen's name: for my position is no worse than theirs, if we argue altogether from authorities,

units.la: Contra Semiobstructionem Epilepticam, CAPVT X.
units.tr: Against Epileptic Semiobstruction, CHAPTER X.

units.la: § 1. Nterim, quia secus visum fuit Fernelio, & pendet ab illo totus chorus saltantium, & inter hos Montanus noster : fas est sequamur vestigia illorum. Fernelii verba sunt, 5. Pathol. 3. Hæc tamen (obstructio) inquit, non assatim, aut penitus obturat spirituum ductus sed ejus etiam nonnihil præterfluit, quo cerebrum concussione adnititur, quidquid nonnium est, excutere: In his qui non agnoscit Semiobstructionem, nemo unus est. Tamen idem, 2. Abd. 15. relictâ illâ, Venenum laté inducit, & Epilepsiam pro morbo formæ haberi vult. Pro cujus excusatione nisi dici potest, Epilepsiam perefsentiam retulisse ad obstructionem, per consensum ad venenum : non habeo, quod dicam, amplius. Quidquid fit:
units.tr: § 1. Meanwhile, since Fernel thought otherwise, and the whole troop of dancers depends on him, including our Montanus, it is right that we follow in their footsteps. Fernel's words are (5 Pathol. 3): However, he says, obstruction does not block the channels of the spirits entirely or completely, but some of it still flows past, by which the brain, by its concussion, strives to expel whatever is harmful. Among those who do not acknowledge semiobstruction, there is not a single one. Yet the same man (2 Abd. 15), leaving that aside, says that poison spreads widely and wants epilepsy to be counted a disease of form. In defence of this, unless it can be said that Fernel referred epilepsy in its essence to obstruction and, by sympathy, to poison, I have nothing more to say. Whatever the case:

units.la: § 2. Apud Montanum tantum potuit Semiobstructio, ut ausus fuerit transcribere Gal. 3. Loc. aff. 7. Vbi cum non offenderet, credo, SENNERTVS olim noster : exhibuit nobis alium, 5. Aph. 45. Verum ego neutrubi ullâ indagine subodorari possum, ut ostendo in Patholog. cap. 122.
units.tr: § 2. With Montanus, semiobstruction had such power that he dared to copy out Galen (3 Loc. aff. 7). Where, I think, our SENNERTUS once did not take offence, he showed us another passage (5 Aph. 45). But I can detect no trace of either in any investigation, as I show in the Pathology, chapter 122.

units.la: § 3, Sinc
units.tr: § 3, Without

units.la: § 3. Sine igitur morâ ad Montanum cap.28. versus, ostendi mihi vôlo apud Gal. aut verba ipsa, aut rem non invitâ Minervâ expressam, Obstructio hæc integra non est, sicuti in apoplexiâ, &c. Mox adimo illi φαινόμενον, quo probare vult obstru-ctionem, Pituita copiosa, per os, naresque Epilepticorum excreta, statim paroxy⁠smum solvit. Non fit in omnibus. In quibus igitur non fit, quæ causa solutionis? Apud me vaporis defectus finem facit. Sed fit.
units.tr: § 3. Without delay, then, I want Montanus to show me in Galen, at the twenty-eighth chapter of his work, either the words themselves or the matter expressed not without Minerva's help: This obstruction is not complete, as in apoplexy, etc. Next I take from him the appearance [φαινόμενον], by which he wants to prove obstruction: Copious phlegm, discharged through the mouth and nostrils of epileptics, immediately ends the paroxysm. This does not happen in all cases. In those in whom it does not happen, what is the cause of the cessation? For me, a lack of vapour brings the fit to an end. But it does happen.

units.la: Marginal notes at the right edge are cut off and not legible enough to transcribe. Pituita illa est ex ventriculis cerebri: verum illa non causavit obstructionem ill-am,quae causa fuit τῆς κλάσεως. Quod enim alibi quoque dixi, Quantumvis concutiatur,contrahaturque cerebrum, quis pofsit sibi imaginari, contractionem illam ad musculos usque pertingere? vel ideo, quia falsum est, nervos trahere habenæ instar? Si cerebrum comparetur manui trahenti, musculus equo tracto, quod est, 7. Vf. p. 14. N. necesse est, cerebrum tantopere cedere, quantopere manus ab equo retrorsum abit. At quod est spatium illud tam amplum, in quod se abscondat? Sed & nervi non sunt liberi, ut lorum habenæ est: quin firmiter alligati sunt partibus illis, in quas mittunt propagines. Nec dicat mihi quis, comparationem eousque extendi non debere. Debet omnino, si effectus
units.tr: That phlegm comes from the ventricles of the brain; but it did not cause that obstruction, which was the cause of the concussion [τῆς κλάσεως]. For, as I have said elsewhere too, however much the brain is shaken and contracted, who can imagine that this contraction reaches as far as the muscles? Or is it because it is false that nerves pull like the reins of a bridle? If the brain is compared to a hand pulling, and a muscle to a horse being drawn (as in 7 Vf. p. 14, N.), it is necessary that the brain yield as much as the hand moves back from the horse. But what is that space so large into which it could withdraw? Yet nerves are not free, as the rein is to the bridle; rather they are firmly tied to those parts into which their branches run. Nor let anyone tell me that the comparison ought not to be pushed so far. It certainly ought to be, if a similar effect is to be expected.

units.la: . effectus similis sperandus sit. Quamobrem non oportet subsistere in motu illo naturali æquivoco: sed inquirere in animalem seu univocum.
units.tr: . if a similar effect is to be expected. Therefore one must not rest in that natural, equivocal motion, but must inquire into the animal, or univocal, motion.

units.la: § 4. Vt igitur ad rem veniamus, Montanus dicit cap.29. se ideo rejecturum Fernelii,2. Abd.15. argumenta, ut doctrina Gal. fiat illustrior; ea vero perspicuè falsa est, si adstringas cerebri ventriculis: videamus è longinquo, quo modo comatur, poliaturque hæc Phryne.
units.tr: § 4. So, to come to the matter: Montanus says in chapter 29 that he will therefore reject Fernel's arguments (2 Abd. 15) so that the doctrine of Galen may become clearer. But that is plainly false if you hold to the ventricles of the brain. Let us look from afar at how this Phryne is adorned and polished.

units.la: I. Fernelii argumentum (quod Erastus etiam præponit aliis) est, Si Epilepsia est à femiobstruēlione ventriculorum , ut Apoplexia à totali : omnem Epilepsiam precedet Apoplexia.Hoc verò refutat omnium feculorum experientia. Respondet Comes; Non sequitur. Si repente irruat apoplexia,repente etiam fit integra ventriculorum repletio.Miserabilis refponsio,quam ideò Eraftus;Anat. p.189. variis incommodis urget: Quæ dum avertere vult Montanus in Ant-Eraft f.124. b. se dignum facit, ut cum Erafto loquar. Nituntur enim omnia falsæ hypothesi , Apoplexiam fieri obstructis ventriculis cerebri.Ego hæc addo. I.Fatuum est credere, hos tam diversis comitatos symptomatis morbos,fieri ab unâ causâ, II.Futilis est hypothesis, Ventriculos esse ossi-
units.tr: I. Fernel's argument (which Erastus also places before the others) is this: If epilepsy comes from a semiobstruction of the ventricles, as apoplexy comes from a total one, then every epilepsy will be preceded by apoplexy. But the experience of all ages refutes this. The Count replies: It does not follow. If apoplexy comes on suddenly, the filling of the ventricles is also sudden and complete. A wretched reply, which Erastus (Anat. p. 189) presses with various difficulties. While Montanus wishes to avert these (Anti-Erastus p. 124 b), he makes himself worthy of my speaking with Erastus. For all these arguments rest on the false hypothesis that apoplexy is caused by obstructed ventricles of the brain. I add these points. (1) It is foolish to believe that diseases with such different symptoms come from one cause. (2) The hypothesis that the ventricles are workshops of the spirits is futile. (3) It is a silly opinion that in apoplexy the ventricles are so filled that the brain cannot contract, while in epilepsy the filling is slight enough that it can. (4) Such a great contraction is imaginable only if there are transverse fibres here, and there are none. Indeed, that something of the kind happens here is shown by the paralysis that follows. Well, since you yourself affirm that compression does not occur because of the abundance of humours? But I spare him.

units.la: cinas spirituum. III. Stulta est opinio, In apoplexiâ ventriculos ita impleri, ut cerebrum fe non possit contrahere : in epilepsiâ modicam esse impletionem, ut possit. I V. Imaginabilis est contractio tanta, cum fibræ transversæ hic nullæ sint. Imò verò esse heic tale quid, persuadet paralysis subsequens. Eja vero, cum tu ipse affirmes, ob copiam humorum non fieri compressionem? Sed parco.
units.tr: § 5. II. The argument is drawn from what anatomical experience has taught. He proudly rejects this. I, however, will say that Fernel ought not to be charged with the disgrace of claiming he saw what he did not see. That putrid humour, whether it lay settled within the skull and dura mater or gathered in the substance of the brain itself, could have given off such a vapour as I want, but it could not fill the ventricles. Perhaps it can be said that Fernel was slightly mistaken about the choroid plexuses, in which he said he had found phlegm, since they are glands, as Bauhin and others observe. Meanwhile, this very point attacks semiobstruction. Nor does Montanus gain anything when he presses the supply of spirits from the book On the Use of the Pulses (2). He gains even less when he calls on Avicenna, who never wanted to be Galen's ally.

units.la: § 5. II. Argumentum petitur ab iis, quæ experientia Anatomica docuit. Hanc illefuperbè rejicit, Ego veró dicam, Fernelio non debere objicitantam turpitudinem,ut dicat fe vidisse,quæ non vidit. * Humor enim ille putridus, tam intra cranium & duram matrem refi- dens, quam in ipsa cerebri substantiâ collectus, potuit emittere de fe vaporem talem,qualem volo ego: ventriculos replere non potuit. Fortassis dici potest,minimum, errasse Fernelium in plexibus retiformibus, in quibus pituitam se invenisse dixerit, cum glandulæ sint, ut Bauh. & alii observant. Interim hoc ipsum impugnat semiobstructionem. Nec quidquam agit Montanus cum ex lib. de Vs. pul{.2. spirituum subministrationem urget. Multò minus agit, cum Avicennam advocat, qui socius Gal. nunquam esse voluit.
units.tr: § 5. II. The argument is drawn from what anatomical experience has taught. He proudly rejects this. But I will say that Fernel ought not to be charged with such shamelessness, as to claim he has seen what he has not seen. That putrid humour, whether it settles within the skull and dura mater or is gathered in the substance of the brain itself, could emit from itself a vapour of the kind I describe, but it could not fill the ventricles. It may perhaps be said that Fernel was mistaken about the retiform plexuses, in which he said he found phlegm, since they are glands, as Bauhin and others observe. Meanwhile, this very point tells against semi-obstruction. Nor does Montanus achieve anything when he presses the supply of spirits from his book on the use of the pulse. Much less does he achieve anything when he calls upon Avicenna, who never wanted to be an ally of Galen.

units.la: * Erafius p.190. frigidum facit. voluit. Imò, sum ejus opinionis, Arabem, cum de Vasis ad cerebrum loquitur, intelligere Venas jugulares cum Arteriis foporalibus, quibus obstructis apoplexiam etiam fieri, difficile probatu forte non est, si admittatur, Ventriculos esse officinas spirituum. Hanc autem signânsse Gal. 2, Aph. 42. non credam, quandoquidem inspectio loci satis convincit, Gal. apoplexias vocare in plurali, quæ in rei veritate gradus sunt ejus solius, quæ à putatitiâ obstructione ventriculorum fit. Interim, si Apoplexia illa sanguinea, ut quidam vocant (hanc facilè probabo ex duobus Gal. locis, à Montano citatis, de Cur.per V. S. c. 9. 4. Loc. aff. 2.) fit sine ventriculorum obstructione, profectò ADRASTEAS hæc vox est. Quam cum contemnit frivolâ istâ excusatione, Satis est, si frequentius fit ab obstructione; itemque ineptâ illâ distinctione, Ea quæ per essentiam est, sola est ab obstructione: profectò commiseratione dignus est.
units.tr: * Erastus, p. 190: "it makes cold"; "he wished." Indeed, I am of the opinion that the Arab, when he speaks of the vessels leading to the brain, understood the jugular veins together with the temporal arteries. It is perhaps not hard to prove that apoplexy also arises when these are obstructed, if one admits that the ventricles are workshops of the spirits. But I will not believe that Galen signified this in Aphorism 2.42, since the context of the passage sufficiently shows that Galen uses "apoplexies" in the plural, and that in truth these are degrees of that one apoplexy alone which arises from the supposed obstruction of the ventricles. Meanwhile, if that sanguine apoplexy, as some call it (I will easily prove this from two passages of Galen cited by Montanus, On the Method of Venesection, ch. 9, and Affected Places, book 4, ch. 2), occurs without obstruction of the ventricles, then this word is truly an inescapable necessity [ἀδράστεια]. When he dismisses this with that frivolous excuse, it is enough if it arises more often from obstruction, and likewise with that inept distinction, only that which is by its essence arises from obstruction, he truly deserves pity.

units.la: § 6. III. Argumentum (ut ego di- spono) Epilepsiam ab inunctione hydrargyri non admittere obstructionem, immobile est.
units.tr: § 6. III. The argument (as I set it out) that epilepsy from mercury ointment does not admit obstruction is unshakeable.

units.la: Quam enim longè petita est frigida cerebri intemperies, ab hydrargyri frigiditate introducta? ut & compulsio excrementorum intrò ab ejusdem frigido tempe-
units.tr: For how far-fetched is the cold intemperature of the brain, said to be introduced by the coldness of mercury? And likewise the driving of excrements inward from the same cold temperament?

units.la: temperamento ? Vt jam dici possit, Fernelium quidem expugnasse femiobstructionem : morbum autem formæ non­dum condidisse. Sed & ubi venenum ad­missum fuerit , causa tantum erit, non morbus.
units.tr: So that one could now say: Fernelius indeed overthrew semi-obstruction, but has not yet established a disease of that form. But where poison has been admitted, there will be only a cause, not a disease.

units.la: § 7. Post Fernelium cum Rondele­tio ( quamvis isobstructionem simplici­ter neget ) agit Mont. cap.30. Locus est in Methodo lib. 1. c.36. ult. mihi p. 162. Vbi hominis facilitatem maximopere admiror, Omnes concedent, inquit, spiritum transmeare ad partes cerebra subjectas , per quem motus celebratur respirationis. * Omnes concedent, quod vident : atnon omnes admittent causam à te, ô Monta& shy;ne, datam. Qui subito credunt Galeno, ut tu , Respirationem esse actionem mere animalem : ii subito etiam applaudent tibi. Ar, qui melius institui sunt, & sciunt, esse actionem mistam ex animali & natu& shy;rali, illi dicent, superesse aliquid respi­rationis, sed cum labore & stertore, quod non concurrat utraque causa. Quo modo? Ex cerebro ad musculos thoracis nihil defluit : hinc tantum non immobiles sunt. Ex corde proficiscens ebullitio in pulmo.
units.tr: § 7. After Fernelius, Rondeletius (although he simply denies obstruction) is dealt with by Montanus in chapter 30. The passage is in the Method, book 1, chapter 36 at the end, in my edition p. 162. Here I greatly admire the man's facility. "All will concede," he says, "that the spirit passes into the parts beneath the brain, through which the motion of breathing is carried on." All will concede what they see; but not all will admit the cause given by you, Montanus. Those who at once believe Galen, as you do, that respiration is a purely animal action, will at once applaud you too. But those who have been better taught, and know that it is an action mixed of the animal and the natural, will say that some respiration remains, but with labour and stertor, because the two causes do not concur. How so? Nothing flows down from the brain to the muscles of the thorax; hence they are not immobile, but only nearly so. The ebullition proceeding from the heart into the lungs...

units.la: * Objicit Erasmus. p. 191. Apoplectici quidam subito moriuntur. Videant boni, an tum non possint quam Apoplexia? pulmones & arterias, superest : hincaliqualis fe ostendit respiratio. Ex his intelligant ἐvπδεια suam, qui pro Erafto velitantur, Si ad thoracem descendere pofsunt spiritus, possunt etiam ad alias partes, adeoque fieri κλόν Epilepticus eo modo,quo Eraftus vult. Quin imò sciant tales, Lieblero non esse gratu n hoc auxilium, quippe qui diserte dicit, Anat. f. 190, Sine spiritu, ex cerebri ventriculis derivato,contingere. Quàin re dum Galenum pretendit,& omnesita sentire affirmatnimis liberalis est.
units.tr: Erasmus objects, p. 191: some apoplectics die suddenly. Let good men see whether they cannot then breathe in some way, since the lungs and arteries remain; hence some kind of breathing shows itself. From these points let them understand their own ready wit [εὐπορία], those who wrestle on behalf of Erastus: if spirits can descend into the thorax, they can also descend into other parts, and so convulsion [κλόνος] can occur in an epileptic in the way Erastus wants. Indeed, let such people know that this help is not welcome to Lieblerus, who plainly says, Anat. f. 190, that it happens without spirit being drawn from the ventricles of the brain. In this matter, while he appeals to Galen and claims that all agree with him, Montanus is far too generous.

units.la: § 8. I. Rondeletii argumentum est,
units.tr: § 8. I. Rondeletius's argument is this:

units.la: si crassus & vifcidus humor ventriculos cerebri obstrueret, cessaret motus omnis, ut in paralysi aut certè debilior fieret. Nunc tamtum abest ut cesset, ut etiam validior fiat. Non cessat, Montanus ait, quia non est integra obstructio. Hem tibi! Die mihi etiam, cur motus fit vehementior, ut Eraftus explicat Rond. mentem? Sed transeat : Si spiritus descendunt è cerebro,cur non sentiunt Epileptici ? imò im- pune secantur & uruntur? Non laborat ἀισθησις, sed ομωεισθησις,five sensus communis, Eleganter! Dico cum Erasto, p. 191. Manet immotum hoc, si obstructio in cerebri ventriculis fieret, pro ratione majoris aut minoris obstructionis debilitaretur motus : non autem, vult dicere, angeretur. Intelliguntur autem hæc omnia cum limitatione, siquidem ventriculi sunt ἐξωσιμένα spiritus animalis.
units.tr: If a thick and viscid humour obstructed the ventricles of the brain, all motion would cease, as in paralysis, or at least would become weaker. Now, far from ceasing, it becomes even stronger. It does not cease, Montanus says, because the obstruction is not complete. Well, there you are! Tell me too, why does the motion become more vehement, as Erastus explains Rondeletius's meaning? But let that pass. If spirits descend from the brain, why do epileptics not feel? Indeed, are they not cut and burned with impunity? It is not sensation [αἴσθησις] that is lacking, but common sense [κοινὴ αἴσθησις], as they say. Elegantly put! I agree with Erastus, p. 191: this remains unshaken, that if obstruction occurred in the ventricles of the brain, motion would be weakened in proportion to the greater or lesser obstruction; but it would not, he means to say, be increased. All these things, however, must be understood with the limitation that the ventricles are the receptacles of the animal spirit.

units.la: § 9. Cæterum, quia Montanus hei examinat sententiam Erafti tantoperè nobilitatam, Cur in Epilepsia pereat ex sensus, & motus? fas est diligentius paulò considerem us. Quod adsensum, inquit, reête fortasis sic disseruit. Fortasis, inquam ego. Cum enim ex propria oris consefione, detentæ sint facultates, tam principes, quam ministræ: quis mihi perfuadeat, solum sensum tactus superesse? Cum (repeto) & visus perierit, & auditus, & olfactus: quis mihi præstet tactum, sub quo gustum comprehendo? Atqui spiritus animales non deesse, ostendit servata quoquo modo in talibus respiratio? Iam ego dixi, Longe aliam causam esse respirationis servatæ. Hac admisså, corruit altera illa ex toto. Ergò dici nullatenus potest, rectè assignatam fuisse causam servati sensus. Quid igitur de motu? Cur motus fiat turpissime labitur, inquit. Cur? Cum motus non fiat, nisi præcedente cognitione vel intellectus vel sensus; neutrum verò horum adsit: quei dari heic potest ratio motus? Tum quid Eraftus? In Anatome, p.193. ut & in DD. confugit ad actiones eas, quæ fiunt à nobis non sentientibus, v.g. cum ambulamus in somno, loquimur &c. Huic ego respondeo, quod supra, Ostendat mihi similitudinem horum motuum cum motibus convulsivis, & fortassis credam. Quod enim Montanus ait in Ant-Erast. f. 126. a. Erastus non probavit, motus Epilepticos celebrari ab imaginatione, verissimè dictum est. Et cum hac attestatione abjicio & conspuo omnia illa, quæ Erastus scripsit trecentis versibus, ut Montanus numerat, à p. scilicet 192. ad. 210. simulque ea, quæ idem Montanus redhostiit, in Ant-Erast. à f.124. b. ad f. 132. a, idque ob eam causam, ne boni, quibus temporis thelaurus ƺere cointra Charus eit, cogantur subire molestiam illam legendi tot nugas.
units.tr: § 9. Moreover, since Montanus here examines the opinion of Erastus, so greatly ennobled, namely why sense and motion perish in epilepsy, it is right to consider it a little more carefully. "Erastus, he says, perhaps reasoned rightly about sensation." Perhaps, I say. For since, by the patient's own confession, the faculties have been held back, both the principal and the subordinate ones, who would persuade me that only the sense of touch remains? Since (I repeat) sight has perished, and hearing, and smell, who guarantees me touch, under which I include taste? And yet does the preservation of breathing in such people show that the animal spirits are not lacking? I have already said that the cause of the preserved breathing is quite different. Once this is admitted, the other falls entirely. Therefore it cannot be said in any way that the cause of the preserved sense was rightly assigned. What then of motion? "Why motion occurs, he slips most shamefully," he says. Why? Since motion does not occur unless preceded by cognition, either of the intellect or of the senses, and neither of these is present, what reason for motion can be given here? Then what does Erastus do? In the Anatomy, p. 193, and also in the Doctors, he takes refuge in those actions which we perform without sensing, e.g. when we walk in sleep, speak, and so on. To this I reply as before: let him show me that these motions are similar to convulsive motions, and perhaps I shall believe him. For what Montanus says in Anti-Erastus f. 126 a, that Erastus did not prove that epileptic movements are brought about by imagination, is most truly said. And with this testimony I cast off and spit upon all those things which Erastus wrote in three hundred verses, as Montanus counts them, namely from p. 192 to 210, together with those which the same Montanus has answered in Anti-Erastus from f. 124 b to f. 132 a; and this so that good men, to whom the treasure of time is dear, may not be compelled to suffer the trouble of reading so many trifles.

units.la: § 10. II. Rondel. argumentum ab autoritate Gal 8.Vs p.6. pendet, Naturam ideè purgasse cerebrum per infundibulum dictum, ne crebrà homo Apoplexiâ (hanc enim in Codd. Gal. esse, non Epiobservat ) laboret. Hoc infundibulum, cum ventriculis continuum, patere in Epilepticis inde manifestum esse, quod cessante paroxysmo, effluat pituita, Epilepsiæ causa. Hoc argumento nihil excogitari posse ineptius, ait Montanus, ineptus ipse.Cur enim non directe respondet imo concedit,Ex accidenti fieri? Quam vero suave est illud, Excussa post paroxysmum excrementa, non esse ex ventriculis, sed ex choana! Oportet valde bonus Geometra fuerit, qui ventriculorum finem ab ipsis ventriculis tam caute absciderit! Sed & qua ratione abscidit,qui in vestigio concedit,pituitam e ventriculis sensim extrudi, & desinere paroxysmum, non in instanti? De hoc argumento judicium Erafti est p. 210. Nescire fe quam validum fit.Mont. in Ant-Eraft. f.134. b.respondet,pro vali- do habuisse,cum probarit.Imo vero refutavit p.21 1.cum negat semper effluere. Quo igitur deponit, vult dicere, cum nihil notatu dignum effluit? Refutavit quin etiam denuo p.217. & 218. cum ipsi Montano ostendit 6 Interdum. Quo ipso vali-de prosternitur Semiobfrusttio.
units.tr: § 10. II. Rondeletius's argument rests on the authority of Galen, book 8, verse 6, p. 6: Nature therefore purged the brain through the so-called funnel, lest man suffer frequent apoplexy (for this is what the Galenic codices have, not epilepsy, as he observes). This funnel, being continuous with the ventricles, is evidently open in epileptics, since when the paroxysm ceases phlegm flows out, the cause of epilepsy. Montanus says that nothing more foolish than this argument could be devised, and that its author is foolish himself. For why does he not reply directly, or rather concede, that it happens by accident? How pleasant is that: the excrements expelled after the paroxysm are not from the ventricles, but from the choana! He must have been a very good geometer who so carefully cut off the end of the ventricles from the ventricles themselves! But also, by what reasoning does he cut it off, who at the same time concedes that phlegm is gradually pushed out of the ventricles, and that the paroxysm ceases not instantly? Erastus's judgment on this argument is at p. 210: he does not know how strong it is. Montanus, in Anti-Erastus f. 134 b, replies that he held it to be strong, since he has proved it. Indeed he refuted it at p. 211, when he denies that it always flows out. What then does he hold down? He means to say, when nothing noteworthy flows out? He refuted it again at p. 217 and 218, when he showed Montanus that it sometimes happens. By this alone semi-obstruction is strongly overthrown.

units.la: § III. Ejusdem Rond. argumentum facit Montanus id, quod Rond. de amplitudine ventriculorum attulerat, ob quam proxyfmus nec facile fiat, nec facile solvatur. Hoc ille temere prolatum esse ait.Si vere ita sensit,cur utitur Puto?Revera,tota illa concameratio, quam in tot ventriculos secuerunt Ariftotele posteriores,in homine vivo latissima est, &
units.tr: § III. Montanus treats as the argument of the same Rondeletius what Rondeletius had brought forward about the size of the ventricles, on account of which the paroxysm neither easily occurs nor easily ceases. He says this was put forward rashly. If he really thought so, why does he use "I think"? Truly, that whole vaulted chamber, which the later Aristotelians cut into so many ventricles, is very wide in a living man, and

units.la: & pateft commodè inde argumentum capi contra femiobftructionem illam. Quâ in re consensum habeo Erafti, Anat. f.210. Et quid?Cum tot argumenta jusbeant nos deferere ventriculos, &venire ad corpus : quid temerè reluctamur? Sed & Galenum, ab Adrafteà inductum, cò venisse, difficilè probatu non est.
units.tr: and from this a convenient argument can be drawn against that semi-obstruction. In this matter I agree with Erastus, Anat. f. 210. And what? Since so many arguments bid us abandon the ventricles and turn to the body, why do we rashly resist? But that Galen, led on by Adrastea, came to this point is not difficult to prove.

units.la: § 12. Poftrefutata, ut putat Montànus, Rond. argumenta de Obftr. eodem c.30. f.142. accingit fe examini sententiæ Rondel. propriæ. Ea est, ut rectè proponit, Conevulfionem fieri à materiâ,non crassâ, sed tenui: eaque non obstruente, sed mordicante et vellicante cerebrum. Heic cum videret constrictum fe argumento Rond. ex 2. Cauf. fym.2. quà de Palpitatione, sumto, nec non variis Epilepticorum historiis: oratorie incipit prædicare mirum Gal. artificium in diverso argumentandi modo. Quod illud verò est? Res ipsa quidem valdè tenebricosa est: puto autem latérein illis verbis, Gal. in palpitatione addit motum, qui motus potius quam subitus ortus et recessus indicat palpitationem & flatu fieri.
units.tr: § 12. After Rondeletius's arguments on obstruction have been refuted, as Montanus thinks, in the same chapter 30, f. 142, he sets himself to examine Rondeletius's own opinion. It is, as he rightly sets out, that convulsion is caused by matter that is not thick but thin, and that it does not obstruct but gnaws and plucks at the brain. Here, seeing himself hard pressed by Rondeletius's argument from the second cause, symptom 2, which is taken from palpitation, and also from various histories of epileptics, he begins rhetorically to proclaim the wonderful art of Galen in a different mode of arguing. What then is it? The matter is indeed very obscure; but I think the trick lies in those words: Galen, in palpitation, adds motion, which motion indicates that the palpitation arises and recedes suddenly, and that it is caused by flatulence.

units.la: Τί πρὸς ταῦτ᾽ ἐπιθυμεῖ ἐνίοτε ... κατὰ λέξιν;
units.tr: What does he wish to say in answer to these things, sometimes [Τί πρὸς ταῦτ᾽ ἐπιθυμεῖ ἐνίοτε ... κατὰ λέξιν;], word for word?

units.la: Ex multis hoc unum, Est λογομαχία, in quâ explicandâ quis jubeat me immo-
units.tr: Of the many points, this one is a logomachy [λογομαχία]. Who would order me to linger over explaining it?

units.la: rari? Interim hoc video, Galenum quidem hoc argumentandi genere prorsus confirmare sententiam meam: Rondeletium autem tacitè irein castra mea, dum in historiis allatis fumos loquitur, auras, nidores, odores, ventos, vinum, iram: imò Vaporesquoque. Quid istud vero est? Nec Montanus longè abit à me, fatendo palpitationem fieri à flatu crasso, qui exitum non habeat: necEraftus, Anat. f.208. cum ait, Flatus crassos palpitationem efficere,dum exitum quaerunt,ut non coagant partes animale, addit. A pari enim dicam, Eadem ratio Epilepsiæ est, siquidem non in ventriculis concludi dicamus vaporem,sed in corpore cerebri,unde in muficulos proficiscatur. Nec quidquam refert, fi ventriculos illi nufpiam dimittunt, cum nulla verisimilitudo illos adjuvet. Multò minus, fi Averroëm ex alto defpicit, & Medicum ex libro vocat. Fortassis ne Comes quidem ipse multò melior practicus fuit, ut § qui ruri degeret, & in opere suo exafciando totos 25. annos insumeret. Hoc non dico ideo,ut carpam illum, imitatione * Erafti: quin laudo industriam elaborandi potius libros, quam properandi ad nundinas Francofurtenfes.
units.tr: Meanwhile I see this: Galen, by this kind of argument, wholly confirms my opinion. Rondeletius, however, while speaking in the cited histories of fumes, breezes, steams, odours, winds, wine, and anger, and even of vapours, silently fights on my side. What is that? Nor is Montanus far from me in admitting that palpitation comes from a thick wind that has no outlet. Nor does Erastus, Anat. f. 208, when he says that thick winds produce palpitation while seeking an outlet, so that they do not clog the parts of the animal, add anything to the contrary. For by the same reasoning, I say, the same account holds for epilepsy, since if we say the vapour is not shut up in the ventricles but in the substance of the brain, from which it passes into the muscles. Nor does it matter if they nowhere let the ventricles go, since no probability supports them. Much less does it matter if he looks down from on high on Averroes and summons the physician from a book. Perhaps not even Comes himself was a much better practitioner, since he spent a full twenty-five years polishing his work. I do not say this to carp at him in imitation of Erastus. Rather, I praise the diligence of working over books rather than hurrying to the Frankfurt fairs.

units.la: § In Ant-Eraft. f. 97,4.
units.tr: § In Ant-Eraft. f. 97,4.

units.la: * In Anat. p. 102. furtenfes. Sed fuerit πεφιλησ ... non duplici ipse itinere huc tendit? Altero, cum ait, Si à flatibus fieri dicat Averroës, dandum hoc illi esse, quod in indicationibus non discrepet à Gal. Altero, cum concedit, Non omnem epilepsiam fieri ab obstructione ventriculorum cerebri: sed quandam à vaporibus, & eam quidem raro. Voluntarium enim hoctotum est. Nec obstat, quò minus dicam ego, Omnis epilepsia, & semper, sitá vaporibus. Et quid cogit nos ad amplexandam cáusarum varietatem, cum, ut non semel dixi, symptomata sint eadem? Et hæc quidem ab Adrastéa certò sunt: tu autem credas, Non satisfieri illi, si quoquo modo ad unam, alteramve quæstionem respondeatur: oportet omnia omnibus consentiant, Hoc demum infallibile Veritatis documentum est.
units.tr: * In Anat. p. 102. But let it be [πεφιλησ ...]; does he not come here by a double route? By one, when he says that if Averroes says it is caused by winds, it must be granted to him that he does not differ from Galen in the indications. By the other, when he concedes that not every epilepsy comes from obstruction of the ventricles of the brain, but some from vapours, and that rarely. For all of this is voluntary. Nor does it hinder me from saying myself that every epilepsy, and always, comes from vapours. And why does it compel us to embrace a variety of causes, since, as I have said more than once, the symptoms are the same? These things are certain from Adrastea. But you may believe that it will not satisfy him if one question or another is answered somehow; all things must agree with all. This, at last, is the infallible proof of truth.

units.la: § 13. Antequam hinc abeam, monendus est lector mihi, Recte quidem Rondel. negare, humorem crassum esse causam obstructionis: sed non recte admittere tenuem, Nam ad hunc quoque extendit se vis demonstrationis Galenicæ. An satis excusavit se vocibus iis, quas collegi supra? Sed & in duobus aliis errat, Non fit obstructio in ventriculis: sed in corpore cerebri. Præcedit quidem vellicatio expulsionem : sed praecedit hane obstructio.
units.tr: § 13. Before I leave this point, the reader must be warned by me that Rondeletius rightly denies that thick humour is the cause of obstruction, but wrongly admits thin humour, for the force of the Galenic demonstration extends to this too. Has he sufficiently excused himself by those words which I collected above? But he errs also in two other points: obstruction does not occur in the ventricles but in the substance of the brain. Vellication indeed precedes expulsion, but obstruction precedes that.

units.la: § 14. Tandem Montanus, cap. 31. Eraftum aggreditur. Vbi ante omnia videtur mihi confultum, ut paulò latius declarem, quae suprà § 3. & 9. leviter tegi. Coftroverfia est, Queifiat motus Epilepticus? Is, inquam, univocus, qui in musculis est? distinctus ab aequivoco illo, quiin cerebro? Ait Eraftus D. 91. Fit ab ipso spiritu animali, naturaliter fe habente, & in substantia, & in quantitate : sed inordinatè & tumultuose moto, quod facultas mandans fit lefa, & confuse imperet omnibus musculis non distincte his vel illis, quantum tendi laxarive debeant. Heic quis non obstupescat ad reinovitatem! Vt enim Montanus f.139. b. recte ait, Implicat duplicem in Philosophia contradictionem. Harum altera est, fi facultas animahis imperat musculis; imperium autem illed nascitur ex appetitu : oportet fana fit facultas appetitrix. Tu vero ipse, ô Erafte, occupatam & vexatam esse adeo feribis, ut alterationem non percipiat, sensu vid. communi; (seu συνασθησις abolitā. Quasi vero, reddit Eraftus, Anat. p. 193. Imaginatio (seu appetitus sensitivus, non possit esse in officio, quiescentibus sensibus! Vnde enim sunt actiones illae, quas in
units.tr: § 14. Finally, Montanus, in chapter 31, attacks Erastus. Here, above all, it seems advisable to me to explain more fully what was lightly covered above in §§ 3 and 9. The controversy is: what is the epileptic motion? Is it, I say, univocal, the one that is in the muscles, distinct from that equivocal one which is in the brain? Erastus says at p. 91 that it arises from the animal spirit itself, naturally disposed both in substance and in quantity, but moved disorderly and tumultuously, because the commanding faculty is injured and confusedly orders all the muscles, without distinguishing how much each should be stretched or relaxed. Here who would not be astonished at the novelty! For, as Montanus rightly says at f. 139 b, this involves a double contradiction in philosophy. The first is this: if the faculty of the soul commands the muscles, and that command arises from appetite, the appetitive faculty must be sound. But you yourself, O Erastus, write that it is so occupied and vexed that it does not perceive the alteration in the common sense, the synaesthesis being abolished. As if, Erastus replies at Anat. p. 193, imagination (or sensitive appetite) cannot function while the senses are at rest! For whence come those actions which we perform in sleep? Or those in delirium?

units.la: somno edimus? quas per delirium? Iam dixi, Ostendatur mihi similitudo harum actionum cum motibus convulsivis, & credam, fi libuerit. Altera est, fi motus di&i sunt à facultate mandante, erunt voluntarii; Atqui, de omnium consensu, sunt involuntarii. Tum ille Anat. p. 297. Cum motus tantum sint duplices, Naturales & Voluntarii; hi autem naturales non sint: restat, ut sint voluntarii. Heic quis tam compositæ mentis fit, qui non rideat? Quod enim in Patholog. cap. 115. dixi, Absurdum maximum est asseverare velle, actionem p.n. fieri ab eădem causâ, à quâ actio f.n. fit. Annon sequetur inde, Dispositionem f.n. quæ sanitas est, esse eandem cum dispositione p.n. quæ morbus est? Ita sanitas fiet morbus, & morbus sanitas. Hoc verò annon subvertit fundamenta artis nostræ? Sed agamus cominus.
units.tr: I have already said: let the likeness of these actions to convulsive motions be shown to me, and I will believe it, if you like. The second contradiction is this: if the said motions are commanded by the faculty, they will be voluntary; but by the agreement of all, they are involuntary. Then he says at Anat. p. 297: since there are only two kinds of motion, natural and voluntary, and these are not natural, it remains that they are voluntary. Here who is of so composed a mind as not to laugh? For what I said in Pathology ch. 115 is this: it is the greatest absurdity to assert that an action of the p.n. arises from the same cause from which an action of the f.n. arises. Does it not follow from this that the disposition of the f.n., which is health, is the same as the disposition of the p.n., which is disease? So health would become disease, and disease health. But does this not indeed subvert the foundations of our art? But let us come to close quarters.

units.la: § 15. In primo argumento ita illum fluctuare, perquam mirum est! Verum est, neque in Apopleƈticis, neque in Epilepticis unquam inventos fuisse ventriculos, vel ex toto, vel ex parte, pituitâ plenos: inveniri autem feré femperichoras cruentos paucos. Illi verò eò venerunt inter dissecandum, inquit Montanus, h.e. Non fuerunt ibi, eum homo moveretur, nec causa mortis fuerunt : sed cum calvaria aperiretur (ferrâ & malleo , sensim collecti ibi sunt. Quâ in re valdè illi consentio. Hinc cadit etiam femiobftructio, quam Montanus ex paucitate ichorum exstruere conatur,
units.tr: § 15. That he wavers so in his first argument is most remarkable! It is true that the ventricles have never been found full of phlegm, wholly or partly, in apoplectic or in epileptic patients; but almost always a few bloody ichors are found. Montanus says those came there during dissection, that is, they were not there while the man was moving, nor were they the cause of death, but gradually collected there as the skull was opened with saw and mallet. In this I entirely agree with him. Hence the semi-obstruction, which Montanus tries to build from the scarcity of ichors, also falls.

units.la: § 16.. Alterum argumentum , à sternutatione sumtum, non est ridiculum, ut Montanus putat, quatenus musculi thoracis & abdominis concutiuntur simul cum capite, ut ego explicavi negotium alibi. Sed nec quod à singultu petitur, admirationem meretur.Est enim convulfio quædam , de Hipp. quoque sensu. Et est utrobique obstructio,quatenus nervis impingitur spiritus quidam flatuofus,qui & musculos dictos,& ventriculum ( qui fi musculus non est, à musculorum tamen naturâ non longè abest, ut in Phyfiolog. probavi ) loco movet.
units.tr: § 16. The second argument, taken from sneezing, is not ridiculous, as Montanus thinks, inasmuch as the muscles of the chest and abdomen are shaken together with the head, as I explained elsewhere. Nor does what is drawn from hiccup deserve wonder. For it is a certain convulsion, in Hippocrates' sense too. And in both there is obstruction, inasmuch as a certain flatulent spirit strikes the nerves and moves the said muscles and the stomach (which, if it is not a muscle, is nonetheless not far from the nature of muscles, as I proved in the Physiology).

units.la: § 17. Litigium de ætatibus inane est, fi ad obstructiones ventriculorum cerebri referre voles.Laborant enim & Apoplexiâ (enes, & Epilepsiâ pueri, quatenus sanguinei sunt. Senes quidem illi, qui ὠχρὸς ἐγγίες dicuntur,& laxius vivunt, in quibus copiâ potius peccat sanguinis, quam ullâ qualitate, quique ( post mortem etiam ) exprobrat Medicis ἀιμεοφ;ὅσις timiditatem , effusus peros , naresque. Pueriautem, puellæve ferè illæ, in quibus malitia superat ætatem, fignoevidentiffimo, sanguinem repere ad & ȷ- ἀάδες, & ἀγωγὴν desiderare refrigeratoriam,& ficcatoriam,ex aq. deftill.alsines, dentariæ majoris,taraxici &c.cum pulv. March. fragm. pretiosis præp.&c.Et hæc est mala illa qualitas, quam Montanus confictam esse aitab Erafto. Quam fi ad variolas & morbillos adstringi patiatur, jam cum illo sum.
units.tr: § 17. The dispute about ages is empty, if you wish to refer it to obstructions of the ventricles of the brain. For old men suffer from apoplexy and boys from epilepsy, inasmuch as both are sanguine. Those old men who are called pale-yellow, and live more loosely, have a fault in the quantity rather than in any quality of their blood; and these, even after death, reproach the physicians with their timidity, with effused eyes and nostrils. Boys, or those girls chiefly, in whom malice surpasses their age, show by the clearest sign that blood creeps to the ... and needs a refrigerating and drying regimen, with distilled water of ... , powder of March ..., precious preparations, and so on. And this is that bad quality which Montanus says was made up by Erastus. If he allows it to be tied to smallpox and measles, then I agree with him.

units.la: § 18. Heic animadversione dignum est, Montanum,in reddendà causà, Apoplexiæ quidem in senibus, Epilepsiæ autem in pueris, vacillare non tantum, sed & vinci ab Adraftéa, Cum enim f.144. b. &iterum f.145. b. corpus etiam cerebri affici scribit: utique dici de illo poteft,quod de Gal. dixi. Quò fit,ut de ipso Montano ja&tari possit dicterium, quod ille de hoste suo, Quidquid afferat contra Veritatem, semper illa emicat.
units.tr: § 18. Here it is worth noting that Montanus, in giving the cause, wavers not only in apoplexy in the old and epilepsy in boys, but is even overcome by Adrastea. For when he writes at f. 144 b, and again at f. 145 b, that the body of the brain is also affected, then what I said of Galen can rightly be said of him too. Hence the saying which he used of his enemy can be thrown back at Montanus himself: whatever he brings against the truth, the truth always shines through.

units.la: § 19. Sed cur sub finem cap. ad Fernelium redit? Vt Colophonem imponat Epilepsiæ. Si, inquit, omnino admittatur Epilepsia in censum morborum formalium: tamen venenum illud causa efficnon morbus. Quo loci ego. Si concedat, venenum illud, non coeleste esse, sed elementare, & quod agat totà substantiâ: fore mihi assi-
units.tr: § 19. But why does he return to Fernelius at the end of the chapter? To put a crown on epilepsy. "If," he says, "epilepsy is admitted at all into the class of formal diseases, that poison is nonetheless the efficient cause and not the disease." To this I reply: if he concedes that the poison is not celestial but elemental, and acts with its whole substance, he will be agreeing with me.

units.la: nem.Possis fortassis & Corruptelam forma excusare, fi intelligas de Cacochymiá, quæ jam διαφθορὰ καὶ σπερμάτων quædam est, 3. Temp.3. B. 2.Aph.17. 3.Meth.2. ut deduxi in Inftit. lib. 3.ca.7. Huc inducere possis Fernelium ideò, quia concedit, auram illam, quæ.3. Loc. aff.7. de pede ad caput subrepebat, habuisse formale quid. Alioquin, fi, quoties supervenit paroxysmus epilepticus, toties corrumpitur forma cerebri,totiesque restituitur: opus habebimus metempsychosi Pythagorică, adeoque Lethæo flumine, è quo animæ Securos latices et longa oblivia potent.
units.tr: You could perhaps also excuse "corruption" as a form, if you understand it as cacochymia, which is already a kind of corruption of humours and seeds (Temp. 3; Aph. 2.17; Meth. 3), as I explained in my Institutes, book 3, chapter 7. You could draw Fernelius into this because he concedes that that vapour which crept from foot to head had something formal about it. Otherwise, if whenever an epileptic paroxysm comes on the form of the brain is corrupted, and then restored each time, we shall need Pythagorean metempsychosis, and the river Lethe, from which souls drink "untroubled waters and long forgetfulness."

units.la: Replica Erafti & Montani, C a p. XI.
units.tr: Reply to Erastus and Montanus, Chapter XI.

units.la: § 1. Eic quiescere poteram, nisi promissa fides urgeret. Dabo igitur ἀξιοφυνμένως quædam, curiofulo alicui non ingrata. Horum primum esto, contra primum Fern. argumentum, cap. füp. § 4. ex Anat. p. 189. quod nunc ita formo. Si ventriculi tam magni subito, et in ictu oculi implent debent, oportet petita illa alibi collecta, et asservata, uno impetu irruat. Vbi autem collectam fuisse dicemus? Non inter calvariam & duram
units.tr: § 1. I could have kept silent here, were it not that my promised word urges me. I shall therefore set down some points, worthy of notice and not unwelcome to any curious reader. The first is against Fernelius's first argument, above in § 4 from Anat. p. 189, which I now set out thus: if the great ventricles must be filled suddenly, in the twinkling of an eye, then the matter must have been collected and stored somewhere else and must burst in with a single rush. Where, then, do we say it was collected?

units.la: matrem : non inter duram & piam matrem:non in ipso corpore cerebri: non in ventriculis. De primis duobus locis ut nemo cogitat : ita neque de duobus alteris ausit quisquam cogitationes institue‘ re.Non de corpore : In hoc enim genita excrementa, sensim & sensim vaporis forte specie, pelluntur in ventriculos.. Non de ventriculis : sunt enim pars recipiens , quod non potest non distinctum esse à mandante. Quod excrementa paulatinâ congestione in ventriculis acerventur , argumentum dat Eraftus , Quia praecinguntur intus piâ matre, nec ulla vasa magna osculis suis hiant in illos: quin(quod ego addo) transverfim eunt, oculi indicio. Quid heic Montanus , in Defenf. f. 124? Canit cuculi cantum.Sed sint haec omnia nihil:Falsa est hypothesis, In ventriculis generari spiritus , ut alibi ostendi. Falso igitur poflit quid veri superftrui ? In his contrà Eraftus stat reito talo.
units.tr: Not between the skull and the dura mater; not between the dura and the pia mater; not in the substance of the brain itself; not in the ventricles. As nobody thinks of the first two places, so nobody would dare to entertain thoughts about the other two. Not in the substance: for the excrements generated there are driven little by little, perhaps in the form of vapour, into the ventricles. Not in the ventricles: for they are the receiving part, which cannot but be distinct from the sending part. That the excrements accumulate in the ventricles by gradual congestion, Erastus gives as an argument, because they are girdled within by the pia mater, and no large vessels open into them by their mouths; indeed (as I add) they run crosswise, as the eye shows. What does Montanus say here, in his Defence, p. 124? He sings the cuckoo's song. But let all this be nothing: the hypothesis that spirits are generated in the ventricles is false, as I have shown elsewhere. Can anything true be built on a false foundation? On these points Erastus stands firm, with his heels cast back.

units.la: § 2. Stat etiam in proximo feq. argumento , ut ego nunc dispono , Si inter bos duos morbos differentia ea est , quae dicitur, Epilepsia semper pracedet Apoplexiam. Hoc vero nunquam est visum: imo contrarium. Epileptici enim fiunt tandem Apoplectici. Hucimmediatè cohaeret tertium, Si Epilepsia est á femiobftructione, pro obstructionis magnitudine et parvitate, magis minus debilitabitur motus; non autem violentior fiet. Quid Montanus? Quod nunquam intelligere potui. Sunt, inquitshi duo morbi ex eádem causá:fcd differtilla modo. Pax! In Defenf. ineptè rhetoricatur.
units.tr: § 2. Erastus also stands on the next argument, as I now lay it out: if the difference between these two diseases is what is said, epilepsy always precedes apoplexy. But this has never been seen; on the contrary, the opposite. For epileptics at last become apoplectic. Immediately connected with this is the third point: if epilepsy comes from a semi-obstruction, motion will be weakened more or less according to the greatness or smallness of the obstruction; it will not become more violent. What does Montanus say? What I could never understand. "There are," he says, "two diseases from the same cause, but they differ in this way." Enough! In his Defence he plays the rhetorician foolishly.

units.la: § 3. Cum Montanus probare vellet, In duobus his morbis non perire omnem motum,attulit respirationem, quæ apud ipsum, & Gal. procul dubio est animalis: respondet Eraftus p.191. non quæri heic de solis thoracis musculis, sed in universum deomnibus in totocorpore. Heic fatendum est, Eraftum egregie frigere. I. cum dicit, Peculiares suas causas habere, curin his morbis sola respiratio superfit? At quæ sunt illæ? Pulcrum est, inquit quidam,quæ nesciás, alio devolvere. I I.cum paulò superius inquit, Si spiritus animales, aut facultates sentiendi, movendique fine spiritu etc. Quid hoc, ô bone, quod utea ris voculá Si? Ego enim suggeram, Dic mihi,utrum velis,Fiuntne actiones à spiritu,tanquam instrumento corporeo : an potius, facultas sola fine corpore id agit? Ambiguum in his fuisse Gal. notum est: quid igitur illud est, Ptex Gal: sententiá sentimus Omnes? Quid sentitis? Qui estis
units.tr: § 3. When Montanus wished to prove that in these two diseases not all motion perishes, he cited breathing, which for him and for Galen is undoubtedly animal. Erastus replies (p. 191) that the question here is not about the thoracic muscles alone, but in general about all the muscles in the whole body. Here I must admit that Erastus is freezing wonderfully. First, when he says that they have their own peculiar causes, why in these diseases does breathing alone survive? But what are those causes? "It is a fine thing," someone says, "to pass off what you do not know onto another." Second, when a little above he says: "If animal spirits, or the faculties of sensing and moving without spirit, etc." What is this, my good man, this use of the little word "if"? For I will put a question to you: tell me which you prefer. Are actions performed by spirit as a bodily instrument, or does the faculty alone accomplish them without any body? That Galen was ambiguous on these points is well known. What, then, is that "in Galen's opinion we all feel"? What do you feel? Who are all these people?

units.la: illi omnes? Revera apud Gal. actiones fiunt à spiritu : ἐεγαις, illius oppositi dogmatis uno,ni fallor,loco tantum meminit. An ita excusare licet incommodum sermonem? Vtro modo fiat,manet hoc, debilitatur ab obstructione motus, non augetur.
units.tr: Indeed in Galen actions are performed by spirit; he mentions that opposing doctrine, unless I am mistaken, in only one passage. Can an awkward phrase be excused in this way? However it happens, this remains: motion is weakened by obstruction, not increased.

units.la: § 4. Friget vero vel maxime,ut supra dixi ex p.193. cum Motus convulforios tribuit spiritu animali. Non nego,iterum dicam, dari tales motus, qui fiant non advertentibus nobis:hoc nego,ullam habere illos affinitatem cum convulforiis. Hoc ipsius frigus ex feq fiet manifestius.
units.tr: § 4. He freezes most of all, as I said above from p. 193, when he attributes convulsive motions to animal spirit. I do not deny, and will say again, that there are motions which occur without our noticing; this I deny: that they have any affinity with convulsive ones. This very coldness will become clearer from what follows.

units.la: § 5. Calcitrat enim Eraftus,Anat. p. 196. dum inquit, Tria sunt in nobis principia motus, I. Appetitus rationalis, ideo hominibus proprius, Voluntas dicta, quae non fit fine cognitione. 1 I. Appetitus sensitivus,eum brutis nobis communis, Phantasia seu Imaginatio vocata. I I I. Natura, ut quidem Gal. Stoicos imitatus, distinguit ab Anima, Mihi, inquit, neque de primo principio sermo est, neque de fecundo: sed de intermedio.Montanus igitur,dum cogit me loqui de primo, putidulum σφιςμα in homonymia committit.Quis te cogit?mi homo. Qui probationem petit,ut Montanus facit,in Ant-Eraft. quoque, f.196, nulla vi utitur. Et hoc est, quod ego dixi nuper,Ostende affinitatem horum motuum.
units.tr: § 5. Erastus kicks out in Anat. p. 196, when he says: "There are three principles of motion in us. I. Rational appetite, proper to humans, called the will, which does not occur without cognition. II. Sensitive appetite, which we share with the brutes, called phantasy or imagination. III. Nature, which, imitating the Stoics as Galen does, he distinguishes from the soul. To me," he says, "the discussion is neither about the first principle nor about the second, but about the intermediate one." Montanus, therefore, while he forces me to speak of the first, commits a rather silly sophism through ambiguity of terms. "Who is forcing you, my good man?" He who seeks proof, as Montanus also does in his Anti-Erastus, p. 196, uses no force. And this is what I said recently: show the affinity of these motions.

units.la: § 6. Convictus ut puto, in animo Eraftus instat p.199. Nulla,inquit, animati corporis actio, quae abeo, quatenus animatumeft,editur,edi potest, nihil animâ couserente, Heimihi, ut aures dolent ad tam scelerata machinamenta! Refutat enim hoc totum reduplicatio Arift. ἡ ἀνθ, quatenus animales sunt. At convulsorii non magis animales sunt, quam terraemotus: fiunt enim utrique à vi externâ. At Gal. 1.Mot. mufc,8. dicit, quod ego dico? Non dicit: loquitur enim de primo motus principio,de voluntate, de quâ tibi sermonem esse negas. Tu verò non debes à Gal. exigere, quod tam diligenter cavet, cum alibi,tum 2.Cauf. fym.2. ubi ait, * Convulsionem ducere musculos ad eam dispositionem, in quam, cum pro naturae lege habebant,ab animali virtute, ut Int. loquitur. In his annon est manifesta contradictio τὰ σαρκὸς, tanquam morbi, qui est ... ab eo, quod est καὶ φύσις, δυνάμει ψυχικῆ? Hoc probo per obliquum ex codem Earto,qui ait p.205. In musculis, neque lumorem esse, qui convulsionem faciat, neque flatum, etc. De humore ut facile confentio: ita flatum esse in Cramfo nostro,concedit ipse, D.78. & aliis. Hinc argumentor, Quod est in infimo gradu,id in sum-mo quoque est; Atqui in Cramfo flatus est. Scio, quid moliatur Montanus, f. 327. a. dum distinguit inter convulsionem, & motum convulforium : sed nihil moror.
units.tr: § 6. Convinced, I think, in his own mind, Erastus presses on at p. 199: "No action of an animate body, insofar as it is animate, can be produced without the soul concurring." Oh, my ears hurt at such wicked machinations! For Aristotle's reduplication, that these are animal insofar as they are animal, refutes all this. But convulsive movements are no more animal than an earthquake is: both come from external force. But does Galen, in On the Motion of the Muscles, book 1, ch. 8, say what I say? He does not: for he speaks of the first principle of motion, of the will, about which you deny there is any discussion between us. Yet you must not demand from Galen what he guards against so carefully, both elsewhere and in On the Causes of Symptoms, book 2, ch. 2, where he says that convulsion leads the muscles into that disposition in which they were when, by the law of nature, they had them, from animal power, as the translator puts it. In these words is there not a manifest contradiction: the affection of the flesh [τὰ σαρκὸς], as a disease, which comes from that which is nature and by a psychic power [καὶ φύσις, δυνάμει ψυχικῆ]? I prove this indirectly from the same author, who says at p. 205: "In the muscles there is neither the humour that makes the convulsion, nor wind," etc. Regarding humour I readily agree; that there is wind in our cramp he himself concedes, in D. 78 and elsewhere. Hence I argue: what is in the lowest degree is also in the highest; but in cramp there is wind. I know what Montanus is aiming at, f. 327a, when he distinguishes between convulsion and convulsive motion, but I do not dwell on it.

units.la: § 7. Victum fuisse Θν ἔσω λόγῳ Erafti, jam probo ex duabus vocibus, quibus utitur in discursu, Proprie & Absolute. Hæ enim arguunt,litem illi esse de nomine. Huc me ducunt verba quoque illa, p. 203. Differunt movere contrahere musculos, &c. Ita enim debebat loqui, Differunt, moveri musculos f.n. quæ fanitas est: & moveri p.n.quæ morbus est. Et hoc ipsum dicit in vestigio, Motus causa est anima cum musculo: vitii causa est morbus.
units.tr: § 7. That Erastus was defeated in his inner argument [ἔσω λόγῳ] I now prove from the two words he uses in his discourse, "properly" and "absolutely." For these show that the dispute between us is about a name. These words of his, p. 203, also lead me here: "They differ: to move, to contract the muscles," etc. For he ought to have spoken thus: "They differ: the muscles are moved" in the sense of health, which is a healthy state; and "are moved" in the sense of disease, which is a morbid state. And he himself says the same immediately afterwards: the cause of motion is the soul with the muscle; the cause of the defect is disease.

units.la: § 8. Victoriam eandem spondet mihi, quod p.204. arripit inanem, & in *Montano jam damnatam distinctionem interconvulfionem & motum convulforium, idque ideo, ut declinet autotoritatem Gal.2. Cauf. fym.1. dicentis, Convulsionem esse à solo morbo. Reverà, est hæc distinctio eadem cum illa, Convulfio alia est legitima, alia spuria.Scio ego, quid differat ... : nescio, quid fit illud,quod facit, ut ... fit * Vide Epist.12.f.34.a.
units.tr: § 8. He promises me the same victory, because at p. 204 he seizes on an empty distinction already condemned in Montanus, between convulsion and convulsive motion, and does so in order to escape the authority of Galen (Caus. sym. 1), who says that convulsion comes from the disease alone. In truth, this distinction is the same as that one: convulsion is one thing when it is legitimate, another when it is spurious. I know what differs ... I do not know what that thing is which makes ... happen. * See Epist. 12, f. 34 a.

units.la: legitimus filius, ⲁⲗ̄ⲟⲩ ꝯ spurius. Ille constituit perpetuam convulsionem, hic interpolatam. Quo graviores súnt febres continuæ intermittentibus: eò spatius est gravior κλόνω. Atque ut operam ludere, qui febres intermittentes vocaret spurias: ita heic mera est novitas, ingrata bonis, quia inutilis.
units.tr: a legitimate son, another spurious. The one establishes a continuous convulsion, the other an interrupted one. As continued fevers are more grave than intermittent ones, so the convulsion is more grave [κλόνος]. It would be as pointless to call intermittent fevers spurious; so here there is pure novelty, unwelcome to good men because it is useless.

units.la: § 9. Quod verò promittit se dicturum de loco illo. 2. Caus. sym. 1. & facit p. 205. quale est? A facultate animali, cuius symptomata sunt tàm convulsiones, quam motus convulsorii, transilit ad naturalem. Non negatur, Cerebrum, à vapore illo irritatum, expellere ad musculos: hoc verò facultatis cerebri expultricis est, quæ tot miliaribus distat ab animali, è cerebro in partes distributā, de quā pugnat homo, quot dici non possunt. Nimirum morbus morbum parit, & quæstio heic est de proximo. Vt enim alibi dixi, Intemperies gignit vaporem: vapor, in cerebrum receptus, ope expultricis ejusdem, pellitur in musculos: musculi, ab illo contractiōnon amplius sub facultate naturali sunt, sed animali. Hanc scalam quia non semper præ oculis habemus, dicimus aliquando, convulsiones esse cerebri affectus, omissis musculis, qui immediatum sunt motus instrumentum. Ex {&}c fundamento fumitur excufatio Gal, qui. 1.Cauf. fym. ult. Epilepfiam dicit effe affectum cerebri. Hoc cum ad motus vitiofos adftrinxiffet Eraftus, p. 205. & vero animadverteret poftea, quantopere obftet conatibus ipfius:juffit delere in Erratis. Et alioquin obfcurum non eft,quam difficulter expediant fe illi, qui in motu cerebri pedem figunt. Qua enim manu contingit cerebrum mufculos ? Per nervos forte ? Hoc ipfimet negant.
units.tr: § 9. As for what he promises to say about that passage at 2. Caus. sym. 1, and what he does at p. 205: what is it? He passes from the animal faculty, whose symptoms are both convulsions and convulsive motions, to the natural faculty. It is not denied that the brain, irritated by that vapour, drives it out to the muscles; but this belongs to the expulsive faculty of the brain, which is as many miles distant from the animal faculty, spread from the brain into the parts, about which the man quarrels, as cannot be said. Clearly disease begets disease, and the question here concerns what is nearest. For, as I have said elsewhere, intemperature generates vapour; the vapour, received into the brain, is driven into the muscles by the aid of that same expulsive faculty; the muscles, contracted by it, are no longer under the natural faculty but under the animal. Because we do not always keep this ladder before our eyes, we sometimes say that convulsions are affections of the brain, leaving out the muscles, which are the immediate instrument of motion. Galen's excuse is taken from this same foundation, in 1. Caus. sym. last chapter, where he calls epilepsy an affection of the brain. When Erastus had tied this to vicious motions, p. 205, and afterwards noticed how greatly it hindered his own efforts, he ordered it deleted in the Errata. And it is not obscure how hard it is for those who fix their foot in the motion of the brain to extricate themselves. By what hand does the brain touch the muscles? Through the nerves, perhaps? These very men deny it.

units.la: § 10. Ex his duo intelliguntur. Alterum, vere dixiffe Galenum, Convulfionem effe a morbo folo, fiquidem fubjectum adaequatum infpicias. Alterum, Montanum quidem acontradictoriis liberum effe : Eraftum autem confufionis reum. A qua nunquam fe liberabit, fi discerit p.2c6. Galenum late accipere vo. cabulum Natura.Multo minus locum in de Cauf.fym.conciliabit cu altero, 3. Loc. aff.7. allata frivola illa diftinctione, in convulfionem proprie & improprie dictam. Haec eft defenfio Gal. Non femper ille defcendit ad mufculos.
units.tr: § 10. From these things two points are understood. First, that Galen truly said convulsion comes from the disease alone, provided you look at the adequate subject. Second, that Montanus is indeed free of contradictions, but Erastus is guilty of confusion. He will never free himself from this if he learns (p. 206) that Galen uses the word Nature broadly. Still less will he reconcile that frivolous distinction, between convulsion properly and improperly so called, which he brings forward in Caus. sym., 3. Loc. aff. 7, with the other passage. This is the defence of Galen: he did not always descend to the muscles.

units.la: § 11. Hinclumen accipiunt illa.p.207. Objicit Montano, Si Epilepfia non eft a folo morbo,fed concurrit vis cerebri, infcite contra nos difputat. Concurrit vis
units.tr: § 11. Here those words at p. 207 offer him light. He objects to Montanus that if epilepsy does not come from the disease alone, but the force of the brain concurs, he argues foolishly against us. The force of the brain concurs

units.la: cerebri expultrix naturalis, ut causa Ꝓmota : non concurrit vis animalis, quae causa est propinqua, quam Eraftus venatur. Exhis patet, quatenus verum fit, quod l.3: c.30:Montanus ait,Certo certius esse,in epilepsia concussionem illam ex cerebro esse.Concussio enim illa,(siquidem ita vecari potest conatus Naturae expellentis) est causa remota. Et hoc est, quod contra Gabucinum dicitur ibidem, Putaffe, nullum alium in epilepsia motum esse quam contractionem cerebri, eamque à natura, non à morbo factam. Imo est alius quoque, Musculorum fc. qui est à morbo. Quo minus opus est obscuro illo Erafti patrocinio, Contractio cerebri non est depravatus ille motus membrorum: imo verò nascitur ab eâ. Hoc enim debebat velle, In ordine causarum, contractio quidem cerebri prior est contractione musculorum : differunt autem, quod cerebri motus est naturalis, musculorum animalis,sed depravatus.
units.tr: as the natural expulsive force of the brain, as a moved cause; the animal force does not concur, which is the proximate cause that Erastus hunts after. From these things it is clear how far true is what Montanus says in 1. 3, c. 30: that it is more certain than certain that in epilepsy that concussion comes from the brain. For that concussion (if indeed the effort of expelling Nature can be so called) is the remote cause. And this is what is said against Gabucinus in the same place: that he thought there was no other motion in epilepsy than a contraction of the brain, and that this was made by nature, not by the disease. Indeed there is another, namely that of the muscles, which comes from the disease. Hence there is less need for that obscure patronage of Erastus, that the contraction of the brain is not that depraved motion of the limbs; rather it arises from it. For this is what he ought to have wished: in the order of causes, the contraction of the brain is indeed prior to the contraction of the muscles; but they differ in that the motion of the brain is natural, while that of the muscles is animal, yet depraved.

units.la: § 12. Ex quo vestigio antequam abeam,monere placuit,Musculorum thoracis in Epilepsia, ut in Apoplexia quoque, aliam esse conditionem, quam reliquorum omnium. Thoracis enim aliquomodo moventur naturaliter, coactiquippe à naturâ aut, fi distinctius loqui me vis,ab ebulliente
units.tr: § 12. Before I leave this point, I wish to remind you that the muscles of the chest in epilepsy, as also in apoplexy, are in a different condition from all the rest. For the chest moves in some way naturally, being moved, to be sure, by nature, or, if you wish me to speak more precisely, by the heat boiling up

units.la: bulliente in corde calore : reliquis nihil uperefle. Hoc probo ex respiratione Hippocrati dicta sublimi, Galeno coacta, cum infigne in corde incendium cogit hominem ad extremam thoracis dilatationem. Hinc occasionem fumo, explicandi fictitiam Gal. contradiftinctioem, de difficultate respirationis in Epiepfia, de qua Montanus multa ex Gabucino. Sufficit hoc unum, Gal.4. Loc.aff.2. neutiquam dicit, In Epilepsia salvam esse respirationem : sed neque per rerum nauram dicere potuit.
units.tr: boiling up in the heart; nothing remains for the others. I prove this from respiration, which Hippocrates called sublime, Galen forced, since a notable fire in the heart drives a man to the utmost dilation of the chest. Hence an occasion arises for smoking out Galen's fictitious contra-distinction, about the difficulty of breathing in epilepsy, about which Montanus says much following Gabucinus. This one thing suffices: Galen, 4. Loc. aff. 2, by no means says that breathing is safe in epilepsy; nor could he say so according to the nature of things.

units.la: § 13. Diffisus, credo, caufe sua Eratus, p.208 .orditur novam telam,ut proet (fi ullo modo possit) motum mufcuorum depravatum in epilepsia, tamen imul esse naturalem. Eho dum, inquis, one absurditatis pervenit? Pervenit cer-. Actiones animales,inquit, aut proprie ta dicuntur,aut improprie. Tu vero,qui ac legis, statim cogita, Labi negotium id quaestionem quid nominis. Sed auiamus, ne insontem damnare videanur.Illas,addit,Montanus vult,has ego. Sunt autem illa, quae eduntur a partius corporis nostri, quatenus anima in-ormatae sunt. Heic enim anima quidem agit:
units.tr: § 13. Distrustful, I believe, of his own cause, Erastus, p. 208, begins a new web, so that he may show (if in any way he can) that the depraved motion of the muscles in epilepsy is nevertheless at the same time natural. Look, you say, to what absurdity has he come? He has come to ... Animal actions, he says, are called either properly or improperly. But you, who read this, think at once that this slips into a question about a name. But let us listen, lest we seem to condemn an innocent man. Montanus wishes those to be the former, I the latter, he adds. Those are the ones which are produced by the parts of our body, insofar as they are informed by the soul. For here the soul indeed acts:

units.la: Vide fis, quam misere fe torqueat in Epift. pro
units.tr: See how wretchedly he tortures himself in the Epistle, for

units.la: muper in margine laudata!
units.tr: just now cited in the margin!

units.la: agit: partes autem sunt instrumentum, quo agit illa.Exemplo sint flatus,qui palpitationem excitant in musculis. Flatus ita heic agunt, ut anima non coagat. Ita purgans medicamentum movet corpus, animâ seu facultate motrice quiescente. Propterea, in palpitatione, pharmacove purgante qui motus est,non recte dicitur animalis. Viden' tu & Recte? Sed fit,quis Sabinorum unquam hoc somniavit? Animalis enim tum dicitur,cum ab animâ,si ita vis, à liberâ voluntate editur. Sit vero hoc quoque: da mihi exempla tuorum motuum, qui quadrent ad motus epilepticos? Palpitatio certe,& purgantis medicamenti actio, tantum absunt à distinctione propositâ,quantum sententia mea à tuâ: imo vero confirmant meam,quatenus fiunt ab externo aliquo, quod vim facit instrumento corporeo, animâ nihil agente. Hoc ita accommodo. Quemadmodum flatus facit palpitationem vi propriâ, postquam, ut puto, receptus est intra membranam musculi,& musculum ipsum,non coagente animâ: ita flatus,in ipsum musculi corpus seu ventrem adductus, facit motum epilepticum, otiosâ animâ. Hoc quia acceptat Erastus in Cramso: oportet acceptet in aliis consulfionibus quoque, quippe quæ disse- rūt. runt inter fe tantum ... Atqui,nec palpitatio, nec spasmus fit, nifi in corpore vivo?Si hoc vult Eraftus,quovis hospitâ pejor est, & indignus, cum quo verbum commutem. Melius igitur speremus de tanto viro, & cogitemus penficulatius,quid potuerit velle? Quærat hoc alius, me fagacior. Ego enim, post cogitationes varias, vario tempore inflituras,mecum & cum amicis, manè, meridiè, vesperi, media noćte, post fursum, deorsumque versum Eraftum: nihil aliud exputare possum.
units.tr: acts; the parts, however, are the instrument by which she acts. Let flatus, which excites palpitation in the muscles, be an example. Flatus here act in such a way that the soul does not co-act. So a purgative medicine moves the body, the soul or motive faculty being at rest. Therefore, in palpitation or in the motion of a purgative drug, the motion is not rightly called animal. Do you see, and "rightly"? But which of the Sabines ever dreamed of this? For it is called animal when it is produced by the soul, if you like, by free will. But let this also be granted: give me examples of your motions that fit epileptic motions. Palpitation certainly, and the action of a purgative medicine, are as far from the proposed distinction as my opinion is from yours; indeed they confirm mine, insofar as they are made by something external that exerts force on the bodily instrument, with the soul doing nothing. I adapt it thus. As flatus produces palpitation by its own power, once, I think, it has been received within the membrane of the muscle and the muscle itself, without the soul co-acting: so flatus, driven into the very body or belly of the muscle, produces epileptic motion, with the soul idle. Because Erastus accepts this in Cramp, he ought to accept it in other convulsions as well, since they differ from one another only ... But surely neither palpitation nor spasm occurs except in a living body? If Erastus wishes this, he is worse than any stranger, and unworthy that I should exchange a word with him. Let us therefore hope better of so great a man, and think more carefully about what he may have meant. Let someone sharper than I ask this. For I, after various thoughts, at various times, with myself and with friends, in the morning, at noon, in the evening, at midnight, after turning Erastus up and down, can make nothing else out.

units.la: § 14. Hac in re ... mè habet futilitas rationum: imò ... sunt. Aut contrarius est, inquit extr. p.208. motui fanorum,aut non. Est contrarius, di- co, quomodo sanitas & morbus sunt contraria. Ergò,motus epilepticus non fit fine anime subsidio. Papæ! Vnde est? Ergò? Imò, quæ est ratio consequentiæ? Bona etenim et mala actio,inquit,necessario sunt ab eådem parte, eademque facultate. Aufer mihi Facultatem. Fitne morbus à facultate? quatenus morbus opponitur sanitati? Ineadem parte esse necesse est, alioqui contrarietas nulla effet: ab eadem facultate esse, quis ausit dicere? Quin foli parti,seu instrumento, ipse diserte transferibit,Epift. 15. f.44. b, Et quid excurro? In
units.tr: § 14. In this matter ... the futility of his arguments troubles me: indeed ... they are. Either it is contrary, he says, to the motion of the healthy, or it is not. It is contrary, I say, as health and disease are contrary. Therefore epileptic motion does not occur without the help of the soul. Oh! Whence does this come? Therefore? Indeed, what is the rule of consequence? For good and bad action, he says, necessarily proceed from the same part and the same faculty. Take away the faculty from me. Does disease come from a faculty, insofar as disease is opposed to health? To be in the same part is necessary, otherwise there would be no contrariety; to be from the same faculty, who would dare to say so? Indeed he himself will expressly assign it to the part or instrument alone, Epist. 15, f. 44 b. And why do I run on? In

units.la: hoc ipso gradu transscribit, cum ait p. 209. Contrarie cause circa idem subjectum versantur: non ausus jungere facultatem prae pudore. Quod tanto facilius creditu mihi est, quo verius est actiones quasdam non esse ab ulla facultate, ut ipsummet docentem audivimus. Pergit, Hæc autem sunt sanitas et morbus. An Hæ voluit scribere? Non enimalio referri potest quam ad causas. Tum vero impropriissima locutio est, & quæ fraudem redolet, Sanæ enim & morbosæ partes sunt subjectum. Fraus est, ut dicere possit, sanitatem et morbum esse dispositiones, quæ non agunt, sed modificant actiones. Quam vero hic sermo Medico indignus est! Qui enim bene institutus est, sic loquitur, Sanitas est dispositio talis, per quam bene agimus: morbus est talis, per quam male. Hic modus in arte nostra tam latam constituit differentiam, ut contrariæ dicantur actiones, quarum altera s. n. fit, altera p.n. Quare, illa quidem fit, & instrumento & facultate bene se habente: hæc, vel alterutro deficiente, vel utroque. Ex his intelligas licet, quam vere absurdum fit, quod aliis objicit absurdum, Fore, ut sanitas constet sine anima, adeoque anima non fit causa efficiens actionum s.n. Intelligas etiam, Partes non fieri morborum instrumen- ta,
