units.tr: In this very way he copies it across, when he says (p. 209): "Contrary causes operate on the same subject." He did not dare to add "faculty," for shame. That is all the easier for me to believe, the more truly some actions come from no faculty at all, as we have heard him teach himself. He goes on: "These, however, are health and disease." Did he mean to write "these"? For they can be referred to nothing but causes. Then indeed it is a most improper way of speaking, and one that smells of deceit: healthy and diseased parts are the subject. It is a trick, so that he can say that health and disease are dispositions which do not act but modify actions. How unworthy of a physician this way of speaking is! For one who is properly trained speaks thus: health is such a disposition through which we act well, and disease is such a one through which we act badly. In our art this manner of speaking makes so wide a difference that actions are called contrary, one of them done according to nature, the other contrary to nature. From this you may understand how truly absurd it is that he objects to others as absurd: that health would exist without a soul, and so the soul would not be the efficient cause of the natural actions. You may also understand that parts do not become the instruments of diseases, unless someone wishes to confuse the agent with the patient. But now I am ashamed of this roundabout phrase [περιδρεψαμένων], perhaps better "minute particles" [λεπτομερῶν].

units.la: [Marginal notes at the right edge are too cut off to read reliably.] ta, nisi confundere quis velit agens cum patiente. Verum, jam me difpudet περιδρεψαμένων, forte potius λεπτο- μερῶν.
units.tr: ta, unless someone wishes to confuse the agent with the patient. But now I am ashamed of this roundabout phrase [περιδρεψαμένων], perhaps better "minute particles" [λεπτομερῶν].

units.la: § 15. Interim nec dissimulare debeo recte facta viri. Non enim injuria urget argumentum suum, p.210, contra femi- nam obstructionem, Nec posse ventriculos to- tos subito impleri, quin præcedat epile- pfia: nec posse subito depleri, quin fequa- tur. Imo, ex fup. p.189. & 190. postis etiam paralysin metuere. Et quid? Ausitne quis (liceat mihi repetere toties dictum) affirmare, hos duos morbos,tam diversis stipatos symptomatis, esse ab eâdem causa, magnitudine differente? Non injuria etiam defendit Averroëm, contra quem nihil solidi attulifle Montanum, rectissimè ait. Vellem fuisse ausum hoc quoque, ut, damnatâ repletione Galenicâ, summam rei detulifiet ad Fumos, seu Vapores Averrois. Tanto magis, quod p.212. ex 3.Loc. aff.7. concludit, Omnem epilepsiam fieri eodem modo, à re videlicet acri, ut non ita pridem ego etiam conclusi,&quatenus verum fit, oftëdi.Per quæ ipsa exponi cupio illa,p.213. Rejiciendam quidem esse femiobftructionem, quod obstent illi insolubilia argumenta: amplexandam contrà esse,in omni epilepfiâ, acrimoniam ftimulantem. Putà, fi detur, ftimulum ilium naturalem definere in noxam animalem. Hoc velle debent fumi Erafti, qui idem femper agunt, &c, Atque hifumi conftituunt tertiam Epilepfiæ fpeciem apud Gal. in de Loc.aff. quam non femper mitiorem efle illâ, quæ per effentiam à repletione , ut Gal. vult, & dixi eo fupra, & confirmat hoc ipfo loco Eraftus.
units.tr: § 15. Meanwhile I ought not to conceal the right things the man has done. For he does not press his argument unjustly, at p. 210, against the obstruction of the womb: that the ventricles cannot be suddenly filled completely without epilepsy preceding, nor suddenly emptied without it following. Indeed, from what was said above at pp. 189 and 190, he even fears paralysis after it. And what then? Would anyone dare (let me repeat it, as it has been said so often) to affirm that these two diseases, surrounded by such different symptoms, come from the same cause, differing only in magnitude? He also rightly defends Averroes, against whom Montanus, as I have said, brought nothing solid. I wish he had dared this too: that, having condemned the Galenic repletion, he had referred the whole matter to the fumes or vapours of Averroes. All the more so since at p. 212, from the Third Book of the Loca affecta (ch. 7), he concludes that every epilepsy comes about in the same way, namely from a sharp matter, as I too have recently concluded, and I have shown how far this is true. By these very points I wish to explain what he says at p. 213: that the obstruction by fumes should indeed be rejected, because insoluble arguments stand against it, but that a stimulating sharpness should be embraced in every epilepsy. Suppose, he says, that that natural stimulus is given, and that it ends in an animal harm. This is what the followers of Erastus ought to want, who always do the same thing, and so on. And these fumes make up the third species of epilepsy in Galen's De locis affectis, which is not always milder than that which arises from repletion, as Galen holds, and as I said above, and as Erastus himself confirms in this very place.

units.la: § 16. Cur Avicenna(p.215,ext.) Epilepfiæ parvæ comparávit fternutamentum, non longè quærenda eft ratio. Quemadmodum fternutamentum conftat duplici motu, Naturali, qui eft cerebri expellentis,& Animali,qui eft thoracis concuffi : ita epilepfia duplicem habet motum,&c. Quare fi Eraftus Galenum & Thaddæum fibi amicos depofcit, portet admittat ἀναγεννᾶν dictam, Irritationem inquam, cerebri jungat cum convulfione mufculorum. Ita cur(114.) Hipp. & Gal. fingultum convulfioni affinem fecerint,in promtu caufa eft, Similitudo motus in excutiendâ noxâ. Vcrtiginem qui elegantes Medici compararint Epilepfiæ, haud fcio. Eftenim fola imaginatio læfa in vertigine, & ob id deliriis vicinior.Interim recte Eraftus, Illuftrant hæc rem , non probant.
units.tr: § 16. Why Avicenna (p. 215, at the end) compared minor epilepsy to sneezing is not hard to find. Just as sneezing consists of a twofold motion, a natural one, which is of the brain expelling, and an animal one, which is of the chest being shaken, so epilepsy has a twofold motion, and so on. Therefore, if Erastus demands Galen and Thaddaeus as his friends, he should admit the so-called irritation [ἀναγεννᾶν], I mean, he should join the irritation of the brain with the convulsion of the muscles. Thus the reason why Hippocrates and Galen made hiccup akin to convulsion is ready to hand: the similarity of motion in shaking off a harm. I do not know which elegant physicians compared vertigo to epilepsy. For in vertigo only the imagination is impaired, and for that reason it is closer to delirium. Meanwhile Erastus is right: these things illustrate the matter, they do not prove it.

units.la: § 17. Epilepsiam simpliciter separari ab obstructione, non feram.
units.tr: § 17. I will not put up with epilepsy being simply separated from obstruction.

units.la: Non est obstructio ventriculorum cerebri ab humoribus vel crassis vel tenuibus : sed est obstructio corporis cerebri, praecipuè, quâ principium nervorum est, à vaporibus crassis, spiritus animales mentientibus. Hi vapores dum per nervos deorsum labuntur in musculos, causantur aIam obstructionem, ut jam toties dixi.
units.tr: The obstruction is not of the ventricles of the brain by humours, either thick or thin; it is an obstruction of the substance of the brain, chiefly where the origin of the nerves is, by thick vapours that counterfeit animal spirits. While these vapours slide downward through the nerves into the muscles, they cause that obstruction, as I have said so many times already.

units.la: § 18. À senibus ductum argumentum, ἀ̔ξ‑ζων est. Nam quantum humores frigidi, crassi, crudi absunt ab epilepsiâ causandâ:tantum senes ab epilepsiâ. Ideo παιδιῶν παιδὸς dicebatur à priscis. Quo ipso Montanus tacitè accusatur, cum Apoplexiam in pueris non raro fe vidisse ait. Fuit syncope cardiaca, quae fi jumentis contingat, dicunt, das Bfut hats erftictet. Haec fi accidat ἀμοιέρεσι quibufdam, subitò moriuntur fine ullo ftertore, ut jam suprà indicavi. His ipsis ἀμοιέρεσι tantum, non autem indistinctè omnibus senibus accidit apoplexia, qui etiam ut plurimum (praesertim, fi venae sectio, vel intermissa fit, vel timidius administrata) mortui jam, pipulo differunt ignavos nostros Medicos, qui venae sectionis terminum statuunt annum 60. Non qui anni sint, videndum est, inquit Celsus, sed quæ vires supersint. Eadem catarrhorum fuffocativorum ratio est. Sed hæc aliena sunt:
units.tr: § 18. The argument drawn from old men is of no account [ἀ̔ξ‑ζων]. For as far as cold, thick, and crude humours are from causing epilepsy, so far are old men from it. So the saying "a child of children" [παιδιῶν παιδὸς] was used by the ancients. By this very saying Montanus is tacitly accused, since he says he has not rarely seen apoplexy in boys. There was cardiac syncope, which, if it happens to beasts, they say: "the blood has choked it." If this happens to certain unfortunates [ἀμοιέρεσι], they die suddenly without any stertor, as I have already pointed out above. Apoplexy happens only to these unfortunates, not indiscriminately to all old men; and these very men, too, for the most part (especially if the bloodletting is either omitted or timidly carried out) are already dead, differing little from our lazy physicians, who set the limit for bloodletting at the age of sixty. It must be considered not what years a man has, says Celsus, but what strength remains to him. The same reasoning applies to suffocating catarrhs. But these things are beside the point.

units.la: § 19. Pueros esse Epilepticos, non ob redundantiam crudorum & crassorum humorum, sed ob malam qualitatem,verissimum est : fi modò qualitatem illam recte accipias. Non enim fine corpore est. Vno verbo, Vapor est, ad bilis naturam tendens, Ideò curatur eo modo,quo dixi. Absque corpore fi capiatur, dici recte potest fictam esse, & nullâ ratione fultam.Cum corpore fas est & MaligAitatem considerare,quæ in pueris Vio- las & Morbillos producit. Hanc per d. morbos vacuari integrè, facilè credo: non obstat tamen, quò minus ex aliis causis maligni creantur vapores, qui quasi recidivam faciant. Hos vapores semper esse acres & mordaces, contrà Eraftum contendero. Indicibilis enim illa,& à totâ substantiâ putredo, fine acri calore non fit,præsertim, quia frigus pofitivum heic non est. Hujus caloris gradum quia nescimus, putredinis etiam gradus meritò ignotus esse dicitur. In hoc calore potius quam in redundantiâ causam mutatæ Epilepsiæ,s. Aph.7. col. loco.Curatur,inquam,quædam Epilepsia ratione ætatis, non quia redundantia non adsit : sed quia calor, corruptionis causa, abest. Vt hactenus recte dixerit Eraftus, Galenum ex hypothesi potius, quam ex rei veritate locutum esse.
units.tr: § 19. That children are epileptic not because of a surplus of crude and thick humours, but because of a bad quality, is most true, provided you understand that quality rightly. For it is not without a body. In a word, it is a vapour tending toward the nature of bile; for that reason it is cured in the way I have described. If it is taken without a body, it can rightly be said to be feigned and supported by no reason. With a body it is right to consider also a malignity, which in children produces violets and measles. I readily believe this is wholly purged away by those diseases; yet it does not stand in the way that malignant vapours are created from other causes, which bring about, as it were, a relapse. I will contend against Erastus that these vapours are always sharp and biting. For that indescribable putrefaction, which spreads through the whole substance, does not arise without a sharp heat, especially since cold is not a positive thing here. Since we do not know the degree of this heat, the degree of putrefaction is rightly said to be unknown as well. Some epilepsy, I say, is cured by reason of age, not because surplus is absent, but because the heat, the cause of corruption, is absent; so that, as far as this goes, Erastus has rightly said that Galen spoke from hypothesis rather than from the truth of the matter.

units.la: § 20. De spumà Epilepticorum (p. 212)
units.tr: § 20. On the foam of epileptics (p. 212)

units.la: consentio Erafto, materiam illius non esse humorem morbificum, è pulmone elatum, quod Montanus vult: sed salivam, ut prædixi, Intantà enim respirationis difficultate, aëri reciprocanti mifcetur aliquid saliva, & fit spuma. Interim, non semper fieri,verum est. Et ita quidem finem suum adepta est Epilepsia: ego verò etiam aliam sarcinam impono meis humeris, ut theoria hujus morbi fiat quam lucidiffima, hoc sumto orationis initio.
units.tr: I agree with Erastus that the matter of that foam is not a morbid humour raised up from the lungs, as Montanus maintains, but saliva, as I said before. For when breathing is very difficult, something of the saliva is mixed with the air as it is drawn back and forth, and foam is produced. It is true that this does not always happen. And so, indeed, Epilepsy has reached its end; but I, for my part, take upon my shoulders another burden as well, so that the theory of this disease may be made as clear as possible, with this as the opening of my discourse.

units.la: Spicilegia Epileptica, CAP. XII.
units.tr: Epileptic Gleanings, CHAPTER XII.

units.la: § 1. Eorum, qui in re literaria verfantur, triplex est ordo, quantum hucusque comperi. Rari quidam sunt, qui & recte instituti sunt abadolefcentiâ, & Veritatis studiosi,folicito, & tantum non suspenso pede inquirunt illam,tam apud antiquos, quam apud noftros, παλαιοῖς ἐξηγηταῖς, ut Græcus aliquis loqueretur,
units.tr: § 1. Of those who are engaged in literary study there are, as far as I have so far found, three kinds. A few are rare: they were properly trained from youth, they are lovers of truth, and they seek it with a careful and almost unhesitating foot, both among the ancients and among our own writers, the ancient expositors (παλαιοῖς ἐξηγηταῖς), so that a certain Greek might say: "Bound to swear by no master's words."

units.la: Nullius adjuvi juvare in verba magistri.
units.tr: Bound to swear by no master's words.

units.la: G 5 · § 2. Plu-
units.tr: G 5 · § 2. Plu-

units.la: § 2. Plures contrà sunt, qui Philofo-phiæ scientiâ tumidi, cæterum, vel divitiis, vel voluptatibus dediti, quærunt sibi nomen, theatrali quadam licentiâ singentes quidvis, Heroftrati inglorium facinus æmulantur.
units.tr: § 2. Others, on the contrary, are puffed up with a smattering of philosophy. Given over either to riches or to pleasures, they seek a name for themselves, inventing whatever they like with a theatrical license, and they imitate the inglorious deed of Herostratus.

units.la: § 3. Qui inter hos medii sunt, Vulcani τὲ ἀμφιγυήεις instar, claudicantes, lapsantesque modò in hanc, modò in illam partem, ob partim judicii infirmitatem, partim ob ignaviam, nullibi sunt firmi.
units.tr: § 3. Those who stand between these two are like Vulcan, "lame on both feet" (τὲ ἀμφιγυήεις), limping and slipping now to this side, now to that. Partly from weakness of judgment, partly from laziness, they are never firm anywhere.

units.la: § 4. Hujus rei illustre exemplum dabo heic. De Epilepsiâ scimus votum fuisse magni Cratonis, Vtinam antè abitum meum, videam essentiam bujus morbi, unà cum curatione rectè explicatam! Nisi fallor, res tam difficilis non est, fi vel Arift. confulamus, vel Gal. suis locis. At verò quia nimis addicti fumus Fernelio, Fuchfio, aliisque, qui sepiæ atramentum in vulgus fparsunt, mansit res indifcuffa.
units.tr: § 4. I will give an illustrious example of this here. We know that it was the wish of the great Crato: "Would that before my departure I might see the nature of this disease, together with its cure, rightly explained!" Unless I am mistaken, the matter is not so difficult if we consult Aristotle, or Galen in his places. But because we are too devoted to Fernel, Fuchs and others, who scatter the ink of the cuttlefish among the crowd, the matter has remained unexamined.

units.la: § 5. Ego verò veritati quasi vexillum erecturus, primum omnium heic dilucidè, & paucis explicabo rem ipsam, (dis 90 ἡμ τρὶς ἐμ κολλα) Deinde volitantes circa hanc lucernam muscas captabo, ne fimplicioribus amplius molestæ sint.
units.tr: § 5. For my part, about to raise the banner of truth, I will first explain the matter itself here clearly and briefly (as the Greeks say, [ἡμ τρὶς ἐμ κολλα]). Then I will go after the flies buzzing around this lamp, so that they may no longer trouble simpler people.

units.la: § 6. Quod ad primum, dixi suprà, Triplicem heic concurrere morbum, Intemperiem, & duplicem duobus locis Obstructionem. Intemperies est, vel in ipso capite, vel in parte quadam inferiori. In capite, dico, comprehendens eã voce quamvis ejus partem, excepto nervorum principio. Et hoc ideo, ut ratio reddi poffit paroxysmorum. Hoc praecipuè notent illi, qui morbum per essentiam diftinguunt à morbo per consensum. Sed qualis est Intemperies? Modò calida: modò, non calida, non frigida, non nulla ex manifeftis; sed totá substantiá.
units.tr: § 6. As to the first point, I said above that three diseases meet here: an intemperie, and a double obstruction in two places. The intemperie is either in the head itself or in some lower part. By "in the head" I mean, in this word, any part of it, except the origin of the nerves. I do this so that the reason for the paroxysms can be given. Those who distinguish disease by essence from disease by sympathy should especially note this. But what sort of intemperie is it? Sometimes hot, sometimes not hot, not cold, not any of the manifest qualities, but intemperate in its whole substance.

units.la: § 7. Ab hac Intemperie genitus Pa- por quidam, vel Åura, vel Flatus, vel Spi- ritus, vel quomodocunque appellare libeat, totá feré substantiá nervis inimicus, certis temporum intervallis, ad principium illorum delatus, obstruit illos. Irritatum ab hoc vapore cerebrum, expellit illum per nervos in musculos. Vltra hos cum ire non possit, facit in illis obstructionem alteram, quam dum solvere properat Natura, fit Convulsio.
units.tr: § 7. From this intemperie a certain vapour is generated, which one may call an air, a breath, a spirit, or however one likes. Almost wholly hostile to the nerves in its whole substance, it is carried at certain intervals to their origin and blocks them. The brain, irritated by this vapour, expels it through the nerves into the muscles. Since it cannot go further than these, it makes a second obstruction in them, and while Nature hastens to dissolve this, a convulsion occurs.

units.la: § 8. Tuverò hoc scito, quod multos fallit, Cerebrum expellit motu æquivoco & infenfili, uno verbo, Naturali. Musculi expellunt unívoco, seu Animali. Qui primo foli fe applicant, non possunt caufam τε κλόνς afferre. Qui conglutinant alterum cum primo, ἀμα ζῶντος
units.tr: § 8. But know this, which deceives many: the brain expels by a motion that is equivocal and imperceptible, in one word, natural. The muscles expel by a univocal, or animal, motion. Those who apply themselves only to the first cannot give the cause of the convulsion. Those who join the other to the first (ἅμα ζῶντος

units.la: ςης δυσερς , & fe aliosque falluntt.
units.tr: ...) both deceive themselves and others.

units.la: § 9. Heic quivis videt,quanti referat neglecta ab initio Intemperies, & ad cognitionem & ad curationem. Quod ad illam,cum tot locis possit latére,quis sibi spondeat fe facilè inventurum? Quod ad hanc,quæ cinnabaris, quod magisterium vitrioli, quæ alia compositio Chymica, indistincte usurpata, poflit tibi promittere certum eventum? Et hæc quidem de primo mihi proposito:venio ad alterum.
units.tr: § 9. Here anyone can see how much it matters that an intemperie is neglected from the beginning, both for knowing it and for curing it. As to knowing it: since it can lie hidden in so many places, who can promise himself that he will find it easily? As to curing it: what cinnabar, what magistery of vitriol, what other chemical compound, used indiscriminately, can promise you a certain outcome? And these things indeed concern the first point I proposed. I come now to the second.

units.la: § 10. Heicin primâ acie colloco ERASTV M, 4. Anti-Paracelf. f. 162. Is primum negat, Morbum illum habere nomen,à quo fymtoma hujus motus depravati pendeat. Non enim omnibus rebus data sunt nomina, inquit v.g. Quis est morbus,qui flernutationem facit, qui singultum? Et addit, Quicunque ille fit, esse in ventriculis cerebri, in quibus cum clusus vapor, vel mordax,vel aliter naturæ inimicus, & peregrinus, ita irritet cerebrum, ut de exturbando illo non minus sollicitum fit, quam in singultu os ventriculi in expellendo,quod molestum est. Hæc ille:
units.tr: § 10. Here I place Erastus in the front line (Anti-Paracelsus, p. 162). First he denies that the disease has a name from which the symptom of this depraved motion depends. For not all things have been given names, he says, for example: what disease causes sneezing, what causes hiccup? And he adds: "Whatever it is, it lies in the ventricles of the brain, where a shut-in vapour, either biting or otherwise hostile and foreign to nature, so irritates the brain that it is no less anxious to drive it out than the mouth of the stomach is, in hiccup, in expelling what is troublesome." So he says.

units.la: § 11. Quæ intuens quis mirabitur, tam prope ad rem accessisse magnum hunc virum! Certè agnoscit veram caufam proximam,Faporem,fi modò agnoffe etiam voluisset verum locum affectum, Corpus, inquam, potius cerebri, quam ventriculos. Ex corpore enim cum fit via in musculos; ex ventriculis cum non fit: quid ambigebat? Studium illud Cerebri in exturbando vapore adverso, quin concussio illa, quid aliud est quam irritatio expultricis cerebri, quam ego urgeo? Vapor ille qua exite potest, quam per nervos, qui sunt apud Gal. cerebrum πνεῦμα. Idem vapor cum mentiatur {spiritum animalem, quei non contrahat musculos eo modo, quo {spiritus animalis solet?
units.tr: § 11. Looking at this, one will wonder that this great man came so close to the matter! Certainly he recognizes the true proximate cause, the vapour; if only he had also wished to recognize the true affected place, I mean the body of the brain rather than the ventricles. For the way into the muscles is from the body; from the ventricles it is not. What was he uncertain about? That zeal of the brain in driving out the hostile vapour: what else is that concussion but the irritation of the expelling power of the brain, which I insist upon? That vapour can get out only through the nerves, which Galen says are the brain's pneuma. Since the same vapour pretends to be animal spirit, why should it not contract the muscles in the way that animal spirit usually does?

units.la: § 12. Sed demus hoc humanitati. Si paulo diligentius inquiramus in morbum tam sternutationis, quam singultus, inveniemus, Galeno fatis cognitum fuiffe, Est morbus in superficie. Vide Patholog. c.191. & feq. Quo loco commodum incidit mihi, Cum heic quoque fit duplex irritatio, in cerebro altera, in musculis alteratannon tribus dictis morbis addendi sint hi duo, ut numerus fiat quinarius? Non debent: quia non lædunt peculiarem actionem. Imo vero sunt actiones, non symptomata. Iamque stabilio sententiam meam ex 5.Aph.5. ubi hæc sunt verba: Non potest fieri convulsio corporis, qui principium nervorum afficiatur. Asse- ctio čtio alia cum non fit, quam transmissio corporis alicujus tenuis, quod per nervos musculis communicetur : apparet, quod dico.
units.tr: § 12. But let us grant this to humanity. If we inquire a little more carefully into the disease of sneezing as well as into hiccup, we shall find that Galen knew it well enough: "It is a disease of the surface" (see Pathology, c. 191 and following). Here it occurs to me opportunely that, since there is a double irritation in this case too, one in the brain and the other in the muscles, these two ought to be added to the three named diseases so that the number becomes five. They ought not, because they do not injure a peculiar action. Indeed they are actions, not symptoms. I confirm my opinion from Aphorisms 5.5, where the words are: "A convulsion of the body cannot occur unless the principle of the nerves is affected." An affection, however, is nothing other than the transmission of some subtle body that is communicated through the nerves to the muscles. What I say is plain.

units.la: § 13. ErafloP LATERVS jungatur velideo quia in motu defendit eandem absurditatem, quod video paucis notum efle. Locus est Prax.tract.r. mihi f,33. Ad cujus lectionem cum fatis diu me praeparaffem, nec non tempus captaffem, quo integris viribus effem : primo statim intuitu nauseam accepi.Cum enim ait, Sensus quidem (tam internos, quam externos) aboleri.quod spiritus animales effundantur,seu profundantur, adeoque vacuum dereliclum cerebrum, & destitutum proximo animae instrumento, non pofit manere in officio : motus autem esse majores, validiorefque,quod exclusi e cerebro spiritus confertim ruant in genus nervosum, &c tantum non tumultuarie moveant,&c. Hac de re quo magis cogitabam, eo minus capiebam. Videbam equidem,in motu plane Eraftéum esse : in sensu alium esse voluisse, non potuisse. Si enim omnino ita fit,ut scribit,quaero, A quo morbo id accidat? A qua causa morbus ille pendeat? Duas ille quidem causas profert, Alteram,quae in Epilepsia per essentiam obtineat, nimiam mentis, cogitationumque
units.tr: § 13. Let me also bring in Erastus, since in the matter of motion he defends the same absurdity, which I see is known to few. The passage is in Practice, tract. 1, f. 33. Having prepared myself for reading it for quite a long time, and having waited for a moment when my strength was whole, I felt nausea at the very first glance. For when he says that the senses (both internal and external) are abolished, because the animal spirits are poured out or spilled, and so the brain is left empty and deprived of the instrument nearest to the soul, and cannot remain in its office; but that the motions are greater and stronger, because the spirits expelled from the brain rush headlong into the nervous kind and move almost tumultuously, and so on, the more I thought about this matter, the less I understood it. I saw, to be sure, that Erastus was plainly in the wrong about motion; in sensation he had wished to be otherwise, but could not. For if it is really so, as he writes, I ask: from what disease does this come? On what cause does that disease depend? He does indeed offer two causes: one, which in epilepsy holds by its essence, an excessive intensity of mind and of thoughts;

units.la: intentionem; alteram, quæ in eádem per consensum, irritationem cerebri, quod molestum est excutere cupientis: verunetamen, quo modo hæ causæ eadem symptomata creent,assequi non potui.Nimia mentis intentio immobilem facere potest hominem: at hic contrarius status est illi, de quo agimus. Irritatio cerebri præerequirit causam irritantem, quæ p.n. sit. At spiritus sunt s.n. & nunquam irritant ad sui expulsionem. Eodem modo, spiritus,in musculos impulsi,sunt illis s.n. quo igitur modo irritant? Copiâ fortassis? Tum verò cogitationes instituere cæpi de curatione. Si enim omninò itase res habet,quas indicationes præbebit? Cum igitur invenirem s.69.Nolle se secundum causas digerere,sed per modos operandi procedere:dixi,Insolens profectò hoc est,eò à Methodo medendi alienum!Cum animadverterem, incertum illi esse, Humores, & vapores evacuet,revellat,derivet,aliò ducat &c.subiracundus abjeci librum cum voce,Non intelligo. Et quid? Estne hæc vera & legitima causa,in quâ inveniendâ tantopere se excruciarint,& veteres & neoterici Medici, invicemque contrarias opiniones prodiderint, Cur abolitis sensibus, motus nihilominus aliquandiu persistere possit:Si Epilepsia recté est in censu functionum laefarum, quei poffis exfpectare ab illâ motus f. n. Sed tempero mihi,
units.tr: intensity; the other, which in the same disease holds by sympathy, an irritation of the brain, troublesome to one who wishes to shake it off. However, I could not grasp in what way these causes produce the same symptoms. An excessive intensity of mind can make a man immobile, but this state is the opposite of the one we are discussing. An irritation of the brain requires an irritating cause, which must be present; but the spirits are themselves something, and they never irritate for the sake of their own expulsion. In the same way, spirits driven into the muscles are, for those same reasons, something; by what means, then, do they irritate? Perhaps by their quantity? Then I began to think about the cure. For if the matter really stands so, what indications will it give? When therefore I found in section 69 that he is unwilling to arrange things according to their causes, but proceeds through modes of operation, I said: "This is surely unusual, and far from the method of healing!" When I noticed that he is uncertain whether it evacuates, revulses, derives, or draws the humours and vapours elsewhere, and so on, I threw the book aside in irritation with the words, "I do not understand." And what then? Is this the true and legitimate cause, in finding which both ancient and modern physicians have tormented themselves so much, and have handed down opinions contrary to one another? Why, with the senses abolished, can motion nevertheless persist for some time? If epilepsy is rightly counted among the functions that are harmed, what can one expect from it concerning motion? But I restrain myself.

units.la: § 14. Eandem fortunam quia expertusfum in SAXONI Æ praxi, dicam aliquid de illo quoque. Heic fciendum eft. Opera quidem ejus omnia ab Vffenbachio noftro edita fuiffe Francofurti, anno 1603. fub titulo Panthei: praxin autem fcorfim ib. anno 1610. à Leandro Vailaco, fub infcriptione Prognofeum, potius Praelectionum practicarum. In hac pofteriori edit. l. 1. c. 14. laudo quidem, quod σπλάγχνα καὶ σπερμάτων diftinxerit: fed quod fubjectum ad totum genus nervofum extenderit, non probo.
units.tr: § 14. Since I have had the same experience with the practice of SAXONIUS, I will say something about him too. Here it must be noted: his works were all published by our Uffenbach at Frankfurt in 1603 under the title Pantheus, while his practice was published piecemeal, in 1610, by Leandro Vailaco under the title Prognoses, or rather Practical Lectures. In this later edition, book 1, chapter 14, I do praise his distinction between the viscera and the seeds [σπλάγχνα καὶ σπερμάτων], but I do not approve of his extending the subject to the whole nervous genus.

units.la: Patet enim ex fuperioribus, folum mufculum unà cum tendine, ficubi habet, fubjectum effe: nervum autem non nifi canalem. Vnde intelligitur, quei fiat, quod, praecifo nervo, ceiet convulfio? Intelligitur etiam, quomodo excufanda fit Galeni, fi quae eft, varietas. Quod enim ipfe ait, locum non habet. * Dico autem, cum nervum accufat, loquitur ex mente illorum, qui habent adinftar trahere illum volebant: cum mufculum producit, ex propria, & ad rei veritatem: cum tendi-
units.tr: For it is clear from what has been said above that only the muscle, together with its tendon where it has one, is the subject, and the nerve is only a channel. From this it can be understood how it happens that convulsion follows when the nerve is cut. It can also be understood how Galen's inconsistency, if it is one, may be excused. For what he says does not hold. * I say that when he blames the nerve, he speaks in the mind of those who wished to draw it by analogy, but when he names the muscle, he speaks from his own view and in accordance with the truth of the matter. When he names the tendon,

units.la: * Loca allegat 5. Aph. 1. & 60. 4. Aph. 65. Lo. Hipp. Aph. 16. 4. Praef. pulf. 19. tendinem, præcipuam musculi partem nominat, licet non in omnibus fit.
units.tr: * He cites the passages 5 Aph. 1 and 60; 4 Aph. 65; Hippocrates, Aph. 16; 4 Praef. pulf. 19. He names the tendon as the chief part of the muscle, although this is not so in all cases.

units.la: § 15. Porro, quæ deinceps fcribuntur de efficiente convulsionis, proba quidem mihi sunt: verum in conclusione, ibi, Itaque sciendum, spasmum esse duplicem cæc. hæreo, tanquam mus in pice. Distinguit quidem convulsionem factam à fiente, antiquam à recenti; Costractos, dicam ego, à convulsis: sed non dicit distinête, quod de utraque causâ Hipp. repletione & inanitione dicere debebat. Vt prorsus videatur mihi dicendum esse, vacillare heic industriam Editoris. Quamobrem conversus ad Panthei I.r..c. 11.& 13. reperio quidem ibi quoque convulsionem recentem & antiquam : sed acervum causarum tam inconditum, ut defperabundus iterum absolvam me illo, Non intelligo. Interim hoc tantum dico, Contractos hodie dictos plane hinc abesse debere. Laborant enim, ipso fatente, moibo, vel in situ, vel in Figurâ. Ego ad Situm magis inclino, & quidem speciem illam, quæ σύμφυσις dicitur. Duo enim articuli illi non debent esse connati, fiue, ut clarius dicam, continui, sed contigui. Quæ causa est, cur conciliatio quoque locorum Gal. pugnantiü stare non possit, Contractionem quidem, (ut ita loquar) esse à solo morbo : convulsionem autem à morbo & facultate simul. Fortassis, nec opus est hac curá.Diserté enim Gal. 2, Caus. sym.1.& 2. morbo foli transcribit convulsionem: ubi veró facultas est ? Ipse quidem Sax. locum nullum affert: Salius autem, Nor. in Altim. c.13. dat nobis.3. Loc. aff.7. Ego verò nihil aliud reperio quam comparatio nem cum singultu. Hanc jure repudio,quia nullum simile currit quatuor pedibus,adeoque collatio instituitur tantum,quatenus utrobique motus est. Coronidis loco id annoto , In confusà illa causarum acie reperiri nonnulla, quæ sapiunt Ob/fruětionem nostram tam cerebri, quam musculorum, eamque à vaporibus potius,quam humoribus crassis : verum, seligere illa nolo.Interim molestum mihi est, quod tanti faciat locum 12. Meth. ult. qui multimodis mihi sufpeuus est,ut alibi demonstravi. Præcipuè Congelatio perquam odiosa est & oculis & auribus meis.
units.tr: § 15. Further, what is written next about the efficient cause of convulsion seems sound to me. But in the conclusion, where it says, "Therefore it must be understood that spasm is of two kinds," I stick like a mouse in pitch. He does indeed distinguish convulsion caused by a full body from that of an empty one, and an old convulsion from a recent one. I would call them "contracted" as distinct from "convulsed." But he does not say clearly that Hippocrates ought to have discussed both causes, repletion and emptying. So it seems to me that the editor's diligence wavers here. Therefore, turning to Pantheus, book 1, chapters 11 and 13, I do find there too a recent and an old convulsion, but a heap of causes so jumbled that, in despair, I again release myself from it with "I do not understand." For now I say only this: those today called "contracted" should plainly be left out of this discussion. For they suffer, as he himself admits, a disease either in position or in figure. I lean more toward position, and specifically toward the kind called symphysis [σύμφυσις]. For those two joints ought not to be grown together, or, to speak more plainly, continuous, but only contiguous. This is why the reconciliation of Galen's conflicting passages cannot stand: the contraction (so to speak) comes from the disease alone, while convulsion comes from the disease and the faculty together. Perhaps this trouble is not even necessary. For Galen, in On the Causes of Symptoms, book 1, chapters 1 and 2, expressly assigns convulsion to the disease alone; but where then is the faculty? Saxonius himself cites no passage at all. Salius, however, in On Altimarus, chapter 13, gives us three passages, Aff. 7. But I find nothing except a comparison with hiccup. I rightly reject this, because no likeness runs on four feet, and so the comparison holds only insofar as there is motion on both sides. By way of a crown to this, I note this: in that confused array of causes, some things can be found that smack of obstruction both of the brain and of the muscles, and that come from vapours rather than from thick humours. But I do not want to choose those. Meanwhile it bothers me that he sets such store by the last chapter of the twelfth book of the Methodus, which in many ways I suspect, as I have shown elsewhere. Above all, "congelation" is extremely offensive to my eyes and ears.

units.la: § 16. De MASSARIA, Saxoniæ
units.tr: § 16. On MASSARIA, of Saxony

units.la: antagonistà, 1.Pract.18. hoc miror imprimis, quod det Galeno symptoma hoc esse solius morbi: simul tamen obtinere velit,esse ex altero quoque genere, quod morbi & facultatis seu naturæ conjun- ćim
units.tr: Antagonist, 1 Pract. 18. I am especially surprised by this: he grants to Galen that this symptom belongs to the disease alone, yet at the same time he wishes it to be held that it also belongs to the other kind, which is joined with the faculty or nature.

units.la: {s}tim est. Cum enim sint ἐνδεχόμενα, quo modo uni-rei convenire possunt? Tamen est actio, inquit. Non est: est symptoma. Si omninò est actio,ita est, ut virgo corrupta est virgo. Omnes concedunt esse actionem depravatam. Imò, est actio communis,regerit. Explica, ut intelligam. Scio quid sit actio communis seu publica, v.g.ventriculi & hepatis coquentium pro toto corpore: hoc quid simile est? Scio etiam,utramque ventriculi & hepatis actionem, publicam & privatam, se-orsim edi à quatuor facultatibus ministrantibus dictis,licet distinctè dicere non possim, quo inter se ordine procedant: sed heic quid simile est? Rursus, ex Avicenna ait,2.i,do&t.3.c.1. est actio accident-alis. Explica, dico iterum. Scio,in iis naturæ operibus, in quibus ad unum essectum complendum plures partes, ἐνπλέχεια agentes,ut supra locutus sum, concurrunt, quasdam partes esse per accidens, v.g. ad sanguificationem lien pet accidens venit, tam apud Avicen. quam apud Galenum:sed quid heic simile? Lien (ut explicatius dicam) ad officium suum laudabiliter perficiendum, opus habet quatuor d. facultatibus: heic ecquid tale? Interim,non negabis,inquit, facultatis ante malis opus esse nerveos & musculos contrahe-re.
units.tr: For since these are contingent things [ἐνδεχόμενα], how can they apply to one and the same thing? "Still, there is an action," he says. There is not; there is a symptom. If there is altogether an action, it is so in the way that a corrupted virgin is a virgin. "All agree" that there is a depraved action. Indeed, there is a common action, he retorts. Explain, so that I may understand. I know what a common or public action is, for example that of the stomach and liver in digesting for the whole body; but what is similar to this here? I also know that both the public and the private action of the stomach and liver are performed separately by the four named ministering faculties, although I cannot say distinctly in what order they proceed; but what is similar to that here? Again, he says, following Avicenna (Canon, book 2, doctrine 3, chapter 1), that there is an accidental action. Explain, I say again. I know that in those works of nature in which several parts concur, intertwined [ἐνπλέχεια], to complete one effect, as I have said above, some parts are there by accident; for example, in the making of blood the spleen comes in by accident, both in Avicenna and in Galen. But what is similar here? The spleen, to carry out its office properly (to put it more clearly), needs the four ministering faculties. Is there anything like that here? Meanwhile, he says, you will not deny that before the disease of the faculty there is need for the nerves and muscles to contract.

units.la: r e. Proh hominum fidem! De statu f.n. loqueris tu : de statu p.n. ego. Ideò sic explico ex fup. Quemadmodum motus naturalis fit à spiritu animali benè fe habente, in musculo benè disposito: ita motus praeternaturalis fit à vapore, spiritum animalem mentiente, & musculum ita disponente, ut contra voluntatem agere cogatur, Hoc cum fiat, tam in verà & per essentiam convulsione, ut loquuntur illi, quam infalsà, & per consensum : quam dabitis mihi differentiam ? Symptomata plenè gemina sunt, ne quid aliud dicam. Profecto, fi aliquis veritatis sensus in nobis effet, vel tandem pœnitere nos debebat futilis hujus distinctionis ! Et quidni ita loquar ? Cum ut jam dixi, & multoties alibi, eadem utrobiqùe sint symptomata, quis mihi persuadeat, illam quidem fieri à Repletione & Inanitione : hanc autem à spiritu flatuoso ? Imò, quia ista duo tot patent incommodis, quot dici non possunt; cum contrà in vapore, ut libenter loquor, omnia sint plana: quid moramur ? Concludo igitur, Omnis convulsio est à morbo : morbus ( ratione musculi ) est Obstructio : causa est Vapor : Vaporis causa est Intemperies.
units.tr: Good heavens! You speak of the state of the natural functions; I speak of the state of the non-natural ones. Therefore I explain it thus, from what has gone before. Just as a natural motion arises from animal spirit that is well disposed, in a muscle that is well arranged, so a motion contrary to nature arises from a vapour that counterfeits animal spirit and so disposes the muscle that it is compelled to act against the will. Since this happens both in what they call true convulsion, through the essence itself, and in false convulsion, through sympathy, what difference will you give me between them? The symptoms are wholly twin, not to say anything else. Truly, if there were any sense of truth in us, we ought at last to be ashamed of this futile distinction! And why should I not speak so? Since, as I have already said, and many times elsewhere, the symptoms are the same on both sides, who can persuade me that the one comes from repletion and emptying, and the other from flatulent spirit? Indeed, since those two explanations carry as many difficulties as cannot be told, whereas in vapour, as I gladly say, everything is plain, why do we delay? I conclude, therefore: every convulsion comes from a disease; the disease, as regards the muscle, is an obstruction; the cause is vapour; the cause of the vapour is an intemperature.

units.la: § 17. ALTIMAR VM quia li- benter
units.tr: § 17. Since ALTIMARUS gladly follows MAFFARIA

units.la: penter sequitur Maffaria ( uterque enim xque què studiosus est Gal.) videamus hujus quoque conatus. Locus est 1. Meth. 13. qui persuadet mihi, Maff. ex hoc fonte naufiffe aquam suam. Ait enim, Voluntatem, in cerebro residentem, edere motus [f.n. absque hoc principio fi fit, fieri motus p. n, à causà quidem morbificà, sed non fine operà facultatis ( hanc vocat ille functionem ) irritatæ. Hoc accepifle videri vult ex 2. Cauf. fym. 2. de Palp. & Trem. 8. Tum verò re- pentè pro causis surrogat Replesionem & Inanitionem Hipp. contentus, credo, laude illà, quam Gal. 3. Loc. aff. 6. pleno ore decantat, profectò immeritiffimo.
units.tr: (for each is equally a keen admirer of Galen), let us examine his efforts too. The place is Meth. 1.13, which persuades me that Maffaria drew his water from this spring. For he says that the will, residing in the brain, produces motions, [f.n. without this principle, if it happens, motion p.n. comes about from a morbific cause, but not without the operation of the faculty (he calls it the function) that has been irritated]. He wishes it seen that he took this from Causis Symptomatum 2, De Palpitatione et Tremore 8. Then, all at once, he substitutes repletion and evacuation for causes, being content, I believe, with that praise which Galen sings with full mouth in Locis Affectis 3.6, most undeservedly.

units.la: § 18. Hujus Censor, SALIVS,
units.tr: § 18. Of this critic, SALIUS

units.la: Notis in Alt. c.13. duo tantum in istis defiderat. I, Quod omiserit convulsionis speciem eam, quæ fit à spiritu flatuofo, Cauf. fym. 1, c. II. Quod à morbo fieri semper velit, cum in unâ illâ specie tantum fit verum, quæ per efsentiam fit, 3. Loc: affect.7. Ego heic obiter in genere doleo vicem Veritatis, quæ deseritur sæpicule ab iis, qui videri volunt ipsius studiosissimi esse. Sed ita homines fumus!
units.tr: in his notes on Altimarus, chapter 13, misses only two things in these. First, that he has omitted the kind of convulsion that arises from flatulent spirit, Causis Symptomatum 1, c. 2. Second, that he always wants it to come from disease, whereas it is true only of that one kind which comes through essence, Locis Affectis 3.7. Here, in passing, I grieve in general for the fate of Truth, which is often abandoned by those who wish to seem most devoted to her. But such are we men!

units.la: § 19. Ab ALTIMARO cupiam audire,
units.tr: § 19. From ALTIMARUS I should like to hear

units.la: audire, Quomodo defectus voluntatis ut ipse loquitur, causari possit motum? quidem tam violentum?tam doloro sum tam periculosum? Deinde, fi a solo fit defectu, quid opus est irritatione, quam irritatio vestigio agglutinat? Irritatio vero cum non fiat absque corpore: unde fit illud, quale? Tertio, fi veræ sint causæ illæ duæ Hippocraticæ, quam habent connexionem, vel cum defectu, vel cum irritatione, vel cum utroque? Quarto, quibus oculis usus, suis an alienis? convulsionem apud Gal. fieri legerit, non a morbo solo, sed a facultate quoque? Ego enim, non in 2. tantum, sed & in 1. 1. de Cauf. fym. diferentiam invenio mentionem solius morbi. In de Palp. c. 8. & ult. ubi alioqui deseft hujus materiæ, & veræ causæ declaratio: ne meminit quidem hujus rei. Quamobrem dico audacter, Altimarus labitur memoria. Annon hoc quoque dicere licet, Participare illum non parum de delirio Eralti.
units.tr: how a defect of the will, as he calls it, can cause a motion so violent, so painful, so dangerous? Next, if it arises from defect alone, what need is there of irritation, which irritation sticks to the trace? And since irritation does not occur without the body, what kind of body is it, and how is it so? Third, if those two Hippocratic causes are true, what connection do they have, with defect, with irritation, or with both? Fourth, what eyes did he use, his own or others'? Did he read that Galen says convulsion arises not from disease alone but from the faculty too? For I find mention of disease alone not only in Causis Symptomatum 2 but also in 1.1, and in De Palpitatione c. 8 and the last chapter, where otherwise the discussion of this matter and the declaration of the true cause is lacking; he does not even mention the thing. Therefore I boldly say that Altimarus slips in his memory. May one not also say that he shares not a little in the delirium of Eraltus?

units.la: § 20. A SALIO postulo, Ostendat
units.tr: § 20. From SALIUS I demand that he show

units.la: mihi tertiam illam speciem, quæ à spiritu flatuofo, in de Cauf. fym. Est enim 3. Loc. aff. 7. 2. ut & 5. Aph. 1. licet 8. x. 3. 3. Q. neget, invenifle fe tertiam causam, præter Repletionem & Inanitionem. Vt ut fit, Ostendo illi quid amplius in de Cauf. fym.
units.tr: me that third kind, which arises from flatulent spirit, in De Causis Symptomatum. For it is in Locis Affectis 3.7, and also Aphorisms 5.1, although he denies (Q.) that he has found a third cause besides repletion and evacuation. However that may be, I show him what more there is in De Causis Symptomatum.

units.la: Locutus in universum de omni convulsione, duos proponit modos,à priscis doctos, quibus fiant convulsiones,& ait, Sÿ- ve igitur ad principium tensis, five spiritus influxu impletis musculis, voluntarii motus beantur, etc. Heic vides,ò Sali, duas ve- terum sententias de motu voluntario positas, de quibus conultat, Sive, inquit, fiat hoc modo, trabenti- bus nervis, fragm. de Cauf. refp. five hoc modo, impletis spiritu musculis, 1. Sent. Hipp. 10. eodem modo fiet quoque motus fl. 3. seu convulforius. Hinc affumo illud, Motus f.n. fit, impletis musculis spiritum animali. Ergò motus p.n. fit, impletis musculis vapore, spiritum animalem mentiente. Vbi id moneo, Interpretem Galeno vim facere,cum ... vertit Flatus. Loquitur enim de motu f.n. qui fit à spiritu, non àflatu,cum distinctè agimus. Cum ergò dico, Motus f.n. fit ita, Motus p.n. fit ita: Galeni personam fumo, depositâ propriâ.
units.tr: Speaking generally of every convulsion, he sets out two modes, held by learned men of old, by which convulsions happen, and he says: "Whether, therefore, the muscles are filled either by tension at the origin or by influx of spirit, voluntary motions are produced," etc. Here you see, Salius, the two ancient opinions on voluntary motion which he consults. "Whether," he says, "it happens in this way, with nerves being drawn" (fragment, De Causis Respiratoriis), "or in this way, with muscles filled by spirit" (Sententiae Hippocratis 1.10). In the same way a motion f.n., or convulsive motion, also happens. Hence I take this: motion f.n. happens when the muscles are filled with animal spirit. Therefore motion p.n. happens when the muscles are filled with vapour, which counterfeits animal spirit. Here I note that the interpreter does violence to Galen when he renders it as flatus. For he speaks of motion f.n., which comes from spirit, not from flatus, since we are treating the matters distinctly. So when I say, motion f.n. happens thus, motion p.n. happens thus, I assume Galen's persona, having laid aside my own.

units.la: § 21. Heic liceat mihi excursionem facere geminam. 1. Gal. cum facit alternativam illam, five ita fit, ab Adraftéa victus facit, quod facit. Tacitè enim damnat Repletionem & Inanitionem, quæ sunt inania nomina, II. Idem acci- ditilli 4. Loc, aff. 2. Q. cum ait, In Epi- * 3. Loc. aff. 6. D. lepfiâ
units.tr: § 21. Here let me make two digressions. First, when Galen makes that alternative, "either it happens thus," he does what he does, vanquished by Necessity [Ἀδράστεια]. For he tacitly condemns repletion and evacuation, which are empty names. Second, the same thing happens to him in Locis Affectis 4.2 (Q.), where he says: "In epilepsy

units.la: lepfiá ventriculi cerebri magis laborant, quam corpus:in Apoplexiá contrà.Cum enim hcic quoque duæ effent antiquitus sententiæ de utroque hoc affectu, quarum una in ventriculis illos collocabat, ut hodie, altera in corpore: conciliationem paritheic Gal. ut utriusque patro-nos faciat sibi obnoxios. Quare repeto superius illud Sÿ vobis, ò Amici,libet amplectli illam veterum Gal. sententiam, quæ de ventriculis: cur mihi non licet defendere Veterum alteram, quæ de corpore? Sed nec perinde est, cum ventriculis omnia adversentur, corpori omnia consentiant, Ita, repletioni & inanitioni omnia sunt contraria, spiritui flatuofo passim obviam itur.
units.tr: the ventricles of the brain suffer more than the body; in apoplexy, on the contrary." For since here too there were two ancient opinions about each of these affections, one of which placed them in the ventricles, as today, the other in the body, Galen seeks a reconciliation so as to make the patrons of both bound to him. Wherefore I repeat what I said above: "Yes, my friends, I am willing to embrace that opinion of the ancients of Galen, the one about the ventricles." Why am I not allowed to defend the other ancient opinion, the one about the body? But it is not the same, since everything opposes the ventricles, while everything agrees with the body. So repletion and evacuation are contrary to everything, while flatulent spirit is met everywhere.

units.la: § 22. Tandem hoc quoque addo, Salium non videri assecutum esse Altimari mentem.Expressè enim morbo jungit facultatem animalem, tam in effentiâ, quam in consensu, * Quod cum Gal. nufpiam docuerit, nec in rei veritateita fit; facilè absolvo Salium. Et quæ verifimilitudo ducit nos eò,ut de Epilepsiâ per essentiam dicamus hoc, per consensum aliud? Symptomata enim sunt eadem,dico iterum. Neque verò effentia hæc eadem,quæ inaliis morbis, Quod enim suprà quoque dixi, Vt ratio reddi possit paroxyf-
units.tr: § 22. Finally I add this too: Salius does not seem to have grasped Altimarus' mind. For he expressly joins the animal faculty to the disease, both in essence and in consensus. Since Galen nowhere taught this, nor is it so in fact, I readily acquit Salius. And what likelihood leads us to say that epilepsy is one thing through essence and another through consensus? For the symptoms are the same, I say again. Nor is this essence the same as in other diseases. For, as I said above also, so that a reason can be given for the paroxysm-

units.la: * Vide infrà par. g. 33 . [illegible, ~10 letters] paroxysmorum, oportet Intemperies illa [?] ixa vel intra calvariam fit, vel extrà; in capite, inquam, seu tertio ventre.
units.tr: * See below, par. g. 33. [illegible] of the paroxysms, that intemperies must be either within the skull or outside it: in the head, I say, or in the third ventricle.

units.la: § 25. NICOLAVS PISO quia
units.tr: § 25. Nicolaus Piso, because

units.la: in Praxi non pauca εὐθ ... describit ex Altimaro, jure ipsius assecla fuerit, Intemperies in quibusdam etiam ab ipso discedit, veluti in proposito negotio. Cum enim ille ne meminerit quidem Epilepsiæ, nisi quatenus sub genericâ appellatione hæc : cauté hic, à nobis notioribus orsus, Epilepsiam pertractat l.1. c.19. & mox [?]. feq. Convulsiones. Mihi cursim notare libet quædam. I. Quam verè dicit, mortuum à quo symptoma motus depravati pendet, esse Obstructionem: tam malè juni-
units.tr: Because in his Practica he describes many things ([εὐθ ...]) from Altimarus, and so is rightly regarded as Altimarus's follower, yet in some matters he departs from him, as in the present business. For although he does not mention epilepsy at all except under the general name of this condition, here, cautiously beginning from things better known to us, he treats epilepsy (book 1, chapter 19) and soon after convulsions. I wish to note a few points briefly. I. As truly as he says that the obstruction on which the symptom of depraved motion depends is the cause, so badly does he join intemperance to it. For intemperance would lie hidden under alteration, unless I am mistaken.

units.la: bit illi Intemperiem. Hæc enim sub alteratione lateret, nisi me decipio. I I. Latitudinem epilepsiæ valdè obscurè describit. Ergo ita concipio. Gravissima est, cum octo[?] rupantur omnes sensus, tam interni, quam externi, & subitò cadunt ægri subini, cum concussione totius corporis, pociferatione incondità, & spumà circa ps. Minus gravis est cum sensuum unus alter superest, cum tantillo corporis motu. Levissima est, cum sensus quidem bolentur, motus autem nulli apparent. In hoc genere sunt illi, qui præsentiunt, at possint fe reclinare in lectum, aut fe-
units.tr: II. He describes the extent of epilepsy very obscurely. So I conceive it thus. It is at its most severe when all the senses, both internal and external, are destroyed, and the sick suddenly fall down with a shaking of the whole body, an unformed cry, and foam at the mouth. It is less severe when one or another of the senses remains, with a slight movement of the body. It is mildest when the senses are indeed disturbed but no motion appears. To this kind belong those who sense the attack coming but are able to lie down on a bed, or to sit

II I· Cum admittit distinctionem inter Convulsionem legitimam & spuriam, incautus est, ut dix anteà I V. Incautior multò, cum parten affectam agnoscit solum cerebrum, & quidem fecundum ventriculos, pituit obscssos. V. Incautissimus, cum Epilepsiæ jungit Apoplexiam, nec discrimen ullum dicit, nisi Semiobstructionem. V I Extremè ineptus, cum distinguit ventri culos. V II. Infigniter fallit & fallitur cum consensisse ait veteres in humorem crassum & lentum, qualis pituita & me Iancholia. V I I I, Nonminus fallit,cun credit flatum crassum posse facere idem quod humores crassi, IX. Sententiam juniorum, quos vocat, non intellexit cum ait illos voluisse, Obstructionem heic nullam esse, sed tantum molestum rei noxiæ. Sed quæ est illa res noxia? Quæ vel quantitate, vel qualitate lædat? Ego hoc tantum, Qualitas sine corpore quomodo id facit? Cætera sino.
units.tr: down, some of whom say, "It was as if snow had fallen, as if a bird had flown through my head." III. When he admits a distinction between legitimate and spurious convulsion, he is careless, as I said before. IV. Far more careless when he says the affected part is the brain alone, and indeed according to the ventricles, with the humours obstructed. V. Most careless when he joins apoplexy to epilepsy and admits no difference except a half-obstruction. VI. Extremely foolish when he distinguishes the ventricles. VII. He is remarkably mistaken, and misleads, when he says the ancients agreed on a thick and viscous humour, such as phlegm and melancholy. VIII. He is no less mistaken when he believes that thick wind can do the same as thick humours. IX. He did not understand the opinion of those he calls the "younger" authors when he says they wanted no obstruction here, but only something troublesome to the harmful thing. But what is that harmful thing? Does it injure by quantity or by quality? I say only this: how does a quality without a body do it? I leave the rest.

units.la: § 24. In spasmo duo tantum noto I. Videri illum Cerebrum exculpare velle, cum utitur 7 Interdum, II. Convulsiones ad latera non dari. Addo, II I ex Epilepsiâ, Non procul abesse ab Erasto rafto illis verbis, Quod dum fit, fpiritus borat etc.
units.tr: § 24. In the spasm I note only two things. I. That he seems to wish to excuse the brain when he uses the words "sometimes". II. That convulsions do not occur on the sides. I add, III. From epilepsy: not far from Erastus is that rafter, in the words "which, while it happens, the spirit roars", etc.

units.tr: § 25. Iachinus, in the ninth Rhazes, chapter 13, at once stumbles at the start by confusing spasm (πάσμὸν) and convulsion (σπάσμα). But this would be a small matter, were it not that from it hangs the most absurd dogma, that the solution of continuity is the cause of this symptom. But this is also a trifle. The most serious thing is that he takes up the long-exploded dogma that the nerves pull the muscles as reins pull a horse. Hardly less serious is that he brings in here what we have called "Contraos". Galen, indeed, is not without reason accused by Rhazes of being inconsistent in explaining the diseases that produce this symptom; yet Iachinus himself should also be accused, partly because he is no less inconsistent, and partly because he leaves Galen under the knife, as the old proverb has it. As for Galen, I have already said what part of it there is, above in chapter 9, as in Pathology, chapter 113. Now I add this: Galen, conquered by Adrasteia, did not know that our spirit is natural [πνεῦμα ... φυσικὸς], as he calls it in the same passage. Also in On the Places, book 3, he gives us a certain bad breath rising from the shin. The third cause in Aphorisms 5.1 [δι᾽ εἰς] points the same way: a bite. Here the windy spirit makes too much trouble and fills both pages, as Linius says somewhere; that is, it causes every convulsion.

units.la: convulsionem, Hunc fi Iacch. distinxisse ab humore, rationem reddere potuisset cur modo paralysis fiat, modò convulsio fit à flatu, quippe qui ex Greek... ut cum Arift. loquimur, qui flatus Obfructionem causatur: Paralysis fit ab humore tenus & aquoso, qui Intemperiem frigidam, humidamque introducit, non fine tameni Obfructione. Quod adrem nostram suffi cit mihi, quod inter morbos hujus fymptomatis habet etiam Flatus tendentes quia iidem locum habent apud Iacch. inter omni per consensum convulsione: nono ego dico heic plura, nisi hoc, In Epilepsia c.14. quia jungit illam simpliciter Apoplexiæ, ab eademque ventriculorum obstructione fieri vult, quia iterum tractum nervorum nobis occinit: licet nobis esse quietis.
units.tr: If Iachinus had distinguished this from humour, he could have given the reason why paralysis arises from humour, while convulsion arises from wind, which causes obstruction, as we speak with Aristotle. Paralysis arises from a watery humour that introduces a cold and moist intemperance, yet not without obstruction. That is enough for my purpose: among the diseases of this symptom he also counts the tending winds, because they have the same place with Iachinus among all convulsions by consent. I say nothing more here, except this: in On Epilepsy, chapter 14, because he simply joins it to apoplexy and wants it to come from the same obstruction of the ventricles, he again sings to us of the drawing of the nerves. We may be content with that.

units.la: § 26. Inhac censurâ quia negligi nostrum debet VALLESIVS, vir alioqui fummus, quamvis forte post Eraftum indicem cedere debuisset: age videamus pauci. Pertendit is §. Controverf. 16. Vtactio aliqua, v. g. [?]otus, fiat, duo requiruntur, & instru[?]enti f.n. dispositio, & Spiritus animalis [?]raefentia. Horum alterutrum si laboret, [?]uis non videt actionem impediri ? Non majoris momenti [?]st diftinctio, quam parat inter Conjulsio- [?]em & Concussionem, quâ ( concussione ) [?]ddita, vult sublevare Galenum. Est enim [?]neré voluntaria. Ejusdem farinæ est al[?]era, jam sepius rejecta, inter conjulsio[?]em legitimam & spuriam ? Quis enim [?]x veteribus docuit? Norant illi ab aliis conjulsionibus differre Epilepsiam in hoc, quod in illis quidem musculi maeant contracti toto paroxy smi temposin Epilepsia autem reciproco motu gitentur : non tamen satum controveriæ movebant Epilepsiæ, quasi legitima on esset. Dicis forte, Quæ causa est buus varietatis? In convulsionibus, quateaus ab epilepsia distinguuntur, vapor imactus tam est crassus, ut natura expellere llum non possit, ideo moriuntur feres- gri in primo paroxysmo, ut ita dicam : in H
units.tr: § 26. In this criticism Vallesius must not be neglected, a man otherwise most outstanding, though perhaps after Erastus he ought to have given way. Let us examine a few points. In § Controversia 16 he maintains that the convulsive motions in epilepsy come from the will... even if, he says, they happen only without freedom, through a hindrance of power. Here who does not at once see the opposite in the added words? For since no voluntary action happens without the faculty of transmission (as I prefer to say), how shall I imagine an action to occur without the faculty being transmitted? I explain. For some action, for example a motion, to occur, two things are required: the disposition of the instrument, and the presence of animal spirit. If either of these is impaired, who does not see that the action is impeded? If it is impeded, how does it happen? How is it, if it is not? If a virgin is corrupted, how is she still a virgin? The distinction Vallesius makes between convulsion and concussion, by which (concussion) he wishes to help Galen, is of no greater weight. For it is indeed voluntary. Of the same stuff is the other distinction, often rejected already, between legitimate and spurious convulsion. For who taught this from the ancients? They knew that epilepsy differs from other convulsions in this, that in those the muscles remain contracted for the whole duration of the attack, but in epilepsy they are thrown into a reciprocal motion; yet they did not raise the controversy that epilepsy was not a legitimate convulsion. You may perhaps ask, what is the cause of this variety? In convulsions, insofar as they are distinguished from epilepsy, the vapour is so thick that nature cannot expel it; therefore the sufferers die in the first attack, so to speak: in

units.tr: epilepsy it is thinner, so that it gradually breathes out and relaxes the limb, until, another vapour being supplied from the brain, the limb contracts again. Epilepsy therefore differs from the others by degree. Thus within epilepsy itself there are marked degrees, according to the greater or lesser harshness of the symptoms, as I said not long ago. To these Celsus refers in book 3, chapter 23: sometimes with stretching of the limbs, sometimes without it. And Vallesius is wrong to say that concussion is always present in the comitial sickness; he could have learned otherwise from Avicenna, and even from the little women of Nórica. For they call it Dag stille fraisch lich, as long as they are held by the senses without motion; after it has come on, they say Sets ifts aufgebrochen. But see, I beg you, whoever you are, how ingenious Vallesius is! In epilepsy, he says, there are motions; in convulsions there are not. There are no reciprocal motions, therefore there are no motions. For when in emprosthotonos the body bends forward, is that not a motion? So too in opisthotonos. So too in tetanus, which is called a tonic motion. How beautiful, indeed, is this explanation of Galen's mind! Convulsion comes from the disease alone, therefore it is without motion! This force is indeed plain. For palpitation, which Galen joins to convulsions, is with motion. If anywhere from this opinion

units.tr: If Galen departs from this view anywhere, it is not of great importance.

units.la: § 27. IOVBERTVS, tract. de fluentiâ & causis convulsionis, quia & trafto & Vallefio consentit, non potest heic praeteriri. Hoc ille recte, quod Repletionem & Inanitionem pro causis proximis non agnoscit; rectè quoque illud, quod in cerebro recipit ἐςἰδρωσα : sed male, quod non explicat fe, quod fit cor- pus illud Exiguum & Tenue, à quo fit itatio;pejus,cum Invitis quidem accide- re ait, sed vi animali (quae motrix καὶ πρὸς ill dicitur) lacessitâ & coactâ. Hoc vero quid est dictu, mihomo? Irritari, lacefsiri, cogi est facultatis expultricis naturalis,non animalis,quae duae facultates profecto sic confunduntur, Rursus, fi Voluntarium adimitur huic motui, quâ fronte iterum dabitur illi? Fit enim oratio huic similis, Motus in convulsione non fit à spiritu animali, ut distinctè lo- quar: motus idem fit ab animali. Sed & hoc non fatis commodè,quod,de morbo proximo interrogatus, Vnitatis solutionem affert, Nec fatis est,ex.2. Prorrh, 20. dolorem proposuisse. Inauditum enim est in arte nostrâ, Vim naturalem expul- tricem fieri non posse,nisi à morbo. Sed & dolor,qui in musculis est,est à Materiâ exiguâ,tenuique, è cerebro (puto) huc tramissâ, tramifsà,quæ quid aliud fit, quam Papæ refer: Hic fcil.cogere potest ad actionem, implendo ventres musculorum, doloremque causando: non autem Spiritus animaecui negatus est aditus, & qui, si omnino adesset, dolorem non faceret. Et quid ego Erroneam, sucatam, ex sophismatis involutam sententiam, pluribus exagito? Præstiterat profecto portenta talia opinionum averso potius vultu contemnere, quam meditatá oratione refutare. Verum, quidquid fit, ideo fit, O fugite hinc juvenes!
units.tr: § 27. Iobertus, in his treatise on the flux and causes of convulsion, agrees with Trallian and Vallesius, so he cannot be passed over here. He rightly does not recognise repletion and emptying as proximate causes, and he rightly holds that the brain admits a watery effusion [ἐνίδρωσις]. But he is wrong that he does not explain what that small and thin body is from which the irritation comes. Worse, he says that it happens to the unwilling, but by an animal power (which is called motive) that is provoked and compelled. What on earth does that mean, my friend? To be irritated, provoked and compelled belongs to the natural expulsive faculty, not the animal one, and these two faculties are clearly confused. Again, if the voluntary is taken away from this motion, with what face is it given back to it? His statement amounts to this: "The motion in convulsion does not come from the animal spirit, to speak distinctly; the same motion does come from the animal." But he does not do this very well either, in that, when asked about the proximate cause, he offers the dissolution of unity, nor is it enough to have put forward pain, as in Prorrhetics 2, 20. For it is unheard of in our art that the natural expulsive power can be produced except by disease. Moreover, the pain that lies in the muscles comes from a small, thin matter sent over, I think, from the brain, which is what else than a "Pappae!" (an exclamation of wonder). Here, namely, it can force the muscles to act by filling their bellies and causing pain; but it is not the animal spirit, to which access has been denied, and which, if it were present at all, would not cause pain. And why should I go on at length about this erroneous, muddled opinion, tangled up in sophisms? Surely it would have been better to scorn such monstrous opinions with averted face than to refute them in a laboured discourse. However that may be, here too it is so: O flee hence, young men!

units.la: § 28. TH. A VEIGA, virtantus, Com. in 3. Loc. aff. 6. f. 368. tam nudus est, in numerandis speciebus & causis convulsionum, ut me pudeat illius.
units.tr: § 28. Th. a Veiga, in his commentary on the third place affecting..., chapter 6, page 368, is so bare in enumerating the species and causes of convulsions that I am ashamed of him.

units.la: VALLESIV S, utad illum redeam, in iisdem Com. valdè molestus est. I. De humore vel slatu indistinctè loquitur, II. De cerebro patrat idem, nec ventriculorum, nec corporis mentione factâ. In hoc solo placet, quod Obstructionem causatur, cujus materia, in aliâ parte generatâ, obstruat aliam. Hoc facilè accommodàro sententiæ meæ, si modò dare mihi volucrit, hanc ipsam materiam ex cerebro ad musculos didi. O fugite hinc juvenes!
units.tr: Vallesius, to return to him, is very troublesome in the same commentary. (1) He speaks indistinctly of humour or wind; (2) he does the same about the brain, without any mention of the ventricles or of the body. He pleases only in this, that he says the obstruction is caused by matter generated in one part which blocks another. This I could easily fit to my own opinion, if only he were willing to grant me that this very matter is sent from the brain to the muscles. O flee hence, young men!

units.la: § 29. PEREDA in Pafchal. lib. 1. C. 14. VIr
units.tr: § 29. Pereda, in Paschalis, book 1, chapter 14. A man

units.tr: chapter 14. A man otherwise careful, is here most unlike himself. The proof of this is that he explains Galen's statement about the nervous kind, in Aphorisms 5, x, falsely, from other passages which have muscles specifically. He ought first to have warned of this and rejected it, and then to have brought the truth into the open. Therefore I again rebuke him: O flee hence, young men!

units.la: § 30. Hoc celeufinate utarheic omni jure in CAPIV ACCIO, quem alias non magni facio , prejudicio accepto ab incomparabili SCHERBIO, qui ajebat , Nimis multas , easque inutiles habere distinctiones , quae legentis cerebrum tantum non diffindant. Hac in parte non fieri illi injuriam, ostendere libet Epilepfie exemplo. Hanc 1.Pract.17. contingere ait, laborante cerebro., & fecundum ventriculos,& fecundum poros. Per Poros fi intellexit corpus, cur non locutus est cum an- tiquis? Tum vero quis non intelligat, conjunxisse illum duas veterum fententias, quarum altera Ventriculos volebat. altera Corpus. Sed cur conjunxit? Credo, ut causam redderet diversorum Epilepfiæ symptomatum, Quei hoc? Detentionem sensuum omnium refert ad corpus : motum convulfivum ad ventriculos:Artificium plane Dædaleum: Ego ab Hs uno vapore peto omnia, Detentio sensuum fit, occupatis à vapore vasis, per corpus cerebri di(persis : motus,occupatis ab eodem musculis.Prioris assertionis fundamentum est,quia facultates principes exercentur in corpore cerebri,non in ventriculis : serviles in singulis sensoriis, quæ nervos suos habent à corpore, non è ventriculis. Posterioris, quia, ut sæpè dixisinimaginabile est,tantoperè contrahi cerebrum, ut musculi simul trahantur. Vnde intelligitur, mitigandum esse id, quod de partibus nervosis dicitur ex s. Aph.1. Solis enim musculis id debetur. Quem verò nodum in scirpo quærit, cum concedere non vult Galeno, Epilepsiam esse convulsionem ? Quod addit, Motum depravatum fieri, quia facultas influit, est inter ea, quæ nemo intelligit. Differt enim depravatio ab abolitione. Nec id quisquam assequatur, Motum animalem esse abolitum, ratione facultatis : depravatum, ratione musculorum. Mi Capivacci,non est heic quæstio, ut dixi, de abolitâ actione, sed de depravatâ : quæ quia ponit rem in actu, oportet etiam positivum quid sit. Id verò est Papor.Qui verò ex ventriculis afficiantur(si modò ulli afficiantur ) τῶν ἀνεξεσυνῶν εst. Et hæc quidem prima divisio est.
units.tr: § 30. Here, with every right, I use the Celsinate; against Capivaccius, whom otherwise I do not think much of, I take the prejudice from the incomparable Scherbius, who said that there are too many distinctions, and useless ones at that, which hardly split the brain of the reader. I want to show with the example of epilepsy that he is not wronged in this matter. In Practice 1, 17, Capivaccius says that this (epilepsy) happens when the brain is affected, both according to the ventricles and according to the pores. If by "pores" he meant the body, why did he not speak as the ancients did? Then who would not understand that he joined two old opinions, of which one wanted the ventricles and the other the body? But why did he join them? I believe so that he could give the cause of the different symptoms of epilepsy. How so? He refers the detention of all the senses to the body, and the convulsive motion to the ventricles. A clearly Daedalean device! I, by contrast, derive everything from one vapour. Detention of the senses happens when the vessels, dispersed through the body of the brain, are occupied by vapour; the motion happens when the muscles are occupied by the same. The foundation of the first assertion is that the principal faculties are exercised in the body of the brain, not in the ventricles; the subordinate ones in the individual sense organs, which have their nerves from the body, not from the ventricles. The foundation of the second is that, as I have often said, it is unimaginable that the brain should contract so strongly that the muscles are dragged along at the same time. Hence it is understood that what is said of the nervous parts from Aphorisms 1 must be softened, since that is owed only to the muscles. But what knot does he seek in a rush, when he will not grant to Galen that epilepsy is a convulsion? As for his addition that the motion is depraved because the faculty flows in, this is among those things that no one understands. For depravation differs from abolition. Nor would anyone grasp that the animal motion is abolished with respect to the faculty, but depraved with respect to the muscles. My dear Capivaccius, the question here is not, as I said, about abolished action but about depraved action, which, since it places the thing in act, must also have something positive. That, however, is the Pappae. As for whether they are affected from the ventricles (if indeed any are affected), that is of the things which are not understood. And this, indeed, is the first division.

units.la: § 31. Altera est, Epilepsia alia est legi-
units.tr: § 31. The second division: epilepsy is of two kinds. One is legitimate

units.la: tima, & fit vel à repletione, vel ab inanitione: alia spuria, & fit à morsu seu irritatione. De hac idem est judicium, est conferruminatio duarum sententiarum, quarum altera hoc volebat, altera illud. Dico ego, quod jam sæpius dixi, omnis epileplia, imò omnis convulsio, est ab eâdem causâ. Symptomata enim sunt eadem, nisi quod in epilepsiâ motus est interruptus.
units.tr: and arises either from repletion or from emptying; the other is spurious and arises from a bite or irritation. My judgment on this is the same as before: it is a patching together of two opinions, one of which held this and the other that. I say, as I have often said already, that every epilepsy, indeed every convulsion, has the same cause. For the symptoms are the same, except that in epilepsy the motion is interrupted.

units.la: § 32. Tertia huic affinis, Legitima est
units.tr: § 32. The third division, akin to this one, is that the legitimate kind

units.la: solius morbi: spuria est morbi simul & facultatis. Illa, ratione mulculorum est, ut ego loqui mallem. hæc, ratione cerebri. Egregium philosophema! Quod ille tamen probat ex 3. Loc. aff.7. 1.Caus. sym. ult. Quidquid fit, quia à tanto viro est, non videtur indignum explicatiunculá. Hoc fecero, occasione captâ abiis, qui Epilepsiam dicunt esse morbum compositum, si de genere loquaris: sed morbi plures complicantur, cum morbus morbum gignat. Et hoc est, quod suprà proposui considerandum. In Epilepsiâ sunt tres morbi, Intemperies, H6 à qua
units.tr: belongs to the disease alone, while the spurious kind belongs both to the disease and to the faculty. The first, as I would prefer to put it, concerns the muscles; the second concerns the brain. What an outstanding philosophy! He proves it, however, from 3. Loc. aff. 7. 1. Caus. sym. ult. Whatever the case, since it comes from so great a man, it does not seem beneath a little explanation. I will do this, having taken the occasion from those who say that epilepsy is a compound disease, if you speak of its genus; but several diseases are combined, since one disease begets another. And this is what I proposed above to consider. In epilepsy there are three diseases: an intemperature, from which

units.la: * In rei veritate) Si quis tamen ita velit, cum eo pugnandum non est. Est enim quastio Logica: ut ex Diff. morb, alt, Capparet. à qua vapor: Obstructio in cerebro, àvapore facta : Obstructio in musculis ab eodem vapore. Interim postrema hæc Obstructio est morbus ille, à quo pendet motus depravatio, cum præcedentes causæ locum subeant. At tu mihi vide anxium & dubium docendi modum penes illos, qui rem non intelligunt? Omnis convulsio est vitium motus univoci, qui voluntarius est. Ad hunc inducendum, opus est cerebri motu æquivoco, qui naturalis. Hos duos motus quia non distinguunt, quis credat illos bene docere? Vnde intelligitur, ad vitandum motum voluntarii, quo de agimus, fatis est morbus. Verum enim vero, quia vitium fine facultate cerebri expultrice (naturali) non fit, confundunt illam cum voluntario seu animali. De aliis ergo quæsiti, de cepis respondent.
units.tr: * In truth) If anyone nevertheless wishes to put it this way, one need not quarrel with him. For it is a question of logic, as is clear from Diff. morb. alt. Capparet., that from which there is a vapour: an obstruction in the brain made by the vapour; an obstruction in the muscles made by the same vapour. Meanwhile this last obstruction is the disease on which the depravation of motion depends, since the earlier causes take its place. But look here, you who do not understand the matter: is this an anxious and doubtful manner of teaching? Every convulsion is a fault of voluntary motion, which is univocal. To induce this, there must be an equivocal motion of the brain, which is natural. Since they do not distinguish these two motions, who would believe they teach well? From this it is understood that, to avoid the voluntary motion of which we speak, the disease is enough. Yet since the fault does not arise without the expulsive faculty of the brain (the natural one), they confuse it with the voluntary or animal one. Thus when they are asked about one thing, they answer about onions.

units.la: § 33. Quarta distinctio in epilepsiam per essentiam & per consensum, bene habet, si recte explicetur. Quod enim dixi nuper, ut paroxysmorum ratio reddi possit, oportet in capite (accepto vocabulo pro toto, quod collo insidet) intemperies aliqua fit, mater vaporis; non secus accin consensu intemperies est viticeris alicujus, aut etiam alius partis, ut historia nos docent.
units.tr: § 33. The fourth division into epilepsy by essence and epilepsy by consent is sound, if it is rightly explained.
