For what I said recently, so that the reason for the paroxysms can be given, is that there must be some intemperature in the head (taking the word for the whole, which sits upon the neck), the mother of the vapour. Likewise in consent the intemperature is the fault of some viscus or of another part, as histories teach us.

units.la: § 34. Quinta, in Vaporem & Mine- ram, non minus eget explicatione, Rer
units.tr: § 34. The fifth division, into vapour and matter, needs no less explanation.

units.la: illum intelligit causam propinquam: pec hanc, remotam. Hanc dum facit quemvis humorem, eumque vel pituitosum, vel melancholicum: excellenter fallitur. Non enim sufficit quivis vapor, à quovis calore simplici elatus: oportet subsit putredo, aut potius corruptio substantialis, unde vapor talis, qualis dictus est. Ab hoc tali vapore pendet argumentum A- verrois, quod est ἀπoδείξεως instar. Porrò, quam elegans est Vaporis consideratio triplex, in Copia, Quantitate, Quiete! Multò elegantius, cum consensum ducit, vel à vaporosa substantia, vel à qualitate! Loquitur quidem feré ita Gal.in 3.illo de Loc. aff, sed ex ore Pelopis præceptoris. Propterea, recte Vall. in Com. ait, Opus esse substantia. Longe elegantiffimum est, quod Qualitatem facit duplicem, spiritalem & materialem! Suprà omnes cœlos est Intemperies exufu, & non ex usu! Sic nimirum distinctio parit fubdiftinctionem, hæc rursus aliam, atque ita in infinitum. Profectò, non risu, sed flagris digna sunt talia Ἀεπισκέα, quæ tamen progemmis habent Capivacciani nostri! Talia fc. labra tales lactucæ decent! Atque ita me absolvo.
units.tr: He understands it as the proximate cause, not the remote one. While he makes this vapour out of any humour, whether phlegmatic or melancholic, he is grossly mistaken. For any vapour raised by any simple heat is not enough; there must be putrefaction underneath, or rather a substantial corruption, whence comes a vapour of the kind described. Averroes' argument depends on this kind of vapour, and it is like a demonstration [ἀποδείξεως]. Moreover, how elegant is this threefold consideration of vapour: in abundance, in quantity, in quiescence! Far more elegantly, when he derives the consent either from a vaporous substance or from a quality! Galen, in that passage of Loc. aff. book 3, does indeed speak roughly so, but from the mouth of his teacher Pelops. Therefore Vallesius rightly says, in his Commentary, that there must be a substance. Far the most elegant of all is that he makes the quality twofold, spiritual and material! Above all the heavens is an intemperature from burning, and not from use! So, of course, one distinction gives birth to a subdistinction, this in turn to another, and so on to infinity. Truly such unconsidered trifles [ἀεπισκέα] deserve not laughter but the whip, yet our Capivaccio has them in abundance! Such lips suit such lettuces! And so I take my leave.

units.la: § 35. Vin' tu plures? Nulla res facilior fuerit, siquidem otium tibi grave fit. Equidem fateor, hactenus me miram ex his voluptatem cepisse, partim, quod publicum Veritati praeconium vulgarim, & hoc ipso hymnum cecinerim DEO meo: partim, quod Mendacium è latibulis protraxerim, ut vel pueris nota fiat turpitudo illius. Sed jam fatur sum, & cogito de alio & utiliore labore, idque hac occasione.
units.tr: § 35. Do you want more? Nothing would be easier, if you find the leisure tedious. I confess that so far I have taken a wonderful pleasure in these matters, partly because I have proclaimed Truth's praise publicly and so sung a hymn to my God, and partly because I have dragged a lie out of its hiding-place, so that its shamefulness may be known even to children. But now I have had enough, and I am thinking of another and more useful labour, and on this occasion.

units.la: § 36. Cum primis statim studiorum meorum annis, in doctrinâ Convulsionum inclinarem ad Flatus Peripateticos, idque autoritate viri incomparabilis, Doctoris mei nunquam fatis laudati, D. PH. SCHERBII; alterâ verò ex parte, quasi catenis me illigatum teneret Repletio & inanitio Hipp. à tot illustribus animabus defensæ: diu fluctuavi, tanquam navis, quæ in anchoris stat. Hinc enim propellebant me quidem Flatus: illinc autem rursus repellebant me difficultates, ad quas respondere non poteram. Temporis interea cum veniret adolefcens, qui defensum vellet Hipp. admisi, visurus, fi vel hac occasione è fluctibus expedire me possem. Et favit Fors fortuna adcò, ut, lectione & meditatione multiplici adjutus, Flatus quidem plane ad-miserim,
units.tr: § 36. In the very first years of my studies, I was inclined in the doctrine of convulsions toward the Peripatetic flatus, and that on the authority of an incomparable man, my teacher, never sufficiently praised, D. PH. SCHERBIUS. On the other hand, as if repletion and emptying of Hippocrates, defended by so many illustrious souls, held me bound in chains, I wavered for a long time like a ship that stays at its anchors. For on the one side the flatus drove me forward; on the other, difficulties, to which I could not reply, drove me back again. Meanwhile, when a young man came who wished to defend Hippocrates, I admitted him, intending to see whether, on this occasion at least, I might extricate myself from the waves. And Fortune favoured me so much that, helped by repeated reading and meditation, I entirely admitted flatus,

units.la: {y} Tum Tiber. miferim, Repletionem autem cum Inanitione dimiferim. Nec poenitet facti, ἀεγόρα ἀὼ γὰρ ἀεὶ τοῦτο ἀδικοῦ ἀπολογῶ.
units.tr: {y} Then, Tiber.: I admitted flatus, but I dismissed repletion together with emptying. Nor do I regret the deed: "for I always defend this" [ἀεὶ γὰρ τοῦτο ἀπολογοῦμαι].

units.la: De Convulsione ψόγος κοὶ ἀντιθέσεις, CAP. V. T. XIII.
units.tr: On Convulsion: Censure and Objections, CHAP. V. T. XIII.

units.la: ΘΕΣΕΙΣ.
units.tr: THESES.

units.la: Omen. 1. σπασμός, ὁ, Græcis eft morbus, quo de agimus, de quà voce duo sunt notanda.
units.tr: 1. Spasmos [σπασμός] is, in Greek, the disease we are discussing. Two things must be noted about this word.

units.la: 2. Alterum. Distinguendam esse ἀπό τῆς σπάσεως, quod alias & πλευρὰ dicitur, & ῥήγμα, & pertinet ad Continui solutiones, cum mufculus totus per transverfum rumpitur, quod in palæstris veterum fæpe accidebat.
units.tr: 2. First, it must be distinguished from [ἀπὸ τῆς σπάσεως], which elsewhere is also called pleura and rhegma, and which belongs to the solutions of continuity, when a whole muscle is torn across. This often happened to the athletes of the ancient wrestling-schools.

units.la: 3. Alterum, Esse quidem τὸ σπασμὸς omninò generi-cum hodiè tamen ufurpari à Latinis, tanquam Latinum, de prima & leviffimâ convulsionis specie, quam nos den Krampf vocamus, & Italorum quidam, il Gramfo, aut la Cramfa.
units.tr: 3. Second, spasmos is indeed a general term, but Latin writers today use it as if it were Latin, for the first and mildest kind of convulsion, which we call der Krampf. Some Italians say il gramfo or la cramfa.

units.la: 4. Convulsio nofiratibus familiaris vox eft. Fortaffis melius Contractio dicetur, ἀπὸ τῆς σπάσεως quippe. Olim Diffentio vocabatur, ut eftapud Cælium Aurel. Celsus Rigorem nervorum nuncupat, & ad cervicem folam adftringit, incommo-dè
units.tr: 4. Convulsio is a word familiar to our countrymen. Perhaps contractio would be the better name, from spasis. Formerly it was called dissentio, as in Caelius Aurelianus. Celsus calls it rigor of the nerves and confines it to the neck alone, which is inappropriate

units.la: de utrumque. Sed & difficulter applica- tur Epilepsiæ : ne dicam,facilè confundi posse cum rigoribus febrilibus. Nec pla- cet additio Nervorum. Nisi enim profluvium habeat, ut olim Hipp. & Arift. frustrà fuerit.
units.tr: for either term. Nor is it easy to apply it to epilepsy, not to mention that it could easily be confused with the rigors of fever. The addition "of the nerves" does not please me either. Unless it has a flux, as Hippocrates and Aristotle once said, it would be pointless.

units.la: 5. Sed fit : ducit nos appellatio hæc ad * definitionem nominis, quæ sola sub hoc initium locum habet, Convulsio est motus depravatus musculorum, cum præter voluntatem versus principium suum trahuntur.
units.tr: 5. But let that be. This name leads us to the definition of the term, which alone has a place at this starting point: convulsion is a depraved motion of the muscles, when they are drawn, against the will, toward their origin.

units.la: 6. *Hæc vel universalis est, cum totum corpus patitur : vel particularis, cum certæ partes, 3 Loc. aff. 6. A.
units.tr: 6. This is either universal, when the whole body suffers, or particular, when certain parts suffer (Galen, De locis affectis 3.6).

units.la: 7. Vniversalis est motus vel interpolatus, vel continuus.
units.tr: 7. The universal kind is either intermittent or continuous.

units.la: 8. Interpolatus ἐπίλυσις, ἢ ἐπιλυσία dicitur Græcis, Subintelligitur autem Ἀλεβαῖα, & est idem cum τὸ ἀπάλυσις Ἀλεβᾶν, ut utrobique fit Interceptio venasum. Ita autem videtur,ibi quidem τὸ ἐπὶ poni ἀνὶ τὲ ἀπὸ ,cum intendit significationem: utrobique autem significare non quamcunque Interceptionem, sed ὑεhementem ἐν periculosam. Eatenus enim τὸ Ἀαρέσθα differt ab utroque composito, ἐπὶ & , ἀπολυσία.
units.tr: 8. The intermittent kind is called by the Greeks epilysis or epilysia, and the word understood is [ἀλεβαῖα]; it is the same as the [ἀπάλυσις] of the veins, since in both cases it means an interception of the veins. It seems that there the preposition epi is used instead of apo when it expresses intensity. In both cases it signifies not just any interception but a vehement and dangerous one. In this respect the word differs from both compounds, epi and apolysis.

units.la: 9. Hac ratione simul accesserimus ad * Definitio nominis.
units.tr: 9. In this way we have at the same time come to the definition of the name.

units.la: * Differentia.
units.tr: * Difference.

units.la: [?]v ἱερῶν κόσμων, μαγνum (non sacrum )morbum Veterum: simul absolverimus nos à Supernarum partium prebenfione, quam somniant quidam.
units.tr: The [sacred] disease of the ancients, which is not sacred but great: at the same time we shall free ourselves from the seizure of the upper parts, which some dream of.

units.la: 10. Epilepsia(nam hoc solo vocabulo utemur) varios habet gradus, quæ species heic (ut à priscis habemus) non mutant ut in Apoplexiâ. Gravissima est; quando cum motu reciproco,quem ἀλό- vocantilli, abolentur omnes sensus, h.e. tam interni quos Facultates principes vocamus, Ratio, memoria, imaginatio: quam æterni, Visus,auditus &c. Hæc fit, cum totum cerebri corpus (nullo modo ventriculi)unà cum principio nervorum occupatur. Minus gravis est, cum pereunt quidem sensus omnes: salvus autem utę cunque motus est. In his servari ex sensibus potest solus tactus. Iterum, minus gravis est, cum vel foli interni pereunt: vel foli externi: vel, salvis utrisque, motus tantum. Hæc omnia fieri, ex historiis probatu facile est.
units.tr: 10. Epilepsy (for we shall use only this word) has various degrees, and these species do not change here, as the ancients held, as they do in apoplexy. The most severe is when, with the reciprocal motion which they call [ἀλό-], all the senses are abolished: the inner ones, which we call the leading faculties (reason, memory, imagination), and the outer ones (sight, hearing, and so on). This happens when the whole substance of the brain is seized, together with the source of the nerves, but never the ventricles alone. Less severe is when all the senses perish but some motion is still preserved in some way. In these cases only touch can be kept of the senses. Again, less severe is when only the inner senses perish, or only the outer, or, with both intact, only motion. That all these things happen is easily proved from histories.

units.la: 11. Et hæc de Interpolato motu: in Continuo separo me à Celso, ut jam dixi, qui ad cervicem adstringit. Quamvis enim fieri posse non negem: tamen Græcorum doctissimi alligârunt ad totum corpus unà cum artubus.
units.tr: 11. So much for the intermittent motion. In the continuous kind I separate myself from Celsus, as I have said, who confines it to the neck. For though I do not deny it can happen, the most learned of the Greeks bound it to the whole body together with the limbs.

units.la: 12. Ἐμπεφυόθνον enim vocârunt, cum spina tota versus anteriora vergit, artusque violenter extenduntur.
units.tr: 12. For they called it [ἐμπροσθότονον] when the whole spine bends forward and the limbs are violently stretched.

units.la: 13. Oπʼ̈Θȫ Θ̇ν, cum eadem in arcum incurvatur, & artus flectuntur, brachiis quidem pectori appressis, pedes autem clunibus appropinquant.
units.tr: 13. [ὀπισθότονον] is when the same body is curved into a bow and the limbs are bent: the arms are pressed to the chest, and the feet draw near the buttocks.

units.la: 14. Τεταν̇ες (ita enim scribo) cum tum corpus riget, quasi tonico motu actum.
units.tr: 14. [τέτανος] (for so I write it) is when the whole body becomes rigid, as if driven by a tonic motion.

units.la: 15. An quia ab hoc posteriori sunt duo priora, scribendum est ἐμπροσθέν & ὀπισθοτέρ(ω) Ἐrrante enim primo scribā, erratum manet, sæpe inquit Gal. Accedit, quod facilè probatu non fit, ὑπο esse idem cum τά τεταν̇ς.
units.tr: 15. Or, because the two former ones derive from this latter, should we write [ἐμπροσθότονος] and [ὀπισθότονος]? For once a scribe has erred, the error remains, as Galen often says. Add that it is not easy to prove that [ὑπο-] is the same as the tetanic ones.

units.la: 16. Hæ tres species ab Epilepsiâ differunt, quod in illis sensuum tam internoꝛum, quam externorum nulla fit læsio, l. de Diff. symp. 3.
units.tr: 16. These three species differ from epilepsy in that in them there is no injury to the senses, internal or external (On the Differences of the Symptoms, book 3).

units.la: 17. An Catalepsis & Catoch est Tetanus quidam, licet cum Epilepsiâ communicet ineo, quod sensus & motus hcic quoque ligati sint? Vide Pathologica nostra, cap. 124.
units.tr: 17. Are catalepsy and catochus a kind of tetanus, although they agree with epilepsy in that the senses and motion are bound in them too? See our Pathologica, chap. 124.

units.la: 18. An spasmus universalis est Tetanus leuior? Constant enim sensus, quod vidi. Particularem qui non expertus fit, vix puto esse hominem, licet particularia nomina non habeat.
units.tr: 18. Is universal spasm a milder tetanus? For the senses remain, as I have seen. I hardly think anyone exists who has not experienced a particular spasm, even though it has no particular name.

units.la: 19. His contrà gaudent Convulsiones reliquæ. Strabifmus enim in oculo eft, licet morbus in fitu quoque effe poffit. Convulfio canina in labiis & buccis, quam vis paralyfis etiam effe poffit Priapifmus & Satyrifmus in pene. Accenfent his quidam & Sternutationem, quam Epilepfiam parvam vocant : & Singultum, quem ipfe Hipp. convulfionibus annumerat.
units.tr: 19. The remaining convulsions, on the contrary, are free of this. Strabismus is in the eye, though the disorder can also lie in the position of the eye. Canine convulsion is in the lips and cheeks, though it may also be a paralysis. Priapism and satyrism are in the penis. Some also count sneezing, which they call a small epilepsy, among these, and hiccupping, which Hippocrates himself reckons among the convulsions.

units.la: 20. *In caufis indagandis non oportet ire ad Repletionem &c Inanitionem Hipp. 5. Aph. 1. 6. Aph. 39. Tanto enim intervallo abfunt à vera Philofophia, quanto Cerletani Italorum,ut veriffimè (non ex odio Medicorum,ut Mercurialis judicat) Averroës 5. Coll. 1. Quò minus videre poffum,cur Gal. 3. Loc. aff. 6. tantopere commendârit! Qui admittunt, in Epilepfia per effentiam tantum volunt, & quidem Repletionem folam : in Epilepfiâ per confenfum Flatus (feu vaporesquod profecto indigniffimum eft. Eadem enim funt fymptomata, ut toties dixi, quarum caufas ex flatibus habes, ex repletione non habes.
units.tr: 20. In seeking causes we ought not to go to repletion or emptiness (Hippocrates, Aphorisms 5.1 and 6.39). They are as far from true philosophy as the Cerretani of Italy are from it. Averroes (Colliget 5.1) truly says this, not out of hatred for physicians, as Mercurialis judges. I cannot see why Galen (On the Places Affected 3.6) so strongly commended them! Those who admit these causes want epilepsy to arise only from essence, and indeed only from repletion, and from consent only from flatus (or vapours), which is truly most unworthy. For the symptoms are the same, as I have said so often; their causes you have from flatulence, and not from repletion.

units.la: 21. Ire igitur ad Meteorologica Arift. oportet, & confiderare artificium veterum planè divinum, quo modo à φαινο-μένων Nobis notis, tranfitum fecerint ad ὑλεσγήν, Naturâ nota, five à fenfibus ad intelle&um.
units.tr: 21. We must therefore go to Aristotle's Meteorology and consider the wholly divine method of the ancients, by which they passed from the [phenomena] known to us to what is known by nature, that is, from the senses to the intellect.

units.la: * Caufæ. telle!tum. Hoc faciam du!tu SCHERBII, τε Ϙευζὶς, idque hæc natà occafione.
units.tr: * Causes. Intellect. I shall do this under the guidance of Scherbius, and it arose on the following occasion.

units.la: 22. Cum anno 1601. de Terræmotu contra Ariftot. disputaret DD. TAVRELLV S, præceptor item meus, & ego inter Opponentes, quos vocant, effem, varia SCHERBIVS mecum contulit super hoc negotio, subinde accommodans ad Epilepsiam, à quâ, præ aliis convulsionibus, ordiendum esse ajebat. Hæc ita explicabat.
units.tr: 22. In the year 1601, when Doctor Taurellus, also my teacher, was disputing about earthquakes against Aristotle, and I was among those called opponents, Scherbius conferred with me on various points in this matter. He repeatedly applied them to epilepsy, which, he said, should be taken first before the other convulsions. He explained it thus.

units.la: 23. In Macrocosmo terræmotus à flatibus fieri, inter alia Φαινόμενα docet hoc, Quod certis locis incipiunt, è quibus veniunt ad vicina, ab hisiterum, ad vicina, & sic deinceps, usque dum alicubi erumpant. Hinc ego colligo hoc ἐνεργεῖς Oportet ergo tale corpus fit, quod & φοβερὸν & κινητικὸν fit. Quæ duo requisita in quo reperias, quam in ἐν ψυχρῷ ἀ πνεύματι Ariftotelico?
units.tr: 23. In the macrocosm, he taught, earthquakes arise from winds. Among other phenomena he notes this: they begin in certain places, from which they pass to neighbouring places, and from these again to their neighbours, and so on, until they break out somewhere. From this I infer the following: the body must be such that it is both [fearful] and [moving]. In what will you find these two requisites better than in the Aristotelian [cold wind]?

units.la: 24. Superioribus annis, cum totum hoc opidum, noctu circa horam terriam, ita concuteretur, ut plerique nostrum è somno excitaremur (inter hos me quoque cfle, non falso prædico, interfabar ego)
units.tr: 24. In former years, when this whole town was shaken at night, about the third hour, so that most of us were roused from sleep (I myself, I do not falsely declare, was among them)

units.la: * Vide Cefalp.2. Quaft. Med 16. Adde Vicomercatum in Meteorol. Arift. f. 107. aut.131. aliis quæ ed. Venetæ. ego) annon postea comperimus, ante mensem forte idem sensisse Rhenanos, & post hos Francos : post mensem Austrios & Vngaros? Quæ ratio motus hujus fucceffivis Reverà montium ille casus est λόγῳ ἀπόσπη ἀδξαν βιαζόμεν, ut Philosophus loquitur.
units.tr: * See Cesalpinus, Quaestiones Medicae 2.16. Add Vicomercatus on Aristotle's Meteorology, f. 107 or 131, and other editions in Venice. Did we not afterwards learn that perhaps a month earlier the people of the Rhine had felt the same, and after them the French; and after a month the Austrians and Hungarians? The manner of this motion, as it spreads in succession, is really a falling of mountains, a violent tearing away, as the Philosopher puts it.

units.la: 25. In Microcosmo, (addebat) eodem modo Convulsiones fiunt, præcipuè Epilepsia. Quam enim rationem dabimus subiti illius accessus? & rursus subitæ illius solutionis?
units.tr: 25. In the microcosm, he added, convulsions arise in the same way, especially epilepsy. For what account shall we give of that sudden onset? And again of that sudden cessation?

units.la: 26. Idem Φαινόμενον jubet nos fperè nere ventriculorum cerebri obstructionem, & quidem à frigidis, crassisque humoribus, quod profecto nimis populare est: è contrario cogitare de corpore cerebri, è quo via est in nervos, cum è ventriculis non fit.
units.tr: 26. The same phenomenon bids us reject an obstruction of the ventricles of the brain, and indeed one caused by cold, thick humours, which is truly too popular a view. On the contrary, we should consider the substance of the brain, from which there is a path into the nerves, since there is none from the ventricles.

units.la: 27. Si enim concedatur, quod tamen per rerum naturam fieri non potest, Ventriculos contrahi : quei verisimile est, contractionem illam ad musculos usque pervenire? Et quæ proportio est inter contractionem tantillam cerebri, & contractionem musculorum tam vehementem? inter motum æquivocum & univocum?
units.tr: 27. For even if one concedes what cannot in fact happen according to the nature of things, that the ventricles of the brain contract, how likely is it that this contraction reaches as far as the muscles? And what proportion is there between so slight a contraction of the brain and so vehement a contraction of the muscles? Between an equivocal motion and a univocal one?

units.la: 28. Si concedatur etiam Galeno motus ille cerebri proprius, quo aërem ex-
units.tr: 28. If one also concedes to Galen that proper motion of the brain by which he wishes us to believe it draws in external air for the making of animal spirits,

units.la: ternum trahere credi vult ad spirituum animalium confectionem, quod tamen reverà quavis fabulâ insolentius est: quis credat,motum illum (ex hypothesi) naturalem trahi posse ad non-naturalem?
units.tr: which in truth is more outlandish than any fable: who would believe that this motion, natural by hypothesis, can be drawn over to the non-natural?

units.la: 29. Prætereà,quis fibipatiatur perfuaderi,musculos eo modo trahi à cerebro, quo ego manu traho lapidem, funialligatum:Oportet in ipsas musculorum cavitates recipi corpus tale, quale defcri- ptum est σφοδ εγ ... quod ex corpore producî potest, ex ventriculis non potest,ceu dixi.
units.tr: 30. So much for that. When, long afterwards, I found these doctrines not only in Aristotle but in Galen himself, they so drew me away both from Galen's own Obstruction and from the Semi-obstruction of Fernelius, Montanus, Massaria and the others of the first class of physicians, that I recoil with my whole mind whenever I hear them. This is especially so since they produce apoplexy from the same cause (for that Gallic modification helps nothing). For what? Can such different symptoms, the most acute and the most protracted, arise from one and the same cause? Based on a hypothesis truly made of straw, that spirit is elaborated in the ventricles of the brain? But these matters we shall examine later.

units.la: 30. Hæcferè illetum: quæ cum longo tempore post non apud Arifl. tantum reperirem, sed & Gal. ipsum, ita me abstraxerunt, tam ab Obstructione Gal. ipsius, quam à Semiobstructione Fernelii, Montani,Massariæ,aliorum primæ classis Medicorum, ut toto animo resiliam, quoties audio. Maximè cum ab eadem causâ (nihil enim promovet modificatio illa Gallica) Apoplexiam quoque generant. Quid enim? Symptomata tam diversa fiant ab eâdem causâ?Morbus acutissimus, & longissimus? cum hypothesi vere straminea, spiritus elaborari in ventriculis cerebri? Sed hæc quidem postea videbimus.
units.tr: 30. These are roughly the things I read. When, after a long time, I found them not only in Aristotle but in Galen himself, they drew me away so much from Galen's own Obstruction as from the Semi-obstruction of Fernelius, Montanus, Massaria and the others of the first class of physicians, that I recoil with my whole mind whenever I hear them. Especially since they produce apoplexy from the same cause (for that Gallic modification helps nothing). For what? Can such different symptoms, the most acute and the most long-lasting disease, arise from the same cause, on a hypothesis truly made of straw, that spirits are elaborated in the ventricles of the brain? But we shall see these matters later.

units.la: 31. Nunc, quia procul omni dubio pofcis me loca illa duorum ducum nostrorum, hem tibi illos !
units.tr: 31. Now, since without doubt you demand from me those passages of our two leaders, here, behold them!

units.la: 32. Philofophus, cum explicuiffet 2.
units.tr: 32. The Philosopher, when he had explained the earthquake in Meteorology 2, adds:

units.la: Meteor. 8. terræmotus, fubdit, O'σαν δὲ ἐχει δ' πνεῦμα δύναμιν, ἡ μόνον ἐκ τῶν ἐν ταῖς γυναικείων ἄεὶ, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐν τοῖς σώμασι τῶν ζώων οὔτε γὰρ πεζῶν ποτὲ ἰ- οἱ ἀναπνοοὶ πνεύματι ἀδ' εἰσὶ κινήσεως. ἐν ἐντὸς δ' ἔχοντι ἰσχὺν, ὥστε πολλὰς ἀπὸ τοῦ πιέζω- φύσεως ἀποδίδωσι ἐκ τοῦ ἡμέτερ... νήσεως τῶν ἀρρωστιῶν. Vbi hoc primum moneo, Videri duas illas voces, πνεῦμα... ἀναπνοοὶ, ἐλλὰ ... more Græcis valdè ufitato, quod explicentur in feq. per ἀέρας, qui non sunt Τremores Gazæ, fed Convulsiones Vallefii, 5.Epid. 49. quo de loco infrà. Tunc fenfus hic erit, Si parva licet componere magnis, quanta sit vis spiritus, exhalationis, vaporis, aut quomodocunque velis appellare, dicere est, non ex iis tantum, quæ in Meteorologicis tractantur à Philosophis : fed ex iis, quæ de Convulsionibus Medici docent. Tam enim violentæ sunt Convulsiones, ut, etiam si plareg adstantium contranitantur, & dirigere velint corpus, non possint.
units.tr: Where I first point out this: the two words "spirit" and "breathings" [πνεῦμα ... ἀναπνοαί], in the very common Greek manner, are explained in what follows by "winds" [ἀέρας]. These are not the tremors of Gaza but the convulsions of Vallesius (Epid. 5, 49), on which passage more below. The sense, then, is this: if small things may be set beside great, consider how great is the force of the spirit, of the exhalation, of the vapour, or whatever else you care to call it. One must say that it is not only such force as the philosophers treat in the Meteorology, but also such as the physicians teach concerning convulsions. For convulsions are so violent that even if the bystanders struggle against them and wish to hold the body straight, they cannot do so. The Greek reads: "...for never does a breath [ἀναπνοή] ... wind [πνεῦμα] ... strength [ἰσχύν] within ... so that many ... from pressing ... nature ... gives ... of our ... diseases" [ὅταν δὲ ... πνεῦμα ... δύναμιν ... ἰσχὺν ... ἀποδίδωσι ... τῶν ἀρρωστιῶν].

units.la: 33. Idem 7.Hift. ult. de Somno.3.ad
units.tr: 33. The same, in the seventh book of the History, final passage, on Sleep, chapter 3, adds:

units.la: Epilepsiam puerilem refert, quam fieri ait in iis, qui copiosiori & flatulentiori alimento utuntur. Quam ob caufam & vinum prohibet.
units.tr: He describes puerile epilepsy, which he says arises in those who use a more copious and flatulent diet. For this reason he also forbids wine.

units.la: 34. Hanc Philosophi mentem qui non perceperit ex iis, quæ scribit Medicus duobus locis, 2. Cauf. (sym. 2. D. & de Trem. & Palp. ult. A, ille, vel ἀξύνετος, ut Philosophus est, vel aliquod interesse habet, ut ficloquar, veluti ipse ex Thucydide, 3. Vt p. 10.
units.tr: 34. Whoever has not grasped the Philosopher's meaning from what the physician writes in two places (in the Causes of Symptoms, book 2, and in On Tremor and Palpitation, end, A), either is unintelligent, as the Philosopher is, or has some interest in the matter, as I may put it, just as he himself says, following Thucydides (book 3)...

units.la: 35. Hoc Θαυμάζωμεν fi stabiliero alio est videntiori, dabifie mihi manus, ὁ Φιλόσοφλόγος, quo nomine scio te apprime gaudere? Antequam id narrem, revoco tibi in memoriam axioma Physicum, quod de hocipso negotio Piccolominus habet in Metetrol. quà de Terræm, f. 932. edit. Francofurt. Nullum reperiri motum violentum, qui non supponat motum f.n. à quo pendeat. Quare, fi quæratur, quod fit illud, & unde visilla invicta, quæ cohiberi non possit, quæque omnia Imperio premat, & vinclis & carcere frenet? Respondebitur, Animadversum fuisse, & olim à Gal. præceptoribus, 3. Loc. aff. 7. & posteà à nostrorum plurimis, quos vidimus dereeft apud Schenk. 1, obser. 189. & seq. in quibusdam Epilepticis eximo pede, ex tibia, ex coxendice, ex utero, ex liene, ex ventriculo, &c. ascendere aliquam quandam frigidam, ut fere loquuntur, ad cerebrum, quà ibi concepta, subito, [illegible, ~6 letters]ubitò,& facultates omnes dispereunt,& motus convulforii incipiunt. Hanc auam negabisne proportionem habere ad latum Ariftotelicum?
units.tr: 35. Will you, philosopher, give me your hand, if I establish this "wonder" against a more discerning opponent? You know that I am especially fond of this name. Before I tell it, let me recall to you a physical axiom which Piccolomini states on this very matter in his Meteorology, on earthquakes, p. 932, Frankfurt edition: no violent motion is found that does not presuppose a motion from which it depends. Therefore, if it is asked what that thing is, and whence comes that invincible power which cannot be restrained, which overrules everything and holds in check by chains and prison, the answer will be that it has been noticed, both by Galen's own teachers (book 3, Loc. aff., ch. 7), and afterwards by many of our own people whom we have seen, as is found in Schenck (book 1, obs. 189 and following), that in some epileptics a certain cold thing, as they commonly put it, ascends to the brain from the tip of the toe, from the shin, from the hip, from the uterus, from the spleen, from the stomach, etc.; once conceived there, suddenly [illegible] all faculties perish and convulsive motions begin. Will you deny that this has a proportion to the Aristotelian wind?

units.la: 36. Non negabo dicis, sed discere cuiam, Quid heic naturale fit ; cum vapor fit .n. Vapor ipse est p. n. nec quæstio est iac de re.Quemadmodum in terræ mou flatus p. n. naturaliter movetur furum:ita heic vaportendit sursum ad ceebrum,è quo iterum deturbatus à viexultrice, quæ ipsa naturalis est,facit καὶ ἀέρου lum. Nimirum calvariam penetrare on potest, subsistere ibi minus : quare, uà vià patet, nervos ingreditur, & inde h musculos fertur.
units.tr: 36. I do not deny it, you say, but I want to learn what is natural here, since the vapour is itself a vapour, and the question is not about that. Just as in earthquakes a wind is moved naturally upward, so here the vapour tends upward to the brain, and, being driven down again from there by a force which is itself natural, it produces the wind and the air. Certainly it cannot penetrate the skull, and it cannot stay there for long; therefore, by whatever way is open, it enters the nerves and is carried from there to the muscles.

units.la: 37. Inquis, Hoc in Epilepsia per connfum tantum habet locum ? Ex hypothesi ialenicà inquam ego. Ea verò non unam abet instantiam, & hanc præcipuè. uod, fi effentia eo modo accipiatur, ut aliis morbis, ratio nulla dari possit aroxyfmorum. Quamobrem non raro hihi occurrit hoc ὅτι δὲ οὐ, Nullam daEpilepsiam per essentiam. Tamen, ne ovator videar, eam dicam, in quâ caput tfedes intemperiei illius, quæ flatum Elepticum gignit. Hæc intemperies post esse tam intrà,quam extrà calvariam, cepto principio nervorum. Hoc enim I ; occupa-
units.tr: 37. You object: does this have a place only in epilepsy by consent? I say, by the Galenic hypothesis. But that hypothesis does not have only one instance, and this one especially. For if the essence is understood in the way it is in other diseases, no reason can be given for the paroxysms. Therefore it often occurs to me that this "but that is not so": there is no epilepsy by essence. Yet, lest I seem to be a boaster, I will call it that in which the head is the seat of that intemperature which produces the epileptic wind. This intemperature is afterwards located both within and outside the skull, the beginning of the nerves having been occupied by it. For when this is occupied,

units.la: occupato, causæ non est, quin semper laboret æger.
units.tr: when this is occupied, there is no reason why the patient should not always suffer.

units.la: 38. Altera instantia est, Inexplicabilis, est, quomodo Epilepsia per eflentiam fiat à Repletione & Inanitione: per consensum pudità flatu seu vapore mordente, irritante. Nec quidquam sublevat, quod Gal.3. Loc. aff.7. A. Inanitionem aspellit, cuncta aliis locis, quibus ingenere loquitur agnoscat. Multò minus juvat, quod findi dicti cap.ut & alibi, Epilepsiam per consensum sensum, & raro fieri ait, & mitiorem esse. Iam enim alii anté me obfervárunt, ut trumque esse falsum, & simplici inverfio ne refellendum, Non minus frequente esse alterà. Non minus sævam alterà.
units.tr: 38. The second instance is inexplicable: how epilepsy by essence arises from repletion and inanition, and by consent from a biting, irritating wind or vapour. Nor does it help that Galen, in book 3, Loc. aff., ch. 7, acknowledges inanition, in all the other places where he speaks in general terms. Much less does it help that in the same chapter, and elsewhere, he says that epilepsy by consent is rarer and milder. For others before me have observed that each of these claims is false, and that it must be refuted by a simple reversal: the other kind is no less frequent, and the other is no less savage.

units.la: 39. Sed sint vera hæc omnia: Quod modo humor crassus, frigidus, glutinosus; quomodo pituita & melancholia quæ obstruunt ventriculos, possunt eam dem inferre symptomata, quæ facit valde poracris, ex bile v.g. æruginosà. 5. Aph. 1. qui irritando agit: Quin, ut iterum dicam sunt symptomata tam sibi similia, ut pe ritiffimi dubitent aliquando, per effent tiam ne fit affectus, an per consensum?
units.tr: 39. But suppose all this is true: how can a thick, cold, glutinous humour, such as phlegm and melancholy which obstruct the ventricles, produce the same symptoms which very bitter bile, for instance the verdigris-coloured kind (Aphorisms 5, 1), produces, acting by irritation? Indeed, as I say again, the symptoms are so alike that the most skilled physicians sometimes doubt whether the affection is by essence or by consent.

units.la: 40. Propterea veni in hanc fententiam, Omnem Epilepsiam esse ab unâ, eamdemque causâ, Vapore, sed cum hac diff ferentia, Vapor alius est à manifestis causis caliditate & siccitate : alius à totâ fubftantiâ. Idcò intemperies quoque duplex est, alia, quæ dicta est, & cui occurrimus aquis taraxici, alsines, fquamatæ &c. in pueris præcipuè : alia est à totâ fubftantiâ,ceu dixi.
units.tr: 40. For this reason I have come to this opinion: all epilepsy arises from one and the same cause, a vapour, but with this difference: one vapour differs from the manifest causes of heat and dryness, another from the whole substance. Hence the intemperature is also twofold: one, which has been described and which we meet with in waters, taraxacum, chickweed, scaly plants, etc., chiefly in children; the other comes from the whole substance, as I have said.

units.la: 41. Hujus consectarium est, ut Epilepfia fit in censu illorum morborum, in quibus pars mandans differt à recipiente, idque ideò,ut ratio paroxysmorum reddi possit,ceu pariter dixi.
units.tr: 41. A consequence of this is that epilepsy belongs to the class of those diseases in which the affecting part differs from the affected part, and this so that the cause of the paroxysms can be given, as I have likewise said.

units.la: 42. Ergone,inquis,Epilepsia jam non est morbus,sed acervus morborum ? Est, & non est. Est : quatenus morbus morbum gignit.Inde est,ut hic fiat ordo. Primus & quidê fundamentalis morbus est intemperies, modò hæc, modò illa, quæ aporé gignit.Secunda eftObftructio in cerebro,ob quam spiritibus negatur aditus, pereuntque sensus universi, tu puta in Epilepfiâ gravissimâ.In minus enim gravibus variant symptomata, pro ratione Obstructionis. Tertius est alia Obstructio in inuículis, ob quam depravatur motus. Non est:quatenus utraque Obstructio tantum habet rationem morbi: Intemperies ratione causæ.Hinc Indicationes, in simplici quidem alterandi,refrigera : in totâ subtantiâ,ure, seca,fi potes.
units.tr: 42. Is epilepsy then, you ask, no longer one disease but a heap of diseases? It is and it is not. It is, insofar as one disease produces another. Hence the order is as follows. The first and fundamental disease is the intemperature, now this, now that, which produces the paroxysm. The second is the obstruction in the brain, on account of which access is denied to the spirits, and all the senses perish, as in the most severe epilepsy. For in less severe cases the symptoms vary according to the degree of obstruction. The third is another obstruction in the muscles, on account of which motion is depraved. It is not: insofar as each obstruction has only the character of a disease, the intemperature having the character of a cause. Hence the indications: in the simple intemperature, indeed, cool; in the whole substance, moisten, dry, if you can.

units.la: ANTIΘEΣΕΙΣ.
units.tr: ANTIΘEΣΕΙΣ.

units.la: 43. Heic subito audio obstrepentem quendam contra §. 38. Argumentum tuum tale est, Vbicunque eadem sunt symptomata, ibi sunt eadem causae, In omni Epilepsia sunt eadem symptomata. Ergo. Major habet hanc instantiam, Diarrhaea, dysenteria, colica habent sua symptomata, & tamen pendent a variis partibus mandibus. Do tibi omnia. Dicam igitur a variis causis, Non potest, Est enim ubique eadem symptomatum congeries, licet humores modo sint ab hac parte, modo ab illa. Ita, unde unde fit vapor ille scelestus, idem agit.
units.tr: 43. Here someone suddenly objects to me, quarrelling with §38. Your argument runs thus: wherever the same symptoms are present, the same causes are present. In every epilepsy the symptoms are the same. Therefore... The major premise has this counterexample: diarrhoea, dysentery and colic have their own symptoms, and yet they depend on various parts of the body. I grant you all of that. I will say, then, that they arise from various causes, but that cannot be said of epilepsy. For the cluster of symptoms is everywhere the same, whether the humours come now from this part, now from that. So, from whatever source that wicked vapour arises, it produces the same effect.

units.la: 44. Stante igitur hoc urgeo illud contra Epilepsiam per essentiam, Non potest dari ratio paroxysmorum. Iamque addo, Cadit hinc simul triplex Epilepsia Gal. 3. Loc. aff. 7, V. & non nisi una manet, illa sc. quam tertio loco numerat. Et quae ratio est, cur ventriculus solus faciat Epilepsiam per consensum? Certe ex quam plurimis partibus accidit tale quid, quale ille ait e ventriculo fieri. Quin lienem numerat ipsemet cap. praeced. 6.E.
units.tr: 44. Granting this, I press the following point against epilepsy by essence: there can be no account of the paroxysms. And I add that from this there falls away at once the threefold division of epilepsy in Galen (Loc. aff. 7). Only one remains, namely the one he lists third. And what reason is there why the stomach alone should cause epilepsy by consensus? Surely something of the kind that he says comes from the stomach arises from very many parts. Indeed he himself, in the preceding chapter (6), counts the spleen.

units.la: 45. Cadit, ut paululum aberrem, triplex quoque Melancholia, Ib. K.O. Per essentiam, ex solo capite: per consensum, ex habitu: hypochondriaca. Nam tertia hæc etiam per consensum est,à ventriculo quidem incipiens, ut rectè definit Gal. sed posteà tam mirabiles mores induens, ut Proteus dicatur à Mercuriali.Propterea itâ concipere sermonem oportet, Melancholia aut per essentiam est, aut per consensum. Hæc rursus, aut ab habitu pendet, aut à visceribus inferiorum ventrium, tantoperè varians symptomatis, quod post ventriculum laboret modò hoc, modòillud viscus; modò plura ex his,modò pauciora.
units.tr: 45. Let me stray a little: the threefold division of melancholy (Ib. K.O.) also falls away. By essence, from the head alone; by consensus, from the habit of body: hypochondriac. For this third kind is also by consensus. It begins, as Galen rightly defines it, in the stomach, but afterwards it takes on such strange habits that it is called Proteus by Mercurialis. Therefore one must speak thus: melancholy is either by essence or by consensus. The latter in turn depends either on the habit of body or on the viscera of the lower belly, and its symptoms vary so greatly that, after the stomach, now this viscus and now that one is affected, now more of these, now fewer.

units.la: 46. Pericilitatur etiam distinctio Epilepsiæ in legitimam & spuriam. Cur enim legitima est illa, quæ fit à Repletione: spuria, quæ à vapore mordente? Omnes sunt æquè legitimæ : omnes sunt ab eâdem causâ : omnes habent eadem symptomata, quatenus sc. Epilepsiæ sunt : omnes habent eosdem curationis sco- pos.
units.tr: 46. The distinction of epilepsy into legitimate and spurious is also in danger. For why is that which arises from repletion legitimate, and that which arises from a biting vapour spurious? All are equally legitimate; all come from the same cause; all have the same symptoms, in so far as they are epilepsy; all have the same aims in cure.

units.la: 47. Propter latitudinem Epilepsiæ,de quâ §10. periclitantur, qui definiunt summum ejus gradum tantum, cum in terram cadunt, & toto corpore convelluntur, &c. Iam enim pauciora & mitiora sunt symptomata : jam plura, sæ- vioraque.
units.tr: 47. Because of the breadth of epilepsy, which I noted in §10, those are in danger who define only its highest degree, when people fall to the ground and are convulsed through the whole body, and so on. For there are then fewer and milder symptoms, and then more and fiercer ones.

units.la: 48. Constat quidem, Epilepsiam esse
units.tr: 48. It is certainly agreed that epilepsy is

units.la: I cum χλέγω ut plurimum; reliquas autem convulsiones cum motu simplici : non conflat, an quemadmodum in Epilepsia aboliti sunt sensus omnes, ita in reliquis quoque sit? Egoex de Diff. sym.3. D.attuli autoritatem Gal. fine experientia nihil afferentis, Non esse. Quare illi, quiajunt Esse, aut experientiam contrariam afferant, aut sileant, Ego certe, quod dixi § 18. in sphaeno universali vidi consistare. An sit, cum solae sunt: non sit, cum Epilepsia illis copulatur?
units.tr: with a clonic motion [κλόνος] usually; but the other convulsions are with simple motion. It is not agreed whether, just as in epilepsy all the senses are abolished, so it is also in the others. I, in my De differentia symptomatum (3), have cited the authority of Galen, who asserts nothing without experience, that they are not. So those who say they are should either bring contrary experience or keep silent. I myself, as I said in §18, have seen it persist in universal sphacelus. Does it happen when the convulsions occur alone, and not when they are joined to epilepsy?

units.la: 49. Hoc temere foliciti sunt quidam, quaerendo, Quâ in re consistat essentia Epilepsia? In medio sunt Gal, verba, in illo de Diff.Sym. E.Epilepsia dicitur, si totius corporis convulsio sit, cum rectricis partis cohibitione, ut Int. loquitur. Ego vero jam dixi, de summo gradu tantum hoc verum esse. Nec tutò quis dixerit, vel in sensu esse, vel in motu: multò minus, In actione animali. Hoc enim esset sub nube latere velle. Dico igitur, reverà quidem in utroque est ut plurimum: dicitur autem à motu, qui magis incurrit in oculos.
units.tr: 49. Some have rashly troubled themselves with this question: in what does the essence of epilepsy consist? Galen's words in the middle of the work On the Differences of Symptoms (E) say that epilepsy is a convulsion of the whole body together with a restraint of the governing part, as Int. puts it. I have already said that this is true only of the highest degree. Nor may anyone safely say that it lies either in sense or in motion, and still less in animal action. For that would be to wish to hide under a cloud. I say, therefore, that in truth it is in both, for the most part, but it is named from the motion, which strikes the eyes more.

units.la: 50. Non minus temere laborant illi, qui crepant Gal. illud, 4.Loc. aff. 2. Q. Epilepsiam esse mediam inter Carum & A-poplexiam. Carus est affectus soporosus, p.n. quidem: sed finiens in sanitatem,idque cum respiratione vel naturali, vel majori, cum somnum toto pectore profiant, ut Virg. canit. Si quando non sequatur sanitas, non Carus fuit, sed Apoplexia inferior gradus. Apoplexia non est affectus soporosus, nisi apud vulgus, quod ex stertore judicat. Eadem ratio est Epilepsia. A vulgo autem exspectes aliquid certi? Quin abjicere oportet talia, quæ morantur bona ingenia.
units.tr: 50. No less rashly do those labour who make a noise about that saying of Galen (Loc. aff. 4, Q. 2) that epilepsy is intermediate between Carus and Apoplexy. Carus is a soporose affection, certainly, but it ends in health, and that with breathing either natural or greater, since people breathe out sleep with the whole chest, as Virgil sings. If health does not follow, it was not Carus, but Apoplexy, a lower degree. Apoplexy is not a soporose affection, except to the common people, who judge it by the snoring. The same reasoning holds for Epilepsy. But are you to expect anything certain from the common people? Indeed such things must be cast off, since they hold back good minds.

units.la: 51. Nescio an dicere audeam : sed quidni? Pueri sunt, qui quærunt, Morbusne sit, proprie accepto vocabulo, an symptoma? Morbus est : sed nomen habet à symptomate. Hic morbus pro causa habet intemperiem, quæ generat vaporem obstruentem.
units.tr: 51. I hardly know whether I dare say it, but why not? There are boys who ask whether it is a disease, taking the word in its proper sense, or a symptom. It is a disease, but it takes its name from a symptom. This disease has as its cause an intemperance, which generates the obstructing vapour.

units.la: 52. Paulò meliores sunt, qui interrogati de sententia Gal. Quale sit symptoma? dicere audent ex 2. Cauf. sym. 1. & 2. Esse actionem læsam, & quidem de genere istarum, quæ fiunt à morbo & natura seu facultate simul. Atqui diserte Gal. ille bis ait, esse à morbo solo. Nimirum, non demittunt se eò, ut libros inspiciant, —ἀνεύης ὀιήσεως ἐμπαθέος ἀσυγὶς, ut versus habet Timonis Phliasii, fi llographi.
units.tr: 52. Those are a little better who, when asked about Galen's opinion on what a symptom is, dare to say, from On the Causes of Symptoms (1 and 2), that it is an injured action, and indeed of the kind that arises from disease and nature or faculty together. Yet Galen says plainly, twice, that it arises from disease alone. Surely they do not stoop to read the books: —ἀνεύης ὀιήσεως ἐμπαθέος ἀσυγὶς, as the verse of Timon of Phlius has it, in the Silloi.

units.la: 53. Nec quidquam juvat illos, quod facultas cerebri expultrix irritata partes heic habet suas. Naturalis enim hæc est. At de animali musculorum quæstio est, in quâ quam infeliciter desudent Erastus, Platerus, Ioubertus, Massaria, alii, notum esse potest.
units.tr: 53. Nor does it help them that the expulsive faculty of the brain, when irritated, has its own parts here. For that is natural. But the question concerns the animal faculty of the muscles, in which it is well known how unhappily Erastus, Platerus, Joubert, Massaria and others have toiled.

units.la: §4. Sed qualis est læsio? Abolita, imminuta, depravata? Non potest simpliciter responderi. Respectu sensuum, in Epilepsiâ quidem gravissimâ, est abolita: in inferioribus autem gradibus, imminuta. Respectu motus est depravata.
units.tr: §4. But what sort of injury is it? Abolished, diminished, or depraved? It cannot be answered simply. With respect to the senses, in the most severe epilepsy it is abolished; in the lower degrees, diminished. With respect to motion, it is depraved.

units.la: §5. De subjecto quæsiti quidam, non superbè tantum responsant, sed & autoritates sputant Gal. Cæl. Aurel. Trall. Cerebrum necessario affici. Non ego nego: sed cupio distinctionem claram & apertam, quam sibi derogant ipsi cum nervositates Plinianas aggerunt. Scio, in hoc reatu Galenum quoque esse §. Aph. 1. sed hoc non excusat.
units.tr: §5. Some who are questioned about the subject not only answer arrogantly but also spit out authorities: Galen, Caelius Aurelianus, Trallian: the brain must necessarily be affected. I do not deny it, but I want a clear and open distinction, which they undermine themselves when they heap up the Plinian nervosities. I know that Galen too is in this fault (Aph. 1), but that does not excuse it.

units.la: §6. Cerebrum affici, certo certius est: volo audire, quâ sui parte? quatenus? quomodo? Nil dubito, dicent, Quatenus ventriculi semiobstruuntur. Res in æternum falsa! Ex ventriculis via in nervos nulla est: sed in palatum, unde etiam derivant ipsimet excrementa pituitosa, quæ in quibusdam visenda se præbent post paroxysmos. Ideo quæram, Habentne ventriculi simul tam sublime officium, ut sint
units.tr: §6. That the brain is affected is more certain than certain. I want to hear: in what part of it? In what respect? In what manner? "Nothing doubtful," they will say, "in so far as the ventricles are half-obstructed." An assertion false for ever! There is no route from the ventricles into the nerves, but into the palate, whence they themselves also drain the phlegmy excrements, which show themselves to be seen in some people after the paroxysms. So I will ask: do the ventricles at once have so lofty an office that they are

units.la: § ... sint ἐρρεσπίεια spiritus ? eorporis tam nobilis ? simul tam despicabile, ut vulgò creditur, ut sint cloaca excrementorum? Non credam, etiam ubi Fides ipsa juramento se obstrinxerit.
units.tr: § ... that they are the ... of the spirits [ἐρρεσπίεια]? Of a body so noble? And at once so despicable, as is commonly believed, that they are sewers for excrements? I would not believe it, even where Faith itself has bound itself by oath.

units.la: 57. Quidquid fit, Cerebrum solum non potest accusari, cum partem culpæ manifestè gerant Musculi. Palpitat quidem Gal. Aph. l.c. cum nominatim stiftit nervos, ligamenta, musculos, tendines: sed non puto pertendere illum velle, omnes has partes ex cerebro oriri, multò minus omnes ad motum hunc vitiatum concurrere.
units.tr: 57. Whatever the case, the brain alone cannot be accused, since the muscles clearly bear part of the blame. Galen certainly wavers in the aphorism cited above, when he names by name the nerves, ligaments, muscles and tendons; but I do not think he means to maintain that all these parts arise from the brain, much less that all of them concur in this depraved motion.

units.la: 58. Quid si petamus explicationem ex 3.Loc. aff. 10. ubi nervos solos habet? Vix possumus, nisi forte cum Hipp. & Arift. qui non raro musculos vocant nervos, loquitur. Acceptemus igitur ὃ ῥαῖον, & quæramus, Quo modo nervos credat huc facere? Procul dubio, trahenda musculos, quomodo habenis equus regitur. At hoc multimodis falsum est, & loquitur ita Gal. non ex propria, sed ex aliena sententia.
units.tr: 58. What if we seek an explanation from Loc. aff. 10, where he mentions only the nerves? We can hardly, unless perhaps he speaks as Hippocrates and Aristotle do, who often call muscles nerves. Let us accept then the [τὸ ῥᾷον] (the easier), and ask: in what way does he think the nerves act here? Undoubtedly by drawing the muscles, as a horse is governed by the reins. But this is false in many ways, and Galen speaks thus not from his own opinion but from another's.

units.la: 59. Quidquid fit: dic mihi clarè & distinctè, Quid cerebrum heic facit? quid nervi? Cerebrum, dico ego, accusare, est cæca assertio. Non & Intemperies, quæ fomitem præbet vapori si si infelici, potest
units.tr: 59. Whatever the case, tell me clearly and distinctly: what does the brain do here? What do the nerves do? To accuse the brain is a blind assertion. Nor can an intemperance, which provides fuel for the vapour of that wicked kind, be in the brain: and that obstruction which produces the paroxysms. So if there is talk of the paroxysms, do not give me the whole brain, but give me that part which contains the proximate cause, the origin of the nerves, whence the motion.

units.la: in cerebro esse : & Obstructio illa , quae paroxysmos gignit. Si ergò de paroxysmis fit sermo,noli mihi dare totum cerebrum : sed da mihi partem illam , quae continet causam proximam , principium nervorum, unde motus.
units.tr: in the brain; and that obstruction which produces the paroxysms. If, then, we are talking about paroxysms, do not give me the whole brain, but give me that part which contains the proximate cause, the principium nervorum, from which the motion comes.

units.la: 60. Nervos apprehendere velle , non minus cæcum est, Duobus enim modis concurrere possunt,aut trahendo musculos , quod falsum est : aut iter præbendo vapori, quod verum est. Proinde dico, Cum sermo est de motu in paroxysmo, locus affectus est Cerebrum, quatenus in se habet principium nervorum : nervus, quatenus (ut dixi) iter præbet vapori ad musculos.
units.tr: 60. To wish to grasp the nerves is no less blind. For they can act on the muscles in only two ways: either by pulling them, which is false, or by providing a passage for the vapour, which is true. Therefore I say: when we speak of the motion in a paroxysm, the place affected is the brain, in so far as it holds the principle of the nerves; the nerve, in so far as (as I have said) it provides a passage for the vapour to the muscles.

units.la: 61. Sed nondum enatavimus. Quid faciendo cerebrum facit motus hos in musculis? Credere velle, fieri cerebro contrahente se , & quasi cotrugante ad expellendum id, quod noxium est : extremæ dementiæ est, præsertim , si hoc addatur. Vnà contrahi omnia συμπᾶν- χῶ & , musculos nervosque omnes.
units.tr: 61. But we have not yet got out of the water. What does the brain do, by acting, to produce these motions in the muscles? To believe that the brain contracts itself, and as it were wrinkles up, in order to expel what is harmful, is the height of madness, especially if this is added: that all things are drawn together sympathetically [συμπάσχω], all the muscles and all the nerves.

units.la: 62. Atqui Gal. hoc scripsit 1. Caus. sym.ult.verbis? Videamus. De somno & vigiliis loquens , hæc habet, ἐμφω ρῆ ... ταῦτα ... ἐν τῷ ἐγκεφαλῷ ... ἀπὸ νεύρων ... μεταβ. Horum verborum sensum esse hunc, non negabis, Quemadmodum propter cerebri affectum qualemcunque, & vi- gilamus, & in lecto subinde nos volutamus : ita propter cerebrum affectum convulsiones incurrimus totius corporis. Ex his generalibus evinces tu mihi modum, quo fiunt motus Epileptici? maxime, quia in vestigio ait, Difficile dictu esse, quae fit causa morbi, a quo convulsiones partium sunt? Vult probare, convulsiones esse ab assectu cerebro : hoc facile est. Sed a qua causa fit : hoc difficile est. Vbi heic vel fomnium modi, quem tu tibi fingis? An latet aliud quid? id vid.quod Arist.docet de somno,3.cum ait, Somnu eo modo fieri, quo Epilepsia? Ego certe pro confirmanda mea sententia, ita induco. Quemadmodum somnus fit, ascendentibus ad cerebrum vaporibus benignis, & relaxentibus (non ad cor, ut parum attenti volunt) ad sensoria, precipue musculos : ita Epilepsia fit, vaporibus malignis affendentibus ad principium nervorum, perque eosdem iterum descendentibus ad musculos, & sensoria reliqua.
units.tr: 62. But did Galen write this in the first book of On the Causes of Symptoms? Let us see. Speaking of sleep and waking, he has these words: [ἐμφωρῆ ... ταῦτα ... ἐν τῷ ἐγκεφαλῷ ... ἀπὸ νεύρων ... μεταβ.]. You will not deny that the sense of these words is this: just as, because of some condition of the brain, we both stay awake and from time to time turn over in bed, so, because of a condition of the brain, we fall into convulsions of the whole body. Will you prove to me from these general statements the manner in which epileptic motions occur? Especially since in the same passage he says that it is difficult to say what the cause is of the disease from which the convulsions of the parts arise? He wishes to prove that the convulsions come from an affection of the brain: that is easy. But from what cause it comes about: that is difficult. Where here is the kind of vapour-fancy that you invent for yourself? Or is something else hidden? Is it that which Aristotle teaches about sleep in the third book, when he says that sleep comes about in the same way as epilepsy? For my part, to confirm my opinion, I argue thus: just as sleep comes about when benign vapours rise to the brain and relax the senses, especially the muscles (not the heart, as less attentive people hold), so epilepsy comes about when malignant vapours rise to the principle of the nerves and, descending again through the same channels, reach the muscles and the remaining senses.

units.la: 63. Scio, corrugationem hanc ab Avicenna esse: verum tantum abest, ut autoritas ipsius vel transversum digitum me moveat loco, ut, quoties video celebrari, exclamem, Aquam ad manus! Tam
units.tr: 63. I know that this wrinkling is Avicenna's; but his authority is so far from moving me even a finger's breadth from my position that, whenever I see it celebrated, I cry out, "Water for the hands!" [i.e. I wash my hands of it]. For

units.la: I
units.tr: I

units.la: enim mihi sordet,ut Cerebro, Margaritaye dignioré putem,quâ tantoPhilofopho.
units.tr: it seems so worthless to me that, as in the case of the brain, I would think a pearl more fitting for so great a philosopher.

units.la: 64. Vt pauca dicam. Quo modo motum univocum preftare potest,quod non, nisi æquivocè, natum est movere ? Certè, cerebrum non nisi æquivocè, seu naturaliter movetur ad expellendum : quo ergò modo movet musculos univocè?
units.tr: 64. To say little. How can a thing which is not born to move except equivocally move the muscles univocally? Certainly the brain is moved to expel only equivocally, or naturally; how then does it move the muscles univocally?

units.la: 65. Sed fit, In motu univoco oportet proportio fit inter movens & motum. At quæ est proportio inter movens æquivocum,& motum univocum? Vt intelligas, Quæ trahunt è longinquo, mediante corpore alio, oportet & proportionē inter fe habeant,& corpus medium tale fit,quod sufficiat moli. Saxum centū librarum ego non movero : sed neque filo traxero, fi omninò alias sufficerem.
units.tr: 65. But suppose it is said: in univocal motion there must be a proportion between the mover and the moved. But what proportion is there between an equivocal mover and a univocal motion? To make this clear: those things which pull from a distance, through some other body in between, must also have a proportion between them, and the intervening body must be such that it is sufficient for the load. I would not move a stone of a hundred pounds, but nor would I pull it with a thread if I were not sufficient at all.

units.la: 66. Vno verbo,ut omnia rectè fe habeant, falsæ sunt duæ hypotheses; altera, in ventriculis fieri spiritus; altera nervos trahere adinftar habenarum. Sed & hoc falsum est,ut dixi, Nervos cum ventriculis esse continuos.
units.tr: 66. In a word, for everything to stand rightly, two hypotheses are false: one, that spirits are made in the ventricles; the other, that the nerves pull like reins. But this too is false, as I have said: that the nerves are continuous with the ventricles.

units.la: 67. Quid igitur ? Rem videmus : quæ causa rei ? Apud me res expeditissima est, quam non semel dixi,Quod in motu f.n. est spiritus, inflans musculum, ut vectis instar rigeat : id in motu p.n. est vapor, spiritum naturalem mentiens, Vtrobique nervus suum habet officium,esse tubi instar. Et huc animus humanus fe penetrare potest. Hoc ipsum non est novum, sed à veteribus perspicuè doctum, Si probabile tantum est, fatis est, siquidem Platoni credimus.
units.tr: 67. What then? We see the thing; what is the cause of the thing? For me the matter is most easily settled, as I have said more than once: in motion of the first kind it is the spirit, inflating the muscle so that it stiffens like a lever; in motion of the second kind it is the vapour, counterfeiting the natural spirit. In both cases the nerve has its own office, being like a tube. And the human mind can penetrate even this far. This itself is not new, but was clearly taught by the ancients; if it is only probable, that is enough, provided we believe Plato.

units.la: 68. Ergò de partibus affectis jam certi fumus? Vtinam!Ingerit enim fe Quercetanus, Tetrade.8. & Cor sufficit Cerebro,Quàin re cum Peripateticum fe praestet, videre oportet, fi quam gratiam in arte nostrà mereatur.Nisi penitiffimè sallor, longius nos abducit, quam par est: Scimus,quid in motu f.n. faciat cor: nos eò non pertingimus, sed in cerebro stamus, praeterquam in unico casu, qui est, Sicor fit pars mandans.
units.tr: 68. Are we now certain about the parts affected? Would that we were! For Quercetanus intrudes himself in the eighth treatise of the Tetrad, and "the heart suffices for the brain." How far he shows himself a Peripatetic, one must see, if he deserves any credit in our art. Unless I am very much mistaken, he leads us further than is right. We know what the heart does in the motion of the first kind; we do not reach that point, but stay in the brain, except in the one case, which is when the heart is the commanding part.

units.la: 69. Heic video τε ἡεπτὶς proceres intercessuros ex 3.Part.4. 4.Part.2. Cor non posse tolerare vitium ullum grave. Quibus ego recentiores oppono observationes,quae docuerunt.Tumores, abfcefsus, vermes, calculos , excrefcentias carneas, & alia talia diu pertulisse. Horum ita affectorum plerosque, vel epilepsiâ laborafle, vel palpitatione cordis, affectu vicino, ut constat ex iisdem observationibus: ita velim mitius agicum Quercetano, homine non malo, ut defcripferunt illum mihi amici.
units.tr: 69. Here I see the leaders going to intervene, from the third part, fourth book, and the fourth part, second book: the heart cannot tolerate any grave vice. Against them I set more recent observations, which have taught that people have long endured swellings, abscesses, worms, stones, fleshy outgrowths and other such things. Of those so affected, most have suffered either from epilepsy or from palpitation of the heart, as a nearby affection, as is clear from the same observations. So I would like them to deal more gently with Quercetanus, who, as friends have described him to me, is not a bad man.

units.la: 70. Vellem etiam persuadere sibi patiantur,non nugari illum planissimè,cum scribit, Facultates principes mansisse in quibusdam integras.Scripsit enim procul dubio, quod vidit. Si enim motus abesse potest : quidni vel interni, vel externi sensus aliquando possint illæsi esse? Quare, ut aliud nomen non habet epilepsia, quæ nihil depravationis ostendit in motu:cur aliud detur illi, in quâ vel hi, vel illi sensus vigeant,vel debiles tantum sint?
units.tr: 70. I would also like them to be persuaded not to think that he is talking utter nonsense when he writes that the principal faculties have remained intact in some people. For he undoubtedly wrote what he saw. If motion can be absent, why should not the internal or external senses sometimes remain unharmed? Therefore, since epilepsy has no other name, though it shows no depravation in motion, why should another name be given to it in which these or those senses are vigorous, or only weakened?

units.la: 71. Et hoc est, quod Avicenna ait, si epilepsiæ jungatur syncope : non obid definit esse epilepsia. Puto autem id fieri in solo illo casu, quem proposui, non quod facultas vitalis in consensum rapiatur:sed contrà potius.
units.tr: 71. And this is what Avicenna means when he says that if syncope is joined to epilepsy, it does not therefore cease to be epilepsy. I think, however, that this happens only in that one case I have proposed, not because the vital faculty is drawn into sympathy, but rather the reverse.

units.la: 72. Quamobrem, si verum est, Mentis,sensuumque læsionem ex eventu conjuncta esse in epilepsia : non video, quomodo non possitalterum absq; altero esse?
units.tr: 72. Wherefore, if it is true that injury to the mind and the senses is conjoined with epilepsy by its outcome, I do not see how the one could not be without the other.

units.la: 73. Quo dato,quis erit proprius epilepsiæ character?non opus est ullo :sedestepilepsia,sive adsit alterutrũ sive utrumq;.
units.tr: 73. Granting this, what will be the proper character of epilepsy? None is needed; it is epilepsy, whether either or both be present.

units.la: 74. Multo minus opus est alio nomine.
units.tr: 74. Much less is another name needed.

units.la: 75. Multò minimè fit convulsio particularis,quæ appellatio jam occupata est.
units.tr: 75. Still less is a particular convulsion, a name which is already taken.

units.la: 76. Neque ulla necessitas est, neque ulla perseitas,conjungi utrumque. Experientia enim aliud suadet.Imò,yerò,dicit.
units.tr: 76. There is no necessity, nor any inherent reason, for the two to be joined. For experience suggests otherwise. Indeed, it rather says the contrary.

units.la: Nisi motus depravetur,sed pereat,eadem erit cum apoplexiâ : Non ex solà motus absentia judicatur apoplexia:alioquin & paralysis & catalepsis effent apoplexiæ.
units.tr: Unless the motion is depraved but perishes, it will be the same as apoplexy: apoplexy is not judged from the absence of motion alone; otherwise paralysis and catalepsy would be apoplexies.

units.la: 77. Sed neque perditio dici ullâ ratione potest absentia motus depravati in epilepsiâ. Malum enim lenius fit, cum absunt symptomata quædam.
units.tr: 77. But neither can the absence of depraved motion in epilepsy be called destruction by any reasoning. For the malady becomes milder when certain symptoms are absent.

units.la: 78. Quare iterum dico, Epilepsia suum habet characterem, fi omninò ita meloqui vis, five detentio mentis sola adsit: five sensuum externorum sola:five motus depravatus.
units.tr: 78. Wherefore I say again: epilepsy has its own character, if you wish to speak in this way at all, whether there is only a detention of the mind, or only of the external senses, or only a depraved motion.

units.la: 79. Quæstio illa inconsultò intruditur, An in apoplexiâ sensus interni ad filentium adigantur? Dico breviter, Non potest simpliciter responderi, sed opus est distinctione,ut in Epilepsiâ. Alias,quæ erit distinctio quatuor apoplexiarum, 2. Aph.42 Scio, Galenum alligare ad respirationem solam ? sed scio etiam, prudentiores quosdam ad alia quoque fymptomata respicere.
units.tr: 79. That question is thrown in without consideration: whether in apoplexy the internal senses are reduced to silence? I say briefly that it cannot be answered simply, but a distinction is needed, as in epilepsy. Otherwise, what will be the distinction of the four apoplexies, Aphorisms 2.42? I know that Galen binds them to respiration alone; but I know also that some more prudent writers look to other symptoms as well.

units.la: 80. Quid verò Noster?Cum applicuifset fe putidæ Obstructioni & Semiobftructioni ventriculorum,mox lapsare incipit cum Gal. cujus ille consilium nunquam intellexit. Id fuit fortè, ut innui suprà, Cum seculo illo non minus graves effent concertationes, tam in Epilepsiâ, quam
units.tr: 80. What, however, does our author do? After he had attached himself to the foul obstruction and semi-obstruction of the ventricles, he soon begins to slip along with Galen, whose counsel he never understood. This was perhaps, as I hinted above, because in that age the disputes were no less grave, both in epilepsy and in

units.la: ip
units.tr: ip

units.la: in Apoplexiâ, Ventriculisne cerebri, an corpori debeantur? quam hodiè conjunxit 4. Loc. aff. 2. ut ab utriusque partis telis immunis esset. In utroque, inquit, & corpus est affectum & ventriculi, sed hac differentiâ. In apoplexiâ corpus potius est affectum, minus ventriculi: in epilepsiâ contrà. Hoc verò per rerum naturam fieri non potest, & qui id clamitant, psittaci sunt.
units.tr: in apoplexy, are the ventricles of the brain or the body owed? He has now joined this question in the fourth book of De locis affectis, chapter 2, so as to stay clear of the missiles from either side. In both, he says, the body and the ventricles are affected, but with this difference: in apoplexy the body is affected more, the ventricles less; in epilepsy it is the other way round. But this cannot happen in the nature of things, and those who keep shouting it are parrots.

units.la: 81. Cum enim certum sit, alii usui corpus servire, alii ventriculos; cui ex his debetur spirituum elaboratio, ei debebitur uterque morbus. At corpori deberi, quemadmodum ventriculis excrementorum collectio, vacuatioque, tam manifestis probatum est argumentis à bonis, sapientibusque, ut non nisi arrogantis fit, aut stulti, restitare velle ulterius.
units.tr: 81. For since it is certain that some parts serve one function and some serve the ventricles, the disease belongs to whichever of these is responsible for producing the spirits. But that the body is responsible, just as the collection and evacuation of excrements is the work of the ventricles, has been proved by such clear arguments from good and wise men that only an arrogant or foolish person would wish to resist any further.

units.la: 82. Verum ergo morbus est corporis: veruntamen hac differentiâ. Apoplexia fit ab humore, uno verbo, à sanguine, in plethoricis, quod probabitur: Epilepsia fit à vapore, quem Pelops vocabat ἀνευμαλαχὴν βοῖαν, ὡσπερ ἀνθρωπος, 3. Loc. affect. 7.
units.tr: 82. The disease, then, is truly of the body; yet with this difference. Apoplexy arises from humour, in a word from blood, in plethoric people, as will be shown. Epilepsy arises from vapour, which Pelops called [ἀνευμαλαχὴν βοῖαν], as a man would say [ὡσπερ ἀνθρωπος], De loc. affect. 3, chapter 7.

units.la: 83. Heic quam pulcrè stat Ille? Primum enim ait, In corpore residerefacultatem: deinde, In superioribus ventriculis solis spiritus generari. Potestne alibi
units.tr: 83. Here, how neatly does he stand? For first he says the faculty resides in the body; then he says that spirits are generated only in the upper ventricles. Can the faculty be anywhere else? Can the spirit, the bearer of the faculty, be anywhere else? And what does his "solis" mean?

units.la: Facultas esse? alibi Spiritus, facultatis bajulus? Et quid sibi vult © Solis? Cum enim in se coeant duo illi, coitusque constituat tertium, qui ipse constitui Infundibulum, quis mihi spondeat, spiritus elaboratos non dilapsuros per os fphenoides in palatum? tanto facilius, quo majora foramina tribuit illi Gal. quanta fc. in ethmoide? Ach nein / fie hupffen hinüber !
units.tr: For when those two meet, and their meeting makes a third, which itself becomes the funnel, who will guarantee me that the spirits, once elaborated, will not slip through the sphenoid bone into the palate? All the more easily, since Galen assigns it larger foramina, as large as those in the ethmoid? Oh no! They hop across!

units.la: 84. Sed transeat, Cum dixiflet, Epilepticos nullo sensu quidquam percipere: non veretur postea affirmare, tactus sensum cerebro superesse, ut rationem reddere possit τ̃ς χλόης. Atqui, dico ego,cerebrum ipsum est infenfile, de Chirurgorum observatione.
units.tr: 84. But let that pass. Having said that epileptics perceive nothing by any sense, he afterwards does not hesitate to affirm that the sense of touch remains in the brain, so that he can give an account of the pallor [χλόης]. Yet, I say, the brain itself is insensible, from the surgeons' observation.

units.la: 85. Dicat,Quam ergo tu causam dabis τ̃ς χλόης. Aliud est causam dare motus cerebri expellentis, qui æquivocus est:aliud musculorum,qui univocus. Hic opus habet sensu : ille non. Si displicet hoc, Vtrobique motus fit à vi externa, & sensu opus non est. Interim loqui nobis ita licet,fierihos motus ab naturá expelente, quod noxium est.
units.tr: 85. Let him tell me: what cause will you give for the pallor [χλόης]? It is one thing to give the cause of a motion of the brain that expels, which is equivocal; it is another to give the cause of the motion of the muscles, which is univocal. The latter needs sense, the former does not. If this displeases you, in both cases the motion comes from an external force, and sense is not needed. Meanwhile we may speak thus: these motions arise from nature expelling what is harmful.

units.la: 86. Atqui dolores habent intenfiffimos? Nescio, an de omnibus fit verum. Acu enim pun&ti, non sentiunt, Anin quibusdam hoc est, in quibusdam illud? Vt enim supra dixi, Superefle quandoque tactum, absurdi nihil est. An habent sensum,sed non percipiunt:quia sensus communis laborat? An post paroxysmum demum percipiunt violentiam vaporis perrum pentis ?
units.tr: 86. But do they have the most intense pains? I do not know whether this is true of all of them. For when pricked with a needle they feel nothing. Is it so in some and otherwise in others? For, as I said above, that touch sometimes remains is no absurdity. Or do they have sensation but fail to perceive it, because the common sense is impaired? Or do they perceive the violence of the vapour bursting through only after the paroxysm?

units.la: 87. Hinc lux accedit illis, quæ ex Avicenná, Heurnio & Capivaccio afferuntur, Reverà confunditur motus naturalis cerebri cum motu animali musculorum. Sed nec potest naturalis ciere animalem, nisi mediante vapore, qui per nervos illabitur, Quæ de vocefuperftite dicuntur, pendent à respirationis parte illâ, quam Naturæ deferimus. Hinc enim vis illa, Necessitas illa, ut cum Gal. loquar, quam Calor ebulliens affert. Hoc ipsum innuit potius,quam dicit.
units.tr: 87. Hence light comes to us from what is brought forward from Avicenna, Heurnius and Capivaccio: the natural motion of the brain is really confused with the animal motion of the muscles. But the natural motion cannot stir the animal motion except by means of vapour, which slips in through the nerves. What is said about the voice surviving depends on that part of respiration which we leave to Nature. For hence comes that force, necessitas, as I shall put it with Galen, which boiling heat brings. He hints at this very thing rather than says it.

units.la: 88. De Erafto & Fontano (addo ego Platerum & Ioub.) rectè ait, Nimis cum imperio agere. Rectè etiam colligit duo absurda. Phantasiâ enim sublatâ necessarió sequetur delirium. Sed neque ratio dari poterit, cur, abolito sensu, maneat motus. Subsunt verò multa alia absurda, de quibus heic cogitari non potest.
units.tr: 88. Concerning Erastus and Fontanus (I add Platerus and Joubert), he rightly says, they act too much with authority. He also rightly infers two absurdities. For if imagination is removed, delirium must necessarily follow. Yet no reason can be given why, sense being abolished, motion remains. Many other absurdities lie beneath, which cannot be considered here.

units.la: 89. Rectissimè Galeno negat, Epilepfiam per consensum mitiorem esse illâ, quæ per essentiam. Non minus rectè Malfariæ, specie differre illam ab hac. Similitudo enim symptomatum identitatem nobis extorquet, 90. Con-
units.tr: 89. He rightly denies to Galen that epilepsy through sympathy is milder than that through essence. No less rightly Malfaria holds that it differs from it in species. For the similarity of the symptoms forces identity upon us. 90. Con-

units.la: 90. Contrà, immensum fallitur, I.Cum morbum, à quo symptoma pendet, à Repletione & Inanitione petit. Inauditum enim est, hæc duo ππ morbos esse. I I. Cum o bftructionem suam probare vult ex spumà copiosà, quæ post paroxysmum prodit. Si enim vera causa effet, semper fieret, non Interdum. I I I. Cum qualitatem dolorificam & venenatam ostentat nobis, nec fe explicat, qualis & quanta fit illa. Revera, nihil docet, qui ita docet.
units.tr: 90. On the contrary, he is hugely mistaken: I. when he seeks the disease on which the symptom depends in repletion and inanition. For it is unheard of that these two are diseases. II. When he wants to prove his obstruction from the copious froth that appears after the paroxysm. For if it were the true cause, it would always happen, not only sometimes. III. When he shows us a poisonous and painful quality, without explaining what that quality is or how great. Indeed, he who teaches thus teaches nothing.

units.la: I V. Cum materiam vaporofam & humorosam, vaporem & humorem indistincte projicit. Quasi vapor & humor possit idem. V. Cum vaporem credit facere Epilepsiam benignam.
units.tr: IV. When he throws out vaporous and humoral matter, vapour and humour indistinguishably. As if vapour and humour could be the same. V. When he believes that vapour makes epilepsy benign.

units.la: 9 1. Galenum non fatis excusat, cur ille solius Obstructionis meminerit? Quasi vaporis nostri non meminerit! Multo minus, cur humorem crassum admiserit? Quasi epilepsia per consensum aliter fiat, quam illa, quæ per essentiam! Quasi crafsus humor ullo modo facere possit epilepfiam! Quasi in ventriculis ulla culpa fit! Et quid hoc verbi est, Vapor obstructionis minus aptus est in corpore, inquam, cerebri.
units.tr: 91. Does he not sufficiently excuse Galen, why he mentions only obstruction? As if he did not remember our vapour! Much less why he admitted thick humour? As if epilepsy through sympathy happens differently from that through essence! As if thick humour could in any way cause epilepsy! As if there were any fault in the ventricles! And what is this phrase: the vapour of obstruction is less apt in the body, I say, of the brain?

units.la: 92. Compressio non est causa proxima, sed remotiffima. Facit illa dolorem: dolor irritat sanguinem ad fluxum: fluxus facit inflammationem : inflammatio suppurata emittit de fe vaporem putri‑ dum : qui denique Epilepsiam causatur. Hoc declaro pulcerrimâ historiâ ex ϛ. Epid.49. apud Vallefium. Puella 20. annorum, latâ manu percussa fuerat finci‑ put, sed per jocum. Hæc cum‑procul dubio effet ex numero illorum, quibus Fontanella illa tardius solidatur, inter quos profiteor meum nomen, ut & filiæ meæ SABIN Æ, statim laboravit vertigine tenebricosâ cum difficili respiratione. Huncego affectum de Epilepsiâ leviori interpretor, Vall. de Catocho. Postquam domum venit, inflammatio successit, non fine febre, quæ inflammatio 7. die, ab‑ fceffu facto, per aurem dextram pus emittit. Verum, superveniente fluxione novâ, inflammatio & febris rediit, accessere convulsiones (ita enim Vall. recte explicat τῆς πρόσω, quemadmodum apud Arift. quoque explicandum esse dixi supra.) novâ die est mortua.
units.tr: 92. Compression is not the proximate cause but the most remote. It produces pain; pain irritates the blood to flux; flux produces inflammation; the inflammation, suppurating, sends out a putrid vapour from itself, which finally causes epilepsy. I make this clear by a most beautiful history from Epid. 5, case 49, in Vallesius. A girl of twenty years was struck on the head with a broad hand, but in jest.
