Since she was without doubt of the number of those in whom the fontanelle closes more slowly, among whom I confess my own name, as also that of my daughter Sabina, she at once suffered dizziness with dark vision and difficult breathing. I interpret this affection as a milder epilepsy, Vallesius on Catochus. After she came home, inflammation followed, not without fever; this inflammation, on the seventh day, the abscess having formed, discharged pus through the right ear. But, a new flux supervening, the inflammation and fever returned, and convulsions came on (for so Vallesius rightly explains [τῆς πρόσω], as I said above it should also be explained in Aristotle). On the new day she died.

units.la: 93. Hæc historia maximi est momenti, & admonet me non dissimilis, quam commemorabo. Quo tempore peftilen‑ tialem heic agebam, anno 1607. in Bac‑ chanalibus, ictus fuerat adolescens quidam, 1 O H. FISCHER, Oetingensis, circa mediam noctem clavâ ligneâ (no‑ftri
units.tr: 93. This history is of the greatest importance, and a not dissimilar one that I shall relate reminds me of it. At the time when I was dealing with the plague here, in the year 1607, in the Bacchanals, a certain young man, Joh. Fischer of Oettingen, was struck about midnight with a wooden club (our people call it a Bohemian ear-spoon) above the right temple. After six hours he was found dead in bed.

units.la: ftri vocant ein Böheimscher Ohrlöffel/ supra tempora dextra, qui post sex horas inventus fuit mortuus in lecto. Triste spectaculum! Iussi sumus ab Senatu Academico, CL. DD. SONERVS, collega posteà meus, & ego, inspicere caver, & caput aperire. Ingredientibus statim apparuit spuma circa os copiosa, tempora dicta livida, cum manifestà loci depressione. Heic, inquam ego, est sedes mali: oportet aperire caput! Cum igitur chirurgi, factà cruciformi incisione, cutim detraxissent, in calvaria apparuere duæ rimæ, quarum altera sesquipalmum lata erat, altera paulò brevior. Ablatà parte, altera quidem illa, & longior penetrabat tabulam utramque: hæc autem eximam tantum. Inter cranium & duram matrem tantũ eratsanguinis extravasati quantũ utraq; manu caua exhaurire nom posset chirurgus, cerebrum subtus liviodum. Quod verò omnem superat admiratio-nem, eo ipso loco, ex adverso fissurarum, dura mater tota erat ossea, Thaleri amplitudine, quasi Natura prævidisset ictum. Hoc os secum habuit D. SONERVS, & stupentibus multis ostendit.
units.tr: A sad spectacle! We were ordered by the Academic Senate, the distinguished Dr. Sonerus, later my colleague, and I, to inspect the body and open the head. As we entered, copious froth at once appeared about the mouth; the temples were livid, with a clear depression of the place. Here, I said, is the seat of the evil: the head must be opened! When therefore the surgeons, having made a cruciform incision, had stripped away the skin, two cracks appeared in the skull, one a span and a half wide, the other a little shorter. The part being removed, the longer one penetrated both tables; the other only the outer. Between the cranium and the dura mater there was so much extravasated blood that the surgeon could not drain it with both cupped hands, and the brain beneath was livid. What surpasses all admiration is that in the very place opposite the fissures the dura mater was entirely bony, the size of a thaler, as if Nature had foreseen the blow. Sonerus kept this bone with him and showed it to the amazed onlookers.

units.la: 94. Superiori anno 1638. cum rusticus, in vicino pago Masch/ aggrederetur
units.tr: 94. In the year 1638, when a countryman in the neighbouring village of Masch attacked

units.la: alterum ligone; is verò pertica illum protruderet: accepto levi vulnusculo in facie sinistrâ, eâ parte, quâ Μῆλον dictum est, supinus cecidit. Accersitus hinc, sexto demum die, chirurgus, tractavit ut potuit: verum, supervenientibus cum aliis, tum Epilepticis symptomatis, mortuus est. 11. die. Rogatus à magistratu opidano, adstiti chirurgis caput aperientibus. In malo quidem fissura nulla: in cerebri autem parte imâ, quà processus mammillares ad nares sunt, inflammatio. Quod verò mirandum, In occipite, κατ' ἀπάγμα, inflammatio altera. Heic à putrefcente utrinque sanguine exiisse vapores ad nervorum principium, & Epilepsiam civisse, quis non videt? 95. Ἀλάλησιν φλεγμονώδη Gal.2. Aph. 42. dum huc facessere jubet Noster, suo more facit. Non enim Gal. de epilepsiâ agit, sed de apoplexiâ. Interim de epilepsia quoque dici posse, vel duæ historiæ allatæ evicerint. Cæterum habet illa διάϑεσις densas difficultates. Ego in Patholog. c.108. penè dubius fui, quò me verterem, quod utrinque probabilia dicantur. Nunc constitutum est mihi ire ad eos velle, qui de ipsâ phlegomone accipiunt. Inflammatio incipiens quidem facit Apoplexiam, cum fusus à calore sanguis Torcu-
units.tr: another with a mattock, the latter pushed him off with a pole. Having received a slight wound on the left side of the face, in that part called the apple [Μῆλον], he fell backwards. Summoned only on the sixth day, a surgeon treated him as best he could; but, with epileptic symptoms supervening as well as others, he died on the eleventh day. Asked by the town magistracy, I stood by the surgeons opening the head. In the wound there was indeed no fissure; but in the lowest part of the brain, where the mammillary processes lie by the nostrils, there was inflammation. What is astonishing: in the occiput, by contrecoup, there was another inflammation. Who does not see that vapours from the putrefying blood on both sides went out to the origin of the nerves and provoked epilepsy? 95. Galen, Aph. 2, 42, speaks of phlegmonous delirium [Ἀλάλησιν φλεγμονώδη]; while our author brings this in here, he acts in his usual way. For Galen does not treat of epilepsy but of apoplexy. Meanwhile, the two histories brought forward have shown that it can be said of epilepsy too. Moreover, that disposition [διάθεσις] presents dense difficulties. In my Pathology, chapter 108, I was almost in doubt which way to turn, since probable things are said on both sides. Now I have decided to go to those who take it from the phlegmon itself. Inflammation beginning does indeed produce apoplexy, when blood poured out by the heat quickly occupies the torcu-

units.la: Tercular occupat confertim : paulò progressa autem Epilepsiam,cum exhalantes à putredine vapores stipant nervorum principium. Heic quis non videt,angustiâ ventriculorum opus non esse?
units.tr: The attack takes hold at once; but if it advances a little, it becomes epilepsy, when vapours rising from putrefaction crowd the source of the nerves. Here who does not see that there is no need for narrowing of the ventricles?

units.la: 96. Tamen cum defendere vellet 1l. Ie,occinit nobis cantilenam,ad quam aures nostræ jam pridem occalluére, Nos oportet, inquit, vel obstructio, vel compressio tanta fit ut integram faciat angustiam: fieret enim apoplexia. Hui,tantumne? Profecto, absque Fernelii fulcro fi effet, jam dudum heic pronus cecidisset interram. Quod cum metueret forte,tantum non Geometricam instituit dimensionem facultatis robustæ & imbecillæ, materiæ paucioris & copiosioris, sensus acuti & obtusi, fenum & juvenum. Quam cum intueor, non possum non suaviter ridere, licet valde indignatùrus fit. Sapiunt enim quandam rerum inanem, propriam illi. Ad eandem refero patientis dispositionem, quæ actionem variet, pronaturæ resistentis vi, &c, Dici quidem possunt hæc pro cathedrá, in facie juvenum rudiorum : in rei veritate vanitates sunt.
units.tr: 96. Yet when he wanted to defend his position, he sang us a tune to which our ears have long since grown hard: "We must suppose," he says, "either an obstruction or a compression so great that it makes a complete narrowing; otherwise it would become apoplexy." Oh, is that all? Certainly, if it were not for the prop of Fernelius, he would long ago have fallen flat on the ground here. Perhaps fearing this, he set up almost a geometrical measurement of strong and weak faculty, of scanty and abundant matter, of keen and dull sense, of old men and young. When I look at this I cannot help laughing softly, though he will be very indignant. For these have a certain empty show of things peculiar to him. To the same he refers the disposition of the patient, which varies the action, the force of nature resisting, and so on. These things may indeed be said from the chair, before a crowd of raw young men; in the truth of the matter they are vanities.

units.la: 97. Porrò,cum Gal.pugnantia videatur scribere,cum 2.Cauf.fym.2.& Trem. & Palp.5. materiam flatulentam caufetur ; at.3. Loc. aff. 5. humorem crassum, frigidamque:conciliationem quaerit bellatulam. Galenus, inquit, obstructionis tantum, non materiae obstruentis indicium capit a subita invasione. Subtilitas altero Scaligero digna! Potestne obstructio separari a materia obstruente? Certe Gal. non potuit, cum πνεῦμα χυμὸν ἐμφέρη Ἰσοθη cau- satur, ἡ φλεγμαλώδη χυμὸν ἐν ἡσιλίαις συν- αλογισθέντα.
units.tr: 97. Furthermore, since Galen seems to write contradictory things, in the second book On the Causes of Symptoms and in On Tremor and Palpitation, chapter 5, he blames a flatulent matter, but in On the Affected Parts, book 3, chapter 5, a thick and cold humour; he seeks a contentious reconciliation. "Galen," he says, "took from the sudden attack an indication only of obstruction, not of the obstructing matter." A subtlety worthy of the other Scaliger! Can obstruction be separated from the obstructing matter? Certainly Galen could not, when he says that the pneuma carries the humour [πνεῦμα χυμὸν ἐμφέρη] ... and that the inflammatory humour is reckoned together with it in the ... [ἡ φλεγμαλώδη χυμὸν ἐν ἡσιλίαις συναλογισθέντα].

units.la: 98. Sed abeat : Quid illud ad rem,
units.tr: 98. But let that go. What has this to do with the matter,

units.la: quod ait, Cum alie quoque causa repente incutiant? Non quaerimus, ex quot, quibusve causis repentinae morborum invafiones accidant: hoc quaeritur, an in Epilepsia crassus humor id possit? Nego ego, propter duas causas, Ventriculi non sunt officinae spirituum: ex motu ventriculorum non potest reddi ratio motus muculorum. Quid illud vero est, Nisi de parti- um sequiorum affectu, et solutione morbi per concoctionem accipiatur? Si non visintelligi, debes negligi. Video equidem, te sequioribus opponere cerebrum, partem principem, in quo sint bi duo morbi:at hoc est probare idem per idem. Quid vero? Cum apoplexia definit in paralysin, sitne per concoctionem? Minime, inquis, Hem tibi materiam concoctionis expertem! At tu Concoctionem praemiseras.
units.tr: You say, "Since other causes also suddenly strike." We are not asking how many or what causes bring on sudden attacks of disease. The question is whether thick humour can do this in epilepsy. I deny it, for two reasons. First, the ventricles are not the workshops of the spirits. Second, the movement of the ventricles cannot account for the movement of the muscles. And what is this that you add, "Unless it is understood of an affection of the inferior parts and of the resolution of the disease through concoction"? If you cannot make it clear, it should be disregarded. I see that you set the brain, the chief part, against the inferior parts, as the seat of these two diseases. But this is to prove the same thing by the same thing. What then? When apoplexy ends in paralysis, does it do so through concoction? "Not at all," you say. Then give yourself matter free of concoction! Yet you had put forward "concoction" yourself.

units.la: Sed cupio audire id, quod nuper dixi, Quae via ex ventriculis est in nervos? Hanc fi ostenderis, Dædalus mihi alter eris. Et quid sibi vult ⊙ Aliquando? Est labantis,& errorem confitentis.
units.tr: But I want to hear what I said recently: what path leads from the ventricles into the nerves? If you show me this, you will be another Daedalus to me. And what does "Aliquando" mean here? It is the saying of one who wavers and admits his error.

units.la: · ἀλλʼ τὶς σαφῶς ἔτως τοῦς ἀγ̓ ἂν ἀρχαῖ.
units.tr: But who has said it clearly and thus, as the ancients did? [ἀλλʼ τὶς σαφῶς ἔτως τοῦς ἀγ̓ ἂν ἀρχαῖ]

units.la: 99. An Hermetici quoque nobiscum sunt,fi demas verborum monstra? Vnius ex illis hæc sunt verba. Hermeticis epifefia fit ex vapore Mercuriali vitriolato, qui ex humore tartareo, aut mucilagine erugenosá exspirat, ⊙ vitrioli tinctuias ⊙ imprefiones circumfert, quas exhalando tempora intervallis malignas, acres,acidas, fbiritibus vitalibus animalibus facile commiscet.
units.tr: 99. Would the Hermetics also be with us, if you removed the monstrous words? These are the words of one of them: "With the Hermetics epilepsy arises from a vitriolated Mercurial vapour, which is exhaled from tartareous humour or verdigris-like mucilage, and carries about the tinctures and impressions of vitriol, which, exhaling at malignant, sharp, acid intervals, easily mix themselves with the vital and animal spirits."

units.la: 100. An eum deferuissent homines nostri flatus veterum, ex quibus ad omnia symptomata responderi potest, ortæ sunt hæ fluctuationes? Quidam enim securi rerum omnium,diffimulárunt motum musculorum. Quibusdam fatis fuit dixisse, sequi motum cerebri. Eraftus, fiduciam in Philosophiâ suâ habens,conatus est ad motum naturaliter fe habentem reducere.Cui cum multa objicerentur obstacula, imprimis, cum fimilitudi- nem motus epileptici cum naturali probare non posset : tubicinem ei subjecit Plaeterus, Hoc cum paulò minus quam K TragiTragicum fit, commendo iis, qui falsa malunt defendere quam vera. Ii vero sciant illud, Maleditus, qui opus DOMINI facit fraudulenter. Θεὸς γὰρ ὁ μυκτη- ρίζεται.
units.tr: 100. Would these fluctuations have arisen if our men had not despised the old doctrines of breathings, from which an answer can be given to all the symptoms? For some, careless of all things, have passed over the motion of the muscles. For some it was enough to say that the motion of the brain follows. Erastus, trusting in his own philosophy, tried to bring back a motion that is naturally conducted. When many obstacles were put against him, chiefly that he could not prove the likeness of epileptic motion to natural motion, Plaeterus set a trumpeter beside him. Since this is a little less than tragic, I commend it to those who prefer to defend falsehoods rather than truths. Let them know that cursed is he who does the work of the LORD deceitfully [Maledictus, qui opus DOMINI facit fraudulenter], and that "God is not mocked" [Θεὸς γὰρ ὁ μυκτηρίζεται].

units.la: De Apoplexia idem tentatum,
units.tr: The same has been attempted concerning apoplexy,

units.la: CAPVT XIV. ΘΕΣΕΙΣ.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIV. Theseis [Θέσεις].

units.la: § 1. Via totiēs jam facta est mentio hujus mali, & est tantum non ἀδιαφορίσιον Epilepsiæ, ut verbo utar Hippocratico; age heic quoque aliquid tale meditemur.
units.tr: § 1. This evil has already been mentioned so often, and it is practically an indistinguishable form of epilepsy [ἀδιαφορίσιον], to use the Hippocratic word. Come, let us consider something of this kind here too.

units.la: § 2. τὸ ἀπὸ τῆς ἀλγήσεως erat olim * proprium victimariorum, cum animalia sacrificanda securi in fronte tam validè percuterent, ut subitò conciderent. Haec animalia cum dicerentur ἀπόπληκτοι (ὁ ἀπὸ ... ) enim intendit) dicti quoque inde fuere hominum illi ἀπόπληκτοι, ἢ ἀπόπληξις, qui subitò conciderent ἐκ ταῦ αὐτοῦ ... vn̄G. Hinc affectus ipse ἀπόπληξία ἢ ἀπο- πληξις.
units.tr: § 2. The term "from the blow" [τὸ ἀπὸ τῆς ἀλγήσεως] was once the peculiar term of the sacrificers, when they struck the animals to be sacrificed on the forehead with an axe so hard that they suddenly fell. Animals so struck were called apoplectic [ἀπόπληκτοι], and from this, men who suddenly collapsed were also called apoplectic [ἀπόπληκτοι], or apoplexy [ἀπόπληξις]. Hence the affection itself is apoplexy [ἀποπληξία].

units.la: § 3. Non dissimile quid cum observarent fieri, & in animalibus & in plantis, βλαβὲς ἢ ἀσεβὲς ( ἀσεβὴς autem Sirius est, seu Canicula ) vocarunt illa, transf-
units.tr: § 3. When they observed something similar happening in animals and in plants, they called such things harmful or impious [βλαβὲς ἢ ἀσεβὲς]. (The impious one is the Dog Star, that is, Sirius or the Little Dog.)

units.la: *Nomen. transtuleruntque id quoq; ad hunc mortui bum, qui appellatus est σεσηεολισμός, quemadmodum ita affecti, Siderati & Attoniti.
units.tr: *Name. They transferred this term also to the death of the sick person, which is called sideration [σεσηπολισμός], just as those so affected are called sidereated and astonished.

units.la: § 4. Eadem affectio cum in plantis φαxεA@ ἢ σφαxεληισμός diceretur : deducta fuit appellatio ad animalia, subito quasi mortua collabentia. Et de hoc malo accipio Hipp.7. Aph.5o. licet Galalio tendat. Hoc additum velim Foëfio in φαxεA@.
units.tr: § 4. The same affection, when in plants it is called phakelē or sphakelismos [φακελή ἢ σφακελισμός], had its name transferred to animals that collapse suddenly as if dead. I take Hippocrates, 7 Aph. 50, to refer to this disease, although Galen inclines otherwise. I would like this added to Foësius on phakelē.

units.la: 5. Porrò cum Apoplectici jacérent immobiles & infenfiles, quomodo etiam Paralytici : orta fuit inde confusio Apoplexie cum Paralysi.
units.tr: 5. Further, since apoplectics lie motionless and insensible, as paralytics also do, a confusion of apoplexy with paralysis arose from this.

units.la: 6. * Hac in re cum multum interfit Practicis : solent illi magnoperè foliciti esse, ut distinctio instituatur, non solum inter duos dictos affectus, sed & vicinos alios.
units.tr: 6. Since this matters greatly to practitioners, they are usually very anxious that a distinction be drawn, not only between the two affections named, but also between other neighbouring ones.

units.la: 7. Cum Paralysi solam symptomatis similitudinem habet. At verò causæ sunt longè diversissimæ. In Apoplexiâ solus est defectus spirituum, cum à cerebro nihil influit,illæsis interim nervis & mufculis. In Paralysi quæ ut plurimum succedit, feré sola spinalis medulla laborat, cum ortis inde nervis, musculis ipsis illæsis. Propterea etiam soli spinæ debent medicamenta topica.
units.tr: 7. Paralysis has only a resemblance of symptoms with apoplexy, but their causes are very different. In apoplexy there is only a lack of spirits, since nothing flows from the brain, while the nerves and muscles remain unharmed. In paralysis, which for the most part follows, almost only the spinal marrow suffers, together with the nerves arising from it, while the muscles themselves are unharmed. For this reason, topical remedies ought to be applied to the spine alone.

units.la: * Dist. à vicinis affectibus.
units.tr: *Distinction from neighbouring affections.

units.la: 8. Apoplexia eft mera obftru&tio, fĩa ̧ multo, adeoque laudabili fanguine incumbente non ventriculis, fed ea cerebri parte, qua Torcular Herophili eft. Paralysis etiam eft obftru&tio, fed fpinali medullæ, nervorumque ab ea orientium facta a parte ferosa fanguinis illius, qui apoplexiam patravit, quod ferum, quia frigidum & humidum, una cum obftru& tione fimul adeft intemperies frigida & humida.
units.tr: 8. Apoplexy is a pure obstruction, caused not by thin but by thick and therefore sound blood, lying not in the ventricles but in that part of the brain where the torcular of Herophilus is. Paralysis is also an obstruction, but of the spinal marrow and of the nerves arising from it, brought about by the watery part of that blood which caused the apoplexy. Because this serum is cold and moist, a cold and moist intemperance is present together with the obstruction.

units.la: 9. Ab Epilepfia ut diftinguant, multa audent. Caufam difficultatis faciunt fibi ipfis, cum deducunt utrumque affe&tum a fi&tiia illa ventriculorum cerebri obftru&tione. Res eft. Vtrobique eft Obftru&tio corporis, quatenus id ventriculis opponitur, aut potius vaforum, perfubftantiam cerebri difperforum. Rurfus, In Apoplexia feorfim, eft obftru&tio a fanguine, ut dixi, laudabili: in Epilepfia, a vapore. Is eft duum generum. Aut enim peccat manifefta qualitate, caliditate, ut fere in pueris: aut occulta, quæ eft a tota fubftantia, quæ & in pueris, & in aliis ætatibus locum habet.
units.tr: 9. Those who try to distinguish these from epilepsy venture a great deal. They make the difficulty for themselves when they derive both affections from that imaginary obstruction of the ventricles of the brain. The matter is this. In both there is an obstruction of the body, insofar as it is opposed to the ventricles, or rather to the vessels dispersed through the substance of the brain. Again, in apoplexy, taken by itself, the obstruction comes from blood which, as I said, is sound. In epilepsy it comes from vapour. This is of two kinds. Either it sins by a manifest quality, heat, as it usually does in children; or by a hidden quality, which arises from the whole substance, and which occurs both in children and at other ages.

units.la: 10. In Epilepfia eft jactatio artuum convulfiva ut plurimum, quâ abfente, fatis eft, fi vel omnes fenfus aboleantur debilitentur, vel aliqui tantum. Et hoc ocant vocant nostrates, ut dixi, das stille fraischlich &c. In Apoplexia est infensibilitas, iterum ut plurimum. Vtrobique respirationis aliquid subest, cum spumâ sere in ore. In Epilepsia seorsim, ut pluri- mum adest vociferatio incondita.
units.tr: 10. In epilepsy there is for the most part a convulsive jerking of the limbs. When this is absent, it is enough if all the senses are abolished or weakened, or only some of them. Our people call this, as I said, "das stille fraischlich" and so on. In apoplexy there is insensibility, again for the most part. In both there is some underlying trouble with breathing, and nearly always foam at the mouth. In epilepsy taken by itself, there is usually incoherent shouting.

units.la: II. A suffocatione uterinâ, quod alia stiam, fatisque horrenda adsint symptomata. Epilepsia vero cum adest, est ipsa quoque à vapore maligno, ex uteri inemperie aliquâ sublato.
units.tr: 11. From uterine suffocation, because other and dreadful symptoms are also present. But epilepsy, when it is present, also arises from a malignant vapour caused by some intemperance of the uterus.

units.la: 12. A Caro facilè distinguitur, si re- piratio fit naturalis: sin, fortassis est Apo- plexia debilis. Id non nisi à posteriori citur. Si enim perfecta succedit sanitas, arus fuit: si Paralysis, Apoplexia.
units.tr: 12. Carus is easily distinguished from it if the breathing is natural. But if the breathing is perhaps weak, it may be a weak apoplexy. This can only be known afterwards. For if perfect health follows, it was carus; if paralysis, it was apoplexy.

units.la: 13. A Syncope simpliciter distà distiminatur, quod tam pulsus, quam repiratio penè totaliter sint ablata, ita tamen,ut feré non diu duret. A Syncope dicum additione Cardiacâ quomodo afferat, diu & anxiè quasivi apud Praticos.
units.tr: 13. Syncope is simply distinguished from it, because both pulse and breathing are almost wholly taken away, yet it does not usually last long. How the so-called cardiac syncope differs, I have long and anxiously sought among the practitioners.

units.la: 14. Ceterum, quia ex solo Gal. didici indem, nullam majorem esse affinitasim, quæque magis decipiat, quàm illa, uæ est inter Apoplexiam & Syncopen dictam Cardiacam: operæ pretium cerim, credam, si plusculum immorer, eliideò, quia nostratibus tantum non cognita est, K
units.tr: 14. Moreover, since I learned from Galen alone that there is no greater affinity, and none that deceives more, than that which exists between apoplexy and the so-called cardiac syncope, I think it worth while to dwell on it a little longer, because it is hardly known among our people.

units.la: 25. Hanc demonstro, partim ex historiis, partim ex Gal. Historiæ docuerunt, quosdam subitò & fine stertore mortuos, inventos fuisse corde sanguini prorsus innatante, salvo, ut puto, cerebro.
units.tr: 15. I demonstrate this partly from histories and partly from Galen. Histories have taught that some who died suddenly and without stertor were found with the heart entirely floating in blood, the brain, I think, being sound.

units.la: 16. Gal. explicans ἀΦωνίας Hipp.4. Acut, 23. sequi ait illam tres affectus, Epilepsiam, Apoplexiam, & Syncopen cardiacam. Epilepsiam intelligo illam, quæ est à manifestâ qualitate, uno verbo, à caliditate, cum sanguis biliofior vapores datacres, dirum istum affectum caufantes. Hoc ut plurimum accidit pueris habitioribus, quos solis refrigerantibus curamus. Et hæc sola Epilepsia rectè dicitur morbus puerilis, seu infantilis.
units.tr: 16. Galen, explaining aphonia in Hippocrates, Acut. 23, says that three affections follow it: Epilepsy, Apoplexy, and cardiac Syncope. By epilepsy I understand that which arises from a manifest quality, in a word from heat, when bilious blood gives off harsh vapours that cause that dreadful affection. This happens mostly to more robust children, whom we treat only with cooling remedies. This epilepsy alone is rightly called a childhood or infantile disease.

units.la: 17. Apoplexiam accipio illam, quam Sanguineam nostri vocant, quamvis præter eam nulla alia fit, ut dicam.
units.tr: 17. I take apoplexy to be what our people call Sanguinea, although no other kind exists apart from it, as I shall say.

units.la: 18. Syncopen Cardiacam (aliquando Cardiaca simpliciter dicitur.) cum fit, quod dixi. Nimirum, ἡ καρδία heic non est os ventriculi; neque eadem est cum Syncope stomachica:sed cor ipsum.
units.tr: 18. Cardiac Syncope (sometimes simply called cardiac) occurs as I have said. Namely, here heart [ἡ καρδία] is not the mouth of the stomach, nor is it the same as stomachic syncope, but the heart itself.

units.la: 19. De hac verba sunt Gal. 1.Caus. sym.7. L. Syncopas cardiacas fieri, affecto principio, quod in corde est. Quod illud verò est? Calidum nativum. Quod quo alio modo subitò exstingui potest, quam si sanguis, diluvii in morem, illud inundet?
units.tr: 19. On this subject Galen's words are in his 1 Caus. Symp. 7: cardiac syncopes arise when the principle that is in the heart is affected. What is that principle? The native heat. How else can it be suddenly extinguished than if blood overflows it like a flood?

units.la: Hoc genere mortis obiisse credo duos magnos in Rep. nostrâ viros, R E M V M & PICCARTVM, quorum alibi commemini.
units.tr: I believe two great men in our commonwealth died of this kind of death, REM and PICCART, whom I mention elsewhere.

units.la: Idem, 2.Aph.21. Syncopis Cardiacis è regione ponit Syncopas fortes, de quibus Hipp. ibi.
units.tr: Likewise, in 2 Aph. 21 he sets strong syncopes opposite cardiac syncopes, about which Hippocrates speaks there.

units.la: Idem 5.Loc.aff. 2. C. gladiatores quosdam ita interiisse scribit, ut ii, qui Syncopa cardiacâ laborant. Puto ego, approperante sanguine ad futuram inflammationem.
units.tr: In 5 Loc. Aff. 2 he writes that certain gladiators died in the same way as those who suffer from cardiac syncope. I think this happened because the blood rushed toward an impending inflammation.

units.la: Hinc ego colligo hoc πρόεισμα, Non omnes, qui subitò moriuntur, apoplectici sunt. Ideò sæpè falli Anatomicos necesse est, qui in solo cerebro, & præcipuè in ventriculis, causam indagant.
units.tr: From this I draw the proposition: not all who die suddenly are apoplectic. Hence the anatomists must often be mistaken, who look for the cause in the brain alone, and especially in the ventricles.

units.la: An ratio distinctionis est? In Apoplexiâ quantumvis forti stertor est, quamdiu id, quod è cerebro, ad complementum respirationis, subministrari solet, non adest. Calidum enim ebulliens durat aliquantulum, pro obstructionis magnitudine. In syncope cardiacâ nullus est stertor, quia statim exsinguitur Calor, non secus ac siquis ignem parvum multâ refutet aquâ, ut cum veteri Poetâ loquar.
units.tr: Is there a reason for the distinction? In apoplexy, however strong, there is stertor as long as that which is usually supplied from the brain for completing the breathing is absent. For the boiling heat lasts for a little while, according to the size of the obstruction. In cardiac syncope there is no stertor, because the heat is extinguished at once, no differently than if someone drowned a small fire with much water, as the old poet says.

units.la: Hoc si locum invenerit, falsus erit Gal.2, Aph.42, cum maximam apoplexiam vocat illam, in quâ respiratio prorsus fit abolita. Eit enim hæc syncope, de quâ agimus. Hac in re fi quis quid melius statuerit, id ratum esto.
units.tr: If this holds, Galen will be mistaken in 2 Aph. 42, when he calls the greatest apoplexy that in which breathing is wholly abolished. For this is the syncope we are discussing. In this matter, if anyone decides something better, let it stand.

units.la: 25. * Consectarium hujus erit, ut non nisi duæ sint Apoplexiæ five gradus five species, 2. Aph. 42. debilis & fortis. Hæc cum insigni ftertore est, quæ etiam finit intra paucas horas. Illa cum mediocri, quæ etiam ut plurimum salutaris est, fi modo salutare est, quod finit in paralysin. Horum aliquot, immediatè ante casum, retulisse ajebat D D. Strobelbergerus, cum apud nos exsularet, sensisse in fe insignem vim alui deponendæ.
units.tr: 25. A corollary of this will be that there are only two apoplexies, whether we call them degrees or species: weak and strong (2 Aph. 42). The strong one has marked stertor and ends within a few hours. The weak one has moderate stertor, and this is usually even salutary, if being salutary is what ends in paralysis. Dr. Strobelberger used to say that some of these people, immediately before their fall, had reported, while he was in exile among us, that they felt a strong urge to empty the bowels.

units.la: 26. Interim, pro tertiâ specie haberi potest Apoplexia parva dicta, cum, ablato motu, sensus superest; quam inter alios habet Spigelius noster 2. Semitert. 16. & habet pro morbo novo.
units.tr: 26. Meanwhile, a third species may be counted the so-called small apoplexy, when movement is removed but sensation remains. Our Spigelius, among others, reckons it in his second Semitertian book, ch. 16, and regards it as a new disease.

units.la: 27. Et hæc prima est differentia à magnitudine: altera petitur à loco affecto. Apud Gal. alia est in ventriculis cerebri: alia in vasis colli, in venis jugularibus, arteriisque foporalibus. Illa describitur. 3. Loc. aff. 10. D. 3. Aph. 23. extr. hæc 4. Acut. 23. & 27.
units.tr: 27. This is the first difference, drawn from size. The second is taken from the affected part. In Galen one kind lies in the ventricles of the brain, and another in the vessels of the neck, the jugular veins and the carotid arteries. The former is described in Loc. Aff. 3, ch. 10, and Aph. 3.23 at the end; the latter in Acut. 4.23 and 27.

units.la: 28. Quo ex loco ingens oritur dubium. Cum enim textu priore ad plethoram referat, atque ideò ad causam calidam:
units.tr: 28. From this passage a great doubt arises. For when in the earlier text he refers it to plethora, and therefore to a hot cause,

units.la: * Differentia.
units.tr: Difference.

units.la: dam : quei textu post. referre potest ad frigus ? Vt ne dubites. Cum dixisset, &c s. fieri tam à siccitate, quam à frigore: subdit, Non esse heic à frigore citate,sed à frigore.
units.tr: ...s... can he in the later text refer it to cold? So that you may not doubt: after saying that it arises from dryness as well as from cold, he adds that it is not here from cold but from...

units.la: 29. Quod difficultatem auget, De Caus. morb, 3. D.E. cum Apoplexiam fieri dixisset ... ab ultima stipatione ut Int. ait, citat locum illum Acut. & Apoplexiis jungit ... affectus, de sententiâ omnium, frigidos.
units.tr: 29. This makes the difficulty greater. When in De Causis Morborum 3 he had said that apoplexy arises from the final compression, as Int. puts it, he cites that passage of Acut. and joins apoplexies with affections which, by everyone's opinion, are cold.

units.la: 30. Quid pro Gal. dici possit, non est mihi curatio : contra Gal. discerte dico, Neuter locus affectus stare potest. Non prior. Si enim in ventriculis spiritus non elaborantur ; neque vero ex ventriculis nulla via in nervos est : non possunt etiam ventriculi causare apoplexiam. Non posterior, ex eodem fundamento. Si enim ventriculi non faciunt spiritus : defectus materiæ spirituum non potest etiam causa sit esse apoplexiæ.
units.tr: 30. What might be said on Galen's behalf is not my concern; I state plainly against Galen that neither place can stand. Not the former: for if spirits are not elaborated in the ventricles, and there is no route from the ventricles into the nerves, then the ventricles cannot cause apoplexy either. Not the latter, on the same ground: for if the ventricles do not make spirits, a lack of the matter of spirits cannot be the cause of apoplexy.

units.la: 31. Hoc ipsum dico contra 4. Præf, puls.11. ext. ubi jungit utrumque locum affectum. ai 3' oiov nvigeis , mis te aAnpa- [Greek] ... perti-
units.tr: 31. I say the same against the 4th Prognostic, comment 11 at the end, where he joins both affected places: [Greek] ...

units.la: que est obstructio , heic quidem ventriculo- rum : illeis autem , vasorum ad ventriculos K pertinentium, quæ sunt jam dicta, non sine tamen reti mirabili & plexibus fecundinis formibus. Dico, inquam, Quia in ventriculis spiritus non gignuntur, vanus estiam heic est labor omnis. Vnde patescit, hanc differentiam esse plane nullam. Indidem claret, & tertiam differentiam, cum dicant, Apoplexiam aut per effentiam esse, aut per consensum, nullam esse.
units.tr: ...and the obstruction is indeed here in the ventricles, but there in the vessels leading to the ventricles, which have been mentioned, not without a wonderful net and plexus-like forms. I say, I repeat, that since spirits are not generated in the ventricles, all labour here is vain. Hence it is clear that this difference is altogether nothing. From the same it is also clear that the third difference is void, since they say apoplexy is either by essence or by consent, and that is nothing.

units.la: 32. Quarta differentia sumitur à matería. Quædam enim dicunt, est ab humore crassó, frigidoque. 3. Loc. aff. 7. 4. Loc. aff. 2. 8. Vi. p. 6. Quædam à sanguine, 4. Acut. 23. Cur. per V.S. 5. extr. Verum enim vero, quia ventriculi jam sunt explosi, cadit etiam commentum de humore dicto. Et est alioquin res nimis popularis, magnam obstructionem non fieri, nisi à crasso corpore, proportionato scil. magnæ cavitati.
units.tr: 32. The fourth difference is taken from matter. Some say it comes from thick, cold humour (Loc. Aff. 3.7; 4.2; Vi. p. 6); others from blood (Acut. 4.23; Cur. per V.S. at the end). But since the ventricles have now been exploded, the fiction about the said humour falls too. Otherwise it is too popular a notion that a great obstruction arises only from a thick body, proportionate, that is, to a large cavity.

units.la: 33. Quin Gal. in 4. illo de Loc. aff. non obscure deserit, & ventriculos, & materiam præscriptam, cum concedit, Apoplexiam partim in ventriculis esse, partim in corpore cerebri, quo modo scil. Epilepsiam quoque, cap. sup. D. 80. Reverà, utibi dixi, Vis hæc est Adraftéas, cujus fulgorem cum ferre non possit, manum prætendit faciei, & fugit.
units.tr: 33. Indeed Galen, in that fourth book De Loc. Aff., does not obscurely abandon both the ventricles and the prescribed matter, when he concedes that apoplexy lies partly in the ventricles and partly in the substance of the brain, just as epilepsy does too (above, ch. 80). For truly, as I said there, this power, which cannot bear its own brightness, stretches a hand before the face and flees.

units.la: 34. Quando igitur Ille, profligatissimus juxtà & occififfimus est,tam in ioco affecto,quam in materiâ, quid faciemus? Vtemur humanitate pristinâ, videbimufque, Annon ex aliis locis exculpi poflit quid Veritati amicum ?
units.tr: 34. Since, then, he is most thoroughly refuted and most blind, both as to the affected place and as to the matter, what shall we do? We shall keep our old courtesy and see whether something friendly to the truth can be drawn from other places.

units.la: 35. Horum primum esto, quod jam dixi, Quia Gal. quasi in bivio Herculis stat nutabundus,rapiemus illum ad nos, oblivione traditis omnibus iis, quæ de ventriculis, ex alienâ sententiâ, loquitur cum hac decisivâ, Est in corpore.
units.tr: 35. The first of these, as I have already said, is this: since Galen stands wavering like Hercules at the crossroads, we shall drag him over to our side, all that he says about the ventricles, taken from another's opinion, being forgotten, and set against it his decisive statement: "It is in the body."

units.la: 36. Hac in re spero faciliorem illum habebimus, fi illi ob oculos ponenus Θεὸς τὰν Φαῖδον Ἰσρατικὸν ... (Greek text) ἐ δυνάμενον ... ἐνχερίδιον... ἠ ... Φύσιν ὅδος βαδίζει, ut loquitur autor. 4.
units.tr: 36. In this matter I hope we shall have him more readily if we set before his eyes [Greek] ... as the author says, book 4.

units.la: Acut.23. & 27. Tunc vid. venas dici intercipi (fieri ἐφανίαν ἢ ... ) cum spiritus non possunt liberè permeare. Hoc enim in vasis fit, non in ventriculis.
units.tr: Acut. 23 and 27. Then the veins are said to be intercepted (when [Greek]) when the spirits cannot pass through them freely. For this happens in the vessels, not in the ventricles.

units.la: Hunc sensum cogemus illum acceptare, quia ipsemet ... quitur,non ... & addit, Ale. ... autem ... tantum abest ab humoribus crassis, frigidisque, quantum ego Romà.
units.tr: We shall force him to accept this sense, because he himself says ... and adds, ... is as far from thick, cold humours as I am from Rome.

units.la: 37. Dicisforte, * Quæ sunt illa vasa? Olim cum Com. in I. de Vf. parte (scriberem, & duplicem agnoscebam Apoplexiam, & duplicia vasa, altera quidem *L.8.n.564. K defcendentia, Sinus & Ductus ab Anatomicis vocatos: altera autem afcendentia, Venas jugulares cum arteriis foporalibus, Rete mirabile, & Plexus chorioideis. Nunc, abdicatá ex toto Apoplexiá hac pofteriori, quam per confenfum vocant alii, recipio priorem, cum hoc additamento, Ne Torcular Nymanni poftbabeatur, quod ille doctis exhibuit, primum in D. anni. 1619. deinde in tract. integro, 1629. V Vitebergæ. Hinc enim præcipuè pendet fubitus ille Apoplecticorum cafus.
units.tr: 37. You may perhaps ask, "What are those vessels?" Once, when I was writing the commentary on the first part of De Vf., I recognised a twofold apoplexy and twofold vessels: one kind descending, which the anatomists call sinuses and ducts; the other ascending, the jugular veins with the carotid arteries, the wonderful net and the choroid plexuses. Now, having wholly abandoned the latter apoplexy, which others call by consent, I accept the former, with this addition: that Nymann's Torcular should not be neglected, which he showed to the learned first in a disputation of 1619, and then in a whole tract in 1629 at Wittenberg. For the sudden fall of apoplectics depends chiefly on this.

units.la: 38. Hac ratione fi abfolvimus nos à ventriculis, & verum locum affectum oftendimus: abfolvimus utique nos fimul ab humoribus craffis, frigidifque & fanguinem amplexavimus.
units.tr: 38. If in this way we absolve ourselves from the ventricles and show the true affected place, we at the same time absolve ourselves from thick, cold humours and embrace blood.

units.la: 39. Hoc fi parum videbitur, hem tibi etiam hunc alterum locum, omni Sole clariorem, cv τῷ Ψεῳ πνεῦμα περὶ Φλέγο-μεις, quem ego librum cum Int. laudare foleo, De Curat. per Venæ fectionem, c.5. ext. in genere quidem de apoplexiá, ait, αἱ γὰρ ἀπὸ ἀπληξίαι καὶ τὸ ὑγιὲς τὸν ταχὺ πνεῦμα ἐπὶ τὴν ἀρχὴν τῆς ζωῆς φυσικῶς ἀπλᾶ: ποχ autem in fpecie fe explicans, de duplici plethorá ait, facere ἀπο-πληξίας, ἢ τὰς φλέβας τῶν Φλεβῶν. Certè, hic ipfe locus perfuafit aliquibus Apoplexiam fanguineam, quam ego unicam & folam agnofco. 40.
units.tr: 39. If this seems too little, here is another passage for you, clearer than the sun, [Greek], which I am accustomed to cite together with Int., On Curing by Venesection, ch. 5 at the end. In general, on apoplexy, he says: [Greek]. Explaining himself specifically on the twofold plethora, he says it makes apoplexies [Greek]. Certainly this very passage has persuaded some that there is a sanguineous apoplexy, which I alone acknowledge as the only one.

units.la: 40. Si velis ex abundanti addere τὴν διὰ ξεῖαν φλεγμονὴν 2. Aph. 42. possis fine violentia.
units.tr: 40. If you wish to add, in addition, acute inflammation [Greek], Aph. 2.42, you may do so without violence.

units.la: 41. His hoc modo obtentis, quidni inclamem iterum adversarios meos? Aut herbam porrigite, ò vos tales: aut docete, quà in re deterioris conditionis sim, quam vos estis! Tamen, si volupe est vobis ulterius morari in cæno humorum vitioforum, quos cloaca ventriculorum suppeditat, non invideo equidem vobis tam sultam ambitionem.
units.tr: 41. With these points secured, why should I not cry out again against my adversaries? Either hand over the herb, you people of that sort, or teach me in what respect I am in worse condition than you are! Yet if it pleases you to linger longer in the mire of vicious humours which the cloaca of the ventricles supplies, I do not indeed begrudge you so foolish an ambition.

units.la: ANTIOEEEIS.
units.tr: Objections.

units.la: 41. Heic primum omnium GALENVM & accuso, & excuso. Accuso: quod. 2. Caus. sym. 2. B. absolute dicat, Apoplexiam esse ... totius corporis. Quin Diff. sym. 3. E. addat, Cum restrictis partis functionibus cohibitis, ut verba Int. habent. Heic enim duo sunt intolerabilia, Alterum, quod affectus duos, tantopere à se invicem dissidentes, confundit, Alterum, quod τῇ ... etiam tribuit ... χέσιν.
units.tr: 41. Here, first of all, I both accuse and excuse Galen. I accuse him because in the second book of Causes of Symptoms he says flatly that apoplexy affects the whole body. Yet in Differences of Symptoms, book 3, he adds "with the functions of the part restrained," as the Interpreter's words have it. For there are two intolerable things here. The first is that he confuses two affections that differ so greatly from each other. The second is that he also attributes to [τῇ ...] the [χέσιν] (...).

units.la: 42. Excuso : loquitur cum vulgo, quod judicat rem ex sola ... ἀνυσίαν. Ac si diceret, Est illa paralysis, quam vulgus dicit, cum simul laditur s ... μονην.
units.tr: 42. I excuse him on this point: he speaks with the common people, who judge the thing from the bare [ἀνυσίαν] (...). It is as if he were saying: "That is the paralysis which the common people mean, when one side is struck together with [μονην] (...)."

units.la: 43. Excuso etiam contrà eos, qui.3. Loc.aff.ro. A.volunt illum idem dixisse cum eo,quod locis jam cit.Expressè enim distinguit, cū apoplexiam quidé toti corpori tribuit:paralysin auté alterutri lateri.
units.tr: 43. I also excuse him against those who want him to have said the same thing in the third book of Affections of the Parts, chapter 10. For there he expressly distinguishes: apoplexy he attributes to the whole body, but paralysis to one side or the other.

units.la: 44. Fortaflis accusare etiam ob id poflit, quod nimis indulgeat vulgo, & hac ratione imperitos ducat in errorem. Non potest, Dat definitionem nominis, quę sumitur à confessâ omniû hominum ratione.Hoc notare volo eos,qui pro definitione essentiali habêt.Hi ipsi in eo quoque fallunt incautos, quod non sinunt illos pervenire ad effentiâ utriufq; morbi.
units.tr: 44. Perhaps someone could also accuse him of indulging the common people too much, and so leading the unskilled into error by this means. He cannot be accused. He gives a definition of the name, which is taken from the admitted reasoning of all men. I wish to note this against those who take it for an essential definition. These same men also deceive the unwary in this, that they do not let them reach the essence of either disease.

units.la: 45. Qui 2. Aph.42. paralysin viderunt,oportet valdè oculati fuerint. Oculatiores, fi apud Celsum 1.3. c.27.eandem vocem repererunt, Est quidem cap. feq. sed cum vulgo loquitur, perinde ut Gal. Hujus rei argumentum fit, quod addit, Nunc utrumque paralysin appellari video.Est enim tacitè improbantis.
units.tr: 45. Those who saw paralysis in the second aphorism of book 2 must have been very sharp-sighted. They would be even sharper-sighted if they found the same word in Celsus, book 1, chapter 27. It is true that the following chapter has it, but he speaks with the common people, just as Galen does. The proof of this is what he adds: "Now I see that both are called paralysis." For this is said by one who tacitly disapproves.

units.la: 46. Qui docere nos volunt, Apoplexiam apud Hipp. esse ἀφωνίαν, nimis praecipites sunt,inspecto vid.uno tantum loco. παλύσιμον esse dicere illis poterat induftriofiffimus Foëfius, fiè demittere fe voluissent. In 4.Acut. non usurpare illum vocem in angustiâ illâ significatione, pro apoplexiâ solâ, autor nobis fit idoneus Gal. ipse. De tribus enim morbis explicat, ut dixi supra.
units.tr: 46. Those who want to teach us that apoplexy in Hippocrates is [ἀφωνίαν] (aphonia) are too hasty, having looked at only one passage. The most diligent Foësius could have told them that [παλύσιμον] is to be said, if they had wished to lower themselves. In the fourth book of Acute Diseases Hippocrates does not use the word in that narrow sense, for apoplexy alone; Galen himself is a reliable witness for us. For he explains it as referring to three diseases, as I said above.

units.la: 47. Miror, quas Turbas meditentur iidem, cum vident, Hipp. transferre ὁ ἀπὸ παλσὶ ad paralysin, & maximè ad particularem? Ista non pertinent ad supinum & ambitiosum : sed ad Foëfium aliquem.
units.tr: 47. I wonder what disturbances these same men contrive, when they see Hippocrates transferring [ὁ ἀπὸ παλσὶ] to paralysis, and especially to the partial kind. Such things do not belong to the careless and ambitious man, but to some Foësius.

units.la: 48. Miror amplius, in quo Parnassῶ fomniârint illimet, Paralysin unius lateris, Apoplexie succedentem, divisum saltem cerebrum torpidum habere? Quis unquam italocutus est? Imò, quis unquam vidit Cerebrum per totum divisum? Hoc enim fine violentiâ extunditur? Quis tandem paralysin ad cerebrum retulit, quæ ad spi-nalem medullam pertinet? Nam hæc verè divisa est, cujus divisionis ratione fit paralysis dextra & sinistra.
units.tr: 48. I wonder even more on what Parnassus these men dreamed that paralysis of one side, following apoplexy, means that the brain is at least divided and torpid. Who has ever spoken so? Indeed, who has ever seen the whole brain divided? For can it be split without violence? And who has ever referred to the brain a paralysis that belongs to the spinal marrow? For that is truly divided, and by the division of it comes paralysis on the right side and on the left.

units.la: 49. Adfomnum cogor referre illud quoque, quod ex. 3 .Loc.aff. 10. refertur. Cum enim hoc tantum Gal, dicat, Apoplexiam vocari πληγὴν, πνευματῶν τῆς νέου ἐν ἀπολεσμένω ἀποθνήσκειν τε καὶ ζῶντος ἀπολλυμένων ὅ: unde est id, Non necessarium aboleri omnes? ὃ Necessarium quidem nufpiam est: ὃ λόγος autem omninò offert mihi Abolitionem. Video, quid mussent de Respiratione: hoc verò ab longè alio de clavo pendet, quem ego fixi supra.
units.tr: 49. I am forced to mention also what is cited from the third book of Affections of the Parts, chapter 10. For when Galen says only this, that apoplexy is called a stroke, and that the animal spirits die and are destroyed in the ..., where does the claim come from that all of them must be abolished? Certainly nowhere is it necessary; but the reasoning itself suggests abolition to me at all. I see what they murmur about respiration, but this hangs on quite a different peg, which I fixed above.

units.la: 49. Video etiam affirmare velle illos, Principes facultates aliquando in hoc malo illasas esse : sed cum addunt, Licet de his sensui non ita manifestum sit, nescio quid fibi velint. An hoc? Inferioribus quidem in gradibus ledi dictas facultates: sed sensum hoc non docere. Si enim quis ex tali apoplexia rediit ad se, & in se ipso animadvertit: quo modo sensus non docuit? Et quid habemus, quod sensus non docuit?
units.tr: 49. I see also that they want to affirm that the principal faculties are sometimes injured in this disease. But when they add, "Although in these cases the sense is not so clear," I do not know what they mean. Does this mean that the said faculties are injured in the lower degrees, but that sense does not teach this? For if someone has come back to himself from such an apoplexy and observes it in himself, how has sense not taught it? And what do we have that sense has not taught?

units.la: 50. De morbo acturus, mirificum facit prologum de laude scientiæ per causas, à quo subito festinat ad locum assectum.
units.tr: 50. About to speak of the disease, he makes a wonderful prologue in praise of knowledge through causes, and from this he quickly hurries to the affected part.

units.la: 51. Recte quidem ratiocinatur cum Gal. Cerebrum esse affectum: sed non reté aspellit Cor. Problematum quidem opus, exotericum quippe, non magni facio: vellem autem legisset, quæ ego scripsi alibi pro Aristotele.
units.tr: 51. He reasons rightly with Galen that the brain is affected, but he does not hit the heart correctly. I do not think much of the Problems, which is an exoteric work; I would have wished he had read what I have written elsewhere on behalf of Aristotle.

units.la: 52. Non minus vellem, considerasset paulo attentius, quæ ex Avicenna, Solenandro, Iouberto, aliis, annotata mihi sunt, Observatum fuisse, morbos cerebri felicius curatos fuisse, habitâ cordis quoque ratione. Et quei per rerum naturam fieri aliter potest, ut, affecto organo proximo, non afficiatur etiam remotum? Est enim catena quædam partium, ad sensum, motumque concurrentium, quâ alicubi diruptâ, quis non intelligit, quid sit futurum de reliquis?
units.tr: 52. I would equally have wished he had considered a little more carefully what has been noted by me from Avicenna, Solenander, Joubert and others: that diseases of the brain have been cured more happily when the state of the heart was also taken into account. And how can it happen in the nature of things otherwise, that when a neighbouring organ is affected, the distant one is not affected too? For there is a certain chain of parts working together for sense and motion, and when it is broken anywhere, who does not understand what will become of the rest?

units.la: §3. Cerebrum laborare, non ut pars similaris, sed ut organica, verum est: sed laborare fecundum ventriculos, salsum est.
units.tr: §3. It is true that the brain suffers not as a similar part but as an organic one; but to say that it suffers according to the ventricles is absurd.

units.la: §4. Ventriculos non esse receptacula excrementorum quia ipsius maximè intererat, cur non stabilivit suis rationibus cur ad argumenta adversaria non refpondit?
units.tr: §4. Why did he not, since it was especially in his interest, establish by his own arguments that the ventricles are not receptacles of excrement, and why did he not answer the opposing arguments?

units.la: §5. Eos, qui distinguunt Cerebrum, in Cerebrum seu corticem cinereum, & Cerebri medullam, oblongatam: nunquam intellexit. Vt neque illos, qui dicunt, Nervos non oriri ex cerebro, sed ex medulla cerebri. Hoc ita probo:
units.tr: §5. He never understood those who distinguish the brain into the grey cortex and the oblong medulla of the brain, nor those who say that the nerves do not arise from the brain but from its medulla. I prove it thus:

units.la: §6. Dicit, non posse nos rationem reddere, cur illa fo cerebro, principes functiones ledantur? Dico, Cerebrum dupliciter confideratur, Aut crasse, ut lanius & coquus: aut accurate, ut Anatomicus. Hic cum dicit, Nervos non oriri ex parte cinerea, quae nervos non attingit; oriri autem ex parte alba, seu medulla, ex qua ad sensum existunt: dimittitne ille cerebrum? id, inquam, totum, quod cranio continetur? Certè pars non est nisi totius pars: ergò, qui dicit totum, dicit ejus partes, & contrà.
units.tr: §6. He says we cannot give a reason why, when the brain is affected, the principal functions are injured. I reply that the brain is considered in two ways: either roughly, as a butcher or cook does, or accurately, as an anatomist does. When the anatomist says that the nerves do not arise from the grey part, which does not reach the nerves, but arise from the white part, or medulla, from which they come forth for sense: does he leave out the brain, I ask, the whole that is contained in the skull? Surely a part is nothing but a part of a whole; therefore whoever says the whole says its parts, and conversely.

units.la: §7. Dicit, Non posse nos distinguere apoplexiam à paralysi universali. Proh hominum fidem! Apoplexia fit, occupato toto eo, quod in cranio continetur, tam cinereo, quam albo, & quidem ita, ut senforia externa, unà cum instrumentis motoriis, non habeant inde commune sensuum & motus instrumentum, Spiritus, ipsis interim partibus non laesis, Paralysis vel totius trunci, vel alterutrius lateris fit, cum pars ferofa sanguinis è cerebro destillat sensim in nervos, atque ita arrigat & occludit, ut spiritus transitum non habeant.
units.tr: §7. He says we cannot distinguish apoplexy from universal paralysis. Good heavens! Apoplexy happens when everything contained in the skull, both grey and white, is occupied, and in such a way that the external senses, together with the motor organs, no longer have from it a common instrument of sense and motion, namely the spirits; while the parts themselves are not injured. Paralysis of the whole trunk, or of one side, happens when a serous part of the blood drips slowly from the brain into the nerves, and so thickens and blocks them, that the spirits no longer have a passage.

units.la: §8. Addo, In Apoplexia est affectum cerebrum, illaesis partibus inferioribus, quarum respectu est morbus in numero, utita dicam. In Paralysi est, ut dixi, assecta medulla spinalis, laesis etiam partibus inferioribus.
units.tr: §8. I add: in apoplexy the brain is affected while the lower parts are unharmed, and it is with respect to these that the disease is counted among those things I will name. In paralysis, as I said, the spinal marrow is affected, and the lower parts are harmed as well.

units.la: §9. Dicit, Non posse nos rationem reddere servate respirationis. Immane telum! Imò nos veram damus causam, tu sallam. Aufertur pars altera respirationis: quei ergò potest esse illaesa? Haec ratio quei nimis vana est? hominum vaniffime. Valet etiam, inquit, in apoplexia illa, in qua respiratio prorsus efl ablata. Non est apoplexia, sed syncope Cardiaca. Atqui Gal. in 2. illo Aph. habet pro primâ specie apoplexiæ? Non refert. Est hic error illi communis cum multis.
units.tr: §9. He says we cannot give a reason for the preservation of respiration. What a monstrous weapon! Indeed, we give the true cause, and you the salt. One part of respiration is taken away; how, then, can it be unharmed? Is this reason too vain? Most vainly of men. He says it also holds in that apoplexy in which respiration is wholly taken away. It is not apoplexy but cardiac syncope. But does Galen not, in that second aphorism, count it as the first species of apoplexy? It does not matter. This error is common to him and to many others.

units.la: 6o. Hei mihi,quod fulmen de longinquo audio! Si substantiam quoque cerebri malum invadat, ut medulla diffluat, & spiritus repente exstinguatur, &c. Sed bene habet, Salmoneus est, non Iupiter. Quem ego:
units.tr: 60. Alas, what thunderbolt I hear from afar! If the substance of the brain also is attacked, so that the marrow flows apart and the spirit is suddenly extinguished, etc. But it is well: he is Salmoneus, not Jupiter. To him I say:

units.la: Sed motos præstat componere fluctus.
units.tr: "But it is better to calm the stirred-up waves."

units.la: Dic mihi, ô nobilissime, siquidem tam certus es ventriculos affici, non substantiam: cur modò, neglectis ventriculis, ad substantiam diversis? Fortassis causam habui.
units.tr: Tell me, most noble sir, if you are so certain that the ventricles are affected and not the substance, why now, neglecting the ventricles, do you turn to the substance? Perhaps I had a reason.

units.la: 61. Fortassis non habuisti! Dic mihi, Reflexe negavit Gal. ulla talia symptomata, quæ subito sunt, ortum posse habere ab intemperie, quod intemperies non nisi succefsu temporis convalescat? Siles? Si de inferiori intemperie, quæ est à manifestis qualitatibus id non licet: quanto minus statuere id licebit de summâ, quæ est corruptio totius substantiæ, & nullo prorsus modo fit in instanti? Hucenim omninò devenire oportet nos si diffluxus locum habet. Sed transeat:
units.tr: 61. Perhaps you had none! Tell me, did Galen not expressly deny that any such symptoms, which come suddenly, can arise from an intemperance, since intemperance does not grow strong except over time? Are you silent? If this is not allowed for a lower intemperance, which arises from the manifest qualities, how much less will it be allowed to decide it for the greatest, which is the corruption of the whole substance and in no way happens in an instant? For we must come to this altogether, if outflow has a place. But let that pass.

units.la: 62. Dic mihi, quæ est illa spiritus exstinctio, quæ à diffluxu pendet? Scio, quid rustici mincentur corrivalibus suis, Sch wil Dif Licht aufslefchen: sed nescio, an in ventriculis cerebri, tanquam in atrio quodam, stet candela, quæ radios suos spargat per totum corpus.
units.tr: 62. Tell me, what is that extinguishing of the spirit which depends on the flux? I know what the country folk threaten their rivals with: "Sch wil Dif Licht aufslefchen" ("I'll snuff your light out"). But I do not know whether a candle stands in the ventricles of the brain, as in some kind of hall, scattering its rays through the whole body.

units.la: 63. Multò minus scio, an, quod quidam voluerunt, quemadmodum atrii parietibus cadentibus, obruitur candela, & exstinguitur: ita etiam in cerebro fiat? Profecto sunt hæc portenta verborum, ad quæ non possum non expavescere, quasi Pan ipse foret in propinquo!
units.tr: 63. Still less do I know whether, as some have wished, the candle is overwhelmed and extinguished as though the walls of a hall had collapsed, and the same thing happens in the brain. These are surely monstrous words, and I cannot help being terrified by them, as though Pan himself were close at hand!

units.la: 64. Tu verò, quisquis es, recipe mecum animum, & para te ad visenda multò ingratiora! Horum. 1.est, cum dicit, Ventriculos in apoplecticis affici, etiam sectio ipsorum post mortem comprobavit. Vbi fi dicam ego, Non est in omnibus utetur rustica occupatione, Si Parolius non vidit, viderunt Coiter & Pareus. Tantumne!
units.tr: 64. But you, whoever you are, take heart with me and prepare yourself to see things much less pleasant! Horum 1. is where he says: that the ventricles are affected in apoplectics has been proved even by their dissection after death. Here, if I say, "It is not so in all cases; the rustic occupation of ..." If Parolius did not see it, Coiter and Pareus did. What arrogance!

units.la: 65. Proba mihi, fi viries, Ventriculos esse officinas spirituum animalium: & dabo tibi ultrò, apoplexiam fieri in ventriculis. Ego verò planissimè tibi probabo, Spiritus fieri in corpore, cujus probationis quæ sequela? Dic tu:
units.tr: 65. Prove to me, if you can, that the ventricles are the workshops of the animal spirits, and I will readily grant you that apoplexy arises in the ventricles. I, for my part, will show you quite plainly that spirits are made in the body. What follows from that proof? You tell me.

units.la: 66. Ego enim rem ipsam aggressus, ab initio ostendo tibi Naturæ genium, Ariftotelem, qui 2. Part. 7. & paulò post 1o. causam afferens finalem, Cur substantia cerebri fit aquea & terrea? uno verbo, frigida & humida? ait, Vt contemperet calorem cordis. Tu verò noli tam crafsè intelligere,quo modo Gal. & alii, Contemperato cordeipfo: fed fpiritibus cordis calidis & ficcis. Hunc fenfum dat nobis Avicenna 1.3. tract. 1. c.2. Averroës,paraphrafi in Arift. & iterum 2. Coll.11. Albertus Magnus 3. Animal.1. c.6. Conciliator, diff.38. Turrifanus in plus quam-commento in Artem. Hucf tendit noftrorum hominum chorus ampliff, quem produxi Com.in 8. Vf.'p. idemque auctior in Phyfiolog.c.183.Vbi cum probatum fit, ut & in Diatriba de Vfu cerebri fecundum Arift. ufum Ariftotelicum cerebri coincidere cum ufu Galenico : probatum etiam fnerit, In corpore cerebri fieri fpiritus, non in ventriculis.
units.tr: 66. For I, taking up the matter itself, first show you the genius of nature, Aristotle, who in Part 2, chapter 7, and a little after in book 1, when giving the final cause, asks, Why is the substance of the brain watery and earthy, in a word, cold and moist? He answers, so that it may temper the heat of the heart. But do not understand this as crudely as Galen and others do, as tempering the heart itself, but as tempering the hot and dry spirits of the heart. Avicenna, book 3, tract 1, chapter 2, gives us this sense; so does Averroes in his paraphrase of Aristotle, and again in Collection 11; Albertus Magnus, On Animals, book 1, chapter 6; the Conciliator, difference 38; Turrisanus in his commentary on the Art. Towards this view tends the larger chorus of our own people, which I brought forward in my commentary on the eighth book, and which is larger still in the Physiology, chapter 183. There, since it has been proved, as also in the Diatriba on the Use of the Brain, that according to Aristotle's use the use of the brain coincides with the Galenic use, it has also been proved that spirits are made in the substance of the brain, not in the ventricles.

units.la: 67. Vbi liceat mihi interloqui,Maximi femper ponderis fuit argumentum, quod ab adverfarii teftimonio peteretur. At verò Gal. ipfe 8. Vf. p.13. 7. Sent. Hipp.3. 3.Loc. aff.7. non eftalienus à corpore cerebri. Idem probat rationem Arift.3. Prorrh.20. 12.Meth.21. Calorem turbare,frigus quietem dare.Et hoc planiffimè ab Adraftéa eft. Ab eadem eft infelicitas Gal. in probanda intentione fua, præcipuè in motu cerebri,quem ideò architectatus eft, ut aërem, ad ventriculos deduceret, pro conficiendis fpiritibus, fpe
units.tr: 67. Here I may interject. An argument drawn from the testimony of an opponent has always carried the greatest weight. But Galen himself, in the Use of the Parts, p. 13, in the Seventh Commentary on Hippocrates, book 3, and in On Affected Parts, book 3, chapter 7, is not alien to the substance of the brain. He also supports Aristotle's argument in Prorrhetics 3, chapter 20, and in Metaphysics 12, chapter 21: heat stirs, cold brings rest. And this is quite plainly from Adrastea. From the same source comes Galen's failure in proving his own purpose, especially concerning the motion of the brain, which he devised so that air would be drawn into the ventricles for making the spirits, a hope that is forever vain, and which I think I have demonstrated in a special digression in my commentary on the third verse of the part.

units.la: in perpetuum vana, quod demonstrasse me putoin Digressione peculiari Com.in 3. Vs. part.
units.tr: (continued) ... vain forever, which I think I have demonstrated in a separate Digression in my Commentary on the third part of the Verses.

units.la: 68. Argumenta contra ventriculos quia latiusculè deduxi in d. Physiolog. c.204. satis mihi sit nunc temporis delibasse tantum, 1.Ibi fit spiritus, ubi actio sit. At verò in corpore sit. Corpus enim agit, non accidens. II. Spiritus si agere debet, oportet sub imperio animæ maneat,in vasis inquam. Postquam enim in æquor illud ventriculorum egressus est, quid cogit illum iterum in angustias illas nervorum? De naturâ enim ipsius est disfundere se. III. Sed nihil sit hoc. Ventriculi interius cinguntur piâ matre, quæ negat & egressum & regressum. IV. Superiores duo ventriculi cum pateant in subjectum tertium, & hic in Infundibulum, quod aperitur in os sphenoides, & consequenter in palatum: quis spondebit,spiritus hac non exituros. V. Ventriculi cum nervis continui non sunt, sed cum corpore.Sunt enim cerebrum ἀεπἈνρῶες, quo modo Gal. solet loqui. VI, Ventriculi jam habent aliud officium, quod cum hoc stare neutiquam potest.
units.tr: 68. I have set out the arguments against the ventricles at greater length in my Physiology, chapter 204; for now it is enough for me to have touched on them only lightly. I. Spirit is where the action is. But the action is in the body, for the body acts, not the accident. II. If the spirit is to act, it must remain under the command of the soul, in the vessels, I mean. For once it has gone out into that sea of the ventricles, what compels it to return again into those narrow nerves? For it is in its nature to spread itself abroad. III. But let that pass. The ventricles are enclosed on the inside by the pia mater, which forbids both going out and coming back. IV. The two upper ventricles open into the third, and this into the infundibulum, which opens into the sphenoid bone and consequently into the palate. Who will guarantee that the spirits will not leave by this way? V. The ventricles are not continuous with the nerves, but with the body; for they are the cerebrum [ἀεπἈνρῶες], as Galen is wont to say. VI. The ventricles already have another office, which can by no means stand alongside this one.

units.la: 69. Hoc officium probo his argumentis. I. Structura ventriculorum, præsertim considerata in sectione universarolii, planissimè convincit calcitrones factos fc. esse eductioni excrementorum. Desinunt enim quà dixi, Imò est unus ventriculus, quo modo Hipp. & Arift, olim æstimabant. I I. Glandula pituitaria;extra duram matrem,in fellà fphenoidis statuta, clarà voce id testatur. Quia agnominatio, tot seculis probata, vult idem. I I I. Gemini in palatu meatus, 8. Vf. p.6. ext: volunt hoc ipsum. I V. Sternutatio,admirabiliffimum naturæ opus, non patitur nos alió ire. Videmus enim plerosque post illam aut expuere, aut nares emungere. V. Si quis fugat lingua cœlum palati, quod I l], Bauh. me docuit,elicit pituitam. V I. Praxis Medica docet, apophlegmatifmos in affectibus cerebri plurimum posse.
units.tr: 69. I prove this office by these arguments. I. The structure of the ventricles, especially as seen in the dissection of the whole head, plainly shows that the little cups were made for the drawing off of excrements. For they end where I said; indeed there is only one ventricle, as Hippocrates and Aristotle once thought. II. The pituitary gland, placed outside the dura mater in the sella of the sphenoid, testifies to this in a clear voice; for the name, approved through so many centuries, means the same. III. The twin passages in the palate (Vesalius? see the eighth book, p. 6) want this very thing. IV. Sneezing, a most admirable work of nature, does not allow us to go elsewhere; for we see most people after it either spit out or blow their noses. V. If someone tickles the tongue or the palate's roof, as Bauhin taught me, it draws out phlegm. VI. Medical practice teaches that expectorants are very powerful in affections of the brain.

units.la: 76. Atqui in Apoplecticorum capitibus inventa fuit pituita? Si naturaliter ibi est,præsertim in frigidioribus & humidioribus, quid miri? Vbi pituita non est, aqua tamen est? Est, & vidi. At verò aqua illa est ferum capitis, quod colligitur in his cavitatibus,dum patera ferrâ & malleo concutitur. Et hæc quidem tam folida sunt, ut nec Herculem timeam!
units.tr: 76. But was phlegm found in the heads of apoplectics? If it is there naturally, especially in those who are colder and moister, what is strange about that? Where there is no phlegm, there is still water? There is, and I have seen it. But that water is the serum of the head, which collects in these cavities when the skull is struck with an iron bowl and a hammer. And indeed these things are so solid that I would not fear Hercules himself!

units.la: 71. Quid ILLE? (Et hoc alterum est) In assertione ventriculorum suorum tam timidè agit,ut facilè appareat illum fine gere, Duo superiores forte foli hoc nomine sunt digni, inquit, Cur, mi DD? quis ante te hoc dixit? Gal. quidem praestantiores ait esse hos duos: tamen contemni non vult reliquos. Et quei contemni possunt, siquidem continui sunt, & spiritus (ex hypothesi) ibi perficiuntur? Sapientia igitur hac propria est Nostri, quam vel obiter inspiciamus. Si prohibetur in superioribus spirituum generatio: quomodo spiritus, qui non sunt, suffocantur in inferioribus? Altera sapientia est in illis, Qui exitum non invenit. Cum enim ibi sit Infundibulum, quem alium exitum sibi optet? In nervos forte? Nulla cum nervis communio ventriculis est, ceu dixi. Sed gradum facit. ciamus.
units.tr: 71. What about HIM? (And this is the other point.) In asserting his ventricles he acts so timidly that it readily appears he is without guile. "Perhaps only the two upper ones deserve this name," he says. "Why, my dear sirs? Who said this before you?" Galen indeed says these two are more excellent; yet he does not want the others despised. And how can they be despised, since they are continuous, and the spirits (on the hypothesis) are perfected there? This wisdom, then, is peculiar to ours, which we may look at even in passing. If the generation of spirits is forbidden in the upper ones, how are the spirits, which do not exist, suffocated in the lower ones? There is another piece of wisdom in them: "one which does not find an exit." For since there is an infundibulum there, what other exit does he wish for it? Into the nerves perhaps? There is no communication between the ventricles and the nerves, as I said. But let us move on.

units.la: 72. III. Angustia illa, inquit, duplex
units.tr: 72. III. That narrowing, he says, is double

units.la: est, aut si maxi, triplex. Quei hoc intelligam? Cur mihi disjunctivam Aut obtrudis? Cur Obstructionem, quae generis locum habuit supra, jam speciem facis? Cur eidem Angustiam surrogas? Et alioqui mirum mihi accidit, non attulisse sex illas Gal. causas, Cauf. morb.7. quas Montanus explicat 4. Morbo 4. qua de re infra in morbis Cavitatum.
units.tr: or, if you prefer, triple. How am I to understand this? Why do you thrust an alternative (disjunctive) on me? Why do you now make obstruction, which above had the place of a genus, into a species? Why do you substitute narrowing for the same thing? Besides, it strikes me as strange that he did not bring up those six causes of Galen, which Montanus explains in Caus. morb. 7, Morb. 4, on which matter see below, in the diseases of the cavities.

units.la: 73. IV. Obstructio illa fit, pergit, a materia crassa et copiosa, sive humor fit, sive vapor: Mirabilis sermo! Idemne possunt humor
units.tr: 73. IV. That obstruction, he goes on, arises from matter that is thick and abundant, whether it becomes humour or vapour. Wonderful language! Can humour and vapour be the same thing in these terms?

units.la: humor & Vapor? his quidem terminis? Nam alias vaporem posse occidere, non nego: verum id fit suffocando, adeoque causa mortis in thorace potius est, quam in capite. Mirabilior est, qui pituitam & melancholiam sociat cum sanguine! Quis enim ventriculos sanguine oppletos in apoplecticis vidit unquam? Et quâ fronte jungit sanguinem cum humoribus istis excrementitiis? De acrimonia enim & mordacitate quæ inspergit, irrita sunt. An Apoplexiam sanguineam cogitavit? Rideo! Pessime enim accomodavit, fi hoc voluit.
units.tr: Humour and vapour? In these terms at least? For I do not deny that vapour can otherwise suffocate; but this happens by suffocating, and so the cause of death lies in the chest rather than in the head. More marvellous still is he who joins phlegm and melancholy with blood! For who has ever seen the ventricles filled with blood in apoplectics? And with what face does he join blood with those excrementitious humours? For the sharpness and biting quality he sprinkles in are beside the point. Did he think of sanguineous apoplexy? I laugh! For he has applied it very badly, if this is what he meant.

units.la: 74. Compressio abiifdem causis oritur, subdit, Ab iisdem causis, quo modo? Non dubito errorem calami esse, quem longiffime exprobrare tibi poteram, fi mores tuos sequerer. Sit igitur: fit ab extrinsecus incidentibus, casu, itu, &c. Sed quâ ratione causat? Est omninò remota causa, quæ dolorem afferendo humores ciet ad Tor-cular. Quo dato, quid hoc negotii est? Ἀλφεῖος Φλεγμονὴ Gal. 2. Aph. 42. Pofteft quidem σφύγμος illa tale quid ciere: verum σφυγμὸς causa demum est compressio.
units.tr: 74. Compression arises from the same causes, he adds. From the same causes, how so? I do not doubt this is a slip of the pen, which I could reproach you for at length, if I followed your manners. So be it: it arises from external incidents, by chance, by blow, and so on. But by what reasoning does it cause this? It is altogether a remote cause, which by inflicting pain stirs the humours towards the press. Granted this, what business is that? [Ἀλφεῖος Φλεγμονή] Gal. 2. Aph. 42. That pulse [σφύγμος] can indeed produce something of the kind; but the pulse [σφυγμὸς] is in the end a cause only through compression.

units.la: 75. VI. συνέχεσις, subsidentia, quæ corporis cerebri est, cum concidit fornix illa, uti fabulantur, quæ quâ fronte de-
units.tr: 75. VI. Syncope [συνέχεσις], subsidence, which belongs to the body of the brain when that vault collapses, as they fable; by what face is it attributed to a defect of spirits?

units.la: L sectus
units.tr: L, cut off

units.la: fectui fpiritunm tribuitur ? Et quomodo consonant sibi ista? Non est à defectu spirituum : deficit spiritus duobus modis , etc. Quei vero à subsistentiâ devenis ad obstructionem Carotidum ? Aquibus cur sejungis sphagitidas? Rursus,quid subsidentia commune habet cum vapore , spiritus genitos dissipante ? Ex his tantum fastidii mihi obrepit, ut non possim diutius heic stare? Adeo verum est illud, ⁊ jejunè ambitiosis non nisi jejunè ambitiosa exspectaris possunt. Vestri, ô adolescentes, me miseretsquos cymbala ista inania tam miserè raptant,aguntque!
units.tr: Defect of spirits? And how do these things agree with each other? It is not from a defect of spirits: the spirit fails in two ways, and so on. But how do you pass from subsidence to obstruction of the carotids? And why do you separate the sphagitides from these? Again, what has subsidence in common with vapour, which dissipates the spirits that have been generated? Does so much disgust creep over me that I cannot stay here any longer? So true is that saying: from the inept and ambitious one can expect nothing but inept and ambitious things. Your men, O young men, I pity you, whom those empty cymbals so wretchedly snatch up and drive about!

units.la: O fugite annales Vetusti , chartamque cacatam!
units.tr: O flee the ancient annals and the befouled paper!

units.la: Censura brevicula thesium Erafti de morbis totius substantiæ, CAP. XV.
units.tr: Brief Censure of Erastus's Theses on the Diseases of the Whole Substance, CHAPTER XV.

units.la: § 1. Ntequam deseram ἀρχεῖν λόγοι Fernelii de morbis formaliter, libuit paululum degustare distas theses. Primo autem omnium monere oportet lectorem, Erratum fuisse à scribâ,cum solos morbos totius substantiæ præscripsit. Agitur enim de morbis quoque materiæ. Deinde, erratum fuisse ab ipso autore cum morbos formæ non satis dilucide separat à morbis materiæ.
units.tr: § 1. Before I leave Fernelius's [ἀρχεῖν λόγοι] on diseases of form, I thought it worth briefly tasting his distinct theses. First of all, however, the reader must be warned that the scribe erred when he wrote only "diseases of the whole substance," for the discussion concerns diseases of matter as well. Then the author himself erred in not separating diseases of form clearly enough from diseases of matter.

units.la: § 2. In D. 46. non possum concoquere,quod ait, Materie, fine temperamento considerate , qualitates ad instrumentalium morborum constitutionem concurrere. Quomodo fine temperamente? Laxitas v.g. & mollities profecto non sunt fine temperamento. Ergo fi sunt non absque temperamento, sunt etiam morbi intemperies. Et hoc pertinet ad difficultatem illam: Qualis morbus fit color flavus cornea, per quem omnia videntur flava? I. Alexandrinus , & alii referunt ad morbos organicos. Nullo modo. Est morbus temperiei, quatenus ad temperiem pertinet Modus substantiæ dictus. Cornea debet habere talem modum substantiæ , ut ad albedinem inclinet potius, quam ad nigredinem.
units.tr: § 2. In D. 46 I cannot stomach his statement that qualities, considered in matter without temperament, concur in the constitution of instrumental diseases. How can they be without temperament? Laxity and softness, for instance, are certainly not without temperament. So if they are not without temperament, they are also an intemperies of the disease. This bears on that difficulty: what sort of disease is the yellow colour of the cornea, through which everything looks yellow? John Alexandrinus and others refer it to organic diseases. By no means. It is a disease of temperament, insofar as it belongs to the temperament called the mode of substance. The cornea must have such a mode of substance that it inclines towards whiteness rather than blackness.

units.la: § 3. Quæ D.feq. dicuntur, valde mi- hi insolentia sunt.Quæ enim sunt ille tuæ qualitates?Explicate. Ventriculi & hepatis actiones quâ de causâ non sunt fimilares? Suntenim alterationes. Eadem viscera voluntad stringentia , quatenus à calidis laxantur & dissolvuntur. Adftrictio enim omnis à frigore est. Sensus acrimoniam esse ab ἀδοσυγκρισια facile ét est, ut & odorum, saporumque diff Mihi pariter àmodo substantiæ Argumento fit, quod, mutato victu, multa talia mutantur.
units.tr: § 3. What the following section (D.) says seems very strange to me. For what are those qualities of yours? Explain them. For what reason are the actions of the stomach and liver not similar? For they are alterations. The same viscera are contracted by the will insofar as they are relaxed and dissolved by warm things. For all astringency comes from cold. That the sense of sharpness arises from [ἰδιοσυγκρασία] idiosyncrasy is easily known, as is also the case with smells and flavours. Likewise, for me the argument for the mode of substance is this: when the diet changes, many such things change.

units.la: § 4. Recte censet D.94.tolerantiam frigoris, caloris, laborum multas habere causas : è quibus tamen temperationem materiæ rejicio, & substituo animi firmitatem, aut mollitiem, licet sub consuetudine comprehendi possit. Ita D. 50. Ingenii & cogitationum celeritas omnino est actio similaris. Sequitur enim temperiem spirituum. Hinc deliria fiunt, vel calidioribus, vel frigidioribus effectis spiritibus.
units.tr: § 4. D. 94 rightly judges that tolerance of cold, heat and labours has many causes. Of these, however, I reject the temperament of matter and substitute firmness or softness of mind, though this may be included under habit.
