So too D. 50: speed of wit and thought is altogether a similar action, for it follows the temperament of the spirits. Hence deliria arise when the spirits are made either warmer or colder.

units.la: § 5. D. 52. Recte abjicit Struthiocameli ὀνυχοβαφυακ, partim, quod non fatis constet τὸ ὁ ᾱ, An concoquat? partim, fi constet, non fieri tamen aliter, quam in aliis animalibus, Calore, inquam, quodam suo. Tu vide Marg. supra cap.6.
units.tr: § 5. D. 52 rightly rejects the ostrich-camel [ὀνυχοβαφυακ], partly because it is not sufficiently established whether the bird digests [τὸ ὁ ᾱ], and partly because, if it is established, it does not happen otherwise than in other animals, by a certain heat of its own, I say. See the marginal note above, chapter 6.

units.la: § 6. Méntem Gal. de duplici temperamento D, 53. non fatis explicat. Et quid est, Illa fine subjecto intelligit ur? præfertim, quia mox ait, Vna cum subjecto? Breviter, Temperamentum quodammodo duplex est.* Aut enim est primarum qualitatum tantum, unde dicitur aliquid Calidum, frigidum, & c. Aut est, non primarum tantum, sed & fecundarum, & tertiarum & quartarum, unà cum modo substantiæ, unde dicitur aliquid Tale, simpliciter. Tribus verbis, Est id, quod Comple-
units.tr: § 6. Galen's doctrine of the double temperament, D. 53, is not sufficiently explained. And what is meant by "understood without subject," especially since he soon says "together with the subject"? In brief, temperament is in a way double. For either it concerns the primary qualities only, whence something is called hot, cold and so on; or it concerns not only the primary but also the secondary, tertiary and quaternary qualities, together with the mode of substance, whence something is called simply "such." In three words, it is what the philosophers call the complexion, the whole substance, according to Galen.

units.la: * Vide supra c, 6.parag.6. xum vocant Philosophi, Totam fubftantiam Gal. Hinc intelligitur, quatenus Temperamentum à Totâ substantiâ differat, aut non differat. An autem Tota substantia fit idem cum ἰδιοσυγκρασία, profectò valdè nescio.
units.tr: * See above, chapter 6, paragraph 6. Hence it is understood how temperament differs from the whole substance, or does not differ from it. Whether the whole substance is the same as idiosyncrasy, I truly do not know.

units.la: § 7. Contrà scio, & valdè scio, falli Eraftum,cum D.56.negat,Totius fubftantiæ morbos recte separari à morbis Temperamenti, Si enim nihil aliud,solus ille Gal. locus persuadeat 13.Meth.6. penè extremo,ubi ait, Eorum, quæ qualitate sola sunt contraria,methodum esse: quæ totâ substantia non esse. Hoc verò nolunt Ferneliani rapere ad se, sed triumphare ante victoriam. Vt enim dixi, Temperamentum est quasi duplex, Totaque substantia tantum abest à morbis formalibus istorum novatorum, quantum album à nigro. Proptereà rectè ait Eraftus, Materia non agit: Forma non agit: sed Totâ ita temperatum. Hoc totum est causa proxima actionis f. n. hoc ipsum læsum est causa proxima actionis p.n. seu Morbi.
units.tr: § 7. On the contrary, I know, and know well, that Erastus is mistaken when in D. 56 he denies that the diseases of the whole substance are rightly separated from the diseases of temperament. For if nothing else, that single passage of Galen (13 Meth. 6, near the end), where he says that the method applies to things contrary only in quality and not in the whole substance, persuades me. The Fernelians do not wish to snatch this for themselves, but they triumph before the victory. For, as I said, temperament is in a way double, and the whole substance is as far from the formal diseases of these innovators as white is from black. Therefore Erastus rightly says: matter does not act, form does not act, but the thing as a whole, so tempered, acts. This whole is the proximate cause of the action (f. n.), and this very thing, when harmed, is the proximate cause of the action (p.n.), or of the disease.

units.la: § 8. Rectissimè idem D.57.quod nos suprà aliquoties, Non, si quædam agunt tota substantia, propterea morbi introducuntur tales. Hoc sæpius repetendum est, ne convalescant illi, qui dant nobis integros tractatus de Occultis morbis. Idem rectè ait D. 58. Non,si medicamenta quaedam agunt totâ substantiâ, ideò aliud quid aguntaut aliter,quam quae temperamento. Theriaca quid facit? Calefacit.
units.tr: § 8. Quite rightly the same author in D. 57 says what we have said above several times: it does not follow, if certain things act through the whole substance, that such diseases are therefore introduced. This must be repeated often, lest those convalesce who give us whole treatises on hidden diseases. He rightly says the same in D. 58: if certain medicines act through the whole substance, it does not follow that something else is done, or done otherwise than by temperament. What does theriac do? It warms.

units.la: § 9. Prudenter D.61. accusat facilitatem illorum, qui perinde esse dicunt, quo modo appellent hos morbos, Substantia,an forma? Egregia ratio! Appellent igitur caelum terram, & terram caelum. Imprudenter D.62. dat illis, Formam magis esse causam actionum, quam Temperamentum, Non est heic alia forma quam temperamentum. Quò facilius creditu est,quod D.63. ait, Gravissimum esse errorem, putare, singulas corporis partes habere peculiares formas! Ego verò hoc etiam addo, Non minus gravem esse errorem, quin salsissimum in Philosophiâ Peripateticâ, Animam esse in toto corpore, & tam pariter in singulis ejus partibus.
units.tr: § 9. Prudently, D. 61 accuses the facility of those who say it makes no difference by which name these diseases are called, substance or form. A fine argument! Let them then call heaven earth and earth heaven. Imprudently, D. 62 grants them that form is more the cause of actions than temperament; here there is no other form than temperament. How much more easily is what D. 63 says believed, that it is a very grave error to think the single parts of the body have peculiar forms! I add this, however: it is no less grave an error, indeed a most false notion in Peripatetic philosophy, that the soul is in the whole body and equally in each of its parts.

units.la: § 10. Quae à D.66. usque ad finem κοινῶς & Fern. affert, non repeto, ne Camarinam moveam bonis ingratam.
units.tr: § 10. What he brings forward from D. 66 to the end, and Fernel's [κοινῶς], I do not repeat, lest I stir up Camarina, which is unwelcome to good men.

units.la: § 11. Eadem causa est, cur non vocem huc Louberti illa dicit, 1.contra Fernel.f.199. ed. Francofurtenfis. Claudicat multis modis.
units.tr: § 11. For the same reason I do not cite here those words of Louberti against Fernel, p. 199 of the Frankfurt edition. He limps in many ways.

units.la: AD LIBRVM. IV.
units.tr: TO BOOK IV.

units.la: De morbis Organicis, CAP. XVI.
units.tr: On Organic Diseases, Chapter 16.

units.la: § 1. IN ordine doctrinæ hoc statim desidero, quod Montanus cap. 1. exponat, Quid sit morbus Organicus (seu Instrumentalis) antequam doceat, Quid sit Organum seu Instrumentum, quod facit cap. 2.
units.tr: § 1. In the order of teaching, I miss at once that Montanus, in chapter 1, explains what an organic (or instrumental) disease is before he teaches what an organ or instrument is, which he does in chapter 2.

units.la: § 2. Rerum igitur ordinem secutus, ante omnia dico, sed paucis, quid Græcis sit ὄργανον? quid Latinis Instrumentum? Inde enim lucem accipiet quæstio, Quâ in re consistat essentia partis Organicæ, Instrumentalis, Dissimilaris? Nam ita quoque appellatur.
units.tr: § 2. Following the order of things, then, I first say, though briefly, what organon [ὄργανον] means to the Greeks and what instrumentum means to the Latins. The question of what the essence of the organic, instrumental, or dissimilar part consists in will be clearer from this, for that is also what it is called.

units.la: § 3. Quemadmodum essentia partis similaris sita erat in Temperamento, quæ Qualitas est, & qualitas unicuique illarum propria, quo Temperamento, quâ Qualitate eò usque mutatâ, ut actio lædatur, morbus erat similaris, qui Intemperies dicebatur: ita essentia partis Organicæ, Instrumentalis, Dissimilaris collocata est certâ dispositione partium similarium omnium, ad constitutionem Dissimilarium concurrentium, quâ dispositione catenus vitiatâ, ut actio lædatur, morbus est Dissimilaris, Organicus, Instrumentalis.
units.tr: § 3. As the essence of a similar part lay in its temperament, which is a quality, and each part's quality is peculiar to it, so that when that temperament or quality is altered far enough to harm its action, the disease is similar and is called intemperies, so the essence of an organic, instrumental, or dissimilar part is located in a certain arrangement of all the similar parts that come together to make up the dissimilar parts. When this arrangement is spoiled to the point that the action is harmed, the disease is dissimilar, organic, and instrumental.

units.la: § 4. Hæc § 4. Heic subito umbram nobis facit distinctio vetus partium, non in Similares & Dissimilares, uti nos: sed in Organa seu Instrumenta, Diff. morb. 4. Heic enim dicitur, Partium alię sunt Instrumenta primi ordinis: aliæ secundi: aliæ tertii; aliæ quarti. Quanto melius in primâ acie collocatur nostra hæc distinctio, &, subjicitur subdistinctio, Diffimilarium aliæ sunt primi ordinis, aliæ secundi, &c. Vt fiat hæc oratio:
units.tr: § 4. Here, at this point, an old distinction of parts casts a shadow over us. It is not the distinction into Similares and Dissimilares, as we make it, but into Organa or Instrumenta, in the Differentiae morborum, book 4. There it is said that some parts are Instrumenta primi ordinis [instruments of the first order], others of the second, others of the third, others of the fourth. How much better our distinction is placed in the front line, and a subdistinction is added: some of the dissimilar parts are of the first order, others of the second, and so on. Let the argument be put this way:

units.la: § 5. Partes sunt vel Similares, ut Caro, fibra, membrana, vena, arteria, nervus &c. vel Dissimilares, ut Auris, oculus, nasus, os &c. Dissimilarium alia est μονοειδής, alia πολυειδής: τῶν πολυειδῶν rursus alia magis & minus. Hæc res exemplo declaretur.
units.tr: § 5. Parts are either Similares, such as flesh, fibre, membrane, vein, artery, nerve, etc., or Dissimilares, such as ear, eye, nose, mouth, etc. Of the Dissimilares, some are μονοειδής [of one form] and some πολυειδής [of many forms]; and of the τῶν πολυειδῶν [of the many-formed], some are more and some less so. Let this matter be made clear by an example.

units.la: § 6. Brachium v.g. est pars dissimilaris, & ea quidem compositissima, seu quarti ordinis. Dividitur enim primum in partes tres majores, Brachium, Cubitum, & Manum; summa iterum dividitur in tres minores, Carpum, Metacarpum & Digitos, quæ sunt instrumenta tertii ordinis. Rursus, digiti singuli in tria internodia, quæ sunt instrumenta fecundi ordinis. Hi tandem subjiciebant illi Similares nobis dictas, vocabantque instrumenta primi ordinis.
units.tr: § 6. The arm, for instance, is a dissimilar part, and a very compound one, that is, of the fourth order. For it is first divided into three larger parts, the upper arm, the forearm, and the hand. The hand is again divided into three smaller parts, the wrist, the metacarpus, and the fingers, which are instruments of the third order. Again, each finger is divided into three joints, which are instruments of the second order. These in turn underlie those we call similar, and these we call instruments of the first order.

units.la: Hac in re consistit demum confusio, quæ adegit Fuchfium eò, ut dixerit, Partes quasdam esse instrumenta, sed non partes Instrumentarias, quo quid ridiculum magis?
units.tr: In this matter lies the confusion that finally brought Fuchsius to say that certain parts are instruments but not instrumental parts. What could be more ridiculous?

units.la: § 7. Cefpitavit Montanus quoque, qui Instrumentum hoc primum confundit cum definitione partis instrumentariæ, quæ est 1. Meth.6. Instrumentum est pars illa, quæ perfectam edere potest actionem, ut oculus visionem, brachium apprehensionem, & sic de cæteris.
units.tr: § 7. Montanus also stumbles here, since he confuses this first instrument with the definition of an instrumental part, which is in Meth. book 1, chapter 6: An instrument is that part which can produce a complete action, as the eye produces vision and the arm grasping, and so on for the rest.

units.la: § 8. Cæterum, ut perfectio hæc intelligatur, operæ pretium fuerit repetiisse ex cap.8. §6. distinctionem, quam 1ll. D. ab Aquapendente acceptam fero, inscius, si illo prior quis habet. Actio persecta, aut ab uno instrumento editur (intelligè, non sine affluxu facultatis desuper) ut visio ab oculo: aut à pluribus, συνεχέως agentibus, h.e. tantum concurrente unâquaque, quantum per naturam suam potest, ut exemplo motus, ex ejusdem cap. § 11. liquet.
units.tr: § 8. Moreover, so that this completeness may be understood, it will be worth repeating from chapter 8, § 6, the distinction which I have received, unaware whether someone had it before him, from the most illustrious Dr. Fabricius of Aquapendente. A complete action is produced either by one instrument (understand, not without an inflow of faculty from above), as vision is produced by the eye, or by several, acting together (συνεχέως), that is, each one contributing only as much as it can by its nature, as the example of motion makes clear in § 11 of the same chapter.

units.la: § 9. In utroque ordine est una aliqua pars, quæ sola agit, quam ideò etiam principem vocant, qualis in oculo humor Crystallinus, in brachio Musculus: huic cæteræ omnes subserviunt tantum, & dicuntur, non agere, sed aliquid conferre partiagenti. L 5 § 10.
units.tr: § 9. In each order there is some one part which alone acts, and for this reason they also call it the principal part. In the eye this is the crystalline humour, in the arm the muscle. All the others serve it only, and are said not to act but to contribute something to the part that acts. Book 5, § 10.

units.la: § 10. Iam, ut fiat hæc actio perfecta, oportet bene & f.n. fe habeant omnes partes,non principem tantum,sed omnes illæ,quæ quovis modo concurrunt,quod vulgò dicimus usum præbere; ut lædatur actio, non necesse est lædi semper principem, fatis est lædi quamcunque ex usum præbentibus.
units.tr: § 10. Now, for this complete action to occur, it is necessary that all the parts be well and sound, not only the principal part but all those which concur in any way, which we commonly call lending their use. For the action to be harmed, it is not necessary that the principal part always be harmed; it is enough that any one of those lending their use be harmed.

units.la: § 11. Ergò fi pars organica hæc est, estne heic quoque tale quid, quale in fimilaribus fuit Qualitas, in quo effentia morbi organici consistit?Est omninò. Hoc verbo quidem barbaro, sed apto ad rem, Organifationem voco. Quemadmodum igitur in morbis Similaribus vitium oriebatur excessu unius aut alterius Qualitatis,prout pars quælibet temperata naturaliter est: ita in Difimilaribus seu Organicis fi contingat partium fimilarium quandam diflocari, ut vitietur compofitio, est & dicitur morbus organicus.
units.tr: § 11. If, then, the organic part is of this kind, is there here also something like the quality in the similar parts, in which the essence of organic disease consists? Certainly there is. I call it organisation, a barbarous word, but apt for the matter. Just as in similar diseases the fault arose from an excess of one or another quality, according as each part is naturally tempered, so in dissimilar or organic diseases, if it happens that some of the similar parts are dislocated so that the composition is spoiled, it is, and is called, an organic disease.

units.la: § 12. Hoc explico. Quemadmodum domus,navis,omnia artificialia constant ex variis partibus, variâ materiâ conftantibus, ita inter fe dispositis, hac figurâ, hoc numero,hac magnitudine, hoc situ, ut omnia in usu sibi respondeant: ita in corpore humano quatuor sunt, quæ faciunt, ut organum fit aptum usui suo.
units.tr: § 12. I explain this. Just as a house, a ship, and all artificial things consist of various parts made of various materials, arranged among themselves in this shape, this number, this size, and this position, so that all correspond to each other in use, so in the human body there are four things which make an organ fit for its use.

units.la: § 13. Quatuor illa sunt, Conforma-
units.tr: § 13. These four are conformation,

units.la: tio, Alg' ἀπαοις: numerus, ἀεἰθμος ὁ: magnitudo, μίγεθ· π̈:situs, ϑεσις ἡ κοιναυία. Rursus, Conformatio tria sub se habet, Figuram, σχῆμα: superficiem, ἐπιφάνειαν: ca-vitates, κοιλίας, ἡ κοιλόπητας, ἡ πόρος, ἡ ὀδύς &c. Hincadeò morbi Organici sunt sextuplices, quos itaimmitto in possessione.
units.tr: [ἀπαοις]; number [ἀριθμός]; magnitude [μέγεθος]; situation [θέσις]. Again, conformation has three things under it: figure [σχῆμα]; surface [ἐπιφάνεια]; cavities [κοιλίαι], passages [πόροι], ways [ὁδοί], and so on. Hence organic diseases are sixfold, and I shall leave them in their possession as they are.

units.la: § 14. Pulcrè, quisquis ille fuit, qui scripsit l.de Constit. art. cap.3. ait, Deum & Naturam, cum hominem formarent, usum pro ideâ habuisse. Huc eunt lib. de V su partium, qui monstrant, hanc partem fuisse solidam, firmamque, ut hoc faciat: hanc fluidam, ut de loco in locum transferri possit: hanc aëriam, ut serviat liberis actionibus. Et hę sunt partes Hipp. Rursus, intersolidas hanc esse crassam, hanc tenuem: hanc membranosam, hanc carneam: hanc canalis instar pertusam, hanc cæcam, & sic deinceps.
units.tr: § 14. Whoever he was who wrote the book On the Constitution of the Art, chapter 3, rightly said that God and Nature, when they formed man, had use before them as their idea. To this belong the books On the Use of the Parts, which show that one part was solid and firm so that it might do this, another fluid so that it might be transferred from place to place, another airy so that it might serve free actions. These are the parts of Hippocrates. Again, among the solid parts, one is thick, another thin; one membranous, another fleshy; one pierced like a channel, another blind; and so on.

units.la: § 15. Harum partium singulæ ut agere possint, quod à Naturà illis demandatum est, oportet I, ita sint conformatæ & superficie tali, & figurâ tali, & cavitatibus seu viis tot & talibus. Horum uno aliquo mutato, triplex sit organicorum morborum genus, in Conformatione dictum.
units.tr: § 15. For each of these parts to be able to act as Nature has commissioned it, it is necessary, first, that it be so formed, with such a surface, such a figure, and so many and such cavities or ways. If any one of these is altered, there arises a threefold kind of organic disease, called by the name of conformation.

units.la: § 16. Onnes et. II. hoc numero sint: III, h. sudine. I V. hoc interse L 6 situs.
units.tr: § 16. The second is number; the third, magnitude; the fourth, situation.

units.la: situ. Horum aliquo vitiato, fit alius ternarius organicorum morborum,suo quodque nomine appellatum. Quare morbi organici in universum sex sunt,eo ordine explicandi,quo inventi sunt.
units.tr: Situation. When one of these is vitiated, another triad of organic diseases arises, each called by its own name. Hence organic diseases are six in all, to be explained in the order in which they were discovered.

units.la: § 17. Antequam id fiat,removendus est obex magni ponderis, ut videtur quibufdam. Quaeritur, An, quemadmodum in partibus fimilaribus, Temperies illa cujusque partis certa, pendens ex quatuor elementorum miftione, dicitur Galeno Facultas, aliquando Anima ipsa : ita quatuor illa, quae in partibus diffimilaribus confideramus,possint etiam dici? Mihi res ab omni probabilitate videtur abesse.
units.tr: § 17. Before this is done, a barrier of great weight, as it seems to some, must be removed. The question is whether, just as in similar parts the fixed temperature of each part, depending on the mixture of the four elements, is called by Galen the faculty, and sometimes the soul itself, so those four things which we consider in dissimilar parts can also be called that. To me the matter seems entirely without probability.

units.la: § 18. Ne videar φορὰ ... ut jam dudum visus sum, declaro. Ita quidem est, πόσῳ ἐπιστήμης in arte nostra est iste, Confiderat mista,quà mista sunt,non-autem quà animata etiam.Quare?Quia fervato λόγῳ μίξεως fervat animam. Hinc adeo fit, ut μίξιν suam, κρᾶσιν suam (jam enim non distinguo)audeat Medicus appellare Animam, Facultatem, Formam substantialem, licet hanc nullatenus attingat, contentus formā illā inferiore, Temperamento, quippe quod alterabile est,cum superior,Anima,non fit. Ita quidem in fimilaribus & qui hoc improimprobant, imperitiæ merito accusantur: sed quâ fronte quærimus tale quid in diffimilaribus? Vt enim essentia morbi fimilaris consistit in hoc, in Temperamento, in Qualitate, quam modò ita voco, modò ita, quia usui nihil derogat: ita essentia morbi diffimilaris consistit in Organisatione, quæ non potest participare de nominibus istis.
units.tr: § 18. Lest I seem to wander, as I have done for some time, I declare it. It is so: in our art, as far as the science goes, the physician considers the mixed things as mixed, not as animated also. Why? Because while the principle of mixture is preserved, the soul is preserved. Hence it happens that the physician dares to call his mixture, his crasis (for I no longer distinguish them), the soul, the faculty, the substantial form, although he does not touch this at all, content with that lower form, temperament, which is alterable, since the higher, the soul, is not. Indeed, in similar parts, those who disapprove of this are rightly accused of ignorance; but with what face do we seek such a thing in dissimilar parts? For as the essence of a similar disease consists in this, in temperament, in quality, which I now call by one name and now by another, because it takes nothing away from use, so the essence of a dissimilar disease consists in organisation, which cannot share in those names.

units.la: § 19. Imò, dicunt quidam, & inter hos Montanus noster, Vt tria hæc unum sunt, Temperies bona, Facultas integra, Sanitas: ita hæc tria unum quoque erunt, Organisatio mala, Facultas læsa, Morbus. Quin Galenum quoque docuisse ajunt, Et συμμετρίαν similarium esse substantiam, formam, facultatem: & συμμέλειαν diffimilarium esse substantiam, formam, facultatem instrumentalem.
units.tr: § 19. Indeed, some people say, and among them our Montanus, that just as these three things are one, good temperament, sound faculty and health, so these three will also be one: bad organisation, damaged faculty and disease. They even claim that Galen taught that the substance, form and faculty of similar parts are symmetry [συμμετρία], and that the substance, form and instrumental faculty of dissimilar parts are symmeleia [συμμέλεια].

units.la: § 20. Profecto superbissimè hæc jactantur! In similaribus ita est, ut dixi, Medicus sumit sibi hanc licentiam, cum nomen rei superioris tribuit rei inferiori, & Animam vocat, quod Temperamentum est: in diffimilaribus nihil opus est, nec Gal. eò audaciæ pervenit, quantum mihi compertum est.
units.tr: § 20. Truly, these claims are made with the greatest arrogance! In similar parts it is as I said: the physician takes this liberty when he gives the name of the higher thing to the lower and calls temperament the soul. In dissimilar parts there is no need for this, and, as far as I have discovered, Galen did not go to such boldness.

units.la: § 21. Atqui actio omnis, proprie & per se, est partis similaris: tribuitur autem toti instrumento, ex accidenti & fecun-
units.tr: § 21. Yet every action, properly and in itself, belongs to a similar part, but it is attributed to the whole instrument accidentally and secondarily.

units.la: dario? Non do tibi signum Vniversale, Omnis. Verum est, quod dicitur in iis tantum instrumentis, quae sola edunt operationem, v.g. Oculus visionem. Falsum est de iis,que per entelechiam agunt, in quibus tota aliqua pars est princeps, v.g. Musculus in apprehensione, docente ipsomet Gal, 1. Vf. part.
units.tr: Do I not grant you the universal sign, "all"? It is true of those instruments alone that perform an operation by themselves, for example the eye in vision. It is false of those that act through an entelechy, in which some whole part is the leader, for example the muscle in grasping, as Galen himself teaches in book 1 of On the Use of the Parts.

units.la: § 22. At tu,o bone, de tribus esto monitus, antequam ad specialem tractationem venias. I, Alio respectu dicitur, actio est totius compositi, non formae, non materiae: alio,actio est totius v.g. oculi;alio,humoris crystallini in oculo.II. Gal. non semper accuratus est in facultatis nomine. Alias enim ita vocat temperamentum oculi proprium(ut in exemplo perfiftam) alias commune, facultatem visoriam influentem.Sic in ἀμαυρωσει,salvo oculi instrumento,cecitas adest, propter defectum spiritus visorii.III.Apud eundem Gal. partium unius instrumenti quatuor sunt ordines: Vna agit: aliae sunt fine quibus non:aliae, cum quibus melius: aliae tutelae gratia, ad quam refero Ornatum. Hac proportione quadam sunt in iis quoque, quae per entelechian agunt. Atq; hinc pendent Morbi in usu, in quibus quidam sunt mirificiffimi. Dictum enim est, actionem laedi, non tantum, quando pars praecipua laborat: sed & cum una ex inferioribus.
units.tr: § 22. But you, my friend, must be warned of three things before you come to the special treatment. First, the action is said to belong to the whole compound in one sense, not to the form or the matter; in another sense, the action belongs to the whole, for example of the eye, and in another sense to the crystalline humour in the eye. Second, Galen is not always exact in his use of the word faculty. Sometimes he calls the eye's own temperament its faculty (to keep the same example), and sometimes the common faculty, the visual power flowing in. Thus in amaurosis [ἀμάυρωσις], with the eye's instrument unharmed, blindness is present because of a lack of visual spirit. Third, according to the same Galen there are four orders of parts in one instrument: one acts; some are needed without which it cannot act; some are needed with which it acts better; and some are for protection, to which I refer ornament. In a certain proportion this holds also for those things that act through an entelechy. From this depend diseases in use, some of which are remarkably wonderful. For it has been said that the action is harmed not only when the principal part is affected, but also when one of the lower parts is.

units.la: De morbis Organicis Conformationis in figura, CAPVT. XVII.
units.tr: On the Diseases of Organic Conformation in Figure, CHAPTER XVII.

units.la: § 1. Conformatio cum consistit in tribus, orditur Montanus cap. 3. à figurâ : sed multa non necessaria infercit. Hoc laudabile est, quod docet, Figuram tum lædere tantum, cum actionibus officit : hoc contra reprehensibile, quod confundit statim cum morbis in situ.
units.tr: § 1. Since conformation consists of three things, Montanus, in chapter 3, begins with figure, but he introduces many unnecessary matters. It is commendable that he teaches that figure is harmful only when it interferes with actions; it is blameworthy that he at once confuses it with diseases of position.

units.la: § 2. De φoξοῖς Græcis vocatis multa inania disputat. Manet enim hoc, φoξοὶ sunt illi, quibus vel alterutra, vel utraque deest σεγοόλη, itaque fit Caput acuminatum. In quibus utraque abest, ii caput habent rotundum, seu orbiculare, qualis est scillæ radix. Vnde concludo, Periclis caput omninò fuisse tale, nec magis illum fuisse σχυοxεῖφαλον, quam φoξὸν, verum hoc modo, quo dixi. Qui quoniam callidiffimus fuit, repetendum est illud, Tum defectum prominentiarum esse in vitio, cum actiones capitis lædunter. Quamdiu enim angustia calvariæ non obest rectæ cerebri conformationi, res benè habet. Novi enim aliquot tales, qui astu-
units.tr: § 2. Concerning those called oxoi by the Greeks [ὀξοί], he argues many empty things. For this remains: the oxoi are those in whom either one or both of the ridges on the top of the head [σαγίττα] are lacking, and so the head becomes pointed. Those in whom both are missing have a round or orbicular head, such as the squill bulb. Hence I conclude that Pericles' head was entirely of this kind, and that he was no more a skytocephalos [σκυτοκέφαλος] than an oxos [ὀξός], but in the way I have described. Since he was very clever, that saying must be repeated: the lack of prominences is a fault only when the actions of the head are harmed. For as long as the narrowness of the skull does not hinder the proper conformation of the brain, all is well. I know some such people who were very shrewd,

units.la: (No marginal notes on this page.) astutissimi erant : novi & stupidos;
units.tr: (No marginal notes on this page.) very shrewd indeed; I also know stupid ones.

units.la: § 3. De iis qui βλαισοὶ ἢ βλαισοὶ dicuntur, moneo, Vocem aliquando latissimè patere, pro omni omnium partium distortione, quo nomine Blæsi à Latinis vocantur illi, qui quovis modo linguâ tubant. Aliquando genibus solis tribui, sed tam pro iis, quibus introrsum curvantur, quam quibus extrorsum. Aliquando alteri vitio tantum, cum introrsum fleƈtuntur, quo malo qui tenentur, Valgi Latt. dicuntur, aut Vatiæ. Tum verò oppositum ci vitium peculiare nomen habet, apud Græcos quidem ποῖ, ἢ ποιδὸς, ἢ ποιδὸς, apud Latt. autem Varus. Hæc à quibusdam per incuriam invertuntur, à quibus deceptus ego, Com. in 3. Vs. part. n.146. nunc retraƈto. Quibus se jungat Montanus, nescio : tu videris. Pariter non video, quid sibi velit illis, Hæc vitia non semper esse morbos : sed aliquando symtomata. Hoc enim forte dixisse debuit, quod ab initio, Non semper esse morbos, sed vitia; tum videlicet, cum non lædunt actiones. Et hanc distinctionem observant etiam I Cti.
units.tr: § 3. As for those who are called blaisoi [βλαισοί] or blaisoi, I warn that the word sometimes has a very wide meaning, covering every distortion of all the parts, and under this name the Latins call blaesi those who lisp in any way. Sometimes it is applied to the knees alone, both to those bent inwards and to those bent outwards. Sometimes it is applied only to the other defect, when the legs bend inwards; those who suffer from this are called valgi or vatiae by the Latins. But the opposite defect has a special name of its own: among the Greeks [ποδός], and among the Latins varus. Some people through carelessness reverse these terms, and I, deceived by them, retracted this in my commentary on the third part of the Vsus partium, no. 146. With whom Montanus agrees I do not know; see to it yourself. Likewise I do not see what he means by saying that these defects are not always diseases but sometimes symptoms. He ought perhaps to have said what he said at the beginning: they are not always diseases but defects, namely when they do not harm the actions. The jurists also observe this distinction.

units.la: § 4. Non minus stupeo ad illa, Morbus est, non figura, sed figuræ vitium. Imò morbus est, non in figurâ, sed in parte, hoc, illo modo figurâtâ. Et est alioquin hic error Montani, Omnes morbos, quo ad suum fundamentum, pertinere ad primam Qualitatis speciem. Huic contraibat SCHERBIVS, ὁ πνεῦμα, Vbicunque parti,quæ est fundamentum, accedit ἀμελεία, ἀμελεία illa est morbus.
units.tr: § 4. I am no less astonished at his statement: "It is not the figure that is the disease, but a fault of the figure." Indeed, the disease is not in the figure but in the part, shaped in this or that way. And moreover this is Montanus' error, that all diseases, as far as their foundation goes, belong to the first species of quality. Against this Scherbius argued in Greek [ὁ πνεῦμα]: wherever a part which is the foundation is affected by negligence [ἀμέλεια], that negligence is a disease.

units.la: § 5. Cujus dicti occasione ventilare placet id, quod Montanus habet fine cap.6. Morbus figuræ facit aliquando morbum in cavitate. v.g. Nasus compressus seu fimus facit angustiam in meatu narium, unde difficilis respiratio. Heic, inquit, fimitas est causa continens. Nihil minus, ajebat ILLE. Imo hoc exemplum conficit causam continentem. Vt enim Gal, docet. 2. Nat. hum. 1. Causa continens primo lædit actionem. At heic angustia primo lædit actionem. ..
units.tr: § 5. On the occasion of this saying I am pleased to examine what Montanus says near the end of chapter 6: a disease of figure sometimes produces a disease in a cavity. For example, a nose that is compressed or flattened makes a narrowing in the passage of the nostrils, whence breathing is difficult. Here, he says, flatness is the containing cause. "Nothing less," that man used to say. Indeed this example proves the containing cause. For as Galen teaches in book 2 of On the Natural Faculties, book 1: a containing cause first harms the action. But here the narrowing first harms the action.

units.la: De morbis Conformationis in cavitati- bus, CAPVT. XVIII.
units.tr: On the Morbid Conformations in the Cavities, CHAPTER XVIII.

units.la: § 1. Avitates hę, vel κοιλόπνες sunt: vel κοιλίαι vel πόρος vel σύρων vel ὁδοί. De his agens Mont. c.4. duplex morborum genus constituit, & recte. Alii enim sunt in cavitatibus ftrictioribus, aut ctioribus, quos Obstructiones mox appellabo: alii in laxioribus, patentioribus que, quos Defluxiones.
units.tr: § 1. These cavities are either κοιλόπνες [hollow spaces], or κοιλίαι [bellies], or πόροι [passages], or σύριγγες [tubes], or ὁδοί [ways]. Concerning these, Montanus in chapter 4 sets out a twofold kind of disease, and rightly so. For some lie in the narrower or tighter cavities, which I shall shortly call obstructions; others lie in the looser and more open ones, which are defluxions.

units.la: § 2. De his cum Gal. duobus locis egerit (de Dift. & Cauf. morb. c. 7. ext.) non minus jejuné quam obscuré, prodente Montano ipso : quid faciemus!
units.tr: § 2. Galen treated these in two places (On the Differences and Causes of Diseases, ch. 7, end), and did so no less meagrely than obscurely, as Montanus himself reports. What are we to do!

units.la: § 3. Cum Pathologica scriberem, videremque SCHERBIVM in omnibus secutum esse Montanum, secutus sum ego quoque: sed parcè. Cum postea Institutiones pararem, & totum istud, quod Montanus tribus cap. inciperet fordere; conversus sum, partim ad correctiones, partim ad explicationes, quoquo modo exculpavi Galenum.
units.tr: § 3. When I was writing the Pathologica, and saw that Scherbius had followed Montanus in everything, I followed him too, but sparingly. Later, when I was preparing the Institutiones, and wanted to rework all that Montanus had begun to set out in three chapters, I turned partly to corrections and partly to explanations, and in whatever way I could, I defended Galen.

units.la: § 4. Nunc paucis me absolvo, & diconon Morbi in Cavitatibus duplices sunt, quemadmodum cæpi dicere. Alii sunt Obstructiones, cum viæ, vel ex toto, vel ex parte inferciuntur, ut jam non amplius spatium fit transitui humorum, spirituumve naturalium. Alii sunt defluxiones, ῥεύματα, ῥευματισμοί, ῥευματισμοί ἀλγηδόνες vocatæ priscis : quin ἀλγηδὼν ἡ ἀλγηδονώδης, ἀπόστασις, μετάστασις, ἀπόσταξις, & fi quas alias voces habent illi, quibus significant translationes humorum, varumve de parte in partem.
units.tr: § 4. Now I will finish in a few words. Diseases of the cavities are twofold, as I began to say. Some are obstructions, when the passages are either wholly or partly stuffed, so that there is no longer room for the passage of humours or natural spirits. Others are defluxions, called by the ancients ῥεύματα [flows], ῥευματισμοί [rheumatisms], ἀλγηδόνες ῥευματικαί [rheumatic pains]; indeed ἀλγηδὼν ἡ ἀλγηδονώδης [pain that causes pain], ἀπόστασις [withdrawal], μετάστασις [transfer], ἀπόσταξις [dripping], and whatever other words they have that signify the transfers of humours, or their movement from one part to another.

units.la: § 5. Huc duo imprimis perpulerunt me. Alterum, nostrorum, tam Theoreticorum (ut sic dicam) quam Practicorum finitertas. Cum enim oratio Gal. atque adeo adeò ipsa rerum evidentia vellet duos sibi oppositos morbos: quid facerem de Soliditate Fuchfii, Argenterii, Planeri, aliorum? Cum pariter viderem, plerisque omnibus aquam hærere, in describendo multorum symptomatum morbo proximo:non potui non animum applicare ad desertas Ἀλγέσεις ῥευματικὰς, & fi quo alio modo appellabant veteres. Podagra v.g. eftfymptoma, dolor quippe, cujus morbi? Omnes tacent, etiam Ill. SENERTVS, qui novissime scripsit, & feorfim,fortassis,quia locum pro illà non invenit.
units.tr: § 5. Two things above all drove me to this. The first is the timidity of our people, both theoretical (so to speak) and practical. For since Galen's account, and indeed the very evidence of things, requires two opposed diseases, what was I to do with the solidity of Fuchsius, Argentier, Platter and the others? Since I likewise saw that nearly all of them were stuck, when describing the proximate cause of many symptoms, I could not help turning my mind to the abandoned rheumatic pains, and to whatever other name the ancients gave them. Gout, for example, is a symptom: it is pain, of course, but pain of what disease? All keep silent, even the illustrious Sennert, who wrote most recently and separately, perhaps because he found no place for it.

units.la: § 6. His poteram me absolvere, nisi scirem, Animadversiones me promisisse in Montanum.Spes autem est,non omninò me ingrata allaturum, nec prorsus inutilia iis,qui Veritati suum deferunt honorem, ob-partám ab hostibus victoriam.
units.tr: § 6. I could have excused myself from all this, if I did not know that I had promised Animadversions on Montanus. There is hope, however, that I shall offer things not wholly unwelcome to those who give Truth her due honour, and not altogether useless to them, in return for the victory won over their enemies.

units.la: § 7. Recte Avicennam culpat, qui morbos in cavitatibus angustis,uno verbo,Obstructiones,facit duplices,aliosReceptaculorum, seu trium vasorum proprie dictorum Medicis,venarum,arteriarum, nervorum: alios Ventriculorum, seu cavitatum majorum, Ventriculi sc. speciatim sic dicti,cum intestinis, & gulā Ventriculorum cerebri & cordis,cavitatum renum & vesicæ utriusque,&c. Reverà,omnes hi morbi aliò spectant.
units.tr: § 7. He rightly blames Avicenna, who, in narrow cavities, that is, in obstructions, makes two kinds of disease: some of the receptacles, or of the three vessels properly so called by physicians, veins, arteries and nerves; others of the ventricles, or larger cavities: the stomach, specifically so called, with the intestines and gullet; the ventricles of the brain and heart; the cavities of the kidneys and of the bladder, and so on. In truth, all these diseases look elsewhere.

units.la: § 8. Ventriculus sic dictus (nisi sitâ saburrâ, quæ pertinet ad Errorem externum ) fi non possit expellere chylum, laborat intemperie frigidâ, vel solâ, vel cum siccitate,humiditateve. Cum aliunde influxit quid,est ῥευματισμὸς, Si gula & larynx non admittant cibum, potumve propter inflammationem:quis cogitet de obstructione? Et sic de cæteris,ne frustrà tempus terâ.Proinde,quæ dicit ille de differentiâ affectuum vię ab affectibus conceptaculorum,suâ ineptitudine corruunt.
units.tr: § 8. The stomach so called (unless it is burdened with foul matter, which belongs to the external error), if it cannot expel the chyle, suffers from a cold intemperature, either alone or with dryness or moisture. When something has flowed in from elsewhere, it is a rheumatism. If the gullet and larynx do not admit food or drink because of inflammation, who would think of an obstruction? And so with the rest, lest I waste time. Therefore what he says about the difference between affections of the passage and affections of the receptacles collapses under its own absurdity.

units.la: § 9. Ferneliũ,qui incôfideratò sequitur Arab.meritò accusat,quod unũ genus morbi bis descripserit.Tantò magis,quod nominamutârit,ne frustrà fapuiffe videatur.
units.tr: § 9. Fernel, who follows the Arabs without consideration, is rightly accused of describing one kind of disease twice, and all the more so because he changed its name, as if he might seem not to have wasted his labour.

units.la: § 10, In explicando Gal. labitur multimodis. Primò enim ineptè amplificat Leoniceri errorem, In Græco est μεΐγεθος τε καὶ πληθος, Hæc ille vertit, Tam magnitudo, tam multitudo, quasi duo forent. Noster, quasi de industriâ opem illi ferens,Aut in magnitudine,aut in multitudine. Neutrum admittunt particulæ expletivæ τε καὶ. Quo loco fi quis dixerit, ὁ μείζων καὶ πληθος non esse ἰσοδύναμον mutaffe expletivas, in ἢ vel ἀλλ' : huic dicetur,quamvis ἰσοδυ- ναμεῖ. γαμξ̃ν non fint:non ob id recte mutatæ funt voculæ illæ. Quamobrem pro ϖλήθ@ olim legi ϖλέτ@ : poftea comperi, Planerum in D. de Morb. org. voluiffe μήκ@ , eodem plane fenfu. Hac habita correctione Gal.quidem recte fubdiderit illa, ποῦμα δὲ ποῦ ψ νοσήματ@ : ineptiffime autem Montanus, V triufque vitium,aut in exceffu effe,aut in defectu.Caeterum,in his ipfis Gal. verbis infignis eft ἀχυ@ἀοψίω, quam ego damno , mutatá lectione ex l.de Cauf. Senfus enim vult, ποῦμα δὲ τεσσάρων ἀλλοῖα. Hinc perfuaderi fibi patiatur Montanus,fex illa,quæ numerat, exceptâ Obftructione,non effe,vel Modos, vel Species , vel Differentias : fed partim Morbos alii generis, partim Modos obftructionum. Hoc non vidiffe,vel Planerum, vel Scherbium,mireris forte ? Quia nimis amabant Galenum ? Ego fine affectu dico, quod res eft,hinc facto initio.
units.tr: § 10. In explaining Galen he slips in many ways. First, he foolishly magnifies Leoniceno's error. The Greek reads μέγεθός τε καὶ πλῆθος [magnitude and multitude]; he renders this "tam magnitudo, tam multitudo" [as much magnitude, as much multitude], as if there were two. Our author, as though deliberately lending him aid, gives "either in magnitude or in multitude." The expletive particles τε καὶ allow neither reading. In such a place, if someone says that ὁ μείζων καὶ πλῆθος is not equivalent to ..., and that the expletives were changed into ἢ or ἀλλ', he will be answered that, even though they are not equivalent, those little words were not rightly changed on that account. Hence I once read πλέτος for πλῆθος; afterwards I found that Platter, in his De morborum organicorum, wished for μῆκος [length], in exactly the same sense. With this correction made, Galen rightly adds those words about the other kinds of disease, but Montanus most foolishly says that each fault lies either in excess or in defect. Moreover, in these very words of Galen the word ἀχυ... is conspicuous, which I reject, the reading having been changed from the book De causis; for the sense requires "of four different kinds" [ἀλλοῖα]. Let Montanus allow himself to be persuaded by this: the six kinds he enumerates, with obstruction excepted, are not Modes, Species or Differences, but partly diseases of another kind and partly modes of obstructions. Are you perhaps surprised that neither Platter nor Scherbius saw this? Because they loved Galen too much? I speak without bias, as the matter stands, having made a start here.

units.la: § 11. Coalitum,σύμφυσιν,caufam effe,falfum eft.Imo eft morbus in fitu. Falfum & hoc eft,σύμφυσιν capi heic eo modo, quo in l. de Off. De naturali enim συμφύσει eft fermo ibi: heic de p.n. Talis σύμφυσις cum fit in ἀπόλυσις dictis, cur morbum in fitu confundimus cum morbo in viis?Rurfus,cum vitium conformationis in gemino poro bilario,2 Temp.6. extra dubium fit morbus in numero excedente, quod Montanus expressè dicit, Plures numero, f. 155. b. In excessu multitudinis, f. feq. a. cur huc arcessit? Eadem est ratio occlufionis labiorum, uteri, narium : sunt enim morbi in situ. Hac in re quam miserè fe torqueat Planerus D. 16. & feq. vide, fis, ipsus, vel ideo, quia D. 22. resumit. Quot ergo heic sunt cefpitationes enormes?
units.tr: § 11. That coalition, σύμφυσις [growing together], is a cause, is false. It is rather a disease of position. It is also false that σύμφυσις is taken here in the sense it has in the book De officiis: there the discussion concerns natural symphysis, here the non-natural. Since such a symphysis is among the so-called ἀπόλυσεις [releases], why do we confuse a disease of position with a disease of the passages? Again, since a defect of conformation in the double biliary pore (2 Temp. 6) is beyond doubt a disease of excess in number, which Montanus states plainly ("more in number," fol. 155b; "in excess of multitude," fol. following, a), why does he bring it in here? The reason is the same for the occlusion of the lips, of the womb, and of the nostrils: they are diseases of position. See how miserably Platter twists himself in D.16 and following, and whether he himself, perhaps for this reason, resumes the matter at D.22. How many monstrous stumblings there are here!

units.la: § 12. Ἐμφεγξις, Obstructio, ut in rei veritate sola huc pertinet, & proprie rapit ad fe curationem, ceu Planerus loquitur, quia morbus est, non causa:ita inanis est distinctio, fi integra fit occlufio, vitium in multitudine esse; fi non integra, in magnitudine. Vno verbo, Multitudo debet hinc facessere: quia ad Numerum pertinet. Et hoc volo exaudire Planerum quoque.
units.tr: § 12. Ἐμφραξις [obstruction], since in the truth of the matter it alone belongs here, and properly carries the cure to itself, as Platter puts it, because it is a disease and not a cause: so empty is the distinction that, if the occlusion is complete, the fault lies in multitude; if not complete, in magnitude. In a word, Multitude ought to depart from here, since it pertains to Number. And I want Platter to hear this too.

units.la: § 13. Σπενοχωρία, angustia, quam facit vel tumor aliquis p. n. vel excrefcentia, quo modo huc facit? Tumor est morbus perse : excrescentia est morbus per fe. Illi, ἐπιμεῖνως, per refultantiam, accidit angustia, quam facit morbus : hæc, morbus in numero est, cui pariter accidit anguftia. Tu scito, Planerum D. 26. uti verbis Montani.
units.tr: § 13. Στενοχωρία [narrowness], which some swelling or outgrowth causes: how does this fit here? A swelling is a disease in itself; an outgrowth is a disease in itself. To the former, by secondary effect, there accrues the narrowing which the disease makes; to the latter, a disease in number, narrowing likewise accrues. Know that Platter, at D.26, uses the words of Montanus.

units.la: § 14. Ψαλμὸς, compressio, meo judicio, non differt ab Angustia, & congessit Gal.tantum varia nomina,quibus Medici tum utebantur. Quo modo pingat Plan. D.28,videat,qui vult.
units.tr: § 14. Ψαλμός [compression], in my judgment, does not differ from narrowness, and Galen merely collected the various names which physicians then used. Let whoever wishes see how Platter depicts it at D.28.

units.la: § 15. Ξυνίζωσις, confidentia, ne pilo quidem melior est prægressis duabus. Et quomodo quadrat exemplum Montani de vesica plena? Plan. D.24. & 25. mera verba dat nobis.
units.tr: § 15. Ξυνίζωσις [contraction] is not a whit better than the two preceding. And how does Montanus's example of the full bladder fit? Platter, at D.24 and 25, gives us mere words.

units.la: § 16. Ἀναισθησία quoties intueor, toties indignor! Quo modo enim causa, quæ affectum contrarium habet, stare potest cum iis, quæ memorata sunt? Et videtur displicuisse ipsi Gal. qui non explicat debito modo. Nec expediverit rem, qui excusationem illius meditari volet,In fine cap. de Diff. vocat ἐυφωνίαν, ut in de Cauf. κ̈ννωσιν. Ne diutius te moer, Tam non potest referri ἀνασύσωσις ad viarum angustias, ut fit, ceu dixi, ex advero oppositus affectus, is, inquam, qui constituit Διαγνώσεις ξυνῳκῆσις, suprà §. 4.
units.tr: § 16. Whenever I look at ἀναισθησία [insensibility], I am indignant! For how can a cause that has the contrary affection stand together with those things already mentioned? Galen himself seems to have been dissatisfied with it, since he does not explain it in the proper way. Nor will he have clarified the matter who wishes to devise an excuse for it. At the end of the chapter On the Differences he calls it εὐφωνία [good sound], as in the book De causis he calls it κίννωσις. Not to weary you further: ἀνάσυσις [recovery of breath] cannot be referred to the narrowness of the passages, as I said, since it arises from a genuinely opposed affection, the one, I mean, which constitutes the diagnosis mentioned above, §4.

units.la: § 17. Rebus Gal. sic stantibus, non fatis intelligere heic possum, cur Mont. cap.5. inchoët expositionem cap.7. de Diff. morb.
units.tr: § 17. With Galen's matters standing thus, I cannot understand why Montanus, in chapter 5, begins the exposition that appears in chapter 7 of On the Differences of Diseases.

units.la: Non mala fit melior causa patrocinio. Videamus strictim quædam.
units.tr: A bad cause is not made better by advocacy. Let us look briefly at some points.

units.la: § 18. Cum videret, reliquis causis ad-di την ἀναστασιν, exficcationem, fi verti ita potest; exsiccatio autem fit Intemperies; quid ait? Quod non intelligo.
units.tr: § 18. When he saw that he had added to the other causes ἀνάστασιν [την ἀναστασιν], exsiccation, if it may be rendered so, and exsiccation becomes intemperies. What does he mean? I do not understand it.

units.la: § 19. Quia dixerat in σηνογωεία, Δαί-μα, καὶ συνιζήσεως, aliquando esse unum morbum, aliquando duos; & verò per exemplanonsatis declaraverat: allaborat vir eximius, ut lucem tenebris asserat. Revera πεπείσεγ est.
units.tr: § 19. Because he had said that in συνοχωκία [σηνογωεία], δαῖμα [Δαί-μα] and συνιζήσεως there is sometimes one disease and sometimes two, and had not explained this clearly enough by example, the eminent man labours to bring light out of darkness. Indeed, it is a matter of πεπείσθαι [πεπείσεγ] (being persuaded).

units.la: § 20. Morbum morbum parere quia scripserat, vult nos docere, quando id fiat? Pax!
units.tr: § 20. Since he wrote that one disease begets another, does he wish to teach us when this happens? Peace!

units.la: § 21. Non majoris momenti sunt Dubitationes,quas cap.6.habet.Primam jam occupavi,Morbine an Causæ sint sex dicta πολυμορφα? Sunt partim causæ, partim morbi,ut dixi. ἀδρομυσία admitti potest.
units.tr: § 21. The Doubts he raises in chapter 6 are not of greater weight. I have already dealt with the first: whether the causes are six, called πολυμορφα [πολυμορφα]? They are partly causes and partly diseases, as I said. ἀδρομυσία [ἀδρομυσία] may be admitted.

units.la: § 22. Occupavi & alteram,quod Gal. alibi modò plura sex illis numeret, modò pauciora. Loquitur modò cum his, modò cum illis, quia accurationem nemini promisit. Et hoc malo, quam verborum latiorem vel pressiorem significationem. Interim recté dixit, In vocabulis esse repugnantiam, in re nullam.
units.tr: § 22. I have dealt with the other too: that Galen elsewhere sometimes counts more than those six and sometimes fewer. He speaks sometimes with these and sometimes with those, because he never promised accuracy to anyone. I prefer this to a broader or narrower meaning of words. Meanwhile he rightly said that there is a contradiction in the words, but none in the thing.

units.la: § 23. De σεγγώσει omissa recté ait, Non posse excusari factum. In reliquis parco & mihi & aliis. Velle enim omnia producere, quæ Gal. varia occasione scribit, insaniæ simile fit...
units.tr: § 23. On what is omitted concerning σεγγώσει [σεγγώσει], he rightly says that the deed cannot be excused. In the rest I spare both myself and others. For to wish to bring out everything Galen writes on various occasions is like madness...

units.la: De morbis Conformationis in superficie CAPVT XIX.
units.tr: On the diseases of Conformation in the surface, CHAPTER XIX.

units.la: § 1. [I]N his subitò Montanus ( & quis non ex nostris? ) cap.7. provolat ad asperitatem & lævitatem, cumulatis exemplis impertinentibus.
units.tr: § 1. Here Montanus suddenly rushes (and who among our own people does not?) in chapter 7 to roughness and smoothness, piling up examples that have nothing to do with the point.

units.la: § 2. Maximè urgere videtur, quod Hipp. ( ut hinc incipiam ) 2.in 6.Epid.4. jubet Exasperare & Lævigare. Me verò, cum diligentius intueor, exempla longè alió ducunt.
units.tr: § 2. The strongest weight seems to lie in Hippocrates (to begin from him) in the second book of the Epidemics, section 6, where he orders us to roughen and to smooth. But when I look at the matter more carefully, the examples lead in quite a different direction.

units.la: § 3. Horum primum apud Gal. est Faucium asperitas,quæ tuflim facit. Ego verò censeam esse Continui-solutionem, quæ dolorem facit. Quin, fi malum diutius duret, Vlcus, quod vel Phthisis doceat ex destillatione.
units.tr: § 3. The first of these in Galen is the roughness of the throat, which causes coughing. I, however, would hold that it is a solution of continuity, which causes pain. Indeed, if the injury lasts longer, it becomes an ulcer, as phthisis teaches us from its discharge.

units.la: § 4. Alterum est, scabrities cutis omnis. Ego verò putem, symptoma esse hoc, quod pendeat ex transmissione viπoforum humorum è visceribus, & jam morbum ex viis laxis.
units.tr: § 4. The second is roughness of the whole skin. I, however, would think this a symptom which depends on the passage of the sharp humours out of the viscera, and already a disease of the loose passages.

units.la: § 5. Tertium, nifallor, est Dysenteria ipsa. Hæc verò ad Continui-solutiones refertur ab omnibus. In hac fi utar muciλαginibus, hordei χλιγεμμοτ, aliis, ad humoris acrimoniam respicio, ad caufam, inquam.
units.tr: § 5. The third, unless I am mistaken, is dysentery itself. But everyone refers this to solutions of continuity. If in this I use mucilages, barley gruel and other remedies, I look to the sharpness of the humour, to the cause, I say.

units.la: M
units.tr: M

units.la: § 6. Quartum est pilorum defectus.
units.tr: § 6. The fourth is loss of hair.

units.la: Hic vero est morbus in numero.
units.tr: This is indeed a disease among the rest.

units.la: § 7. Quintum sordida ulcera sunt, quae abstergentibus exasperamus. Miror ego, quae haec locutio fit? Cum enim fordes auferimus, laevigamus potius. Et quis pro morbo peculiari habeat, cum fit causa fine qua non?
units.tr: § 7. The fifth is foul ulcers, which we roughen by cleansing. I wonder what kind of expression this is. For when we remove the foulness, we rather smooth. And why should anyone count it a peculiar disease, when it is a cause without which the thing cannot happen?

units.la: § 8. Sextum Ventriculi laevitas est, ob copiam pituitae. Hoc accepto: sed ut liceat accommodare rebus meis, de quibus mox.
units.tr: § 8. The sixth is smoothness of the stomach, owing to an abundance of phlegm. I accept this, but let me apply it to my own matters, which I shall come to shortly.

units.la: § 9. Septimum est haemorrhoidum citatio per peffos. Haec quis credat, haemorrhoidum curam esse morbum? Sed admittatur ἀδύνατα: Siquidem illae substiterunt ob tenacem pituitam, clauentem oscula ipsarum, jam hoc quoque pro me est.
units.tr: § 9. The seventh is the summoning of haemorrhoids through the pores. Who would believe this, that the cure of haemorrhoids is a disease? But let us grant impossibilities [ἀδύνατα]: since those haemorrhoids have subsided because of thick phlegm closing their mouths, this too is on my side.

units.la: § 10. Octavum, Palpebrarum ευκees fi curantur cathereticis, quibus praemittitur levius exasperans, quid hoc ad rem? Idem dicam de verrucis, de favis, de aliis.
units.tr: § 10. The eighth, the eyelids' lashes [ευκ ees], if they are cured with caustics, preceded by a milder roughening agent: what has this to do with the matter? I would say the same about warts, about favi, and about other such things.

units.la: § 11. Haec cum talia sint, quae vel ipse saxeus Morychus contemnat, quid Noster? Primum, substituit dentes molares, ex 11. Vf. part. 8. Facile illi do, dentes à Natura ideo factos esse asperos, ut molere possint; nec displicet simile alapidibus mola-
units.tr: § 11. Since these things are of such a kind that even the stony Morychus would scorn them, what does our author say? First, he substitutes the molar teeth, from Galen's On the Use of the Parts, book 11, part 8. I readily grant that the teeth were made rough by Nature so that they might grind, and I do not object to a similar comparison with millstones

units.la: ex 11. Vf. part. 8.
units.tr: from 11. Vf. part. 8.

units.la: molaribus sumtum : sed quid hoc ad morbos? Fortassis quia per senium lævigati,indicatio oritur exasperandi ?
units.tr: taken from the molars; but what has this to do with diseases? Perhaps because, when they are smoothed by old age, the indication for roughening arises?

units.la: § 12. Deinde profert offa fphacelata & cariosa, quæ radimus, inquit. Audio : sed statim subvenit mihi solutio-continui. Paucis. Asperitas illa est causa fine quâ non, perinde ac in sordidis ulceribus.
units.tr: § 12. Then he brings forward bones that are gangrenous and carious, which we scrape, he says. I hear this, but at once the solution of continuity comes to mind. In brief: that roughness is a cause without which the thing does not happen, just as in foul ulcers.

units.la: § 13. Tertiò addit uteri superficiem internam asperam, absque quâ femen receptum iterum effluit. Et hanc causam dant quidam, cur scorta non concipiant. Non semel ego in Anatomiis contrectavi dictam superficiem : sed nihil sensi. Revera, hiant quidem vasa in uteri cavitatem: sed non extant adeo, ut digito sentiri possint.
units.tr: § 13. Thirdly, he adds that the inner surface of the uterus is rough, without which the received seed flows out again. Some give this as the reason why prostitutes do not conceive. I have more than once handled that surface in anatomies, but I have felt nothing. In truth, the vessels do indeed open into the cavity of the uterus, but they do not stand out so much that they can be felt with the finger.

units.la: § 14. Eadem ratio est ventriculi & intestinorum. Vasa enim mefaraica dicta fibrulis tenuissimis obliquè potius, quam rectà progrediuntur, & hauriunt chylum ἀλγεδώς, uti Galenus loquitur. Revera, imaginaria sunt ista omnia, & indigna liberali ingenio!
units.tr: § 14. The same reasoning holds for the stomach and the intestines. For the so-called mesenteric vessels proceed obliquely rather than straight, by very fine fibres, and they draw up the chyle with difficulty [ἀλγεδώς], as Galen says. In truth, all these things are imaginary, and unworthy of a liberal mind!

units.la: § 15. At villosus est intrinsecus ventriculus? Scio : sed quid inde? Pudet me profecto minutiarum istarum, quas tamen jactant omnes! Dicam igitur, quid mihi in mentem venerit.
units.tr: § 15. But is the stomach villous on the inside? I know; but what follows from that? I am truly ashamed of these trifles, which nevertheless everyone boasts of! I shall therefore say what has come into my mind.

units.la: § 16. Legenti mihi <bl>Ἀλφὰ ἐκ ἐεἰδες</bl>, à quibus sternutatio & tussis fiant, 2. Cauf. fym.1. A. Diff. morb. 7. forte fortunâ obtulêre femihi morbi ii, de quibus agimus, quod Gal, expresse dicat, fieri fi exasperetur, quod læve erat.
units.tr: § 16. As I was reading the first book of the Problems [Ἀλφὰ ἐκ ἐεἰδες], from which sneezing and coughing arise (Causes of Symptoms, book 1, section 1; Differences of Diseases, book 7), it happened by chance that the diseases we are discussing were presented to me, which Galen expressly says arise if what was smooth is roughened.

units.la: § 17. Hoc confirmavit mihi duplex Φαινόμενον, Sternutatio fi à nobis excitari potest indito naribus pipere, pyrethro, helleboro, nigellâ, fl. lilii convallium, tacaco: quidni à naturâ quoque ita fiat? Submisso, inquam, acri aliquo humore, vaporéve, qui membranam narium interiorem irritet? Tussis fi à nobis fieri potest comestis amygdalis, præsertim rancidis, juglandibus, avellanis, aliisque talibus: quidni à naturâ quoque id fiat, delabente in asperam arteriam humore acri, & ftimulante membranam internam, valdè alioqui sensilem? Singultus eadem ratione esse videtur, quod ab aliquibus cieri possit, comesto tantum pulvere piperis, us Gal. de fe scribit.
units.tr: § 17. This was confirmed for me by a double phenomenon [Φαινόμενον]. Sneezing can be provoked by us when pepper, pellitory, hellebore, nigella, the root of lily of the valley, or tacamahac is put into the nostrils. Why should it not also happen thus by Nature, when some sharp humour or vapour is sent down which irritates the inner membrane of the nostrils? Coughing can be provoked by us when almonds, especially rancid ones, walnuts, hazelnuts and other such things are eaten. Why should this not also happen by Nature, when a sharp humour drips down into the windpipe and stimulates its inner membrane, which is otherwise very sensitive? Hiccup seems to work by the same reasoning, since it can be provoked in some people merely by eating a powder of pepper, as Galen writes of himself.

units.la: § 18. Quamobrem conclusi, Quæcunque symptomata fiunt à morbo & naturâ simul, in iis morbus, seu difpofitio morbifica est superficies exasperata, aut contrà lævigata.
units.tr: § 18. Wherefore I concluded: whatever symptoms arise from a disease and from Nature together, in these the disease, or morbid disposition, is a surface that is roughened, or on the contrary smoothed.

units.la: § 19. Heic aliquis, voce hac excitatus, Quid fiet inquiat, de morbo opposito? fito? Iam Gal. in fup. dedit mihi sub manus duos casus, alterum quidem, cum villi in cavitate ventriculi ita sunt obruti pituitâ, nihil uti sentiat ventriculus: alterum autem, cum hæmorrhoides non eunt, quod ora ipsarum sint occæcata à pituitâ foris allitâ, quà patere debebant.
units.tr: § 19. Here someone, stirred by this statement, may ask: what will happen with the opposite disease? Already Galen, in the passage above, has put in my hands two cases: one, when the villi in the cavity of the stomach are so buried in phlegm that the stomach feels nothing; the other, when the haemorrhoids do not flow, because their mouths have been blocked by phlegm applied from outside, where they ought to have been open.

units.la: § 20. Hoc posterius accommodo omnibus intestinis, & confirmo pulcerrimâ historiâ, quam accidisse Lipfio, 7ⁿ Ὠ ⃛ Heurnius refert, præf. op. suorum. Laborabat vir eximius melancholia hypochondriaca, &, inter alia symptomata, perpetuò habebat pigram alvum. Credo ego infelicem etiam chyli distributionem adfuisse. Hic, dato aliquando medicamento purgante, pituitam excrevit vifcidiffimam, ita figuratam, quali intestina ipsa exiffent,&c.
units.tr: § 20. I apply the latter to all the intestines, and I confirm it by a most beautiful history, which Heurnius reports as having happened to Lipsius, in the preface to his works [7ⁿ Ὠ ⃛]. A man of distinction was suffering from hypochondriac melancholy, and, among other symptoms, he constantly had a sluggish bowel. I believe that an unhappy distribution of chyle was also present. Here, when a purgative medicine had at some point been given, he discharged a most viscid phlegm, shaped as if the intestines themselves had come out, and so on.

units.la: § 21. Et hæc quidem hactenus visa mihi sunt de morbis superficiei: fi cui difpliceant, det meliora. Ego hinc peto responsum ad dubium Montani,cap.8. Similarefne sint morbi, an inftrumentarii? Inftrumentarii omninò,cum motum yitiofum creent.
units.tr: § 21. And these things, so far, have seemed to me to be said about diseases of the surface; if anyone dislikes them, let him give better. From here I ask for an answer to Montanus's doubt, in chapter 8: are these diseases similar, or instrumental? Instrumental altogether, since they create a faulty motion.

units.la: § 22. Alienum à rebus nostris est alterum: tamen dicam aliquid. Quærit, Asperitas hæc, aut levitas morbosa Cita enim proponi debebat) estne ab alteraM trice,an à formatrice ? Quæro ego, De utrâ asperitate loqueris,Interná, an externâ?Non puto de illâ:ergò de hac.De quâ itafentio, somnium esse, quod ostendi exemplo uteri & intestinorum. Hoc quia sensus stabilit, non est opus aliis.
units.tr: § 22. The other point is foreign to our matters; still I shall say something. He asks whether this morbid roughness or smoothness (for it ought to have been stated at once) comes from the material cause or from the formal cause. I ask: of which roughness are you speaking, the internal or the external? I do not think of the former, therefore of the latter. Concerning which I judge that it is a dream, as I have shown by the example of the uterus and the intestines. Since sense establishes this, there is no need for other proof.

units.la: § 23. Quæ sùbnectit de loco Hipp.in quo ille exasperat, miserè calamitosum est.Non enim de morbo loquitur, sed de opere chirurgico, quo tollit causam fine quâ non.Calamitofius illud est de scabie, leprâ & exanthematis. Morbus est Intemperies: scabrities symptoma est qualitatis tactilis.Et hæc de Conformatione.
units.tr: § 23. What he adds about the place in Hippocrates where he roughens is wretchedly calamitous. For he is not speaking of a disease, but of a surgical operation, by which he removes a cause without which the thing does not happen. What is more calamitous is that he speaks of scabies, leprosy and exanthemata. The disease is an intemperie; roughness is a symptom of the tactile quality. And so much concerning Conformation.

units.la: De morbis in Numero, CAP. XX.
units.tr: On Diseases in Number, CHAP. XX.

units.la: § 1. ACturus Montanus cap.9. de his morbis ex de Diff. morb. cap.8.videtur ante omnia monendus esse de vitio, quod subodoror in codicibus Gal. Ita autem concipio locum, Τῶν μὲν περιπλευόντων, τὰ μὲν ἐν τῷ γένες ἐσιπῶν καὶ Φύσιν, ὡς εἰ καὶ τὰ γένεσθαι δὲ ... ὡς ἐν τῇ ἐφθαλμῷ ὁ πλεῖον, ἡ ἐν ῥινὶ βλαστημός τῆς στρεψόσ.
units.tr: § 1. Since Montanus, in chapter 9, is about to treat these diseases from On the Differences of Diseases, chapter 8, I think I must first warn about a fault which I suspect in the text of Galen. I construe the passage thus: "Of the things that surround [Τῶν μὲν περιπλευόντων]..." and the rest as printed, with the sense that, as in the eye the greater part, or in the nose an outgrowth, is a growth that narrows the passage.

units.la: § 2. Videtur deinde monendus esse idem,ne subitò acceptet omnia,quæ Gal. dicit. Nimirum, ita comparare nos fas est, ut exiis, quæ dicuntur, utiles indicationes hauriamus. At quid boni habemus ex distinctione illâ, Eorum, quæ abundant (tu puta, ita ut actionem lædant) alia sunt f.n. alia p.n. Agimus de morbo, qui est p.n, potestne aliquid in eo cfle, quod fit f. n ʒ Quale quale fit id, quod lædit actionem, certè morbosum est. Seponamus igitur inanias has, & sectemur utiliora. Vide Ioubert. dict.4.
units.tr: § 2. I should also warn the same reader not to accept everything Galen says at once. We must so compare things that from what is said we draw useful indications. But what good do we get from that distinction: "Of those things which abound (for instance, so that they injure the action), some are f.n., others p.n."? We are dealing with a disease which is p.n.; can there be anything in it which is f.n.? Whatever injures the action is certainly morbid. So let us set aside these empty distinctions and pursue the more useful ones. See Jouberts, Dict. 4.

units.la: § 3. Quæro, quomodo faciat hæc exemplum sexti digiti? Licet enim monstrofum fit: incertum tamen est, an morbofum fit? Imò pro roboris indicio habetur in Sacris, proposito Philiftæo illo fedigito, ut hoc tantum dicam.
units.tr: § 3. I ask how the example of the sixth finger bears on this. For although it is a monstrosity, it is uncertain whether it is morbid. Indeed, in Scripture it is regarded as a sign of strength, when that Philistine with six fingers on his hand is set forth; let me say only this much.

units.la: § 4. Quæro etiam, quomodo sensus Gal. non laboret, nisi pterygion & polypus ita collocetur, ut ego collocavi? Vtut enim ἀισϑητήριον fit exercitentia cor- neæ, ut polypus nasi: dici tamen non pofsunt esse f.n. quia lædunt actionem. Nec quidquam juvat oppofitio inter has excrescentias & calculos, lumbricofque. Increpo enim illud, Lædunt actionem.
units.tr: § 4. I ask also how Galen's meaning would not hold unless the pterygium and the polyp were placed as I have placed them. For although the organ of sense is hindered by the growth on the cornea, as by a polyp of the nose, these cannot be called f.n., because they injure the action. Nor does the contrast between these growths and stones and worms help at all. For I object to that very point: "They injure the action."

units.la: § 5. Dicis, Sine injuriâ non potes rejicere distinctionem Gal. Certè, sextus digitus est res naturalis: lumbricus est præternaturalis. Rideo! Quasi lumbricus non codem modo fit naturalis. Vbi ubi enim est,est à naturâ productus. At verò nos confideramus non simpliciter, & Physicè : sed Medicè, & quidem in homine,in quo non minus p.n. est, quam ullum aliud. Indicat enim expulsionem. Nec hilum valet expositio Montani, Lumbricus est ex materiâ inutili,& toto genere p.n. Sextus digitus ex utili &c.
units.tr: § 5. You say: "Without injustice you cannot reject Galen's distinction. Certainly the sixth finger is a natural thing; the worm is preternatural." I laugh! As if the worm were not equally natural. For wherever it is, it is produced by nature. But we consider the matter not simply and physically, but medically, and in man, in whom it is no less p.n. than anything else. For it indicates expulsion. Nor is Montanus' explanation worth anything: "The worm comes from useless matter and is wholly p.n.; the sixth finger from useful matter, etc."

units.la: § 6. Interim accepto monitionem Montani,Istas resin numero,modò morbos efle, modò causas.Morbi sint, cum primò lædunt actionem: causæ, cum interventu alterius. v.g. Polypus est causa: quia lædit respirationem interventu alterius, carnis. An in obstructionibus ab humoribus aliter fe habeat res?
units.tr: § 6. Meanwhile, accepting Montanus' warning, these things are in the number: sometimes they are diseases, sometimes causes. They are diseases when they first injure the action; causes when they do so through the intervention of another thing. For example, the polyp is a cause, because it impairs respiration through the intervention of another thing, the flesh. Does the matter stand differently with obstructions from humours?

units.la: § 7. Hanc in rem, Mont. c.10. tradit duas regulas, ex quibus discere est, I. Quando morbus fit res in numero? quando causa? I I.Quando utrumque,& morbus & causa? Quæ quia paulò meliora sunt quæstionibus Logicis,indicaffe sufficiat. De usu gurgulionis seu columellæ quæ concionatur,ex trivio sunt. Longè enim alia comperta sunt.
units.tr: § 7. To this end Montanus, in chapter 10, gives two rules from which one learns: I. When is a thing in number a disease, and when a cause? II. When is it both a disease and a cause? Since these are somewhat better than logical questions, it is enough to have pointed them out. The use of the little uvula, or little column, which preaches, belongs to the trivium; for quite other things have been discovered.

units.la: § 8. Quæ sequuntur, faciunt mihi suspicionem, Montanum hoc egisse, ut magnum exponeret librum. Quæstio, quam proponit cap.11. paulò minus quam inepta est. Cum morbi in numero duplices sint, vel aucto, vel deficiente : si in numero deficiente sint, cujus partis sunt, illiusne, quæ periit? an illius, quæ requist? Quis ausit dicere, Perditæ esse? Cum periit digitus, aut digiti internodium, jam morbus manus totius est : cum manus summa tota, brachii.
units.tr: § 8. What follows makes me suspect that Montanus did this to lengthen his book. The question he proposes in chapter 11 is rather less than sensible. Since diseases in number are of two kinds, either by excess or by deficiency: if they are in a deficient number, to which part do they belong, to the part that has perished, or to the part that remains? Who would dare to say they belong to the part that has perished? When a finger, or an internode of a finger, has perished, the disease now belongs to the whole hand; when the whole hand has perished, to the whole arm.

units.la: § 9. In seq. capp. 12. 13. & 14. primum quidem proponit objectiones Argenterii contra numerum auctum, ad quas etiam respondit : deinde autem contra deficientem, quas simul diluit. Mihi pauca hæc sufficiant. Vbi indicationes non variant, loquitur Gal. modo cum his, modo cum illis, prout illi morbos varie considerabant.
units.tr: § 9. In the following chapters 12, 13 and 14, he first sets out the objections of Argenterius against the increased number, and answers them; then the objections against the deficient number, which he dissolves at the same time. A few points suffice for me. Where the indications do not vary, Galen speaks now with these, now with those, according as they considered diseases in various ways.

units.la: § 10. Cum dicit Argenterius, In calculo non est sanitas, ergo nec morbus : decipit in figura dictionis, ajebat SCHERBIVS. * Calculus non est morbus, nec ullo modo consideratur ut pars corporis, quod Turrianus volebat : sed calculus in hac parte, cui inhæret, facit dispositionem talem, quæ morbus est. Alopecia, & alii pilorum affectus, sunt morbi in numero : pili enim sunt partes corporis, non abnuente Montano. Quod si curatur defectus ille, non curatis pilis, sed intemperie cutis subjectæ : non id multum refert. Reverà, casus pilorum est.
units.tr: § 10. When Argenterius says, "In a stone there is no health, therefore neither is there disease," he errs in the figure of speech, said Scherbius. A stone is not a disease, nor is it considered in any way as a part of the body, as Turrianus wished. But the stone in this part, to which it adheres, creates such a disposition, and that is a disease. Alopecia and the other affections of the hairs are diseases in number, for hairs are parts of the body, and Montanus does not deny it. But if that defect is cured not by treating the hairs but by correcting the intemperature of the underlying skin, this does not matter much. In truth it is a case of the hairs.

units.la: * Vide Ant. Erast. f. 118 a. M symptoma, & pendet ab intemperie cutis: interim aliter nos loqui nil prohibet, ab evidentiori fc. captà denominatione.
units.tr: * See Ant. Erast. f. 118a. M symptom, and it depends on the intemperature of the skin. Meanwhile nothing prevents us from speaking otherwise, taking the more evident denomination.

units.la: § 11. Quæ cap.15. spargit pro excufando Gal. non sunt magni momenti. Ve enim nuper dixi,non omnia possunt excusari. Res est,tam in partibus agentibus, quam usum præbentibus morbus est,non autem in illis quidem morbus, in his autem causa. Vide dictatum alt. Ioub. in I. de Diff. morb.
units.tr: § 11. What he scatters in chapter 15 to excuse Galen is of no great moment. For, as I said just now, not everything can be excused. The point is this: whether the disease is in the acting parts or in those that supply the use. Not that it is a disease in the former and a cause in the latter. See the other lecture of Jouberts on the first book of On the Differences of Diseases.

units.la: § 12. Caterum, attingit heic Montanus id, quod supra cap. 15, § 8. & 21. ex Ill. D. ab Aquapendente dixi, Actionem alias fieri ab uno instrumento, alias à pluribus κατ' συνεχείαν agentibus. In pofteriori ordine cum sint duæ valdè celebres actiones, vox & sermo, quid dicit Montanus? Quod non capio. Plura illa, instrumenta habere rationem unius. In- terim innuit magis quam dicit, Inter plurainftrumenta, ad unam actionem concurrentia, unum esse; quod fit princeps. Dico igitur, Inter duarum dictarum actionum, Larynx est pars princeps, nisi, mavis, inter laryngis partes, γλωττὶς appellata. Ita in mafticatione quæ est pars princeps? Lingua. Atqui larynx & lingua funt partes diffimilares? Hoc est, quod dico, doctrinam illam departe principe similari non esse universaliter veram. § 13. Hec decisio fervit iis etiā,què c.16: agitantur. Rectè ait Mont: fi rectè intelligas, ex Hipp. & Gal. ξυῤῥοια μία, ξυμπνοια μία, ξυμπαθεία παν(τ)ῶ. Intellectus est. In iis actionibus, quæ obeuntur à pluribus partibus, hoc fit ab hac illud ab hac. Hinc est,ut quo dignius est id,quod laborat,eo plus noxæ afferunt toti actioni. Manus totius actionem esse apprehensionem, rectè dicitur : sed ita, ut manus summa principatum obeat, brachium cum cubis to serviat, quatenus,vel sequimur res apprehendendas, vel distantia fortiter ftringimus. Brachio igitur cum cubito manuque abscissa, perit hoc totum, Apprehendere, sequi,stringere : abscissa manu sumatantum, Apprehendere, & brachio superstiti superest,quodammodo sequi & trudére.lam fi quæras,Quæ pars inter fimilares potissimum hoc præstet dabit tibi Gal: musculos.
units.tr: § 12. Moreover, Montanus here touches on what I said above, in chapter 15, §§ 8 and 21, from the illustrious Fabricius ab Aquapendente: that an action is sometimes performed by one instrument, sometimes by several agents acting in continuity [κατ' συνεχείαν]. In the latter case, since there are two very famous actions, voice and speech, what does Montanus say? I do not grasp it: that those several instruments have the standing of one. Meanwhile he hints, rather than says, that among several instruments concurring in one action, one is chief. I say, therefore: among the two actions named, the larynx is the principal part, unless you prefer, among the parts of the larynx, the one called the glottis. So in mastication, which is the principal part? The tongue. But are the larynx and the tongue dissimilar parts? This is what I mean: the doctrine that the principal part is among the similar parts is not universally true. § 13. This decision serves also for the things discussed in chapter 16. Montanus rightly says, if you understand Hippocrates and Galen rightly: "one flux, one breathing, universal sympathy" [ξυῤῥοια μία, ξυμπνοια μία, ξυμπαθεία παν(τ)ῶ]. The meaning is this: in those actions which are performed by several parts, this is done by this part, that by that. Hence it is that the more important the part that labours, the more harm it does to the whole action. It is rightly said that the whole hand is the action of grasping; but so that the palm holds the chief place, and the arm with the elbow serves, insofar as we either follow the things to be grasped or grip strongly at a distance. So with the arm cut off at the elbow along with the hand, this whole perishes: grasping, following, gripping. With the hand alone cut off, grasping perishes, and the surviving arm retains, in a way, the power to follow and to thrust. Now if you ask which similar part chiefly performs this, Galen will give you the muscles.

units.la: De morbis in Magnitudine CAP. XXI.
units.tr: On Diseases in Magnitude, Chapter XXI.

units.la: § 1. VT morbi in numero duplices erant, § 8. ita in magnitudine quoque (cap.17.) sunt alii in excessu, alii in defectu. Vtrumque accidit, vel toti corpori, vel certæ alicui parti.
