In toto corporc,. corpore, excessus quidem dicatur mihi Obesitas, five solius pinguedinis fit, five solius carnis, five utriusque: defectus autem Gracilitas. Illius exemplum dat Gal. Diff. morb.9. Nicomachum Smyrneum, quem Asclepiades curârit. Ita enim lego. Talis etiam fuit D. Thomas de Aquino. Hujus sunt calidi quidam, qui alimentum omne dissipant, nec unquam corpus accipiunt, etiamsi pinguedine farcias. Talis fuerat SCHERBIVS in adolefcentiâ, ut ipsemet sæpè mihi, sed qui in conjugio corpus sibi conciliârat balneo aquæ dulcis.
units.tr: § 1. Just as diseases are twofold in number, § 8. so in magnitude too (ch. 17) some are in excess and others in defect. Either condition may affect the whole body or some particular part. In the whole body, excess may be called obesity, whether it is of fat alone, of flesh alone, or of both; defect is leanness. Galen (De morb. diff. 9) gives an example of the former in Nicomachus of Smyrna, whom Asclepiades cured; that is how I read it. Thomas Aquinas was such a man too. Of the latter there are some hot-tempered people who dissipate all their nourishment and never gain bulk, even if you stuff them with fat. Scherbius was like this in his youth, as he often told me himself, but in marriage he won a body for himself by bathing in fresh water.

units.la: § 2. Et hoc quidem in latitudine fanitatis, in qua ferè ἀτροφία dicitur in morbis φθίσις Tabes, utroque latè accepto vocabulo.
units.tr: § 2. This belongs to the breadth of health, in which atrophy [ἀτροφία] is commonly called, in diseases, phthisis [φθίσις] or tabes, the word being taken broadly in both senses.

units.la: § 3. Particularis obesitas, ut sic dicam, quibusdam est in cruribus, ut & contrarius affectus. Quidam enim tam crassas habent suras, ut indecorum sit: quidam, passerum instar, exiles, idque in latitudine sanitatis. Montanus etiam linguam ita increscere posse autumat, quod nescio. Idem Priapismum etiam huc accersit, quod plane nego. Est enim à flatibus πνεῦμα (Ita enim malo cum Foëfio quam φύσαμα) in oculo huc facere vel ideo non credo, quia repugnat ὁ ἐτυμος. Particularis culuris atrophia frequens est in artubus.
units.tr: § 3. Particular obesity, so to speak, is found in some people's shins, and so is the opposite condition. Some have such thick calves that it is unseemly; others, like sparrows, are slender, and this within the range of health. Montanus also claims that the tongue can grow in this way, which I do not know. The same man brings priapism in here too, which I flatly deny. It comes from winds [πνεῦμα] (I prefer this reading with Foesius to φύσαμα) in the eye, and I do not believe even this, because the etymology argues against it. Particular atrophy of the calves is common in the limbs.

units.la: § 4. Posthæc cap.18. folicitè admodum disputat Montanus, An perpetuæ veritatis fit, quemadmodum in morbis numeri semper vitiatur etiam figura partis:ita in magnitudinis semper fervetur? Apud me quia τῶν ἀεεργων εἰ, non libet mihi pro Gal. autoritate tantoperè pugnare. Sit,an non fit, perinde esto. Logicum enim est.
units.tr: § 4. After this, in ch. 18, Montanus very carefully discusses whether it is a perpetual truth that, just as in diseases of number the shape of the part is always vitiated, so in magnitude it is always preserved. For my part, I have no wish to fight so hard for Galen's authority on this point. Let it be so or not; it makes no difference, for it is a matter of logic.

units.la: § 5. Idem dictum esse volo de quæftione cap.19. An, veluti in morbis numeri excedentis proponebatur illa diftinctio, quædam esse f. n. quædam p. n. ita heic quoque fit? Ego paucis me expedio, Quidquid lædit actionem, est p.n. quale quale etiam fit. Nec refert, fi Gal. hoc,illudve dixit. Quo minus curo, quid vel Fuchfius comminiscatur, vel Fernelius, vel Montanus ipse.
units.tr: § 5. I want the same said of the question in ch. 19: whether, as in diseases of excess number that distinction was drawn, that some are f.n. and some p.n., the same holds here too. I settle it briefly: whatever hinders the action is p.n., however it is otherwise. Nor does it matter whether Galen said this or that. I care little what Fuchsius, Fernelius, or Montanus himself may invent.

units.la: § 6. Hoc loco.cap.20. & 21. dux noster facit excursionem, An Gal. in definitione morbi intellexerit actiones solitas tantum, adeoque cæcitas, aliique morbi congeniti, non sint morbi? An & quatenus morbi sint dispositiones?
units.tr: § 6. At this point, in chs. 20 and 21, our author makes a digression: did Galen, in his definition of disease, mean only customary actions, so that blindness and other congenital conditions are not diseases? And are dispositions diseases, and if so, in what sense?

units.la: § 7. Quod ad priorem, suscitavit hanc litem Turrifanus in Plusquamcommento, sed præter omnem rationem. Galenus enim absolute loquitur in definitione suâ; è medio vulgo defumtâ. Sed & Autor artis huc non it, cum sermo illi fit deiis actionibus,.quas dudum aliquis exercuerit.
units.tr: § 7. As to the first question, Turrianus raised this dispute in his Super-commentary, but without any reason. Galen speaks absolutely in his definition, which he took from common usage. Nor does the author of the art come into it here, since his discussion concerns those actions which someone has long been exercising.

units.la: § 8. Quod ad posteriorem, ratio dubitandi est, In dispositionibus est ordo partium, qui in numero non est. Montanus refert fe ad superiora, & dicit, Non est in numero numerante,abstractivè: sed in numero numerato, concretivè, cum parte,inquam,quæ numerum subit.
units.tr: § 8. As to the second question, the reason for doubt is this: in dispositions there is an order of parts, which is not present in number. Montanus refers back to what he said above and says: it is not in number as the counting number, abstractly, but in the counted number, concretely, that is, with the part which takes on the number.

units.la: § 9. Verum enim verò cum hinc fequi videretur, Morbum in numero fore substantiam, dicit, Non substantia, v.g. sextus digitus est morbus: sed sextus digitus ita disponit manum, ut fit inepta apprehensioni,ut ficloquar. Hinc liquet, planissimè heic esse ordinem.
units.tr: § 9. Indeed, when it seemed to follow from this that a disease of number would be a substance, he says: it is not a substance. For instance, a sixth finger is a disease, but the sixth finger so arranges the hand that it is unfit for grasping, as I may put it. From this it is clear that there is a plain order here.

units.la: §. 10. Rediens Montanus in viam, cap.22. quærit, Atrophia fitne morbus, an symptoma? Gal. enim dicit utrumque. Est utrumque! Est morbus: quatenus ita affectis perit corpus. Est symptoma: quatenus læsa actio facultatis nutritoriæ est.
units.tr: § 10. Returning to the road in ch. 22, Montanus asks whether atrophy is a disease or a symptom, since Galen says it is both. It is both! It is a disease, insofar as the body perishes in those so affected; it is a symptom, insofar as it is an impaired action of the nutritive faculty.

units.la: §. 11. Excurrens iterum, quatuor integris cap. in locum Gal. Diff. morb. 8. aliquammulta proponit contra Fuchsium & Argenterium. Sum paucis contentus. & ϰⲁⲓ impune possunt dicimorbistam in numero,quam in magnitudine. Quando autem hoc vel illud fit, ingratum fuerit exponere, Logica enim sunt, dico iterum. Vide Ioub. dict. 5. Com. dict.
units.tr: § 11. Running off again over four whole chapters on Galen's passage in De morb. diff. 8, he sets out much against Fuchsius and Argenterius. I will be content with a few words. And one may say without fault that there are more diseases in number than in magnitude. To explain when this or that occurs would be tedious, for these are matters of logic, as I say again. See Ioub. dict. 5, Com. dict.

units.la: De morbis in Situ. Cap. XXII.
units.tr: On Morbi in Situ. Chapter XXII.

units.la: § 1. HEic (cap.27.) Montanus in ipso limine cadit, secutus salsam lectionem Cod. Graecorum, qui habent, Diff. morb.10. συνοχωσ, cum ςτσως deberet esse.
units.tr: § 1. Here (chap. 27) Montanus falls at the very threshold, following the corrupt reading of the Greek codices, who have συνοχῶς [synochōs], when it ought to be στάσις [stasis]. (Diff. morb. 10.)

units.la: § 2. Ni fallor, locus ipse & confusaneus, & obscurus est : ideo manum illi admovi in Patholog.cap.226. Heic,nulla facta in rebus mutatione, hanc solam paraphrasin dabo. Morbi in situ, dicere debet Gal. sunt illi,cum partes vicinae amitttunt rationem situs naturalem,quem fitum, non ζῶν tantum voco, sed & ἐμιλίαν, κοὴ κοινωνίαν. Accidit hoc quatuor modis. Horum primus est,cum,quae contingere fe debent,discedunt à fe invicem, ut in luxationibus & fubluxationibus, Alter est,cum, quae adjacere sibi mutuo debent, fe invicem ingrediuntur, ut in herniis quibusdam,cum per peritonaeum ruptum, dilatatum vel decidit intestinorum aliquod, aut etiam omentum. Tertius,cum,quae disjunctae esse volunt, connafcun-
units.tr: § 2. If I am not mistaken, the passage itself is confused and obscure, which is why I took it in hand in the Pathology, chapter 226. Here, without changing anything, I will give only this paraphrase. Galen says that there are diseases "in position" when neighbouring parts lose their natural arrangement in relation to one another. I call this arrangement not only position [ζῶν] but also association [ἐμιλίαν] and common fellowship [κοινὴν κοινωνίαν]. This happens in four ways. The first is when parts that ought to touch one another come apart, as in dislocations and subluxations. The second is when parts that ought to lie next to each other enter into one another, as in certain hernias, when some loop of intestine, or even the omentum, drops or is pushed through a ruptured or stretched peritoneum. The third is when parts that ought to be separate grow together [connasc-]

units.la: nalcuntur, ut cum pulmo conglutinatur cum pleurâ, hepar cum ventriculo. Huc pertinent & foramina obliterata, in iis, qui ἀρτηρίαι dicuntur. Quartus, cum pars situm suum amittit ob ligamentum vel brevius, vel longius, unde fit, ut trahatur, modò in dextrum, modò in sinistrum: modò longius eat, quam debebat: modò non perveniat, quo debebat. Hæc qui cum Gal. Montano, rerumque naturâ conferre volet, faciat.
units.tr: nascuntur], as when the lung is glued to the pleura, or the liver to the stomach. Here belong also the foramina that have been closed up in those called arteries [ἀρτηρίαι]. The fourth is when a part loses its position because of a ligament that is either too short or too long, whence it happens that it is pulled now to the right, now to the left, now goes further than it should, now does not reach where it should. Let whoever wishes to compare these things with Galen, with Montanus, and with the nature of things do so.

units.la: Dubia quædam in genere CAP.XXIII.
units.tr: Certain doubts in general, CHAPTER XXIII.

units.la: § 1. Bfolutis morbis Organicis omnibus Montanus, cap.28. orditur telam valdè longam, contra Erastum imprimis, & Chr. à Vegâ, qui volebant Morbos hactenus dictos non esse morbos, sed causas morborum. De hoc negotio, vide, si ambagibus caperis, judicium primum Erafti, Anat. p.47. & seq. quidque respondeatur in Ant-Eraft. f.56. b. & seq. deinde, Eraftum iterum, Anat. p.88. & seq. Ant-Eraft. f.67. a. Ego carptim ago.
units.tr: § 1. After completing the organic diseases, Montanus, in chap. 28, begins a very long web of argument, chiefly against Erastus and Christoph à Vega, who wanted the diseases mentioned so far not to be diseases but causes of diseases. On this matter, if you are not put off by the circumlocutions, see first Erastus' judgement, Anat. p. 47 and following, and what was answered in the Anti-Erastus, fol. 56b and following; then Erastus again, Anat. p. 88 and following, and Anti-Erastus fol. 67a. I deal with it piecemeal.

units.la: § 2. Morbi omnes, dicebant isti, non minus quam similares vobis enumerati, Causæ sunt, non morbi. Calculus v.g. est causa continens doloris, non autem morbus.
units.tr: § 2. All diseases, these men said, which have been listed for you as similar parts, are causes, not diseases. A stone, for example, is the containing cause of pain, not a disease.

units.la: bus, Heic primum rideo ineptias. Calculus , per fe consideratus , neque causa est, neque morbus : sed est fundamentum ἀμερογίας hujus , uno verbo , pars morbi essentialis : Calculus enim cum parte,cui insidet,facit hanc ἀμελείαν , quæ morbus est.Deinde,Causa continens,ut illi defcribunt , nihil aliud est quam morbus ipse, ut suprà descripsi ex Langio, aliisque.
units.tr: Here first I laugh at the absurdities. A stone, considered in itself, is neither a cause nor a disease, but it is the foundation of this dyscrasia [ἀμετρία], in a word, an essential part of the disease. For the stone, together with the part in which it lodges, produces this disorder [ἀμέλεια], which is the disease. Then, the containing cause, as they describe it, is nothing other than the disease itself, as I described above from Lange and others.

units.la: § 3. Sunt , qui fine pudore ausint jastare, Morbi in numero deficiente quomodo possunt esse morbi , cum pars abfens non possit agere. Nescio quid dicam amplius?Pueri,quiadhuc sub ferulà sunt. didicerunt hanc regulam ex Loffio,Pofitis causis sufficientibus,& non impeditis, sequitur effectus. Hinc concludunt,fi deest aliquid manui , quo minus apprehendere possit,quid frustrà disputas? Si femur est egressum acetabulo suo , & impeditur ambulatio, quid molestus es?
units.tr: § 3. There are some who shamelessly dare to boast: how can there be diseases in a deficient number, since a missing part cannot act? What more can I say? Boys who are still under the rod have learned this rule from Lossius: when the sufficient causes are posited and nothing hinders them, the effect follows. From this they conclude: if something is lacking to the hand so that it cannot grasp, why do you argue in vain? If the thigh has come out of its socket and walking is hindered, why do you trouble us?

units.la: § 4. Non prudentiores sunt in fimilaribus. Si qualitas illa excedens , ajunt, est morbus , eo modo, quo mediocris est sanitas : morbus & sanitas different tantum fecundum magis & minus.Quid absūrdi? Si qualitas illa fe habet ut quatuor, est sanitas:Si ut quinque vel sex, est morbus. Non oportet ista considerare Mathematicè : sed quatenus latitudo quædam sanitatis est,cum quâ Anima in corpore durare potest. Hinc fit, ut veré dicum fit, In ipso morbo est sanitas quaedam. Nisi enim ita esset, nemo convalescere. Ob hanc eaufam puto etiam in ὑγιεινοῖς concedendam. esse ὑγιεινόν. Propter enim hanc utimur Alimentis. Proptereà recte intelligendum est, quod Arist. in Probl. ait, In sanitate quietem esse in morbo motum. Natura enim in morbo pugnat. Vide Erastum, Anat. p. 36.
units.tr: § 4. They are no wiser about similar parts. If that excessive quality, they say, is a disease in the way that moderate health is health, then disease and health differ only in degree, more and less. What is absurd about that? If that quality stands at four, it is health; if at five or six, it is disease. We ought not to consider these things mathematically, but insofar as there is a certain latitude of health within which the soul can endure in the body. Hence it is rightly said that in disease itself there is a certain health. For unless it were so, no one would recover. For this reason I think that even in things conducive to health [ὑγιεινοῖς] it must be granted that there is something conducive to health [ὑγιεινόν]; for we use foods for this reason. Therefore what Aristotle says in the Problems must be rightly understood: that in health there is rest, and in disease motion, for nature fights in disease. See Erastus, Anat. p. 36.

units.la: § 5. Pergit Mont. cap.29. & de diffimilaribus morbis quaerit, An non sint plures sex descriptis? Gal. enim in de Const. artis requirit Essentiam etiam, Ref. Essentia nihil aliud est, quam temperamentum. Ibi additur σύνταξις ordo, Quo factum est, ut quidam morbos Ordinis velint. Ref.I. Vel hoc etiam argumentum sit, librum de Const. non esse Gal. II. Ordo non differt à situ, quam vis situs latius pateat.
units.tr: § 5. Montanus goes on in chap. 29 and asks, concerning dissimilar diseases, whether there are not more than the six described. For Galen, in the book On the Constitution of the Art, requires also the Essence, and the essence is nothing other than the temperament. There is added the arrangement [σύνταξις], that is, order, on account of which some want diseases of order. Reply: (1) Let this also be an argument that the book On the Constitution is not Galen's. (2) Order does not differ from situation, although situation has a wider range.

units.la: § 6. De morbis Conformationis peculiare movet dubium cap.30. Cur Gal. dispescuerit in tres? Quid ex Curtio dicat Mont. videre possunt, qui volunt. Quid contra Curtium idem, non refero. Ipse distinguit formam essentialem, quae εἶδος sit, ab accidentali, quae μορφή. Cui differentiæ quid opponi poffit, dixi alibi.
units.tr: § 6. Concerning diseases of conformation, Montanus raises a peculiar doubt in chap. 30: why did Galen distinguish them into three? Those who wish may see what Montanus says from Curtius. I do not report what the same man says against Curtius. He himself distinguishes the essential form, which is the species [εἶδος], from the accidental form, which is the shape [μορφή]. What can be set against this distinction I have said elsewhere.

units.la: § 7. Tandem finit cap.31. propofitâ duplici quæftione, An partes organicæ laborare poffint morbis fimilaribus? Et contra; An fimilares morbis organicis?
units.tr: § 7. Finally, in chap. 31 he puts a twofold question: Can organic parts suffer from similar diseases? And conversely: can similar parts suffer from organic diseases?

units.la: § 8. Ad hoc pofterius refpondet negativè, Partes fimilares morbis organicis laborare non poffunt: fi videantur tamen, laborare ut organicas. Heic meritò lucem defideres! Qua enim confideratione fimilares funt fimul diffimilares? An quæftio propofita eft de iis fimilaribus tantum, quæ & funt, & dicuntur: non autem de iis, quæ dicuntur tantum? Venæ, arteriæ, nervi, mufculi reverà funt diffimilares: quia poffunt obftrui. Non concoquo: dico igitur.
units.tr: § 8. To the latter he replies in the negative: similar parts cannot suffer from organic diseases; yet if they seem to suffer, they suffer as organic parts. Here you will rightly miss some light! For in what respect are similar parts at the same time dissimilar? Or is the question asked only about those similar parts which both are and are called such, and not about those which are called such only? Veins, arteries, nerves and muscles are in fact dissimilar, because they can be obstructed. I cannot digest this, so I say:

units.la: § 9. Partes fimilares, quatenus funt fub primâ conftitutione corporis noftri, non poffunt laborare morbis organicis: quatenus fub fecundâ funt (h.e. concurrunt ad factuiram partium diffimilarium) poffunt. Veruntamen, non dicuntur tum laborare ipsæ, fed organum, quod conftituunt. Res exemplo fiat clara: Obftructio hepatis non eft alibi, quamin venis: tamen non dicuntur laborare venæ, fed hepar. Ita de liene, de cerebro, dealiis omnibus.
units.tr: § 9. The similar parts, insofar as they belong to the first constitution of our body, cannot suffer from organic diseases; insofar as they belong to the second (that is, insofar as they contribute to forming the dissimilar parts), they can. Nevertheless, it is not said that they themselves suffer, but the organ which they constitute. The matter will be made clear by an example: an obstruction of the liver occurs nowhere except in the veins, yet it is not said that the veins suffer, but the liver. So it is with the spleen, the brain, and all the others.

units.la: § 10. Ad priusillud refpondet, & redè, Non funt aftimandi morbi ex læsâ
units.tr: § 10. He answers the former point, and rightly, that diseases are not to be judged from the impaired action but from their own nature.

units.la: actione : sed ex suâ naturâ. Inflammatio est inflammatio, five hanc, five illam lædat actionem. Itain oculo licet inflam-matio fit læsio actionis inftrumentariæ : non est tamen morbus inftrumentarius seu organicus,nisi per accidens,quatenus vexat similares partes omnes, quæ ad oculi constitutionem concurrunt. Propterea jam concludit affirmativè, Partes diffimilares possunt laborare morbo fimilari.Hæc cum impugnaffet Eraftus, Anat. p.218, extr. & feq. suscipit illorum defenfionem Mont, in Ant-Eraft. f.141. a, & feq. Tu videris.
units.tr: Inflammation is inflammation, whether it harms this action or that. So in the eye, although inflammation is an injury to the instrumental action, it is not an instrumental or organic disease, except incidentally, insofar as it afflicts all the similar parts which go to make up the constitution of the eye. Therefore he now concludes affirmatively that dissimilar parts can suffer from a similar disease. When Erastus attacked these claims, Anat. p. 218, at the end and following, Montanus takes up their defence in Ant-Erast. f. 141 a and following. It is for you to judge.

units.la: Ad Librum V.
units.tr: Book V.

units.la: De Continui solutione, ejusque causis, CAPVT XXIV.
units.tr: On the Dissolution of Continuity and Its Causes, CHAPTER XXIV.

units.la: § 1. HActenus quia duo summa morborum genera venati sumus, Vnum quidem è natura & conftitutione partium fimilarium, quod Intemperies sub fe habet; alterum autem é naturâ & constitutione diffimilarium,quod morbos Organicos : fi præter has alia fit & tertia natura constitutiove, quâ malè fe habente, malæ fiant actiones, utique de illa agendum erit.
units.tr: § 1. So far we have traced the two chief kinds of disease: the first arising from the nature and constitution of the similar parts, which includes intemperies; the second from the nature and constitution of the dissimilar parts, namely organic diseases. If there is also a third nature or constitution, by whose bad condition actions become bad, that too must be treated.

units.la: § 2. Atqui est tertia quædam natura, communis tam fimilaribus, quam diffimilaribus, Vnio seu continuitas, Ergo erit tertium morborum genus.
units.tr: § 2. Now there is a certain third nature, common to similar and dissimilar parts alike: union or continuity. Therefore this will be a third kind of disease.

units.la: § 3. Quemadmodum igitur partes fimilares sunt unæ,continuæve, unamque actionem edunt; quemadmodum diffimilares sunt unæ,continuæve, unamque actionem perfectam edunt : ita unitate illâ solutâ,utrinque fit morbus, qui Vnitatis seu Continui solutio dicitur.
units.tr: § 3. Just as similar parts are one and continuous and produce one action, and just as dissimilar parts are one and continuous and produce one complete action, so when that unity is dissolved, disease arises on both sides. This is called the solution of unity or of the continuous.

units.la: § 4. Cæterum, quia unum multis modis dicitur, s.Metaph.8. ne qua deceptio oriatur, seligere fas est nobis Vnum illud, quod huc facit. Id verò est, cum ex duobus extremis fit unum.
units.tr: § 4. But since "one" is said in many ways (Metaphysics 8), lest any confusion arise, we may choose the sense of "one" that serves our purpose. This is when one thing arises from two extremes.

units.la: § 5. Hoc cum fiat tam ab arte, quam à naturâ : relinquamus illud, acceptemus hoc.
units.tr: § 5. Since this happens both through art and through nature, let us set aside the first and accept the second.

units.la: § 6. Vnum ergò,aut, fi mavis,Continuum Naturâ eftid, cujus motus eftunus, tempore indivisibilis.
units.tr: § 6. Therefore a one, or if you prefer a continuum, is that by nature whose motion is one and indivisible in time.

units.la: § 7. Hæc definitio licet sitâ pofteriori,ut Monlorius habet tract. de Vniverf. quadrat tamen rebus nostris, fi rectè accommodetur,
units.tr: § 7. This definition, although it comes from a later source, as Montanus gives it in his tract on the universal, nevertheless suits our matter if it is rightly adapted.

units.la: § 8. Accommodatio est,ut dicamus, Vnum & continuum modò distingui, modò non. Distinctio est, Vnum seu Continuum aliud est verè tale, id vid; cujus motus tempore divisibilis non est, & proprie ita dicitur: aliud non verè, cujus motus tempore divisibilis est, & est Continuum, non Vnum.
units.tr: § 8. The adaptation is this: we say that the one and the continuous are distinguished at one time and not at another. The distinction is as follows. That which is one or continuous in the true sense is that whose motion is not divisible in time, and it is properly called so. That which is not one in the true sense, but whose motion is divisible in time, is a continuum and not a one.

units.la: § 9. Hoc ita explicat Montanus. Linea vel recta est, vel flexa. Illius motus magis est continuus: hujus minus, quia angulos habet, secundum quorum angulorum motus, modò hæc pars movetur, modò illa.
units.tr: § 9. Montanus explains this as follows. A line is either straight or bent. The motion of the straight line is more continuous, that of the bent line less so, because it has angles; according to the motions of these angles, now this part moves and now that.

units.la: § 10. Rectæ lineæ respondet os v. g. femoris, per fe. Moventur enim omnes ejus partes simul & semel, & fit non nisi motus unus. Flexæ, idem os femoris, sed dearticulatum cum tibiâ. Potest enim utrumque os simul moveri: potest & alterutrum feorsim, & fit diversus motus, Ita possum movere hunc digitum, immoto altero: possum hujus digiti articulum, immoto vicino.
units.tr: § 10. To a straight line corresponds, for example, the thigh bone taken by itself. For all its parts move together and at once, and there is only one motion. To a bent line corresponds the same thigh bone, but jointed with the shin. For both bones can move together, or either one can move alone, and the motion is then different. So I can move this finger while the other remains still, and I can move the joint of this finger while the neighbouring joint remains still.

units.la: § 11. Et hæc quidem in Philosophia ita distincta sunt: at in Medicinâ non sunt, ratione τῆς προώτης τῆς ἐπιστήμης, qui τὴν ἀκολούθειαν non admittit. Perinde enim Galeno est, five Vnum fit, five Continuum, vocatque fine discrimine λύσιν τῆς συνεχείας ἢ ἑνώσεως, Solutionem vel continuitatis, vel unionis.
units.tr: § 11. These matters are distinguished in this way in philosophy; but in medicine they are not, because of the order of the science, which does not admit the consequence. For Galen makes no difference whether it is one or continuum, and he calls without distinction the "solution of continuity or of union" [λύσιν τῆς συνεχείας ἢ ἑνώσεως], that is, the solution of continuity or of union.

units.la: § 12. Sed quare hic morbus dicitur Communis, tam fimilaribus, quam diffimilaribus partibus? Fortassis, quia semper in utrique fit? Non : sed quia contingere potest utrique.
units.tr: § 12. But why is this disease called common to both similar and dissimilar parts? Perhaps because it always occurs in both? No; rather because it can happen to both.

units.la: § 13. Hoc ipsum multas habet ambages, quas ita supero. Est in similaribus, quoties intemperies alterutra accidit, tu puta, vel cum, vel sine materia. Est in dissimilaribus, quoties Vulnus, Vlcusve. Est in utrisque, quoties Intemperies alterutra supervenit Vlceri, Vulnerive.
units.tr: § 13. This point involves many circumlocutions, which I cut short as follows. It occurs in similar parts whenever either kind of intemperies arises, for example with or without matter. It occurs in dissimilar parts whenever there is a wound or an ulcer. It occurs in both whenever an intemperies supervenes on an ulcer or a wound.

units.la: § 14. Heic quid litigent Erastus, Aunat. p.228. & Montanus,in Ant-Erast. f. 155. a. videant, qui volent : ego enim restà ad Cansas descendo.
units.tr: § 14. Whatever Erastus (Anatomy, p. 228) and Montanus (Anti-Erastus, f. 155 a) dispute here, let those who wish see for themselves; for I hasten straight to the causes.

units.la: § 15. Has intelligere non licet, nisi Montanum distinctione locuplemus,hac vid. Continui solutio alia in oculos incurrit : alia non incurrit.
units.tr: § 15. These cannot be understood unless we enrich Montanus with a distinction: one solution of continuity is evident to the eyes, another is not.

units.la: § 16. Posterior hæc est Intemperies utraque dicta, cum inter fibras partium sentientium insinuat se materiæ, modò parum modò multum, quod tendendo & divellendo dolorem facit. Nimirum, hæc est gemina doloris causa, de quâ multi tam multa.
units.tr: § 16. The latter is called intemperies in both senses, when matter works its way in between the fibres of the sensitive parts, sometimes little and sometimes much, and by stretching and tearing it causes pain. This is indeed the twofold cause of pain, about which many have written much.

units.la: § 17. Prior illa iterum est duplex, & sumitur vel à divisis partibus, vel à causâ dividente.
units.tr: § 17. The former, again, is twofold, and is derived either from the parts that are divided or from the cause that divides.

units.la: § 18. Cum loquor de partibus, dico, Vel in ossibus fit, vel in carne, cæterisque partibus mollibus.
units.tr: § 18. When I speak of the parts, I say that it happens either in the bones or in the flesh and the other soft parts.

units.la: § 19. In ossibus iterum duplex est. Harum una ἀγμα est, ἡ κοίλη speciatim, si propè articulum fit, ἄπαγμα, Latinis Fractura aut Ruptura : altera, ἐνάρθρωσις ἢ ἀλάθρωσις, quæ in Cartilaginibus forte etiam locum habet, Erofio aut Caries. Dicitur etiam πεφηνὸς, quasi πεφηνὸς, Caries.
units.tr: § 19. In the bones it is again twofold. One kind is fracture, which is called [κλάσις] in general, and [ἄπαγμα] if it occurs near a joint; in Latin, fracture or rupture. The other is [ἐνάρθρωσις] or [ἀλάθρωσις], which perhaps also occurs in the cartilages: erosion or caries. It is also called [πεφηνὸς], as if from [πεφηνὸς], caries.

units.la: § 20. In carne vulgò admittitur illa subdistinctio, quod alia Continui solutio fit in Carnosâ substantiâ, alia in Fibrosâ. Ego non admitto, quod caro proprie dicta nihil aliud fit quam recens circa fibras sanguis concretus : qui quomodo feorsim à fibris lædi possit?
units.tr: § 20. In the flesh it is commonly admitted that one kind of solution of continuity occurs in the fleshy substance and another in the fibrous. I do not admit this, since flesh properly speaking is nothing other than blood recently congealed around the fibres. How could it be injured apart from the fibres?

units.la: § 21. Substituo igitur illi aliam, & dico, Alia Continui solutio est in vasis : alia in fibris: alia in utrisque.
units.tr: § 21. I therefore substitute another distinction and say: one solution of continuity is in the vessels, another in the fibres, and another in both.

units.la: § 22. Has differentias agnosco fieri à quatuor causis dividentibus, à Montano cap.2. recensitis.
units.tr: § 22. I recognise that these differences arise from four dividing causes, listed by Montanus in chapter 2.

units.la: § 23. Prima est τρίψις sectio, quæ Vulnus facit, idque vel punctim, vel cæsim, quando & vasa & fibræ læduntur.
units.tr: § 23. The first is [τρίψις], section, which makes a wound, either by a puncture or by a cut, when both the vessels and the fibres are injured.

units.la: § 24. Altera est ἀλάθρωσις, erofio, corrosio, quando à pure substante Vlcus fit, vel etiam ab humoribus acribus exulceratio quædam interior.
units.tr: § 24. The second is [ἀλάθρωσις], erosion or corrosion, when an ulcer arises from a sharp or pure substance, or also when there is an inner kind of ulceration caused by acrid humours.

units.la: § 25. Tertia, est ϑλάσις, contusio, cum absque externo & visibili vulnere, vasa quassantur, ut fiat cxχύμωμε, sugillatio.
units.tr: § 25. The third is [θλάσις], contusion, when the vessels are shaken without any external and visible wound, so that [ἐκχύμωσις], a bruise or ecchymosis, results.

units.la: § 26. Quarta, Ꞓσς,tenfio , quæ fit à multis causis, copiá sanguinis, flatibus, vi externa,&c. de quibus in feq.
units.tr: § 26. The fourth is [τάσις], tension, which arises from many causes: an abundance of blood, wind, external force, and so on, of which more in what follows.

units.la: De partibus fimilaribus excursus Phyfio- logicus Montani. CAP. XXV.
units.tr: On the similar parts: a physiological digression on Montanus. CHAPTER XXV.

units.la: § 1. Ta loquor: excusationem enim, quam profert, non accepto. De nomine tantum hoc moneo, Frustrà exculpare illum velle Galenum , quasi Aristoteli tribuerit, quod Anaxagoræ est. O μοιομερεια enim illa Anaxagoréa longè alió ibat, & παντοιεμέια quoque vocabatur.
units.tr: § 1. I say nothing here, for I do not accept the excuse he offers. I only warn about the name: it is pointless for him to want to exculpate Galen, as if Galen had attributed to Aristotle what belongs to Anaxagoras. For that homoiomeria of Anaxagoras went quite a different way, and was also called "all kinds of parts" [παντοιομέρεια].

units.la: § 2. De definitione partium dictarum acturum, præmonitum voluissem, Primum omnium definiisset ὁ ὁμοιομερὴς: deinde vidisset, An, & quousque partibus his tribui possit?
units.tr: § 2. I would have wished it said in advance that he would treat the definition of the said parts. First of all he should have defined the homoiomeres [ὁμοιομερής]; then he should have considered whether, and how far, these parts can be attributed to them.

units.la: § 3. Ita quidem est, Similare est id, cujus partes, tum inter fe, tum toti fimiles sunt, ideoque idem cum toto nomen habent: Diffimilare contrà, cujus partes non sunt sibi similes, neque possunt eodem nomine vocari. Ita est, inquam: sed profecto rebus nostris simpliciter accommodari non potest,
units.tr: § 3. It is so: a similar thing is one whose parts are both similar to each other and similar to the whole, and so have the same name as the whole. A dissimilar thing, on the contrary, is one whose parts are not similar to one another and cannot be called by the same name. That is so, I say; but certainly it cannot simply be applied to our matters.

units.la: § 4. Hujus negotii difficultas statim inde apparet, quod definitio tradita non competat omnibus, à Gal. numeratis partibus fimilaribus. Imò, quod non constet sibi in numero illarum. Sed recte excusatur,quod iis locis, quos habemus, non fuerit hoc ei propositum: fecerit autem procul dubio in 1, de Similaribus, quos non habemus.
units.tr: § 4. The difficulty of this business appears at once from the fact that the definition given does not fit all the similar parts that Galen enumerates. Indeed, he does not even agree with himself about their number. But he is rightly excused, since in the passages we have this was not his purpose; he undoubtedly treated it in the first book On Similar Parts, which we do not have.

units.la: § 5. Quâ acceptâ ἀπογμυσία, non est opus illâ Argenterii, Galenum modò intueri formam harum partium, modò materiam; ideò jam huc referre, jam illuc.
units.tr: § 5. Having accepted this, there is no need for that point of Argenterius: Galen simply looks now at the form of these parts and now at their matter, and so he refers things now here, now there.

units.la: § 6. Ad rem, Dexterrimè Montanus recipit Fuchii refponfionem, Similarium partium alias revera esse, quod dicuntur: alias videri tantum, & ad sensum esse.
units.tr: § 6. To the point: very skilfully Montanus accepts Fuchs's answer, that similar parts are in truth what they are called, and otherwise only seem so and exist only in relation to the senses.

units.la: § 7. Hanc ex 1.Fac. nat.6. ita declaro, Non est opus nobis heic Physicis speculationibus, quid fit similare,quid diffimilare:quin opus est Anatomiâ solâ. Hæc quascunque & quotcunque dederit nobis similares, (tu puta, quæ ad constitutionem diffimilarium concurrunt) tot erunt. v.g. oculo dissecto, quot repereris partes, è quibus ille componitur, tot erunt oculi partes similares. Et sic de cæteris diffimilaribus.
units.tr: § 7. I explain this from the first book of On the Natural Faculties, chapter 6, as follows. We have no need here of physical speculations about what is similar and what is dissimilar; only anatomy is needed. Whatever and however many similar parts it yields to us (take those which come together to make up dissimilar parts), those will be the number. For example, when an eye is dissected, as many parts as you find of which it is composed, so many will be the similar parts of the eye. And so with the other dissimilar parts.

units.la: § 8. Hoc amplius doceo ex.1. Ex. Anat.4. 2. ejusdem 2. & forte alibi, Anatomia alia exquisita est : alia non est. In hac sufficit inspectio fuperficiaria, & Medica dici potest : in illa accuratiore opus est,& est Physica,quam Medicus aliquando Sophisticam dicit. Scio, quid heic argutari possit quis, contra priícam sapientiam : sed sino.
units.tr: § 8. I further teach this from the first book of the Anatomical Exercises, chapter 4, and from book 2 of the same, and perhaps elsewhere: anatomy is of one kind exact, and of another kind not. In the latter, superficial inspection suffices, and it may be called medical; in the former a more accurate work is needed, and it is physical, which the physician sometimes calls sophistical. I know what someone might quibble here against ancient wisdom, but let it pass.

units.la: § 9. Harum partium numerum qui mecum inire volet,hic esto. I. in ordine est Caro proprie dicta. II. Fibrae. III. Membranae. I V. Venae. V. Arteriae. VI. Nervi. VII. Ligamenta. VIII. Musculi cum Tendinibus suis. IX. Cartilagines. X. Offa. XI, Vngues, XII. Pili. XIII. Glandulae. His superaddo Cutim, Cuticulam, & Membranam carnosam. De his quia periit,ceu dixi, labor Gal. ausus fui ego superioribus annis tale quid. Attigerimne scopum, judicabunt boni & sapientes, fi quando, favente Mercurio, prodibit.
units.tr: § 9. Whoever wishes to count these parts with me, let him take this list: I. in order, flesh properly so called; II. fibres; III. membranes; IV. veins; V. arteries; VI. nerves; VII. ligaments; VIII. muscles with their tendons; IX. cartilages; X. bones; XI. nails; XII. hairs; XIII. glands. To these I add the cutis, the cuticle, and the fleshy membrane. Since Galen's work on these has perished, as I said, I myself in past years ventured something of the kind. Whether I have hit the mark, good and wise men will judge, if it ever appears, with Mercury's favour.

units.la: De nominibus, quae haec faciunt CAPVT. XXVI.
units.tr: On the names that belong to these: CHAPTER XXVI.

units.la: § 1. Pectat quidem haec res ad SOESIVM : verum, quia Montanus ejus personam sibi sumit cap. 11. paucis ego defungar.
units.tr: § 1. This matter pertains indeed to Soesius; but since Montanus assumes his persona in chapter 11, I shall dispatch it briefly.

units.la: § 2. Quod ad Offa, siquidem in universum consideres, addi debet vocibus superioribus χαλαζα: sin in capite solo, quinque sunt morbi apud Hipp. l. de Vuln. cap. quos breviter rememorabo ex Montano.
units.tr: § 2. As for the bones, if you consider them in general, the earlier words should have χαλαζα added; but if you consider the head only, there are five conditions in Hippocrates' book On Wounds, which I shall briefly recall from Montanus.

units.la: § 3. Prima ρωγμη ἡ ρἡξις est, sissura, scissura, Celso Rima. Hæc quia fit à telo gravi, retusoque, dicitur etiam λάσσις ἡ λάσσῳ, Ionicè φλάσις ἡ φυάσμα, Contu- sio. Inter has quæ vix apparet, σχισμὸς dicitur.
units.tr: § 3. The first is rhōgmē or rhēxis [ῥωγμὴ ἢ ῥῆξις], a fissure or split, which Celsus calls rima. Since it is caused by a heavy, blunt weapon, it is also called lasis or lassō [λάσις ἢ λάσσω], in Ionic phlasis or phyasma [φλάσις ἢ φύασμα], a contusion. Among these, the one that hardly shows is called schismos [σχισμός].

units.la: § 4. Τῆς λάσεως species altera est, quæ manifestum sui indicium non præbet. Quâ de quæ controversa sunt inter Hipp. & Gal. vide ipsus apud Montanum.
units.tr: § 4. The second kind of lasis is one that gives no clear sign of itself. As to what is disputed between Hippocrates and Galen on this, see Montanus himself.

units.la: § 5. Tertia est, ἐνλάσεως ἡ ἐσφλάσις, Illisio, cum cranii pars deprimitur. Hujus species apud Gal.in Meth. est ἐγχίσωμα, καὶ καμψεωσις.
units.tr: § 5. The third is enlasis or esphlasis [ἐνλάσεως ἢ ἐσφλάσις], an impression, when a part of the skull is pressed inward. A kind of this, in Galen's Methodus, is enchisōma [ἐγχίσωμα] and kampseōsis [καμψεωσις].

units.la: § 6. Quarta, cum primus & fecundus modus concurrunt.
units.tr: § 6. The fourth is when the first and second modes occur together.

units.la: § 7. Quinta dicitur ἐδες, & διάζωσις, forte etiam ἐκγοσμ.
units.tr: § 7. The fifth is called edes [ἐδες] and diazōsis [διάζωσις], perhaps also ekgosm [ἐκγοσμ].

units.la: § 8. In reliquis ossibus supersunt duo modi, 6. Meth. 5. quorum alius fuit κοινὴ διὰ, per transversum, alius ψιδκενδὸν, per reslexalius ἐκφατνδὸν, partim hoc, partim illo modo. Sed curiosa esse hæc, satetur Gal. ipse.
units.tr: § 8. In the remaining bones two modes remain, as in Methodus book 6, chapter 5: one was koinē dia [κοινὴ διὰ], through the transverse, the other psilokendon [ψιδκενδὸν], by reflection, and another ekphatndon [ἐκφατνδὸν], partly in one way and partly in the other. But Galen himself admits that these are curious matters.

units.la: § 9. Ethæc de ossibus : In carne est
units.tr: § 9. And this is enough on the bones. In the flesh is

units.la: ἀπάσμος quod præcipuum exhibet negotium Græcæ linguæ imperitis, quia confundunt cum τῷ ἀπάσμος ut suprà dixi. Hac de re bis agere voluisse Comitem nostrum, cap. 12. & 29. equidem demiror! Quid ἀπάσμος fit, non debeo repetere, ne Montani culpam in me transferam: Ο ἀπάσμος vel invitis obtrudam, ne porrò claudicent. Ignorantiam fovet, quod malum apud nos infrequens fit, cum in palæstris veterum frequentissimum effet. Docet id Gal. 3. Off. Med. 30. cum ait, Ο ἀπάσμος γίνεται ἀπὸ τῶν μυῶν ἴνας, Spafma fit in fibris musculorum, non circa fibras, tu puta, cum transverfim rumpuntur, sed fine sanguinis effusione. Ejus rei exemplum est 2. Ex. Anat. 4. in rupto toto musculo. Hunc affectum dici Græcis etiam πύρα, ἀπὸ πύρα, ut libenter concedo Foëfio: ita nolim illi sicco pede transita duo illa loca, quæ è tenebris nos in lucem protrahunt. Eidem observatum vellem, cum simplici eadem esse duo composita, ἀπάπρα. Quod quia probavi in Isagog. c. 4. parco jam operæ. Hoc tantum litiganti Montano cap. 30. oggero, Ne postulet à Gal. nominum accurationem, quam nuspiam promisit.
units.tr: The word ἀπάσμος [spasmos], which presents the chief difficulty to those unskilled in Greek, because they confuse it with τῷ ἀπάσμος [tō apasmos], as I said above. I am surprised that our Count wished to treat this matter twice, in chapters 12 and 29! What ἀπάσμος is I need not repeat, lest I shift Montanus's fault onto myself; I will not force ἀπάσμος on the unwilling, lest they go on limping. Ignorance is encouraged by the fact that this disease is rare among us, though it was very frequent in the wrestling schools of the ancients. Galen teaches this in 3 Off. Med. 30, when he says: ὁ ἀπάσμος γίνεται ἀπὸ τῶν μυῶν ἴνας [ho spasmos ginetai apo tōn myōn inas], a spasm occurs in the fibres of the muscles, not around the fibres, as when they are torn across, but without effusion of blood. An example of this is in 2 Ex. Anat. 4, in a muscle ruptured through its whole length. I readily grant to Foesius that the Greeks also call this affection πύρα [pyra], from ἀπὸ πύρα [apo pyra]; but I would not like him to pass over those two passages, which lead us out of darkness into light, with dry feet. I would also wish him to note that the two composites are the same as the simple form, ἀπάπρα [apapra]. Because I proved this in Isagoge c. 4, I now spare the effort. I only throw this at the litigious Montanus in chapter 30: he should not demand from Galen a precision of names, which Galen nowhere promised.

units.la: N 3 § 10. Τεκμ-
units.tr: N 3 § 10. Τεκμ-

units.la: § 10. Τεφῦρα ἡ σφῦρα Vulnus est à telo acuto. Nec alio est opus, nisi forte illo. Cum dicitur, aliud esse in parte carnosâ, aliud in fibrosâ, intelligi forte debere ita, Aliud est in parte musculosa, eine Fleifch Wunde; aliud in fibrosâ,seu tendinosâ,seu excarni.
units.tr: § 10. τεφύρα or σφύρα [tephyra or sphyra] is a wound from a sharp weapon. Nothing else is needed here, unless perhaps that one. When it is said that one thing is in the fleshy part and another in the fibrous part, this should perhaps be understood thus: one thing is in the muscular part, a flesh wound (Fleischwunde); another in the fibrous, or tendinous, or stripped-of-flesh part.

units.la: § 11. Ἁλὰσις ἡ Ἁλόρμα fit à re gravante & comprimente, Contusio. Hujus species ἐκχύμωσις est, sugillatio, cum pars livescit & virescit, fine cutis apertione. Quæ dubia Montanus ciet, nullius momenti sunt. Objectio Argenterii vanissima. Et hoc fatis est:
units.tr: § 11. ἁλάσις [halasis], or ἁλόρμα [halorma], arises from a heavy, crushing thing: a contusion. A species of this is ἐκχύμωσις [ekchymōsis], a suffusion, when the part turns livid and greenish without any breaking of the skin. The doubts which Montanus raises are of no weight. Argenterius's objection is most empty. And this is enough.

units.la: § 12. Satis etiam est dictum, ἕλκος, ulcus, fit per διάβρωσιν ab humore acri. Quæ alia Montanus controvertit, de oppositione carnis & ossium, σήψις sunt, Instantia Argenterii puerilis est.
units.tr: § 12. It has also been said enough that ἕλκος [helkos], an ulcer, arises through διάβρωσις [diabrōsis] from a sharp humour. The points Montanus disputes, about the opposition of flesh and bones, that they are σήψις [sēpsis], are beside the point; Argenterius's instance is childish.

units.la: § 13. Quam grave fuerit explicatu Montano, Quatenus solutio continui fit morbus communis? ex conclusione agnoscas. Indicatâ, inquit, hac à me difficultate, extabit aliquando quispiam, qui eam enodabit. An ego is fuerim, fup. cap. § 3. judicent ii, quibus permissum est judicare. De acromio Gal. vide in Ifagog. laudatis cap. 6.
units.tr: § 13. How hard it was for Montanus to explain in what sense the solution of continuity is a common disease, you may recognise from his conclusion. "This difficulty having been pointed out by me," he says, "someone will at some time arise who will unravel it." Whether I am that man, let those judge who are permitted to judge, above, chapter § 3. On the acromion, see Galen, in the Isagoge, chapter 6 as cited.

units.la: Contra-
units.tr: Contra-

units.la: Controversia una & altera, CAP. XXVII.
units.tr: Controversy One and Another, CHAPTER XXVII.

units.la: § 1. Miratur Montanus cap.20.varietatem ingenii humani de hoc negotio:dabo ego varietatis causam. Vbicunque error committitur ab initio, erratur posteà in infinitum. Hoc Averroem ita proponere intelligo. Viator cum primum pedem ponit extra τὴν Ἀσφόεγν, ut Græci loquuntur, parum id videtur; cum secundum, id quoque parum est; cum tertium, & sic deinceps:at verò cum duravit id per quadrantem horæ, tum demum agnoscit,quantoperè absit à fcopo suo. Ita in disciplinis, cum primus error levis est,excipit hunc alter,qui gravis, & sic deinceps, usque dum ad principium revertatur.
units.tr: § 1. Montanus, in chapter 20, wonders at the variety of human opinion on this matter. I will give the cause of the variety. Wherever an error is made at the start, one goes on erring endlessly. I understand Averroes to put it this way. A traveller who first sets his foot outside [τὴν ἀσφάλειαν], as the Greeks put it, seems to have gone only a little astray. When he takes a second step, that too is a small matter; the third, and so on. But when he has kept on for a quarter of an hour, he finally recognises how far he is from his goal. So in the disciplines: when the first error is slight, another follows it that is more serious, and so on, until one returns to the beginning.

units.la: § 2. Quod ad rem nostram, Veteres docebant, Continui solutionem esse morbum communem, h.e. tam similarem, quam organicum. Hoc quei fieret, cum idem Aver.3. Coll.11. assequi non posset,asseruit, Esse similarem tantum, nullo autem pacto organicum.
units.tr: § 2. As to our matter, the ancients taught that a solution of continuity is a common disease, that is, both similar and organic. Since Averroes could not follow this in his third Collection, chapter 11, he asserted that it is only similar, and in no way organic.

units.la: § 3. Huic tubicinem subjicit Conclliator, Diff.75. In eádem caligine cum. versaretur Argenterius, lib. de Morb. N gen·2.12. & 13. pertendit,Continui solutionem esse causam morbi organici tantum, non vero similaris etiam. Heic tu videas studia partium, satagentium de tutando Galeno!
units.tr: § 3. The Conciliator, Difference 75, sounds the trumpet for him. Argenterius, working in the same fog, in his book On Diseases, chapters 2 and 12, 13, maintains that a solution of continuity is the cause of an organic disease only, and not of a similar one as well. Here you may see the zeal of the factions, busy with defending Galen!

units.la: § 4. Quod mireris, primam defensorum aciem Fernelius ducit, de quo Montanus judicat, Pervertere totam Gal. ductrinam, totam adeo rei naturam,
units.tr: § 4. What you may wonder at is that Fernelius leads the first line of the defenders, of whom Montanus judges that he overturns the whole doctrine of Galen, and indeed the whole nature of the matter.

units.la: § 5. Secundam format Leonicenus in quaestione peculiari, quem Noster refutat quidem, sed nihil solidi affert.
units.tr: § 5. Leonicenus draws up the second line, in a separate question. Our author refutes him, indeed, but brings forward nothing solid.

units.la: § 6. Tertium Argenterius instituit. Huic statim opponit Montanus I. Alexandrinum in Ant-Argent. deinde Argentum ipsum, sub nomine Solenandri, in Apologia, mox I. Alex. in Defenf. contra Ant-Arg. Sed finis est, Machinam esse portentosam & monstrosam, &c.
units.tr: § 6. Argenterius sets up the third line. Montanus at once opposes him with John Alexandrinus in his Anti-Argentarius, then Argentarius himself under the name of Solenander in an Apology, and soon after John Alexandrinus in his Defence against the Anti-Argentarius. But the conclusion is that the machine is monstrous and prodigious, and so on.

units.la: § 7. Quartam dare potest Fuchf. in Institut. qui Alexandrini vitula arat. Verum Montanus noster arguit illum infcitiæ, quæ & rationi & sensui adversetur, &c.
units.tr: § 7. Fuchsius, in his Institutions, may supply a fourth, who plows with a heifer. Yet our Montanus charges him with an ignorance that conflicts with both reason and sense, and so on.

units.la: § 8. Montanus tandem ipse, Argenterio apprehenso, ex propriis ipsius hypothesibus convincere vult, Continui solutionem, & morbum esse non causam: & morbum tam similarem, quam organicum. Quantum proficiat, videat, qui vult, in in longissimâ illa deductione cap.27. Ego,quod dixi,dico denuo,Continui solutio est morbus similaris, qualenus Intemperies dicta, utraque dolorem ciet:est organicus, quatenus Vulnus,ulcusve facit : est uterque, quatenus cum vulnere, ulcerevé; alterutra est intemperies dolorifica.
units.tr: § 8. Montanus himself at last, having taken hold of Argenterius, wishes to convict him from his own hypotheses: that a solution of continuity is a disease and not a cause, and that a disease is as much similar as organic. Let anyone who wishes see how far he gets in that very long deduction in chapter 27. I say again what I have said: a solution of continuity is a similar disease, in so far as it is called an intemperature and both cause pain; it is organic, in so far as it makes a wound or ulcer; it is both, in so far as it is with a wound or ulcer, and either kind of intemperature causes pain.

units.la: § 9. Post hæc omnia peculiariter apprehendit Montanus cap.28. usque ad finem Argenterium juratum Gal.hostem, & ostendere vult, Galenum non fuisse varium in numerandis continui solutione differentiis: verum itafe gerit,ut alio accusatore non indigeat.Dico paucis,& fine affectu,Gal.non erat τῶν ἀχεάϭυτων ,ἀλλα- τῶν ἐρεϭυτων,quod dicunt Græci. Hoc capi volo ita,ut alibi me explicui,In lectione ipsius opus est judicio, Et hac ratione absolvo meâ Iouberto, quem Montanus in Peroratione jure incessit.
units.tr: § 9. After all this, Montanus in chapter 28, right to the end, particularly seizes upon Argenterius, Galen's sworn enemy, and wishes to show that Galen was not inconsistent in numbering the differences of solution of continuity; but he so conducts himself that he needs no other accuser. I say briefly, and without passion, that Galen was not one of the [ἀνεξετάστων] but of the [ἐρευνητῶν], as the Greeks say. I want this understood as I explained elsewhere: in reading him, judgement is needed. And on this ground I acquit my Joubert, whom Montanus rightly attacked in his Peroration.

units.la: Auctarium de Causâ continente,
units.tr: Appendix on the Containing Cause

units.la: CAPVT. XXVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVIII.

units.la: § 1. Via Montanus l.4, c.6. mention fecerat Causæ continentis, de quâ extat integrum scriptum Erasti;& veró Mont. multòante l.2. c.35. & 36. manifestè illam damnárat: Eraftus, Anat, p.101, & feq. resumit negotium. & late tractat. Hujus filum secutus videbo, tam quæ dicit ipse, quam quæ Mont. in Ant-Erast. f. 79. non aliter acsi liber ipse Erafti effet ad manus.
units.tr: § 1. Montanus, in book 4, chapter 6, had mentioned the continent cause, on which Erastus has a complete treatise. Yet Montanus had clearly condemned it in many places, especially book 2, chapters 35 and 36. Erastus takes up the matter again in the Anatome, p. 101 and following, and treats it at length. Following this thread, I shall consider both what Erastus himself says and what Montanus says in the Antierastus, f. 79, as though Erastus's own book were in my hands.

units.la: § 2. Antè omnia libet mihi formare statum controversiæ, ne cum plerisque omnibus parietes in tenebris palpem. Fundamenti loco sit illud, Causam continentem esse ex Philosophiâ Barbaricâ dictâ, é quâ defumferunt Stoici, & inter Medicos Pneumatici, Methodicique defenderunt.
units.tr: § 2. Before all else I wish to set out the state of the controversy, so that I do not grope along the walls in the dark as most people do. Let this be the foundation: that the continent cause comes from what is called Barbarian Philosophy, from which the Stoics derived it, and which the Pneumatici and Methodici among the physicians defended.

units.la: § 3. Hi omnes volebant, Res fublunares consistere non posse, nisi, ut Horatius loquitur, divinæ particula auræ misceatur, nisi Spiritus intus alat, ut Virgil.6. Æn, Vterque enim poëta Stoicus fuit.
units.tr: § 3. All of these held that things beneath the moon cannot exist unless, as Horace puts it, a particle of divine air is mixed in, unless a spirit nourishes them from within, as Virgil says in Aeneid 6. Both poets were Stoics.

units.la: § 4. Hæc particula, hic spiritus nihil aliud est, quàm Anima mundi Platonica, quam omnia vi suâ continere dicunt ita, ut ipsa à nulla aliâ contineatur, ipsa sibi sufficiens.
units.tr: § 4. This particle, this spirit, is nothing other than the Platonic world-soul, which, they say, holds all things by its power while itself being held by nothing else, sufficient to itself.

units.la: § 5. Contra hanc disputat Gal.1. de Pleth.3. D. item 1. adv. Iulian.6. I. Si omnia, inquit, habent hanc causam Continentem, hæc rursus aliam habebit, atque hæc iterum aliam, & ita resibit in infinitum, nisi ad DEVM tandem deveniatur. Contrà eandem Alexander quoque Aphrodif. disputat 1. de Mistione.
units.tr: § 5. Galen disputes against this in Gal. 1, De plethora 3, D; likewise in 1 Adversus Julianum 6, I. If all things, he says, have this containing cause, then this in turn will have another, and that another, and so it will go back into infinity, unless at last one comes to God. Alexander of Aphrodisias also disputes against the same in De mixtione 1.

units.la: § 6. Talis aliqua cum in morbis
units.tr: § 6. When such a thing was also sought in diseases,

units.la: etiam quaereretur , neque certi quid dici posset : itum fuit ad varias sententias.
units.tr: and nothing certain could be said, people turned to various opinions.

units.la: § 7. Quidam Galenum etiam implicuerunt, non in spuriis tantum libris, sed & in legitimis, & ita definierunt, Causa continens est, quā positā, res ponitur : quā sublatā res aufertur. Cum ftoad speculum,addebat SCHERBIVS, imago mea adest : cum abeo,abit & illa.
units.tr: § 7. Some have even entangled Galen in the matter, not only in the spurious books but also in the genuine ones, and have defined it thus: The continent cause is that, by whose positing the thing is posited, and by whose removal the thing is taken away. When I stand before a mirror, my image is present; when I go away, it goes too, SCHERBIUS added.

units.la: § 8. Hoc voluisse ajunt illum 1. Loc. aff. 2. illis verbis, Quo tangente ,certus assectus ( τῷ ) in nobis fit , quoque remoto, subito cessat , id causam credunt esse omnes homines. Ex hac confecisse creditur Vallefius suam, 4. Controv.3. Causa continens est , quae non quidem necessario rem efficit, nec simpliciter positam rem infert : sed alterum tantum, (cil. Quae,dum facit,ita facit, ut,eā sublatā auferatur.
units.tr: § 8. They say Galen meant this in Loc. aff. 1, 2, in the words: "By whose touch a certain affection arises in us, and by whose removal it suddenly ceases; all men believe this to be the cause." From this, Vallesius is believed to have formed his own definition, in Controversia 4, 3: "The continent cause is that which does not indeed necessarily produce the thing, nor simply infer the thing when posited, but only the other (namely, that which, while it acts, acts in such a way that when it is removed the effect is removed)."

units.la: § 9. Quo loco monendi sunt parum cauti,Considerari hanc causam, vel in rebus jam factis,vel in iis,quae sunt in fieri. De prioribus accipiebant Stoici. Quod cum defendere non possent Medici,itum fuit ab aliis ad posteriora. Hoc factum est dudum ante Galenum : ideo Gal. cum illis non raro loquitur. Hoc fecit Vallefius,u'us exemplo pulsus. Pulsus ut faciat , inquit , tres desiderantur causae continentes , Facultas, instrumentum & N. 6. usus : ut deficiat , fatis est , fi una illarum defit.
units.tr: § 9. Here the less careful must be warned that this cause may be considered either in things already made or in those that are in the making. The Stoics took the former. Since the physicians could not defend that, others turned to the latter. This was done long before Galen, which is why Galen often speaks with them. Vallesius did the same, driven by the example of the pulse. "For the pulse to act," he says, "three continent causes are required: faculty, instrument and use. For it to fail, it is enough that one of them be lacking."

units.la: § 10. Quo dato, non jam quæstio erit de unâ continente, sed de pluribus. Non erit etiam quæstio de tali causâ, quam Gal. describit , Quâ positâ, ⅇⅽ. sed de altero tantum, Quâ sublatâ, ⅇⅽ. Non erit tandem quæstio de causâ materiali, quò trahunt quidam,sed deefficiente solâ.
units.tr: § 10. Granted this, the question will no longer be about one continent cause but about several. Nor will it be about such a cause as Galen describes, by whose positing the thing is posited, and so on. It will concern only the other kind, by whose removal the thing is removed. Finally, the question will not be about a material cause, to which some drag it, but about a cause whose failure alone is enough.

units.la: § 11. His præhabitis,conversus ad res nostras, dico. Morbus considerari potest dupliciter, Aut ut jam factus est: aut ut fit. Heic enim subsisto , nec addo cum Pacio, Com.in 1.Meth, col.296. morbum futurum , quem puto cum fiente eundem esse. Tu, qui causam hanc foves, dic mihi, In utro vis illam collocari? An in facto? Non videtur fieri posse. Is enim jam actum habet, jam est in termino motus, æger jam decumbit, adsunt hæc, illa symptomata.
units.tr: § 11. With these things premised, I turn to our own matter and say: disease can be considered in two ways, either as already brought about or as it comes about. For I stop here, and I do not add with Pacius, Commentary on the Method, 1, col. 296, that a future disease, which I think is the same as one that is coming to be. You who favour this cause, tell me: in which of the two do you want it placed? In the completed one? That does not seem possible. For the completed disease already has its act; it is already at the end of its motion; the patient now lies sick, and these symptoms are present.

units.la: § 12. Hoc declaro.In universum ita est, In iis,quæ jam facta sunt, quæ, inquam,ita facta sunt,ut non amplius fiant: in iis,non habet locum Causa efficiens, Effectus enim jam adest,
units.tr: § 12. I explain: in general it is so. In those things which are already made, and made in such a way that they no longer come to be, the efficient cause has no place, for the effect is already present.

units.la: § 13. Nec obstat, fi ulterius progredi possunt. Intelligimus enim cum reduplicatione Arift. Quatenus facta sunt.Eatenus enim ratio efficientis est, ut fit principium unde motus, qui motus simul atque eò devenit, ut aliquid factum fit, ut, inquam, actio fit læsa notabiliter: jam est habitus, quo præfente, cessat motus, & consequenter actio motoris, h.e. caufæ efficientis.
units.tr: § 13. Nor is it an objection that they can progress further. For we understand, with Aristotle's reduplication, "insofar as they are made." For so far the account of the efficient cause holds, as the principle from which motion comes. As soon as that motion arrives at the point where something is made, namely where action is notably harmed, there is now a state in whose presence the motion ceases, and consequently the action of the mover, that is, of the efficient cause.

units.la: § 14. Sed quatenus morbus eftfactum quid? Molestus es. Morbus est terminus motus,non respectu ​τῆς ἀμελείας relationis: sed respectu fundamenti fui, corporis sic affecti.
units.tr: § 14. But insofar as disease is something made? "You are a nuisance." Disease is the terminus of motion, not with respect to the relation [τῆς ἀμελείας], but with respect to the foundation of itself, the body so affected.

units.la: § 15. Nondum capio, dicat quis: Oportet morbus jam eò devenerit, utacquifiverit formam suam. Hæc enim est terminus motus, v.g. in pullo. Dico paucis, Est ita. Verum tu mihi distingue formas substantiales ab accidentalibus. In pullo v.g. forma superior seu substantialis est id, unde dicitur pullus: in eodem est forma quædam inferior, & accidentalis, temperamentum. In medicina quia subsistimus in forma inferiori, is ipse essectus est forma, nec alia in morbis forma est, quam hæc.
units.tr: § 15. "I still do not grasp it," someone may say: "it must be that the disease has already reached the point where it has acquired its form, for this is the terminus of motion, as in a chick." I say briefly: it is so. But you must distinguish for me substantial forms from accidental ones. In a chick, for example, the higher or substantial form is that from which it is called a chick; in the same there is a certain lower and accidental form, its temperament. In medicine, since we rest in the lower form, that very effect is the form, and in diseases there is no other form than this.

units.la: § 16. Hinc ergo exclusi Medici quidam, inficeté ab Efficiente ad Materiam eunt, ne, quod est, vi&i videantur? Sed age, morigeremur illis, hinc facto exordio.
units.tr: § 16. Do some physicians therefore leave the efficient cause and rush shamelessly to the matter, lest what is the case appear to be overcome? But come, let us humour them and make a beginning from this.

units.la: § 17. Materia est duplex, In quā, & Ex quā. Materia in quā est subjectum, est corpus vivens, animatum, aut quomodocunque appellare velis. Apud enim Arist. tam ægrotare, quam benè valere dicuntur de iis tantum, quæ vivunt. Quod quia præsupponitur ab omnibus hominibus, non debuit Fernelius in definitione Partis collocare {Vivens}, ut hoc obiter moneam. Scitur enim de cadavere non agi, vel in Physicis, vel in Medicina.
units.tr: § 17. Matter is twofold: that in which and that out of which. The matter in which is the subject, which is a living, animated body, or whatever you wish to call it. For in Aristotle, to be sick and to be well are said only of things that live. Since all men presuppose this, Fernelius ought not to have placed "living" in the definition of the part, as I may note in passing. For it is known that no cadaver is being discussed, either in physics or in medicine.

units.la: § 18. Hoc enucleandum magis est, Subjectum morbi est duplex. Alterum totum et adæquatum, cum dico, Petrus ægrotat,Paulus, hic,ille. Alterum partiale, cum, ægrotante hepate-v.g. tamen dico, Petrus ægrotat, &c. Virobique morbus duas habet partes essentiales, Materialem & Formalem. Intellige tu materiam in quâ: intellige formam, quam dixi esse in mistis, quâ mista sunt, à quâ forma morbus habet, ut sit talis, v. g. febris. Hæc enim calor est p.n. in quo continetur febris, propter quem calorem dicitur febris.
units.tr: § 18. This needs to be made clearer. The subject of disease is twofold. One is total and adequate, when I say, "Peter is sick," "Paul," "this one," "that one." The other is partial, when I still say, "Peter is sick," etc., though it is the liver that is sick. In either case disease has two essential parts, the material and the formal. Understand the matter in which, and understand the form, which I said is in mixed bodies, by which they are mixed, and from which the disease has its character, as for example fever. For this heat, which contains the fever, is the substance, and because of this heat it is called fever.

units.la: § 19. In hoc calore (ne ab exemplo discedam) duo considerantur, alterum Calor, quà calor, qui est materiale illud, quod quærimus fundamentum relationis: alterum Calor talis, ἀμετρος, in quo est formale illud, quod quærimus ἀμέλεια, relatio ipsa, unde febris dicitur febris, in quo essentia febris est, &c.
units.tr: § 19. In this heat (so as not to depart from the example) two things are considered: one is heat as heat, which is that material thing we seek as the foundation of the relation; the other is heat of such a kind, excessive, in which is that formal thing we seek, the negligence [ἀμέλεια], the relation itself, whence fever is called fever, and in which the essence of fever lies, and so on.

units.la: § 20. Hoc amplius declaro. Sanguis tantum habet caloris, quantū à corde accipit, 1. Temp. ult. ex. Non magis enim tantum requirit calorem, quam tantū. Hincè chorio, lactuca, femine papaveris, Melanzanis hodie Italis dictis, &c. æque (ὡσαύτως inquit Gal. 3. Temp. 4.) sanguis fit, atq; ex allio, porro, cepis: sed non ejusdē gradus. Hic sanguis in alio corpore calet, ut duo: in alio ut tria, in alio ut quatuor. In corpore meo senili fatis est, fi caleat ut duo: fi ulterius incalescat, ut tria, ut quatuor, jam morbus est. Contrà in milite aliquo strenuo, cum calet ut quatuor, bene habet: fi descendat ad duo, ad tria, jam ægrotat. Et sic in Intemperiebus fe habet:
units.tr: § 20. I explain this further. Blood has only as much heat as it receives from the heart, by the first book on temperaments, last chapter. For it does not require more heat than it does... Thus blood is made from chicory, lettuce, poppy seed, the eggplants that Italians now call melanzane, and so on, in the same way (ὡσαύτως, says Galen, On Temperaments 3, 4), as it is made from garlic, leek and onion, but not of the same degree. This blood is hot in one body as two, in another as three, in another as four. In my aged body it is enough if it is hot as two; if it grows hotter, as three or four, it is now a disease. On the contrary, in some vigorous soldier, when it is hot as four, all is well; if it descends to two or three, he is now sick. And so it is with the intemperies generally.

units.la: § 21. In morbis Organicis ita. Sextus digitus (nihil enim prohibet hoc exemplo uti) est materiale illud, est fundamentum illud, est ἀρχέλεγον illud, quo præfente lædit ur actio manus, apprehensio: sextus ille digitus collatus cum quinque reliquis, constituit ἀρχέλεγον illam, relationem illam, formale illud, quod morbus est, lædit que actionem manus.
units.tr: § 21. In organic diseases it is the same. The sixth finger (for nothing prevents us from using this example) is the material element, the foundation, the ἀρχέλεγον, by whose presence the action of the hand, its grasping, is harmed. That sixth finger, compared with the other five, constitutes the ἀρχέλεγον, the relation, the formal element, which is the disease and which harms the action of the hand.

units.la: § 22. Quemadmodum igitur fanguis, consideratus ut pars animalis, à natura fa&tus ad nutritionem corporis, habet rationem infe & sanitatis & morbi, Ulius, cum in hoc gradu est, Hujus, cum in
units.tr: § 22. Therefore, just as blood, considered as a part of the animal, made by nature for the nourishment of the body, has the character of both health and disease (of health when it is in this degree, of disease when it is in that),

units.la: J in alio:ita sextus digitus simpliciter habet rationem morbi, quatenus conformatio est p.n. & per illam apprehensio fit deterior.
units.tr: in another case, so the sixth finger simply has the character of disease, insofar as its formation is against nature and through it the grasping becomes worse.

units.la: § 23. Nimirum, Sanitas & Morbus per fe,ut sunt συμπτωσεις & ἀμπτωσεις, non sunt termini motus, sed mutantur relationes mutatis aliis, ut Arift. loquitur, fundamentis scilicet. Idcirco confiderat Medicus, non calorem tantum, sed & gradum caloris, ut, eo in melius mutato, assequatur finem suum, qui est, ut homo habeat sanguinem rectè sibi contemperatum. Ita sextum digitum confiderat, non tantum ut digitum, sed & ut fupernumerarium, quo refecto, apprehenfio fiat melior. Et hæc est Materia in quâ, quam illi rejiciunt.
units.tr: § 23. Clearly, health and disease in themselves, as they are concurrences and non-concurrences [συμπτώσεις, ἀπτώσεις], are not limits of motion, but their relations change when other foundations change, as Aristotle says. Therefore the physician considers not only the heat but also the degree of heat, so that, when this is changed for the better, he attains his end, which is that the man have blood properly tempered for himself. So too he considers the sixth finger not only as a finger but as a superfluous one, which, once removed, makes the grasping better. This is the matter in which, which they reject.

units.la: § 25. De Materiâ ex quâ, quam recep- tam volunt, loquens Pacius, Com. in Meth.statim nauseam mihi movet diftinctione illâ nudiustertius repertâ, Morbi alii sunt materiales, alii immateriales. Si enim rectè perpendas rem, materiam omnes morbi habent, fundamentum fc, illud relationis,de quo dixi. Sed transeat.
units.tr: § 25. Speaking of the matter from which, which they want to be accepted, Pacius in his Commentary on the Method makes me sick at heart with that distinction, lately discovered: some diseases are material, others immaterial. For if you weigh the matter rightly, all diseases have matter, namely that foundation of relation of which I spoke. But let that pass.

units.la: § 26. Non minus nauseo ad diftinctionem alteram,quamtumvis vetustam, Materia hæc, vel fecundum naturam est, vel præter. Vtenim supra dixi, Quod est p. p.n. eo modo,eo respectu est p.n.quo officit actionibus. Et hæc est consideratio Medica, quæ sola heic regnare debet : at Physica, quæ confiderat rem,ut est à natura producta, debet hinc facessere. Sed transeat hoc quoque.
units.tr: § 26. I am no less nauseated by the other distinction, however old: this matter is either according to nature or against it. For, as I said above, what is contrary to nature is contrary to nature in that respect and to the extent that it hinders the actions. This is the medical consideration, which alone ought to reign here; the physical consideration, which considers a thing as produced by nature, ought to depart from here. But let this pass too.

units.la: § 27. Morbi illi materiales neotericorum, qui sunt? Qui dicunt, habent materiale quid, quod movendum est. v.g. in febribus putridis sunt humores, qui fomitem præbent febri. Ego video, perdere illos hoc ipso dimidium causæ suæ. Dico enim, Si quidam morbi absque hac materia, & consequenter causa continente, subsistere possunt, fit mihi verisimile, omnes poffe illa carere.
units.tr: § 27. What are those material diseases of the moderns? They say that there is something material that must be removed, for example, in putrid fevers there are humours which provide fuel for the fever. I see that by this very claim they lose half of their cause. For I say: if some diseases can subsist without this matter, and consequently without a containing cause, it seems likely to me that all can do without it.

units.la: § 28. Propterea concludo, Quemadmodum nullus morbus est absque materia in quâ ita omnis morbus est absque materiâ ex quâ, de qua illi somniant.
units.tr: § 28. Therefore I conclude: just as no disease is without matter in which, so every disease is without the matter from which, of which they dream.

units.la: § 28. Somniant, dicis? Hæc quidem clarissima injuria est. Somniant, dico. Rogati enim causam afferunt quidquid in buccam venit, Omnium ineptiffimi sunt, qui à materia ad efficientem provolant. Estne materia efficiens? & contra?
units.tr: § 28. They dream, you say? This is indeed a most manifest insult. They dream, I say. For when asked the cause, they bring forward whatever comes into their mouth. Those are the most foolish of all who rush from matter to efficient cause. Is matter an efficient cause? And conversely?

units.la: § 29. Nescio fatis, an prudentiores sint, qui audent vociferari, Causa continens considerari potest, & in efficiente & in materia. Nisi fallor, conciliatio hæc
units.tr: § 29. I do not know well enough whether those are wiser who dare to shout that the containing cause can be considered both in the efficient cause and in the matter.

units.la: debet esse utriusque sententiae, & est planè gemina cum Gal. illâ, Apoplexia partim in ventriculis est, partim in corpore cerebri.
units.tr: Unless I am mistaken, this reconciliation ought to be of both opinions, and it is plainly twin to that of Galen: apoplexy is partly in the ventricles, partly in the substance of the brain.

units.la: § 30. Summa, Efficiens causa non est: quia morbus, quem concipimus ut factum quid, jam est effectus. Materia in quâ non est, ipsis adversariis fatentibus. Restat igitur fit Materia ex quâ, de quâ audire cupio. quid sibi velint? Et ne ab exemplo discedamus, Materia, quæ febrim putridam facit, cujus causæ rationem habet? Antecedentisne, quam προηγούμενα vocant? an Continentis? Si continentem elegeris, regeram ego, Materia illa non potest sustinere nomen causæ continentis, quomodocunque etiam definieris. Cur? Quia sublatâ etiam illâ, tamen febris manet, docente id Gal.
units.tr: § 30. In sum: the efficient cause is not it, because the disease, which we conceive as something made, is already an effect. The matter in which is not it, as even our opponents confess. It remains, then, that it is the matter from which, about which I am eager to hear what they mean. And, not to depart from the example: the matter that makes a putrid fever, what is the reason for its cause? Is it the antecedent cause, which they call προηγούμενα [proēgoumena], or the containing one? If you choose the containing cause, I will answer that this matter cannot bear the name of containing cause, however you define it. Why? Because even when it is removed the fever remains, as Galen teaches.

units.la: § 31. Quæi hoc? Quia est factum quid, quia calor febrilis jam ita est impressus humoribus, ut absque materia duret, quamobrem opus est alterantibus. Quid igitur tandem est materia illa, si non est causa? Est pars morbi essentialis, fundamentum illud de quo jam toties.
units.tr: § 31. Why is this so? Because it is something made, because the febrile heat is already so impressed on the humours that it lasts without the matter, for which reason alterants are needed. What, then, is that matter, if it is not the cause? It is an essential part of the disease, that foundation about which I have said so often.

units.la: § 32. Heiciterum vide mihi, ô quifquis es, conciliationem bellatulam, fimilem illi, quæ fuit § 29, !O, inquiunt, utrumque est, Et causa continens materialis, & pars morbi. Inter hos Montanum esse, Pacius ait,Com. in Meth. col. 306. O Montane, uttecum agam, quomodo non confundis causam cum causato? Ita ignis,qui aquam calefacit, eritidem cum aquâ calefactâ.quo nihil abfurdius.
units.tr: § 32. Look again, you who are whoever you are, at the petty reconciliation, similar to that of § 29: "Oh," they say, "it is both: the containing cause is material and it is a part of the disease." Pacius says that Montanus is among these. O Montanus, let me ask you: how do you not confuse the cause with the caused? In the same way, the fire that heats the water will be the same thing as the heated water, than which nothing is more absurd.

units.la: § 33. Ergone fi materia illa febrilis non est causa Continens, estne Antecedens? Dictum alibi est, vocari hanc caufam ita,non respectu morbi,sed corporis, in quo morbum excitat. Quo praefuppofito, dico, Aut consideratur, quatenus morbum factura est, & ad nos hoc loco & tempore non pertinet : aut quatenus jam fecit. At vero quatenus fecit, quatenus morbum actu constituit,quatenus fine eâ morbus non est:eatenus est, ut dixi, pars morbi essentialis, imo vero morbus ipse.
units.tr: § 33. So if that febrile matter is not the containing cause, is it the antecedent one? It has been said elsewhere that this is called a cause not with respect to the disease but to the body in which it excites the disease. With that premise, I say: either it is considered insofar as it is about to produce the disease, and that does not concern us here and now; or insofar as it has already produced it. But insofar as it has produced it, insofar as it actually constitutes the disease, insofar as without it there is no disease, to that extent it is, as I said, an essential part of the disease, indeed the disease itself.

units.la: § 34. Res declaretur exemplo calculi. Ponamus, antecedentem hujus causam esse pituitam copiosam, ex voracitate collectam .Hæc,quamdiu pituita est,caufa antecedens est:at postquam ita concrevit,ut calculus fit, & obstruat jam est vel pars morbi, vel morbus ipse. Calculus enim per fe, ut materia est p.n. non parit urinæ suppressionem : sed calculus hoc in loco litus, quâ transire debet urina.
units.tr: § 34. The matter may be made clear by the example of a stone. Let us suppose that the antecedent cause of this is an abundance of phlegm, gathered from gluttony. As long as it is phlegm, it is the antecedent cause; but after it has so solidified that it becomes a stone and now obstructs, it is either a part of the disease or the disease itself.
