For the stone in itself, as matter, against nature, does not produce the suppression of urine; rather, the stone lodged in this place, where the urine ought to pass, does.

units.la: § 35. Quem-
units.tr: § 35. Just as-

units.la: § 35. Quemadmodum enim in cultro secante duo sunt, Culter secans, qui est Agens quod; & Acies cultri, quæ est Agens quo; seu ratio & forma agentis : ita in Calculo duo sunt, Calculus ipse, & Calculus obstruens. Hinc Obstructio non est medium quid inter calculum & morbum : sed res quædam unà cum calculo, fine quâ urina non supprimitur. Vt enim actio hæc laudatur, oportet in unum coëant hæc duo, quæ duo jam fimul juncta, fiunt unum, constituuntque unum morbum.
units.tr: § 35. For just as in a cutting knife there are two things, the knife that cuts, which is the agent that (quod), and the edge of the knife, which is the agent by which (quo), or the reason and form of the agent; so in a stone there are two things, the stone itself and the stone that obstructs. Hence obstruction is not something intermediate between the stone and the disease, but a thing that belongs to the stone itself, without which the urine is not suppressed. For when this action is to be named, these two must come together, and these two, once joined, become one and constitute one disease.

units.la: § 36. Hinc patet quam decipiatur Vallefius & alii,qui dicunt, Rem additam esse causam continentem, v.g. calculum, sextum digitum, materiam obstruentem. Qui plura vult, adeat Pacium, Com. in Meth. col. 302. Ex quo loco (sed col. 304.) diluo objectionem, quæ plerisque obstat Galenistis. Dicunt, Quei permitti potest Gal.ut lasionem à calculo factam, vocet Obstructionem, cum actio fit transitoria? At morbus est factum quid. Refpondet rectissimè, Verbalia ista significant duo, & Motum, qui fit, & Terminum, qui factus est. Non enim datur pars ulla motus, in quâ non fit res aliquo modo mota. Itaque qui dicit mutationem, dicit etiam mutatum quid.
units.tr: § 36. Hence it is clear how Vallesius and others are mistaken, who say that the added thing is the containing cause, for example the stone, the sixth finger, or the obstructing matter. Whoever wants more should consult Pacius, Commentary on the Method, col. 302. From that passage (but col. 304) I answer the objection that bothers most Galenists. They say: how can Galen be permitted to call the injury done by a stone an obstruction, since the action is transitory? But a disease is a thing that has been made. He answers quite rightly that these verbal nouns signify two things: the motion that takes place, and the term that has resulted. For there is no part of a motion in which the thing is not in some way moved. So whoever speaks of a change also speaks of something changed.

units.la: § 37. Vt jam denique concludendum fit, Causam, de quâ contendimus, in morbo facto nullatenus esse, Fortassis igitur in morbo fiente seu futuro est? Non enim distinguo, ceu prædixi.
units.tr: § 37. To conclude at last, the cause we are arguing about is in no way present in a disease that has already come about. Perhaps then it is present in a disease that is coming into being, or is future? No, I do not distinguish, as I said before.

units.la: § 38. Heic cautione opus est, ut recte percipiamus Pacii mentem, quæ est, Non est idem dictu, Morbus, & Morbus fiens. Fallit enim à dicto fecundum quid ad dictum simpliciter. Quin oppositum est in adjecto, ut in scholis loquimur. Quare, ut recte docet, Morbus simpliciter dictus est solus ille, qui morbus vere est, ideoque causam continentem non habet: ita fi putes, illum simpliciter ἀνλεπς Θεν, Morbus fiens nullatenus est morbus, nechabet causam continentem, fallēris immensum.
units.tr: § 38. Here caution is needed, so that we correctly grasp Pacius's meaning, which is that it is not the same thing to say "disease" and "disease in the making." For one is misled by moving from a statement qualified in some respect to a statement taken absolutely. Indeed the opposite is contained in the added term, as we say in the schools. Therefore, as he rightly teaches, a disease taken absolutely is only that which truly is a disease, and so does not have a containing cause. So if you think that a disease in the making, taken absolutely (simpliciter), is in no way a disease and has no containing cause, you are greatly mistaken.

units.la: § 39. Hoc enim vult, Morbus simpliciter dictus est revera morbus. quia habet factum quid: at causam continentem non habet, quia est factum quid, & hoc ipso prabet indicationes curatorias. Morbus cum additione dictus, Fiens, non est morbus quidem, & habet causam continentem, sed dat indicationes præfervatorias.
units.tr: § 39. For this is what he means: a disease taken absolutely is truly a disease because it has something made (a factum quid), but it does not have a containing cause, because it is something made, and by this very fact it supplies indications for curing. A disease taken with an addition, the disease in the making, is indeed not yet a disease, and it does have a containing cause, but it supplies indications for prevention.

units.la: § 46. Vt enim suprà dixi, Oportet feorfim ponere ea, quæ sunt, feorfim ea, quæ fiunt, ut secure dicere possimus.
units.tr: § 46. For, as I said above, we must set apart those things that are, and set apart those that are coming into being, so that we can speak with certainty.

units.la: Hæc, quæ facta sunt, non habent causam continentem: hæc, quæ fiunt, habent.
units.tr: Those things that have been made do not have a containing cause; those that are coming into being do have one.

units.la: § 41. Dicis, Quid illud est, Non est morbus quidem? Aliter confiderat morbos ὁ θεραπευτὴς: aliter ὁ ὑγιεινός. Ille curat morbos, indicatione sumtâ à dispositione stabili, quæ morbus est. Hic, indicatione captâ à causâ morbificâ, quæ παθεἶναι ἀλλοίωσις (non morbus) præservat à morbo.
units.tr: § 41. You ask, what is that "not indeed a disease"? The physician of diseases (therapeutes) considers diseases in one way, and the physician of health (hygienos) in another. The former cures diseases, taking his indication from a settled condition, which is the disease. The latter, taking his indication from the morbific cause, guards against disease, which is an alteration of the passions (not a disease).

units.la: § 42. Et hoc est, quod alibi monui, Causam indicare, absurdum dictu non est: sed in ὑγιεινή. Absurdum, quin falsum est in θεραπευτική. Habitus athleticus est morbus? Nemo dixerit. Hipp. tamen solvere illum jubet venæ sectione. Unde hic est indicatio venæ sectionis? ✓ more bo futuro magno, nisi præoccupes.
units.tr: § 42. This is also what I have elsewhere pointed out: to indicate the cause is not absurd to say in the hygienic art; but in the therapeutic art it is absurd, indeed false. Is an athletic condition a disease? No one would say so. Yet Hippocrates orders that it be dissolved by venesection. Whence then comes the indication for venesection here? [The rest of this unit is corrupt in the scan and cannot be restored with certainty.]

units.la: § 41. Et hoc est, quod Gal. non uno loco docet, Cum proprie loquimur, curationem à præservatione distinguimus, & alterum mandamus huic, alterum illi. Cum improprie etiam τὴν ὑγιεινὴν curare dicimus.
units.tr: § 41. This is also what Galen teaches in more than one place: when we speak properly, we distinguish cure from prevention, and we assign the one to one and the other to the other. When we speak improperly, we also say that the healthy condition (hygieine) is cured.

units.la: § 42. Cum grano igitur salis accipiendum est, quod Pacius & alii scribunt. Morbus siens apud Gal. non est morbus, sed παθῶν. Est, cum proprie loquimur: at vero cum non distinguimus morbum & παθῶν, curationem & præservationem, non est. Non semper accurati fumus in nominibus,ut neque opus est : modò res non confundantur, Et hinc pendet vel assertio vel negatio Causæ continentis, ut dicam.
units.tr: § 42. Therefore what Pacius and others write must be taken with a grain of salt: a disease in the making, according to Galen, is not a disease but a passion (pathon). It is so when we speak strictly; but when we do not distinguish disease and passion, cure and prevention, it is not so. We are not always exact in names, nor need we be, provided that the things are not confused. And on this depends either the affirmation or the denial of the containing cause, as I shall say.

units.la: § 43. Ex his erudiri possunt, qui subfidium sibi quærunt ex 1. Loc. aff.2. tu puta,ut in morbo etiam facto Continentem extundant. Causa continens est, dicunt, quà tangente, fit in nobis τὸ ἁπτόμενον. Dico ego, Gal. heic τὸ ἁπτόμενον proprie accipit, quatenus morbo opponitur, & eatenus concedo causam continentem, de ἐπιστῆμαι, inquam,non de ἐπιστήμη.
units.tr: § 43. From these points those may be taught who seek support for themselves from the first book, On the Places Affecting (Loc. aff.), book 2, and who try to make the containing cause hold even in a disease already made. "The containing cause," they say, "is that by whose touching there comes to be in us the thing touched (to haptomenon)." I reply that Galen here takes "the thing touched" strictly, insofar as it is opposed to disease, and to that extent I concede a containing cause, of the knowledge (epistemai) I say, not of knowledge (epistême).

units.la: § 44. Atqui,nihil est fine causâ?Nisi decipi vis,dicas,Nihil fit fine causâ.Intεrim, quæ jam sunt, non omnia habent causam.
units.tr: § 44. But is nothing without a cause? Unless you wish to be deceived, say: nothing comes to be without a cause. Meanwhile, things that already exist do not all have a cause.

units.la: § 45. Minimum, inquit, in iis factis concedes mihi,ubi sunt plures causæ Antecedentes ? Vid. ut illam dicam Continentem, quæ effectui proxima est ? Non concedo. Constituto enim eo, quid fit causa continens? permittere non oportet, ut nomen tribuatur antecedentium alicui,ne finiat res in litem nominis. In rei veritate, antecedentium nulli hoc competit,ut eâ ablatâ tollatur causatum,Ergo nulla etiam illarum dici potest Continens, ita aqua calefacta, sed abigne remota, calet aliquandiu: febris putrida manet, etiam purgatis humoribus.
units.tr: § 45. "At the very least," he says, "you will concede to me in those cases where there are several antecedent causes." Do you see that I call that one the containing cause which is nearest to the effect? I do not concede it. For once it has been settled what the containing cause is, one must not allow the name to be given to some one of the antecedents, lest the matter end in a quarrel over names. In the truth of the matter, this belongs to none of the antecedents, so that when it is removed the effect is removed. Therefore none of them can be called containing. Thus water heated, but removed from the fire, stays warm for a while; a putrid fever remains even when the humours have been purged.

units.la: § 46. Tantò autem folicitiores esse oportet nos hac in re, quod non fatis constet, quò inclinârit Gal.In 1.enim illo de Loc. aff. modò agnoscere videtur causam continentem in morbis factis: modò negare. Agnoscere, cum ait, ςυιοτε μιᾶ χρίεῖς ροτῆ,μνο temporis momento curari dolores quosdam colicos ex pituitâ vitreâ. Negare, cum post aliquammulta dicit, τὴν φύσιν ἱᾶσθαι μικρὰ πνεῦμα πάλιν, Naturam curare parvas quasdam assectiones.
units.tr: § 46. We ought to be all the more careful in this matter, because it is not sufficiently clear towards which side Galen inclined. In the first book, On the Places Affecting, he seems at one time to acknowledge a containing cause in diseases already made, and at another to deny it. He acknowledges it when he says that certain colic pains from glassy phlegm are sometimes cured in a single moment of time. He denies it when, after a good many pages, he says that nature cures again certain small affections.

units.la: § 47. Iam ergò, per longas quamvis ambages, huc pervenimus, quo nemo (quantum mihi compertum est) hactenus eorum, qui vel pro Causa continente scripserunt, vel contra illam, Causa contine-ns (non Stoica illa, è cœlo petita, sed quæ pertinet ad res fientes) datur, & non datur. Datur ἐν ὑγιείᾳ, quatenus illa curat fientes morbos, seu, qui in herbâ sunt adhuc, indicatione præfervatoriâ acceptâ à Causâ morbi. Non datur ἐν θεραπευτικῇ, quatenus illa morbos factos sub manu habet, indicatione curatoriâ sumtâ à morbo ipso.
units.tr: § 47. So, though by long detours, we have at last arrived at the point which no one (as far as I have found) of those who have written either for the containing cause or against it has reached: the containing cause (not that Stoic cause drawn from the heavens, but the one that pertains to things in process of becoming) both is and is not. It is in health [ἐν ὑγιείᾳ], insofar as it cures morbid processes that are still developing, or those that are still in the herb, by the preventive indication taken from the cause of the disease. It is not in therapeutics [ἐν θεραπευτικῇ], insofar as it has to deal with disease already formed, by the curative indication taken from the disease itself.

units.la: § 48. Vbi fi quis iterum quærat, Quid fit id, quod vulgò, in morbis materiali-
units.tr: § 48. Here, if someone again asks, what is that which is commonly called the containing cause in diseases described as material?

units.la: bus dictis, Causa continens dicitur? Dixi non semel, & est sæpius dicendum, quia audire nolunt illi, Est pars morbi, est fundamentum relationis, à quo ferè morbi denominantur, ut docet regula Melanchthonis, cuius memini. Hæc pars morbi non est simul causa, ut nuper dixi.
units.tr: I have said more than once, and it must be said again and again, because those people refuse to hear it: it is a part of the disease, the foundation of the relation from which diseases are for the most part named, as the rule of Melanchthon teaches, which I have mentioned. This part of the disease is not at the same time the cause, as I have just said.

units.la: § 49. Ex quo statim manifestus fit error Erafti, Anat. f. 105. cum ait, questionem de nomine esse. Parum quidem refert, quo quis utatur nomine: sed magni refert, ut res unaquæque suo gaudeat. Quid autem insolentius, quam Partem rei subsistentis vocare Causam ipsius: & contra, Causam dicere partem? Fit enim consu̇cio causæ & causati, ut jam innui.
units.tr: § 50. Nor does this furrow help, the claim that Galen wrote about the thing but abstained from the name. For in many places he also used the name. Let Montanus be consulted on Antonius Erastus, f. 81 b.

units.la: § 50. Nec quidquam facit huc sulcrum, Galenum scripsisse rem: à nomine abstinuisse. Multis enim locis etiam nomine usus est. Videatur Montanus in Ant. Erast.f.81.b.
units.tr: § 50. Nor does it help the case that Galen wrote about the matter while abstaining from the name. For in many places he also used the name. Let Montanus be consulted in his Antierastus, folio 81 b.

units.la: § 51. Dicat aliquis, Qui causam continentem in Pathologicis simpliciter damnasti quei potes jam ex parte recipere? A's ἀντίθεσις... ἐμφάσεις. Volo au- tem hanc sententiam poni juxta alteram, & liberum fieri judicium, Vtra sit melior?
units.tr: § 51. Someone may say: "You simply condemned the containing cause in pathology; how can you now accept it in part? [ἀντίθεσις... ἐμφάσεις]." I wish, however, that this opinion be set beside the other, and that the judgment be left free: which is the better?

units.la: CAPVT XXIX.
units.tr: CHAPTER 29.

units.la: § 1. NE parum honorificè tractaffe videar Eraftum mèum, conferam huc pauca ex Anat. p. 111. & feq. digito fimul intento in ea, quæ Mont. habet, Ant-Eraft, f. 82.b.
units.tr: § 1. Lest I seem to have treated my Erastus too disrespectfully, I shall here set down a few points from Anat. p. 111 and following, with my finger also pointed at what Montanus says in Anti-Erastus, f. 82b.

units.la: § 2. I. Argumentum eft ἀπεχνον, innitens autoritati Gal. 1. Loc. aff. 2. Non urgeo jam τὸ ἀπὸ quod Valleriola, & alii:fed dico, loqui Gal. cum vulgo, quod non diftinguit caufam à parte. Hoc facio ideò, ne arietem in Montani Caufam continentem, quam ille ftatuit Intemperiem frigidam inteftinorum. Periculum enim eft, necogamur illam recipere in aliis quoque.
units.tr: § 2. I. The argument is inartificial [ἄτεχνον], resting on the authority of Galen, Loc. aff. 2. I no longer press the τὸ ἀπὸ that Valleriola and others press. I say instead that Galen speaks with the common people, who do not distinguish cause from part. I do this so as not to run my head against Montanus' containing cause, which he holds to be a cold intemperature of the intestines. For there is a danger that we would be forced to accept it in other cases too.

units.la: § 3. II Eft f. 112. à definitione Caufæ continentis, Omnis caufa, &c: Montanus negat minorem, & rectè.
units.tr: § 3. II. It is from f. 112, from the definition of the containing cause, "every cause, etc." Montanus denies the minor premise, and rightly so.

units.la: § 4. Pro II I. habet Montanus autoritatem Arift. 2. Poft. quod rejicit ille f. 81. a. quemadmodum etiam alterum ex Hipp. de Vet. Med, f. 80.b.
units.tr: § 4. For the third, Montanus relies on the authority of Aristotle, Posterior Analytics 2, which Erastus rejects at f. 81a, just as he also rejects the other one from Hippocrates, On Ancient Medicine, at f. 80b.

units.la: § 5. Idem Eraftus, refutaturus Montani argumenta, hypothefin quandam ftatuit, quam f. 83.b. fimpliciter negat effe fuam.
units.tr: § 5. Erastus himself, about to refute Montanus' arguments, lays down a certain hypothesis, which at f. 83b he flatly denies to be his own.

units.la: § 6. I. Sophifma, ut Montanus appellat ex l.2. c.36. fubeunt artis noftra fundaméta, Intemperies non recté diftingui in nudas & cum materiá. Refpondet ille, Ant-Eraft. f.84. a. Ego tacere malo vel ideò, quia non video, quid faciat ad Caufam continentem. Saltu etiam fupero, quæ apud Eraftum funt à p.113. ufque ad p.120. Nec non illa, quæ in AntEraft. ufque ad novam rubricam f.87.b. Idem facere cogor, nifi rifum perfolvere velim bonis,de iftis, quæ cumulat Eraftus ufque ad p.126. Idem de iis,quæ in Antraft.ufque ad f. 90.b.
units.tr: § 6. I. A sophism, as Montanus calls it, from book 2, chapter 36, undermines the foundations of our art: that intemperies is not rightly divided into bare and with matter. He replies in Anti-Erastus, f. 84a. I prefer to keep silent, partly because I do not see what it has to do with the containing cause. I also skip over what is in Erastus from p. 113 up to p. 120, and likewise what is in Anti-Erastus up to the new heading at f. 87b. I am forced to do the same with what Erastus piles up up to p. 126, unless I wish to make the good readers laugh. The same goes for those things in Anti-Erastus up to f. 90b.

units.la: § 7. II. Argumentum,ex eodem loco, tractatum ab Eraft.p.127. exagitatum in iifdé Ant-Eraft.f. 91.a.non meretur punctum,ut quidam loquuntur. Idem, cum pace bonorum, dixero de iis, quæ ufque ad p.124. & f,98.Qui enim rem intelligit,infuper poteft habere talia fcitamenta.
units.tr: § 7. II. The argument from the same passage, treated by Erastus at p. 127 and tossed about in the same Anti-Erastus at f. 91a, does not deserve a point, as some put it. With the good men's leave, I will say the same of those things up to p. 124 and f. 98. For whoever understands the matter can have such trifles at hand.

units.la: § 8. Quę de Chimeris,& monftris Africanis dicuntur à p.143. ufque ad p.150, contra c.33.l.2;quæitem in Ant-Eraft. à f.98.ufq; ad f.101.b.relinquo monftrofis ingeniis. Et quid fruftra laboro? Iifdem transfcribo,quæ ab Erafto ufq; ad p.187. & Montano ufque ad f.120.intiuduntur.
units.tr: § 8. What is said about chimeras and African monsters from p. 143 to p. 150, against chapter 33 of book 2, which also appears in Anti-Erastus from f. 98 up to f. 101b, I leave to monstrous wits. And why do I labour in vain? I transcribe the same things that are brought forward from Erastus up to p. 187 and from Montanus up to f. 120.

units.tr: Apoplexy is not a drowsy affect, 13.50. That it differs from paralysis, 14.7.57; from epilepsy, ibid. 9.10; from uterine suffocation, ibid. 11; from Caro, ibid. 12; from syncope and cardiac syncope, ibid. 13. Sudden death is not its pathognomonic sign, ibid. 24. Another sign, ibid. 25. Only one species, differing in severity, ibid. 31. This is called sanguineous, 10.5.17; 14.17.38. The species are degrees, 14.25. Small, what? ibid. 26. No difference in the location of the affect, ibid. 27, 29. It is not in the ventricles but in the body, or the vessels, ibid. 34, 36. That it is in both places: what is this called by sense? 13.80; 14.32. Water found in the cerebral ventricles, whence does it come? 10.15. Are the internal senses false? 13.79. Do children suffer from it? 11.17. By which senses does it become familiar? ibid., and 10.17. How it occurs.

units.la: de Morbo qui agit, agit etiam de Sanitate, 1.4. de utroque quid censeat vulgus, 1b. 5.9, ex hac censura non fit nisi definitio nominis. nominalis, nullo autem modo essentialis, Ibid. 2. 19. Ἀλόγως Gal. non est genus Logicum, Ib. ideo nec morbus est Qualitas, Ibid. 15.16. 17.20.21. verum genus Logicum morbi (ita etiam Sanitatis) Ib. 8.18.19. hinc fit definitio essentialis, Ib. 8. interim ex definitione illa Gal. nominali, additis aliunde aliis, fieri potest definitio essentialis Medica, sed non Logica: Ib. 19.
units.tr: A discussion of the disease that acts also treats of health, 1.4. What the common people think of both, 1b. 5.9. From this judgement there results only a definition of the name, a nominal one, but in no way an essential one, Ibid. 2. 19. Galen's "unreasonably" [Ἀλόγως] is not a logical genus, Ib.; therefore disease is not a quality either, Ibid. 15.16. 17.20.21. But the logical genus of disease (and likewise of health) is Ib. 8.18.19. Hence arises an essential definition, Ib. 8. Meanwhile, from that nominal definition of Galen, with other things added from elsewhere, an essential definition may be made that is medical but not logical: Ib. 19.
